neighbouring sequence, in the file's own order, on a region and in the 1D browser (§5.8); the `‹ ›`
beside a title is the same two keys as buttons (§5.4). A `contig × contig` block has two axes and no
single neighbour, and does not step. They were `[` and `]`, which a French PC types with AltGr — a
third level, so never a shortcut (§26.6) — and a French Mac with ⇧⌥. Either half of the key the
marks are on steps: over the comma and the full stop on American and British QWERTY, so `,` and `.`
step without Shift, and a key of their own beside the left Shift on AZERTY and most European
layouts, bare for `<` and shifted for `>`. Control with them is the tab beside this one (§5.6).

**Every view has a trail, the 1D browser included**, where it reads `genome → Whole genome → IV →
1,000,001-1,400,000`: a genome opened as tracks has no map to go up to, so its root is the whole
assembly, which is both where a browser opens and the one place above the sequence in front of the
reader — and a picker between that and the genome's Chromosomes table (§5.8), as a map's root picks
between its table and its whole. Without it the row appeared and vanished as the map's eye was
pressed, and the assembly a reader was looking at was named only on a tab and in a foldable column.

**The last crumb is the window alone**, under the crumb that names the sequence: the heading and the
locus box below it print the same place, and a row ending `› IV › IV:1,000,001-1,400,000` above two
more copies of that string is three readings of one fact in three typefaces.

**And a `+` at the coarse end of it**, which asks for a resolution the file does not store: any
whole number of one of its own bins, added up as it is read. §3.4 is where that lives — what the
bar contributes is the stop, starred, in bin-size order, with a `×` to take it back off.

**Nine rungs are chipped; past that the row is a dropdown of every rung.** A `zoomify` ladder that
doubles from 1 kb reaches a megabase in ten rungs and one that walks the 1–2–5 series reaches it in
nine, so nine covers most of the files in the wild — about three hundred pixels of short numbers,
right-aligned into whatever the trail leaves. The cap was six, on the grounds that more would push
the place the reader is looking at off the left of a laptop screen; what it actually cost was the
aim-and-click on the files with the most rungs to aim at, and on the files somebody is most likely
to *add* a rung to, since a ninth stop used to collapse an eight-rung row to a bare slider. Past
nine — a 4DN `.mcool` has eleven — the word `resolution` is followed by a `<select>` holding every
rung in the ladder's own order, each wearing the `*` and the tooltip its chip would have, with the
`×` of an added rung after it while that rung is the one being read. It was the slider and one chip,
which between them said how many rungs there were and which was being read, and named the rest
only to a reader who hovered the slider.

**The resolution is not a segment of that trail.** A rung of a `zoomify` ladder (§3.4) is the same
file drawn more or less finely: it does not contain the crumbs after it and clicking it does not go
anywhere, so it sits at the **far end of the bar, past the coordinates**, where the controls over the
picture belong. It spent a release as the second crumb, between the file name and the table, which
read as *this file, then this resolution, then these chromosomes* and put a control readers change
constantly at the one end of the row they scroll past on the way to the box they type in.

**Past the resolution, at the far end of the bar, the total the maps are drawn to** (§6.5): a box
labelled *contacts*, empty and showing a pale `e.g. 10M` until a reader clicks into it, and —
with two maps or more on screen — two chevrons after it that type the shallowest map's total or the
deepest's. It is on the bar rather than on a card for the reason the resolution is: it is a control
over the whole picture, and over every task, not a step of the trail. It is one element for the life
of the file, re-seated at the end of the row on every render rather than rebuilt with it, because the
trail is redrawn on every pan and a box rebuilt under the cursor loses what is being typed into it.

**A one-rung file is drawn without the slider.** There is nothing to slide along, so the row reads
`resolution  1 kb  +` and the `+` is the only control on it — which is §8.5's rule, not an exception
to it: a control that cannot keep its promise is absent rather than greyed, and a plain `.cool` is
the commonest file a lab opens. The slider arrives with the second rung, which is what the `+` makes.

Up to nine rungs it is a **slider over a row of labelled stops** rather than a dropdown, and the
stops say `1 kb`, `50 kb`, `1 Mb` rather than `1000`, `50000`, `1000000`. A ladder is an *ordered*
thing with a fixed number of rungs, which is exactly what a slider over stops shows — how many there
are, which one you are on, and which way is finer — and a dropdown of raw bin counts shows none of
the three and asks the reader to divide before the number means anything. Both halves write the
same value: the stops are real radio inputs, so the arrow keys and a screen reader get the list, and
the slider commits on release rather than per rung, since dragging across five rungs must not
re-open the file five times.

**`-` and `+` walk the same stops from the keyboard**, one rung coarser and one finer (*Coarser
resolution*, *Finer resolution*): counted from the stop that is lit, onto a rung the reader added as
onto one the file stores and by the road a press on its stop takes, and stopping at both ends rather
than wrapping — the palette says which end, and at the coarse one that the `+` beside the rung adds
a coarser one. Their hint is the rung they go to, as `<` and `>` name the sequence. They are bound by
what they type rather than where they are, since the two marks stand in different places on QWERTY
and on AZERTY: either half of each key does — `_` and `=` as well — so neither needs Shift, which
`+` takes on both; and an AZERTY PC's minus, the bare half of its 6 key, is still the minus under
Shift or Caps Lock, where it types a `6` (§26.6). In a deck the step is the first map's, which every
map follows (§16.2). The map's canvas zoomed on the same two keys whenever it had the focus — which
it has after any press on it — so the one keystroke would have been a zoom and a re-read at another
grid together; it gave them up (§7.2), and so does a deck's tracks cell (§5.4).
An **mmetacool's entry picker is untouched** and stays where it is, before the root: switching to a
different nested metacool invalidates every crumb after it, so that one genuinely is a step of the
trail.

Pan and zoom are deliberately **not** in it: the hash carries what is being looked at, and one that
rewrote itself on every wheel notch would turn the back button into a scrollback. The one exception is
`focus`, and it is not a live position — it is a window a view *opens* standing on, applied when the
block arrives and never written back, so a link that named a place goes on naming it however far its
recipient then wanders (§8.10). The 1D browser is the other case: there the window *is* what is
being looked at, so its `locus` is in the hash — written in the display form once a gesture has
settled, in place of the current history entry rather than as a new one, so a link names the window
and the back button still walks navigations.

**The newest navigation wins.** A view state that arrives while the previous one is still being drawn
— its file opened, its deck reconciled, its contigs table read — supersedes it: the earlier one stops
at its next step and draws nothing, so a reader quicker than the file never sees a picture of a place
already left, and one place asked for twice is drawn once. A change of colour, score or saved place is
a repaint of the view on screen only once that view has finished mounting; arriving earlier, it is
drawn as the navigation it then is, rather than painted onto the view being replaced. And a state
naming a view this build does not have — which only a stored workspace, a share link or a `?config=`
file can carry — lands on the file's first table, as a link to a view the file cannot answer does,
rather than leaving the tab opening.

### 5.6 Sessions

Several files may be open at once, as tabs — twelve at most (`MAX_SESSIONS`), a ceiling on memory
rather than on the strip, since each tab that has opened something holds a worker and, for a
whole-file view, a matrix. A **session** is one file, its views, its tracks, its annotations and its
settings, and it is a real one: its own reader worker, its own annotation worker, its own stores,
its own DOM. Switching tabs re-parents that DOM rather than rebuilding it, so a map comes back with
its pixels, its zoom and its scroll intact and without a byte re-read.

The address bar names **the active tab and nothing else**. A hash is one view state and there is one
of those on screen; writing several would make every link a description of somebody else's workspace
and make the back button walk a history interleaving three files. The rest of the strip lives in
`sessionStorage` beside the annotations (§8.6), and a restored tab is *named*, not opened — its label
and its view state come back, its worker does not, and clicking it is what reads the file. A tab that
named a local file comes back to the picker with §11's explanation — unless this browser kept a
grant for that file (`state/handles.ts`, where the platform hands one over with the file), and then
a click reopens it as it would a remote one. The file dropped there opens **the map the tab named
inside it** — the `.mcool`'s rung, the `.hic`'s resolution — on the view the tab was showing, alone
or with tracks dropped beside it, which join it: a dropped file is named by its path, and opened at
its root it landed on a rung of its own choosing and on its Chromosomes table instead.

**A closed browser is offered its tabs back, never given them.** Beside the strip, every tab's whole
config — tracks, marks, filters — is kept in IndexedDB (`state/workspace.ts`) and read only when
there is no session storage at all, which is what closing the browser leaves. A record outlives the
build that wrote it, so what each tab was looking at is read by §5.5's reader like a link's. The window then says
*You had 3 tabs open 2 days ago: …* with *restore*, and its × forgets the record rather than hiding
the note: reopening a week's files unasked would reverse the reader's own closing of them, and on a
shared machine would put somebody's unpublished data in front of whoever sat down next.

**The reader's word is *tab*.** Every string on screen says tab — *New tab*, *Rename this tab*,
*Close this tab*, *Share this tab* — and so does every label a screen reader speaks, the rename box's
*Tab name* among them, because a tab is what is on screen and *session* is a word the strip never
shows: "Close this session" read as something larger than closing the thing being looked at.
*Session* stays as the implementation's word, in this document and in the code. The every-tab
file keeps its own name, said as *Save every tab as a file*, because it genuinely is a different
thing. No key closes one: ⌘W is the browser's chord for closing the window, and a binding that is
right about what it does and wrong about what it closes costs a workspace. `o` opens one and
Control with `<` or `>` steps between them — Control on a Mac too, where ⌘< walks a French Mac's
windows and ⌘, is every program's settings — from a box being typed into as well. A tab is renamed in place, by a double-click on it or `F2`: Enter commits, an
emptied box hands the tab back to its file's name, Escape abandons, and Tab commits and goes on to
the next tab's name (§26.8). A middle-click closes one,
and the last is emptied rather than closed, since a window with no tab has nothing to drop a file on.

Four things are per *window* rather than per session, because they are preferences about this window
rather than facts about a file: the theme, the fold and width of each column, and where the reader
has moved its cards (§26.6). The theme's cycle
is ordered against the machine's own scheme — from *system* to the opposite of what the OS is doing,
then to the same as it, then back to following it — so that the first press changes the picture; a
fixed order spends it on the choice that repaints nothing and reads as a control that does not work.

Two tabs on one file share nothing. The per-session memory is keyed on the session id as well as the
URI, so a second view of the same map starts with no tracks, no filters and no marks.

**A tab's note is about its file.** The bar under the strip says what a tab found out about the file
it opened — that a sequence reads as circular (§8.15), that a task set an origin, that a kept edit is
not drawn, that a file is not the one its saved session was made from — and the note is that tab's:
shown while it is in front, and taken down when the tab opens another file, goes back to the picker,
or closes. Another resolution of the same file keeps it. Nothing but its own *dismiss* used to take
one down, so a link that moved a tab from a mouse map to a chicken one left *chrY reads as circular*
over a genome with no chrY. The window's own notes — a workspace with more tabs than the window can
hold — are about the window, and stay until dismissed.

### 5.7 Two files in one square

A second cooler may be opened into the **lower-left triangle** of the same map. A contact matrix is
symmetric, so half of every square on screen is a mirror carrying no information; giving that half to
another file makes the picture asymmetric, which is what the eye reads a difference from.

The split is the **matrix diagonal**, not the viewport's: a cell belongs to the second file when its
row bin exceeds its column bin, wherever the view is. Panning off the diagonal is therefore not a
special case — a trans block above the line shows the first file alone and its transpose shows the
second — and zoom, selection and every other gesture are untouched, because the merge happens once
per read and hands the renderer an ordinary block.

Three refusals, each because the merged picture would otherwise be a lie rather than a limitation:

- **a genome layer** — §8.5's argument applied to a whole matrix rather than to a track;
- **a different bin size** — one grid cannot be two resolutions;
- **a chromosome list differing in count, order, name or length** — every coordinate in the picture
  is an index into one such list. Two spellings of one name, `chr1` against `1`, are not a
  difference (§5.9); one name at two lengths is.

**The card asks for it only once there is a first map.** The zone is labelled *Load a map into the
lower triangle* — not *a second map*, which is what §16's companion cell is called — and it is
absent until a map is open, because a triangle of nothing is a promise with nothing to keep it
(§8.5). A session with no map has one drop zone on that card, asking for a contact map.

The zone takes a file from the desktop and a **row out of the Files column** (§20.5) alike — the
file behind the row read at the drop, through the folder it names, with the credential that folder
lists with and the name a Drive or a Dropbox gives it — and nothing else: it no longer lights for
the card's own grips, nor for a word of text dragged across it. On a session with no map the row is
the first map, through the door every pick takes.

Either file can be closed. Closing the second returns to one map; closing the first promotes the
second, so the map that remains is an ordinary one. *swap sides* puts the other file above the
diagonal, re-opening both rather than relabelling them, since the first file is the one whose axes,
tracks and trail are on screen. `uri2` is part of the view state, so a comparison is a link — for
two remote files, which is the same limit `uri` has always had (§11).

**The second file follows the first across a change of resolution.** A comparison belongs to the file
it is a comparison *of*, so opening another file puts it down; changing rung is not that, and the
reader closed nothing. What carries is the **bin size** rather than the URI, since the second file has
a ladder of its own: `rep2.mcool::/resolutions/1000` beside a 1 kb map is `…/5000` beside a 5 kb one,
looked up in that file's own entries and refused where it has no such rung — which is the bin-size
clause above, seen from the other side, and is said on the card rather than left to be discovered.
The reading carries with it: the operation, and whether the second triangle was hidden.

**Turned, the pair is two bands rather than two triangles** (§17.2). Either map, here or in a deck,
can also be given a name of its own (§16.10).

One colour scale, because the same colour meaning the same count is the stronger claim, and two
libraries of different depth are brought to one depth by **drawing both to one total** (§6.5) — the
chevrons after the breadcrumb's *contacts* box do it in one press — rather than by rescaling the
colours of one. The second key carries the first's numbers, which is what it says: the two triangles
are on one scale. A **match depth** switch used to scale the second file so its 99th percentile met
the first's; it is gone, because it matched the picture and nothing else — the number under the
pointer, and every task run on either file, were still each file's own depth.

This is the design for **two** files and it stays exactly as it is. §16 is the design for N, which is
a weaker claim on the files and therefore a different picture; the two compose, and a session may
hold both at once.

### 5.8 The 1D genome browser

A session may hold a **genome** instead of a file: a list of sequences and their lengths, with tracks
drawn along it and no contact map at all. It is entered by opening, with no map, a `chrom.sizes`, a
bigWig, a bigBed, a FASTA or `.2bit`, a BAM, a VCF, a feature file or a 3D structure (§25.3), and
it is not a second application — the tracks, their cards, their session memory and their renderers
are the ones §8 already specifies. What differs is the coordinate model underneath, and only that:
the axis is the whole assembly laid end to end at one unit per base pair, rather than an axis of
matrix bins. §8.4's rule is unchanged and is what makes this possible at all.

Lengths come from whatever named them, in descending order of trust: a `chrom.sizes` declares them,
and so do a VCF's `##contig` lines (§8.14) and a cytoBand whose bands tile every sequence (§8.22); a
BBI header, a BAM's `@SQ` table (§8.13) and a `.2bit`'s index (§8.21) carry them, and a FASTA is
them; and a feature file yields only the furthest coordinate it mentions — which is a lower bound,
is rounded up, and is labelled as inferred wherever the genome is described. A **label**, and once
per surface: the Genome card's `lengths` row reads `inferred (rounded up)`, the browser's summary
line ends ` · lengths inferred (rounded up)`, and the way out of it — drop a `chrom.sizes` or a
bigWig — is said once, in the card, where the row it corrects is. It was said four times on one
screen, in sentences, of which the longest was the longest line on the page.

The two shapes of session convert into each other. Dropping a `.cool` on the tracks makes the tab its
map, tracks and all; closing the map — the × on its row of the Contact maps card, which the File
card used to carry — falls back to a browser on the cooler's own `/chroms`, with the same tracks
still loaded and the same marks in the Manual annotations card (§8.1), which that road used to
leave out of the column while a browser opened fresh had it. Neither is a new session: the tab, its
id and its memory are the same throughout.

**A genome has a Chromosomes table too.** The trail's root picks between it and *Whole genome*, the
browser, as a map's picks between its table and its whole: the sequences the genome was opened with,
their lengths, and the two columns that are declarations about the molecules rather than about any
map — which are circles, and where each one's origin is (§8.15). A reader with a FASTA and no map
declares them there, and the tasks that read a sequence read them. A row opens its sequence in the
browser. **A map opened over the browser takes them**, for its sequences of the same names and only
where it has declared nothing itself; its first open still measures its circles, which only adds.

**One key walks the three pictures a file with tracks can be**: `v` goes from the map and its tracks,
to the tracks alone, to the map alone, and home. Two of those swap what is mounted and the third does
not, which is why it is a cycle written in one place rather than a toggle in each — a reader pressing
`v` is asking to see the same data with less and then more furniture around it, and where the
boundary between "another view" and "the same view drawn differently" falls is an implementation
detail they should never meet. Tracks-only comes first because it answers "get this matrix out of my
way", which is what a reader with six tracks open wants most often; the map alone follows because
from there the next thing to ask is the opposite.

**The key alone, with no button beside it.** There was one in the region bar, offering the next
stop, and it has gone: the same three states are reachable one row at a time from the eye beside
the map in the column that lists what is drawn, which is where every other thing on screen is shown
and hidden. A second way to do a thing is not a convenience when the first way is a row the reader
is already looking at — it is another control in a bar that has to stay readable at a glance
(§5.4). The cycle stays because a *key* costs the bar nothing and is the fastest road for the
reader who has learnt it.

Nothing is hidden, moved or restyled by any of it. The map alone is the stacks drawing no lanes for as
long as it lasts, which is the same kind of presentation as the turn (§17.4) and reversible in the
same way: three presses come home to the arrangement the reader spent ten minutes on.

**The browser's bar is a box, `go` and the four zoom steps (§5.4), and no title**: the genome is
named on its tab, in the Genome card and in the trail. The one box takes a locus — a single position
opens a window round it — a sequence's name, `*` for the whole genome, and, from the list it drops
as a word is typed, a sequence or a feature of the starred set (§5.4's hit list). Enter goes to the
text where it reads as a place and to the first hit where it does not, and the box keeps the locus
it went to.

The gestures are the map's, deliberately (§7.2): a drag pans, Option- or Shift-drag selects a range
to zoom into, the wheel zooms about the pointer, a **sideways** wheel slides along the axis, a double
click fits, a lane's border resizes it, a drag across it moves its ceiling (§8.8), and its handle, in
the margin before the axis, reorders the stack. `<` and `>` step to the sequence before or after
this one, as they do on a map — the plainest thing anybody does with a genome, and it was the one
view where it had to be typed into the locus box. Two gestures are not the map's. ⌘-scroll over a
lane moves *that* track's ceiling, as it does over a lane beside a map, because it is the adjustment
a genome browser is asked for constantly and a map has no analogue for it. And a drag on the
**ruler** selects a range to zoom into with no modifier at all: the coordinate strip is where a
reader points to say "this much", and it is the one gesture whose meaning its position already
settles, so spending a keystroke on it buys nothing.

**A bar under the stack makes every track taller or shorter together, each in proportion** — the
deck cell's height bar in look (§25.3), under the last lane. A gene model drawn at half the height
of the coverage above it is still half as tall when the stack has doubled: dragged, every lane's
height is the one it had when the drag began times one factor, the stack's foot following the hand,
each lane held to what a lane may be; Escape mid-drag puts them all back; a double click makes the
stack's foot the column's, still in proportion and taller or shorter as the column asks — where
*Stretch the tracks* (`h`) makes them one height — and the arrow keys step it. Only here: not beside
a map, whose lanes are the map's (§8.8), and nowhere in a deck — a tracks cell has the cell's own
bar for the height of the whole picture (§25.3), and the browser leading a deck has neither bar. The
room it, *Stretch* and the canvas itself fill is measured from where the stage stands in the
column's content to the column's foot, less what stands under it — measured against the box the
browser is mounted in, which grows with what is in it, a canvas grown under a tall stack never gave
the height back when the stack was made shorter, and *Stretch* filled that canvas rather than the
window.

**The ruler gains digits as it is zoomed**, and it does that by being told the gap between its own
ticks. Two decimals of a megabase is ten kilobases, so a window narrower than that on a chromosome
measured in megabases wrote the same number under every tick — an axis of `4.60 Mb`, four times over,
under a picture zoomed in to answer exactly the question it was there for. The unit is chosen so that
two decimals can tell one tick from the next, and it steps down when they cannot rather than growing
a third: `4.6 Mb`, then `4,605 kb`, then `4601520 bp`. Nobody reads a fourth decimal off an axis. On
one axis every tick keeps the step's decimals and a four-digit kilobase is grouped like every other
number on screen (§26.1): trimmed per tick, a row read `1.05 Mb 1.1 Mb 1.15 Mb 1.2 Mb`, which is two
precisions alternating along a single ruler.

**How many ticks it draws comes from how wide it is.** Ten was a constant chosen for the browser at
full width, and the same ruler is drawn in a deck cell a third as wide, where ten labels ran into
each other — `1250 kb1255 kb1260 kb` — and a coordinate axis whose numbers touch is the one part of a
browser a reader cannot read around. The gap a label needs is the heatmap's own, so the two rulers of
one genome thin out by one rule. And where the surface around the strip already captions it — the
Chromosomes table's bar says `16 sequences · 12.11 Mb` over it — the ruler draws its boundary marks
and no caption of its own: two captions for one strip say the strip is two things.

**A label at either end of the ruler is kept inside it.** The mark stays on its tick; the label is
nudged back in, two pixels clear of the end, as the heatmap's own axis nudges its labels and a
feature's name is nudged inside its lane (§8.16). A tick on a window's first or last base sits on
the ruler's edge, and a label centred on it was half outside the strip: a deck's tracks cell over
`IV:1,000,001-1,400,000` read `Mb` and `1.4` for `1.0 Mb` and `1.4 Mb`, and the browser over a whole
sequence `bp` for `0 bp` — a cut number is a different number. Nudged in, an end label can reach its
neighbour at the larger text sizes; then the inner of the two is left out, never written over, since
the two ends say where the window starts and stops. A label too wide for the ruler at all is left
out too (`placeTickLabels`).

**The plot is the whole column, not the stack.** The canvas reaches the foot of the column rather
than the foot of the last lane, so pointing anywhere under the tracks names a coordinate, draws the
crosshair and reads every track at it — the axis does not stop where the tracks do, and a view with
two lanes in a tall window would otherwise have a screenful of surface that answers nothing. It stops
at the **start of the axis**, though: the strip before it is the handles' margin and, when it is on,
the track names' column, and neither is a position — so the line stops there and the readout says
nothing, rather than naming a base pair while the arrowhead is on a word. The height is a screen
fact only; a figure is a picture of the tracks, and blank paper under them is not part of it.

**Over the map, where a guide line is drawn, the pointer gives way to it.** The arrowhead is the
wrong shape over a picture being measured: it points from one corner, so the coordinate it names is a
pixel at its tip with a blunt body over everything below and to the right of it — which on a matrix
where a cell can be one pixel is the only thing covering the answer.

**Over the map it is a ring**: Lucide's `locate`, twenty pixels square — the arrowhead's own size —
with its hotspot in the middle: a ring with four ticks, in blue on a white casing so it reads over
paper, dark contacts and every colour between. What it is for is what is *inside* it, the cell under
the hand and the cells round it, whole, and so **the guide lines stop short of it**: every line is cut
where it comes within the ends of the ticks of the hand (a little over eight pixels), so a line through
the hand runs into a tick and none of it crosses the ring. The small open cross the ring replaced left
a hole of a few pixels, which on a 1 kb map is the pixel itself and none of its neighbourhood; a ring
twice this size with the lines running through its middle was a gunsight over the picture rather than a
pointer on it, and put back over the answer the very ink it was drawn to take away.

It is not a second copy of the guide lines: they are at the position the app has *resolved*, through
the middle of a cell that, zoomed in, is wider than the ring, and the ring is where the **hand** is.
So the gap is cut round the hand rather than round the cell, and it follows the hand inside a cell: a
move that shifts the gap is a repaint, and one that changes nothing drawn — a hand in the far corner of
a large cell, clear of both lines — is not. The rays of a turned map and its span guide are cut the
same way. A tap on a touch screen names a cell with no pointer on screen, and there the lines are
drawn whole.

**Over a lane or the 1D browser the arrowhead stays**, crosshair on or off, its tip on the hairline.
It used to be taken away while the hairline was drawn — the line under the hand runs the height of the
stack and names one base pair, so the line was argued to *be* the pointer — and a stack with a line
and no pointer read as a stack the hand had left. The lanes also draw another surface's pointer as
that same line (a cell of a map beside them, a bead in the structure cell, §25.4), so which line was
the reader's own was the one thing the picture stopped saying. There is no cell whose neighbours a
ring could frame; the arrowhead points from its tip, on the base pair the line names, and hangs to
the right of the line rather than across it.

So the ring comes exactly where the map's lines do: while the crosshair is on and the pointer is over
a cell, and not over a label gutter, which holds no cell to draw one at. With the crosshair off there
is no line on any of the three surfaces — the lanes' own hairline under the hand, and the line it
carries across the map, follow the preference too, where they used to be drawn whatever it said, so
a reader who turned the crosshair off watched it leave the map and stay on every track — and all
three show the arrowhead.
The transient cursors stay — the closed hand while panning, the crosshair while a selection is about
to be drawn — because those say what is *happening*, which no guide line does.

Only what follows the pointer goes down there. Everything that describes the *picture* — the sequence
boundaries, the name column's own edge — stops with the tracks: a boundary is a mark *on* the tracks,
and a rule carrying it through a screen's worth of blank space is a divider between two things that
are not there.

Each lane carries two controls of its own, laid over marks its label already paints (§8.8): the
colour chip before the track's name, and the autoscale mark at the end of its range, lit while the
axis is the data's own. Everything else of the lane is the canvas — the layer the two sit in is
transparent to the pointer — so there is no band across a lane where a drag would fail to pan.

The lane's **value range is drawn under its name and edited there**. Under the name because a number
at the far end of a lane has to be paired with its track by eye; edited there because it is, with
the name, what a reader changes on a lane, and a number that is already under its name is a number
that can have a caret put in it. Pointing at either end gives a text cursor and pressing opens a box
at the same size in the same place, so nothing moves when the number becomes editable. Typing a
bound turns autoscale off — that is what typing a bound means — and the other bound comes from the
axis on screen rather than from whatever was last stored, because the axis on screen is the one that
was being read. (The side panel's own boxes seed from the file's whole-genome extent instead: a
panel is not a view, and a number in it must not change when the view is panned.) The track's
**name** is edited the same way, where it is drawn, and commits to the one track it names rather
than to the lane, since an overlaid lane draws a name for each of its tracks. Tab takes either and
goes on (§26.8): a bottom to its top, a top to the next track's bottom, a name to the next track's
name — down the browser's lanes, and beside a map through every stack round it.

Four things the edit refuses, all for one reason — a limit nobody typed must never be stored.
Opening a bound and leaving it alone, or emptying the box, closes it and changes nothing; an
unreadable number and an inverted pair are marked in place with the caret still in them, rather than
silently discarded or answered with the `{0, 1}` axis `resolveLimits` gives an impossible range. And
the edit applies to **every track in the lane**, because a lane draws one range under however many
names it holds — committing to only the first would leave an overlay group as two lines at two
scales under one label, which is the picture the group exists to prevent.

The same layout applies beside a heatmap, on any lane tall enough for two lines. Where a lane is not,
the range goes back beside the name and stops being clickable, because its box would then overlap the
lower border that resizes the lane — an overlap in which the canvas promises a drag and the press
opens a text box is worse than either alone.

The **General column lists the sequences** under the Genome card: every contig, its length, a bar of
its length against the longest, and a click that shows the whole of it. A filter appears above a
dozen of them and the list is capped, because a `chrom.sizes` is as likely to be forty thousand
scaffolds as sixteen chromosomes. Under the list, what the ticks have done — `4 of 16 ticked` — and a
button that undoes it, *show the whole genome*. The count is said of the ticks and not of the list,
because a reader looking at nine rows of sixteen reads *showing 4 of 16* as a claim about the rows.

**A metagenome's card lists its own two units.** Over a picture of genomes — the whole metagenome, a
pair, several ticked — it is **Genomes**: every genome and its length, and ticking any number draws
them against each other (a `selection` of `genomes=`), one included, so the list is not swapped out
from under a reader halfway through ticking a second; none ticked is the whole metagenome. Inside one
genome — the genome view, one of its contigs, several — it is **Contigs**, *of* that genome, with a
`↑ genomes` link back out: ticking draws those contigs against each other (`regions=` with the
`genome` riding along, so the crumb reads `Genomes › G › a × b`), and none ticked is the genome
itself. A name's click goes one level in. Never the file's whole contig list, which is a hundred
thousand pieces of four thousand assemblies and not a picker.

**The map's level heads the card** (§7.3): `bin × bin` or `chromosome × chromosome` over a cooler's
whole genome, all three over a metagenome's, and bins or contigs over a genome or a pair; absent where
the view has only one. It is one question about the map — what one cell holds — and it was three
controls in two places: the Map card's `level` on a genome and a pair, a `Level` card of its own over
the whole metagenome.

Between the Genome card and the sequence list — beside a cooler's map, under the Sequences card —
the **Genome minimap**: the same sequences drawn end to end with the current view marked on them,
one line under it saying what a click and a drag do, and one under that saying where the view is.
The first says the gesture and nothing else — the Genome card above it already carries the sequence
count and the assembly's length — and the second writes the window in the display form (§26.1), so
the strip and the locus bar name the same place with the same digits.

### 5.9 One genome, many nomenclatures

Two files of the same genome disagree about its names more often than they agree. UCSC writes `chr1`,
Ensembl writes `1`, a `.hic` off 4DN writes `1`, a yeast cooler writes `chrI` and the `chrom.sizes`
beside it writes `01`. Every one of those is the first chromosome, and until this section every one
of them was a *different sequence*: a companion panel asked for `chr1` against a file calling it `1`
answered `unknown-label` and showed a blank rectangle under a bar claiming the deck was one
navigation, and a bigWig of the same assembly drew nothing beside a map that spelled it otherwise.

`src/genome/naming.ts` answers one question — *does this name, in this file, mean the same sequence as
that name, in that one* — under three constraints, and the constraints are the design.

**It never silently matches two different sequences.** A wrong match is worse than no match: no match
is a blank panel and a sentence saying why, and a wrong one is somebody else's chromosome drawn under
your label, which nothing on screen would show. So each step is a rule with a reason, `length` vetoes
rather than persuades, and a name whose shape the matcher does not recognise is matched **by its
spelling and not otherwise**. That last clause is what makes this safe on a metacool: assembler
contigs (`NODE_1_length_…`, `k141_9`, `tig00000001`) are opaque ids from independently assembled
organisms and two of them agree by coincidence (§8.5), so no numeral, no accession and no organelle
table is ever applied to one.

**The decisions come from the whole list, not one name at a time.** `X` is the tenth chromosome of
*S. cerevisiae* and the sex chromosome of everything else, and the string cannot tell you which. The
list can: a file that also holds `IX` and `XI` is counting in Roman numerals and its `X` is ten; a
file whose numerals stop at `V` — *C. elegans* is `I`…`V`, `X` — is naming a sex chromosome, and has
no chromosome ten to be confused with. The same test gets *S. pombe* right and gets every numeric
assembly right by never reaching the question. This is why the entry point is an index over a whole
file's sequences rather than a `canonicalise(name)` anybody could call on a string in isolation, and
why what it produces is **forwarded with the request**: a companion resolving the lead's region has
to read the numeral the way the lead wrote it.

Two further list-level rules, and each exists because a real file breaks the obvious version:

- A Hi-C library mapped against a **host plus a yeast spike-in** carries `chr1`…`chr22`, `chrX`,
  `chrY` *and* `chrI`…`chrXVI` in one list. The Roman evidence is overwhelming and the conclusion —
  that this file's `chrX` is chromosome ten — would re-key the host's sex chromosome onto the
  spike-in's tenth. So a list that numbers chromosomes **both** ways does not get to answer the `X`
  question at all: in a list that already counts in Arabic, `X` is the sex chromosome.
- SOAPdenovo, ABySS, Shasta and several binners number their contigs `1`, `2`, `3`. Read as ordinals
  those match `chr1` at the same rung an Ensembl file does, drawing a 4 kb contig under the label of
  chromosome one. Nothing about the string says which it is; the *count* does — no genome has two
  hundred chromosomes, and every draft assembly has thousands of contigs — so past that ceiling a
  bare number is an id and is matched by its spelling only. The ceiling applies per name as well as
  per list, which is what keeps Ensembl's *Drosophila* working: it carries hundreds of scaffolds
  named `211000022278279`, and those are neither chromosomes themselves nor evidence about the file
  that holds them.

Two more rules exist because a name can *look* like a convention without being one, and both were
found by reading real metagenome headers rather than by reasoning about the conventions:

- **The `chr` prefix comes off only when what is left reads as a chromosome.** `Christensenella_1`
  begins with `Chr` and `Chromobacterium_ctg1` with `Chrom`; stripped on sight they become
  `istensenella_1` and `obacterium_ctg1`, two names no file contains and which would then match each
  other's mangling. So a number, a Roman numeral, a sex letter, an organelle, an accession, UCSC's
  `Un_…` or a short letter run in front of a number gets the prefix taken off, and everything else
  keeps its name whole — which is also what a bacterial replicon genuinely called `Chromosome` needs.
- **Pipe decoration is reduced only when a database tag says so.** `MAG_042|NODE_1` and
  `MAG_007|NODE_1` are two organisms' first contigs, and reducing both to `NODE_1` would collide them
  at tier `exact` — the loudest possible version of the one thing this must never do. A header only
  loses its decoration if it carries one of NCBI's own tags (`gi`, `gb`, `ref`, `emb`, …) — and not
  `gnl`, whose `gnl|db|id` names a sequence by both of its fields, so that `gnl|MAG_042|NODE_1` is
  kept whole.

**Length corroborates; it never matches.** Two sequences of equal length are not the same sequence —
a metagenome has thousands of equal-length contigs — so no pair is ever matched *because* the lengths
agree. The implication runs the other way: where a name match is proposed, both lengths are known and
they differ, the match is reported as contested rather than taken quietly. hg19's `chrM` and hg38's
`chrM` are the case that matters — one name, two sequences, two bases apart.

**The ladder**, weakest interpretation first, and every match carries the rung it was reached by:

| tier | example |
| --- | --- |
| `exact` | `chr1` = `chr1` |
| `case` | `Chr1` = `chr1` |
| `decorated` | `ref\|NC_001133\|` = `NC_001133` |
| `prefix` | `chr1` = `chrom1` = `chromosome_1` = `1` |
| `padded` | `01` = `1` |
| `roman` | `chrXII` = `12` |
| `organelle` | `chrM` = `MT` = `MtDNA` = `NC_012920.1` |
| `accession` | `NC_000001.11` = `chr1`; `chrUn_GL000220v1` = `GL000220.1` |
| `version` | `NC_000001.10` ≈ `NC_000001.11` |

`version` is last and is the only rung known to be shaky: the same locus at two assembly versions is
two sequences, so it is offered and flagged rather than taken.

Only two ranges of per-species knowledge are hard-coded, and both are arithmetic rather than tables:
NCBI gave human chromosomes 1–22, X and Y the consecutive block `NC_000001`–`NC_000024`, and mouse
1–19, X and Y the block `NC_000067`–`NC_000087`. Everything else is a rule but the organelles, whose
names no rule relates — nothing derives `MtDNA` from `chrM` — and which are one small closed table of
spellings of a mitochondrion, a plastid and the yeast 2-micron plasmid, with the few reference
accessions a pipeline writes in their place. A real alias table for every assembly is megabytes,
needs a network, and would have to be told which assembly a file is of — which is the question this
whole section exists to avoid asking (C1, C2).

**What is deliberately not equated.** A chromosome arm is not its chromosome: *Drosophila*'s `2L` and
`2R` are separate sequences and neither is `2`, which also keeps wheat's `1A`, `1B` and `1D` — three
homoeologues, one number — apart from each other. The number in front of that letter is capped at two
digits, because FALCON writes its contigs `000001F` and reading one as chromosome 1 arm F would put
an assembler's output into the karyotype namespace. `_random`, `_alt`, `_fix`, `_hapN`, `_maternal`
and `_paternal` stay, because a patch is not the chromosome it patches, nor one parent's copy the
other's. A linkage group keeps its `LG`, because a linkage map is numbered by linkage and an
assembly by length and the two orders agree only by luck. `C`, `D` and `M` are excluded from the
Roman numeral system entirely — no genome has a hundredth chromosome, so a `C` in a chromosome list
is a chloroplast and an `M` a mitochondrion, every time. Organelle
spellings are matched whole and never by prefix, because *S. pombe*'s `MTR` is a mating-type region
sitting in the same file as its `MT`. And **genome names are never matched**: a metacool's genome
layer is independently assembled organisms, and nothing about their names is a convention.

**What is not attempted.** UCSC's `.1` → `v1` scaffold rewrite belongs to the hg38/mm39 generation;
the one before it lowercased the accession and *discarded* the version, so `chrUn_gl000220` cannot be
turned back into `GL000220.1` without knowing the assembly. Those names are left unrecognised rather
than guessed at, which costs a blank lane and a sentence where a guess would cost a scaffold drawn
under another scaffold's label. Two mitochondria in one file — UCSC's hg19 analysis set carries the
legacy `chrM` beside the rCRS as `chrMT`, on purpose — are not resolved either: both land in one
bucket, which makes the bucket ambiguous, which makes the matcher refuse unless a length settles it.
That is the general rule doing the work, not a special case.

**Where it fires, and where it must not.** In `parseMetacoolerRange` the matcher is consulted *after*
both namespaces have been asked literally and the answer would otherwise be a refusal. That placement
is the whole of how the range parser stays a faithful port of `metacooler.ops.range` (§5.4): every
string a file does carry resolves exactly as Python resolves it, in the same order, with the same
genome-wins rule, and a session of one file cannot tell the matcher exists. Only the error case
changed. The same after-the-strict-answer rule governs the ticked selection, the locus box, and
`contigOf`.

**Renaming at load is not enough on its own, and this is the part that is easy to get wrong.** A track
is loaded against the session's map and renamed into *its* vocabulary — but a deck draws the same
track beside every panel, and each panel samples through its own block's axis, so a companion asks
for a sequence by the name **its** file writes. One track, three vocabularies, and the rename can only
ever have chosen one of them. So every place a held track is asked for a name resolves as well as the
range does: the bigWig's refNames, a bedGraph's contigs, a FASTA's sequences, the feature sets the
renderer walks, and — the one with no file behind it at all — a synthetic track's grid, which is laid
out over the map the analysis was *computed on* and drawn beside every other. **Everything drawn at a
place resolves too**: a loop set's rings and arcs, a mark, a rectangle, a called set's corners are
placed through the map's own axis (`LocusAxis.ownName`), which answers a spelling it does not write —
`chrXIV` on a deck cell whose file writes `XIV` — through the same matcher. Asked by the exact name, a
loop set lit on a second map spelled the other way drew nothing there, while its tracks beside it did.

**It says so.** A panel that answered a name it does not itself write prints a line under its heading
naming both spellings and the rule that joined them, and says separately when the two lengths
disagree; the line is cleared whenever the panel stops drawing that picture. The §8.2 overlap report
is computed after the rename and therefore counts a cross-convention match as a match — which is
right when the two are one sequence and a lie when they are not, so a rename whose two lengths
disagree is carried into the report and named there. Without that, the one case most warranting a
word would be the one case that reported a clean bill. `compareRefusal` (§5.7) no longer refuses two files for spelling
one assembly differently — but still requires the same list in the same order, and still refuses two
sequences of one name at different lengths, which is the check that catches hg19 against hg38.

---

## 6. Reader layer

A read-only JS mirror of the Python `MetaCooler` class — same names, same semantics, same errors, no
new concepts.

```ts
class MetaCooler {
  static open(uri: string, source: ByteSource): Promise<MetaCooler>;

  readonly uri: string;
  readonly binsize: number;                    // never null: variable bins are refused (§3.3)
  readonly shape: [number, number];
  readonly info: Record<string, unknown>;      // incl. ordering, assembly
  readonly metadata: Record<string, unknown>;
  readonly genomes: Table | null;              // null for a plain cooler
  readonly contigs: Table;
  readonly chromnames: string[];
  readonly chromsizes: Map<string, number>;

  extent(region: string): [number, number];
  offset(region: string): number;
  genomeExtent(genome: string): [number, number];
  contigExtent(contig: string): [number, number];
  matrix(q: MatrixQuery): Promise<DenseMatrix>;
}
```

Plus `detectLayout` (one `Layout` for what Python asks `is_metacooler` and its siblings, in §3.1's
order), `listEntryNames`, `parseUri`, `parseMetacoolerRange`.

### 6.1 Byte-source abstraction

One interface, two implementations, chosen at construction. h5wasm is imported by `h5/bootstrap.ts`
alone, and no module of the reader or its formats (`metacooler/`, `h5/`, `hic/`, `pairs/`,
`hicpro/`) calls `fetch`: their requests are made by the sources, and by `worker/`, which builds them.

```ts
interface ByteSource { readonly id: string; readonly size: number; readonly isRemote: boolean;
                       mount(): Promise<string>;                 // for h5wasm
                       readBytes(position: number, length: number): Uint8Array;  // through the chunks
                       readExact?(position: number, length: number): Promise<Uint8Array>;
                       close(): void; stats(): SourceStats; }
```

`LocalFileSource` wraps a `File`. `RemoteRangeSource` wraps a URL. Identical downstream.

**A remote read reads ahead where the reads before it say to.** Each miss of the 1 MiB chunk cache
is a round trip, and HDF5 reads a cooler's pixels a dataset chunk at a time — `bin2_id` and `count`
in turn, and `bin1_id` where it is read at all (§6.2), streams through one region of the file — so a
whole chromosome of a 5 GB `.mcool` was 63 round trips of a megabyte, one after another. A miss
within 4 MiB of one of the last eight fetches is that region still being read, and from the third in
a row the fetch runs ahead of it, doubling to at most 16 MiB; the count is kept per region, so a
read of the weights between two pixel chunks does not start it again. A miss far from anything
recent — an index, a header, another sequence — fetches what it asks for and nothing more, so
opening a file costs what it did, and a source opened to read in small pieces (§3.8's `fine`) never
reads ahead. The same chromosome is now 34 requests. A walk across a `.hic`'s chromosome pairs reads
the other way, exactly and not through the chunks at all, planned so its reads are few (§3.6).

**The reader is started before it is asked for anything.** Its worker fetches and compiles h5wasm the
moment it exists, and it used to exist only once a file was opened, so every first open waited for
the runtime between the click and the first byte: 2.6 of the 3.2 seconds a 1 GB `.mcool` dropped on a
fresh tab took to land. It is made when the picker is on screen and the page is idle, and the same
drop lands in 0.3 s — the picker a workspace or a restored tab puts up to ask for a map on this
machine included, where a file dropped used to wait for a reader: a chromosome or a locus of the
timings' three maps (§18.10) took 1.18 s to draw from it, and takes 0.96 s.

### 6.2 Decoding requirements

**String columns.** metacooler writes them as fixed-length `S<n>`, sized by **UTF-8 encoded byte
length** rather than character count (`_str_to_hdf5`), precisely so multi-byte characters are not
truncated. Decode with `TextDecoder('utf-8')` and strip trailing NUL padding; never assume ASCII.
`CORE_COLUMN_KINDS` also permits kinds `O` and `U`, so a file produced by `create cool` may carry
variable-length strings instead — handle both.

**Names are ASCII, and this viewer does not claim otherwise.** `/contigs` *is* cooler's `/chroms`,
and cooler decodes every column of it with an ASCII `.astype("U")` — so metacooler refuses to write a
non-ASCII `/contigs` or `/genomes` name at all (`check_ascii_names` before the first write,
`schema.validate` after the last). A file with one cannot be produced by any documented command, and
supporting a shape the reference implementation will not create is a claim with nothing behind it. The
UTF-8 decode above is still required and still exercised: an **extra `/genomes` column** — an accented
taxonomy is the obvious one — is legal metadata cooler never sees.

**int64 becomes `BigInt64Array`.** `bin1_id`, `bin2_id` and all three offset arrays are int64.
`count` is **int32 at base resolution, int64 wherever counts have been summed** (`binnify`, `merge`),
**and float64 when the source column was float** — `resolve_count_dtype` preserves float sources
rather than truncating them, and `CORE_COLUMN_KINDS` accordingly permits `i`, `u` **or `f`** for
`pixels/count`. Three paths, resolved once at open. Unsigned integer columns are permitted throughout,
so test dtype *kind*, not an exact dtype. Consequences in JavaScript: mixing `BigInt`
with `Number` throws at runtime, not compile time; convert offsets to `Number` once on read (bin
counts are far below 2^53); resolve `count`'s dtype once at open rather than per pixel. **The
conversion is word by word, never a BigInt per element**: the high 32 bits times 2³² plus the low, or
the low word alone into an `Int32Array` (`toNumberArray`, `lowWords`), which is `Number` to the last
bit and was, through `Number(x[i])`, a third of what reading a pixel column cost. And a numeric column
is read out of h5wasm's heap straight into the array handed on, not copied out first as the stored
type and narrowed from that copy.

**A row band never reads `pixels/bin1_id`.** Each pixel's row is `bin1_offset`'s own answer
(`RowIndex`): the index *is* that column run-length encoded, a valid cooler is one on which the two
agree, and cooler's own range query (`CSRReader`) has never read it either. It was eight of the
twenty bytes a pixel of an int64/int64/int32 table inflates, for numbers already in hand. The one walk
that reads it is the deep check (§6.3), which is checking the column against the index and so cannot
take one from the other (`ScanAllOptions.storedRows`).

**A rectangle across the diagonal reads to the lower of its two ends.** Under `symmetric-upper`,
rows `[r0, r1)` against columns `[c0, c1)` that overlap need the pixels whose row is in
`[min(r0, c0), min(r1, c1))` and no others: a stored pixel has `bin1 ≤ bin2`, so one whose row is at
or past the lower end has both its bins past the end of one axis, and is in the block neither as
stored nor mirrored. `planRead` used to read to the higher end and let the scatter throw those rows
away, which a square on the diagonal never notices and a band of `hi` diagonals (rows `[a, b)` against
columns `[a, b + hi)`) paid for on every strip.

**Aggregation accumulates in `Float64Array`.** The format widens counts to int64 precisely because
summation overflows int32; the same applies in the browser.

### 6.3 Validation

Light by default: attributes, group presence, table lengths, `/chroms` soft link, declared-vs-actual
counts. All O(1).

The full Python `validate()` reads whole `bins` columns, the whole `genome_id` column, both offset
arrays and three pixel windows. Acceptable on local disk, unacceptable over HTTP — and the deep check
offered here is not it: it is `check --deep`'s pass over every stored pixel, each in range,
upper-triangular, in order and in the `bin1_offset` slot that claims it, and the integer counts
summing to `attrs['sum']`, with `validate()`'s `/bins` checks left out, since this reader never reads
`/bins` (§3.3), and its report says so. It reads the pixels as stored, even while the map is drawn to
a total (§6.5). Offered as an explicit debug action only: the status bar says **never run** until it
is pressed, and the offer — what a press will scan, and what it costs over a network — is in the
panel the item opens rather than in a second tooltip behind it. The item is absent altogether while
no file is open, since there is nothing to check and a check button that silently does nothing is
what §8.5 forbids — and so is *read* (§12). That includes a tab on the picker, whose reader is
started before anything is chosen (§6.1): the tab handed the bar that worker, so on a tab switched
back to both items came back, a counter of nothing beside a check that failed when pressed. A tab
hands the bar its reader only while a file is open in it.

### 6.4 Balancing

The format specification defines no weights column and `show()` uses `balance=False`. Balancing is
therefore **optional-if-present**, and it is built: when `/bins/weight` exists the score picker
offers `balanced` (§7.5), and a balanced cell is `raw * w[i] * w[j]` — cooler's own definition. A
`NaN` weight marks a bin the balancer dropped; the product is `NaN`, which renders transparent, so a
filtered row reads as absent rather than as empty. Where there is no weight column the entry is not
offered, a link naming it lands on counts, and a read asking for weights anyway is refused by name.
No default weighting is invented.

This is the **one** read of `/bins` in the reader, and it is bounded: two slices of the weight column
for the bins actually on screen, never the whole column, never `/bins/chrom`, and never at all unless
the user asked for balanced counts. §3.3's rule is that *coordinates* never come from `/bins`; they
still do not, and `test/unit/bins-guard.test.ts` still proves it for every unbalanced path.

### 6.5 Drawn to a total — subsampled or oversampled

**The last box on the breadcrumb is a number of contacts** (§5.5), labelled *contacts*. Empty, it
shows `e.g. 10M` as its placeholder, paler than any number the box holds and gone as soon as the box
is clicked, so it reads as *type a number here* and never as a value already in it; every file is
then read as stored. The map's own total — the `sum` that `cooler info` prints, 179,175,551 for the
yeast micro-C — is in the box's tooltip. (It was the placeholder once, and was read as a total
already typed.) A total typed into it draws **every map of the tab to
that many contacts, each on its own**: subsampled where a map holds more, oversampled where it holds
fewer. It reads a total the way a methods section or `cooler info` prints one — `10M`,
`23,000,000`, `2.5e7`, `500k`, `1.2G` — and refuses, in the box and with nothing redrawn, anything
that is not a positive whole number of contacts (`contacts.ts`, the one parser the box and the shell
share). It commits on Enter or on leaving the box rather than per keystroke: `1`, `10` and `10M` on
the way to the number wanted are not three requests to walk the file. Escape puts back what is in
force; an emptied box puts back the files as stored. The total is in the link (`contacts=`) and,
like `cells` (§3.8), belongs to the file rather than to the view: it survives a navigation into a
chromosome and back out.

**A subsample is `cooltools random-sample --count N --exact`**: `N` of the file's `T` contacts, every
subset of that size equally likely, so each pixel keeps a hypergeometric share of its own and the
total is exactly `N`. `--exact` is not offered as a choice, because it is not one: a map captioned
*10,000,000 contacts* that holds 9,998,213 is the thing this box exists not to draw. cooltools holds
the whole map to do it, and a viewer reads a window at a time, so the draw is split where its
distribution splits exactly (`metacooler/resample.ts`):

1. **A census**, once per map: one walk over every stored pixel for each sequence pair's contacts.
   It does not depend on `N`, so a second total costs no second walk.
2. **A split**: each pair's share of `N`, hypergeometric in what is left — a handful of draws.
3. **A band**, on the first read of a sequence: its own block and every block to its right, each
   drawn to its share pixel by pixel in `(bin1, bin2)` order, from a generator seeded by the map's
   seed and the block.

The seed is fixed, so the same total is the same map in every view, in both workers, after a reload
and in the shell. The pixels follow cooltools' distribution and not its generator: a numpy stream is
not reproducible from here, and a subsample is a draw, not a file.

**An oversample is Boost-HiC** (Carron et al., *Bioinformatics* 2019), ported from its Python
(`metacooler/boost.ts`) and held to it by a golden file that Python writes
(`scripts/make_boost_golden.py`): every contact the file has, plus `N − T` more drawn with
replacement from a probability map. Within a sequence the map is Boost-HiC's boosted matrix —
outlier bins taken out by a kernel density on their coverage, ten rounds of SCN, Floyd–Warshall on
`1/cᵅ` with `main.py`'s `α = 0.2`, back to contacts, and the decay with distance put back window by
window — returned **in the file's own counts** rather than in SCN units; a pair with a bin the
outlier filter took out is weighted by the file's own pixel instead, or that bin would come out of an
oversample shallower than everything round it. Between sequences, which Boost-HiC does not model,
the map is the file's own pixels. Each pair's share of the new contacts is
binomial in its share of the old, so the total is again exactly `N`. An oversample is an
**inference** where a subsample is not, and everything that names a drawn map says which it was.

**The map an oversample draws from is a command of its own.** `chromosomix boost <map>` hands
Boost-HiC each sequence's stored counts — the square an oversample hands it (`cisSquare`) — and
writes what `main.py` writes, `boostedmat`: the boosted map over the bins the outlier filter kept, in
SCN units, one square TSV a sequence, its rows and columns named by each kept bin's start
(`--sequences` names some, `--alpha` another exponent). Nothing on screen shows that map, and a draw
from it is a poor way to hold a port to its upstream; with it, `notebooks/validation.qmd` holds the
port to Boost-HiC's own Python cell for cell over whole chromosomes, where the golden holds a hundred
bins (§18.10). A sequence past the limit below is refused by name, as an oversample refuses it, and the
others are still written.

Floyd–Warshall is cubic in a sequence's bins. It runs as a WebAssembly SIMD kernel
(`metacooler/wasm/floyd.c`, built by `npm run wasm:floyd` and committed as base64, bit-identical to
the TypeScript loop it falls back to), which walks yeast's chromosome IV at 1 kb — 1,532 bins — in
about a second and a half. Past **3,000 bins** in one sequence the wait is a refusal better said than
suffered, and it is said by name: the sequence, its bins, the limit, and a coarser resolution as the
way out.

**Balanced reads stay on the file's scale.** A drawn map is `N/T` times the file in expectation, so
each bin's weight is read times `√(T/N)` — where ICE run on the drawn map converges, up to the noise
the draw added. Without it a subsample balanced with the file's weights reads `N/T` times fainter,
and two maps drawn to one total would not be on one colour scale.

**Every task reads the drawn map.** The drawn pixels stand behind the one `PixelStore` every read
goes through (`metacooler/store.ts`), so the views, the pooled reads and every task of §18 get them
without knowing. The analysis worker opens its own mount drawn to the same total and seed, handed the
reader's census rather than walking the file again, and a block the view holds is lent to a task
only when the two were drawn alike (§18.3). A task's framing says the depth —
`subsampled to 10,000,000 contacts (of 179,175,551)` — and its line in the console carries
`--contacts 10000000`, which `chromosomix` takes with the same parser and the same seed (§23). A
figure says it in its caption (§7.2).

**Two maps or more are drawn map by map**, each to the one total, each subsampled or oversampled as
its own depth requires. With two or more on screen — a deck (§16), or a second file in the lower
triangle (§5.7) — two chevrons follow the box: **down** types the shallowest map's total, so every
map is subsampled to it, and **up** the deepest's, so every map is oversampled to it through
Boost-HiC. Matching depth is what a comparison draws a map to another total for, and those are the
two totals it is matched at. A chevron is lit while the box holds its total and names, in its
tooltip, the map whose total that is; both wait, disabled, while a map's total is still being
counted, and the box's own tooltip lists every map's.

**A `.hic` is counted.** Its header's `sumCounts` counts every contact off a chromosome's diagonal
twice — the matrix both ways round — and the demo `.hic` declares 23,827,759 for its 13,681,280
contacts, so that number would have sent the up chevron to a total the file never held. The reader
counts the contacts instead, in the background, on the coarsest rung of the file (the same contacts
in the fewest pixels), and the box shows them when they land.

**In the background means behind every other read.** The census starts on every open, on the
thread every view reads through, so it reads nothing before a request already waiting has been
answered — on an open, the loading screen's — and it walks the file the way §3.6 walks one across
chromosome pairs: each pair's matrix record read only as far as the coarsest rung, which is the
record's first few dozen bytes, and that rung's blocks, all as exact ranges planned together, four
reads in flight. On the 5 GB 4DN map of mouse granule neurons (4DNFI916JQ1Y, thirteen rungs, 231
pairs) that was 456 requests and under 1 MB pair by pair; on the 4DN chicken map 4DNFIRKUYKP4 (630
pairs) it is 419 requests where pair by pair it was 1,258. Reading each record whole first — the
block index of all thirteen rungs, 70 MB, in 1 MiB chunks — was 500 MiB, and held the loading screen
for a minute and a half.
And **it stands aside for as long as a view is reading**, not for one turn: between pairs it waits
until no view's request has run for a quarter of a second (§12), so a chromosome clicked while it
counts is read as if it were not counting. A resample waiting on the census ends the wait, since the
views are then waiting on it. Its progress is its own and is not written on a view's veil: *counting
contacts…* over a chromosome that was loading named the wrong wait.

**What is refused, by name:** counts that are not whole or are negative (there is no contact to
draw); a `square` file, which stores every contact twice; an `.scool`, whose map is a sum of cells
rather than one library; a value column other than `count` while the map is drawn, since a drawn map
is drawn from its contacts; and, for an oversample, a sequence past Boost-HiC's limit. The refusal
takes the map's place — the tab's first map's page offers **read as stored**, and a companion says it
in its own frame — and the box turns red with the reason as its tooltip: a map drawn from the stored
counts under a total that says otherwise would be the one wrong answer.

**What it costs is a walk and a band.** The census reads every stored pixel once per map, and is
handed to every worker that draws the same map. A drawn band is kept while 192 MiB allows, the
oldest redrawn identically when it is read again past that; an oversample adds Boost-HiC for each
sequence as its band is drawn.

---

## 7. Rendering

### 7.1 Defaults match `metacooler show`

The same file must produce the same picture in the CLI and the browser, or every figure in the paper
diverges from what a reader reproduces locally.

- transform `log1p` (with `log10` and `none` selectable)
- colormap `afmhot_r`
- `vmin = 0`; `vmax` = 99th percentile of non-zero values in the **transformed** matrix, recomputed on
  view change, with manual override. A *refine* (§2) is not a view change and does not recompute it:
  a coarse cell is a sum of bins, so a finer block over the same place holds systematically smaller
  numbers, and re-measuring would re-brighten the map for a reader who changed nothing but the
  magnification. The range is measured from the **widest block held** and stays there while the
  reader zooms in; zooming out past it re-measures, which is right, because that reader is looking at
  data that was not in the picture before
- the **cell size** is named in the key, on its own line under the scale's name, and in the exported
  key as well — it is the one fact about a refining map that cannot be recovered from the pixels, and
  a figure that carries it needs no caption to say it
- separators at genome or contig boundaries, in `metacooler show`'s two greys — and **heavier than its
  0.5 and 1**: 1.5 CSS pixels between sequences and 2 between genomes or selection blocks, in every
  picture, since drawn at the larger of the CLI's width and one device pixel a line between two
  chromosomes was half a pixel on a 2× screen and a hairline in a PNG, and the reader lost it on a
  dense map. A line is centred on the device grid by its width, so its whole pixels are solid and only
  a fraction is shared with a neighbour; the PDF carries the widths as they are, 1.125 and 1.5 pt
- ticks in base pairs on any axis that stays inside one contig, and the contig names on any axis that
  does not — `_bin_axis`'s rule, because a bin index is not a position and does not restart at zero
  where the block does. An axis of **several** contigs is then ruled one contig at a time on top of
  those names, each measured from its own first base, because "where in this one am I" is the
  question a reader asks of a whole genome as much as of a single chromosome. Each stretch gets the
  room it actually has — a chromosome with room for no tick carries its name and nothing more, which
  is the rule the names themselves are elided by, and a metagenome's thousands of pixel-wide contigs
  carry none — its own step, since one chosen for the longest chromosome puts no tick on the
  shortest, and no tick on either of its own edges, where the boundary line already is. Above bin
  level there is still nothing: a cell there *is* a contig, and a position inside one would be an
  invention

Both bounds are overridable, as one clip range: two typed numbers and one control back to auto. The
URL carries `vmin` and `vmax` independently, in transformed units, and their absence means auto.
The key in the map's top-right corner prints the same two numbers, the boxes' own, under the score's
name with the transform on it, and each is a button: pressed, it takes a typed bound in place,
emptied it hands that bound back to auto, and left as it was it changes nothing — a bound on auto is
not fixed at the number the key happened to show. The box opens on **that number**, rounded as the
key prints it and as the clip boxes are (`trimNumber`): it opened on the float the scale holds,
`-1.0543182366`, which overflowed the box and left its last digits in view and its sign and first
digits out. Tab goes from the low end to the high one, and on a deck on to the next map's key
(§26.8). A change of transform hands both back, since a bound is a
number in the old transform's units. **Between the two numbers is the ramp they run between**, short
— 48 by 10 pixels — and drawn through the colormap's own colours: on screen a gradient, in a figure
one band a pixel, since a PDF page here has no linear gradient. For a while it was two squares, the
ramp's ends, on the argument that the colours between them were the picture's to show rather than
the legend's; on a ramp that is not a line they are not — the default runs white, yellow, red, black,
and which of the four a cell halfway up is was the one thing two squares could not say.

**Both unit systems on that row are named**, because both are on screen at once: the boxes are in
transformed units, so the row is labelled `clip (log10)` from the transform in force, and the line
under them prints the same pair untransformed, in the units the readout under the pointer gives,
followed by the word for them — `auto · 0.000066 – 0.089 balanced`. Unnamed, the two read as a
contradiction, and a reader who typed the caption's own number into a `log10` box clipped the map a
thousandfold too high. The
line is **absent until a block has been scaled**: `auto · 1 – 10` beside a view that has drawn
nothing is a caption for a picture that is not there. On screen the ramp picker is called
**colours**, which is what a lane's own row calls the same kind of choice; `colormap` is the word for
it here and on the command line, where it is a parameter rather than a label.

**What the app *opens* with is its own choice**, as the overlay defaults are (§7.2). Parity is a
property of the machinery — the same colormap table, the same indexing, the same percentile rule —
not of which entry the picker starts on, so the viewer opens on its own white → yellow → red → black
ramp, and a **cooler with a weight column** opens balanced in `log10` because that is what a finished
assembly's map is read in. `afmhot_r` on raw counts is one item away and still byte-identical, and a
`.metacool` — where the reader is asking how much two contigs touch, which is a count — is left on
the CLI's counts and `log1p` even where it carries weights, on the viewer's ramp like every other
file.

**The percentile is taken over the pixels that are drawn.** Above §7.2's raster
cap a block is pooled, one pixel to many cells, and a scale fitted to the cells
would describe a population no pixel on screen belongs to. Below the cap nothing
is pooled, the two are the same set, and the resolved bounds are bit-identical —
which is where the parity above actually lives, since `metacooler show` renders
at a size that never pools.

The rule above is for **raw counts**, where zero is a true floor. It does not survive balancing
(§6.4), whose values are fractions: `log10` of them is negative almost everywhere — on a 10 kb *E.
coli* map, 0.4% of cells transform positive and a `vmin` of 0 clips the other 99.6% to white. A
balanced block is therefore scaled to the 1st-to-99th percentile of the cells that carry a contact,
and `log10` draws an empty cell at the low end rather than at numpy's `0.0`, which for these values
sits above the whole picture. `metacooler show` never balances, so neither departure touches parity.

### 7.2 Technique

`ImageData` + `putImageData` to an offscreen canvas at matrix resolution, then `drawImage`-scaled to
the display canvas. Pan and zoom are canvas transforms over the in-memory matrix. A colour-vision-safe
colormap is selectable; keyboard pan and zoom are supported — on the focused map the arrows pan,
Page Up and Page Down zoom about the centre a wheel notch at a time, and Home refits — and from
anywhere in the window `0` refits (*Fit the view*, by its place, so AZERTY's bare `à` does) and
Space locks the map onto its diagonal (§8.9). `−` and `+` are not a zoom on a map: they step its
resolution (§5.5), and the wheel, a pinch, the paging keys and the boxes zoom. In the 1D browser `0`
is the whole genome, as a double click is.

**The wheel's two axes mean two different things.** Up and down is the zoom, about the pointer.
Sideways **slides along the picture**, which is what two fingers mean over every genome browser there
is and what they already meant over this app's own tracks — on a map, **the columns alone**, and
**along its diagonal while the view is held on it** (the diagonal lock, §8.9): rows and columns
together, by the same distance, so the diagonal stays where it is on the screen and the picture moves
down the genome under it, as the reference editor's stage (§27.3) has always slid. It slid along the
diagonal always, which a reader who had panned off it to read a stretch of the off-diagonal could not
get out of: letting go of the lock is saying the next slide is meant to leave the line, and a slide
that kept to it anyway was the map overruling the hand. **Every cis block slides that way** while
locked, a block of two stretches of one sequence
included — the off-diagonal window an Option-drag opens, whose diagonal is off the picture: it is
read by separation as the diagonal is, and moving rows and columns together keeps a band parallel to
the diagonal, one distance apart, under the pointer, where the columns alone carried the reader
across distances they had not asked to leave. Such a block used to slide its columns alone, as a
trans block does. Along the columns alone where there is no separation to keep: over a turned band
(§17), whose diagonal already runs across the screen, and over a trans block — two sequences, two
genomes; a picture above bin level slides along its diagonal where its axes share cells, as it
always has. The sideways scroll used to be left to the page so that the
platform's back-and-forward swipe would work over a map as it does over the rest of a document; that
is the wrong trade over the one element a reader navigates *by* sliding, and the swipe still works
everywhere outside the picture. Over a lane stack it means the same thing as over the map, because a
stack is drawn on the map's own axis — the map moving under the pointer while the profile above it
stayed put would read as the two coming apart.

**With ⌘ held, up and down slide too.** Two fingers on a trackpad slide a map sideways and zoom it
vertically, so moving it *up or down the screen* took a drag with the button held — the one
direction of the picture the fingers already on the pad could not reach. ⌘ turns the vertical axis
into a slide as well, both axes at once, so with it held a two-finger drag moves the map wherever the
fingers go and the zoom waits until it is let go. ⌘ and never Ctrl: a trackpad pinch arrives as a
wheel with `ctrlKey` set, and it stays the zoom it is. Over a lane stack ⌘-scroll keeps its own
meaning, that lane's ceiling (§5.8), since the gesture is aimed at the lane under it.

**Touch is a first-class input**, not a fallback: one finger pans, two pinch, a tap opens what it
lands on and a double tap refits. Below 34rem the app is one column — the plot as wide as the screen,
and the key in its corner hidden, since there it covers a real fraction of the data; it stands down
the same way on any plot narrower than 240 px, a narrow cell of a deck's included. Every control
revealed by *pointing* — a tab's ×, a track's colour — is shown outright under `(hover: none)`,
because a control that appears on hover appears never where there is no hover; and every one of them
is inert while it is invisible, so a tap or a click that lands where one is hidden reaches what is
behind it rather than firing a button nobody saw.

**One grid, and one place it is decided.** This is what a refine (§2) re-uses
rather than works around: it asks for a narrower window and *nothing else*, and
the reader plans the grid for it exactly as it plans every other read. A caller
that named its own grid would bypass the widening below and anchor the cells to
wherever the reader had panned to, so a cell's value would change as it crossed
the screen — which is why the plan is never sent by anything driven from a
