viewport.

**A window is read at its own bins up to `denseCellCap`**: the widest square the dense guard
(§9) passes on this machine, and never wider than `RASTER_MAX_DIM`, **16,384** — on a machine
reporting 8 GiB it is the 16,384 that binds. That is what draws a whole yeast chromosome IV at
100 bp, 15,320 bins a side, one bin to a pixel, so that a zoom into it reaches single bins without
another read: 45 s and 2.9 GB in the tab, measured in headless Chromium, where the 4,096 the raster
stopped at before drew it at 400 bp in 9 s and 235 MB. A smaller machine gets a smaller square, from
the same budget, so the window it cannot afford is pooled rather than refused.

A wider block is coarsened **once, in the reader**, into cells that hold at most a capacity of bins
and never part of one sequence beside anything else: a sequence longer than the
capacity keeps cells of its own, cut at its own start, and only the ones too small
to fill a cell share. The capacity is searched for against `POOLED_CELL_CAP`, **4,096**, which is
narrower than the raster on purpose: the pooled read is the one a whole genome takes when no rung
brings it under `denseCellCap` (a ladder's coarser rung often does — the whole yeast genome of a
100 bp ladder is its 2 kb rung, 6,064 bins, read whole), it is not under the dense guard, and its accumulator is sized by this cap — at 16,384 it would be a gigabyte for every
whole-genome view of a large file. Narrower is never pooled twice: the grid the reader builds fits the
raster, and the raster's own pooling is reached only by a block a caller hands it unplanned. The
grid is anchored to the *sequence*, not to the request, so the same base pair falls
in the same cell holding the same sum in every view of it, and a range is widened to
those cell edges rather than starting a grid of its own.

**A block come back to is not pooled again.** The raster is made in two passes: the block reduced to
display values — transformed, pooled to the raster's size, and measured for its automatic range — and
those values coloured. The first is a property of the block, the transform, the balancing and the
neutral value, and of nothing a colormap or a clip can move, so it is kept beside the block for as long
as the block is held anywhere (`pooledOf`), and a view built over a block the reader came back to (§2,
§12) goes straight to the colouring. The colouring writes each pixel as one 32-bit word out of a 32-bit
view of the table — the same four bytes the four byte writes it replaced put down — which took a
3,910-cell chromosome's from 410 ms to 280 ms on the machine it was measured on.

**What is accepted, and stated rather than fixed:** the raster is at most 16,384 px
per axis and a plot is commonly 800–1,600 device pixels, so `drawImage` still
minifies, and its filter averages across cell — and therefore sequence —
boundaries. Every stage before it is exact; this one blends neighbours that are
not neighbours, by up to a few pixels at a boundary. Removing it means performing
the reduction to display size in the app, sequence-aware, which measured 40–66 ms
per frame on the main thread and therefore belongs in a worker. It is a known
limitation of the drawing, not of the data: the numbers behind every pixel, the
readout, the axes and the export are all taken from the reader's grid.

**Keyboard pan and zoom are supported**, so the picture takes focus — and draws **no focus ring**:
not around the map, the 1D browser's strip or a table's viewport. A ring on those surfaces is a blue
frame around the data, which reads as part of the figure; and `:focus-visible` also matches the focus
the app hands the picture after a typed locus and Enter, so a ring kept for the keyboard appeared
after the commonest navigation there is. The picture has a frame of its own.

**Four of the overlay preferences are about the tracks rather than the matrix**, and are shared by
both places the tracks are drawn. Two take ink away: `text` takes every word off them — names,
ranges, feature names — and `fills` takes the shading out from under their lines, which is the
envelope and an area track's own fill together. Both are one thing to the eye and both are context
for a line rather than a series, which is what makes them the first things to go when several tracks
share a lane or a figure is going into a caption. Two add a rule: `outline` along the top of every
track and round every feature's box, and `baseline` along the foot of every lane. They live in the
same store as the matrix's own overlays (`localStorage`, not the hash: §5.5 shares what is being
looked at, not whether the reader likes shading). The app opens on its own overlays rather than the
renderer's, which are `metacooler show`'s: the crosshair and `outline` on, the dividers and the
block labels off (`ui/plotOptions.ts`).

**Everything that leaves the app is on white, in either theme.** A map's PNG and PDF, a deck's, the
1D browser's, a task's figure, a model's and every *Copy this* are laid on white and written in the
light palette's ink, whatever the reader is looking at the app in: the dark theme is a way of
looking at the app, not at the figure. The centre column already wears the light palette in either
theme; what did not was the ground, which was the page's own colour read off the root — so in the
dark theme a map's PNG came out on near-black under ink chosen for white, its exported key a dark
box of near-black text — and a task's figure enlarged into the stage dialog, which follows the theme,
and exported from there. The ground is one white (`FIGURE_BACKGROUND`), and a figure is redrawn for
its export from a hidden node pinned to the light palette (`figurePaper`) rather than from wherever
it is mounted.

**The figure saves as PNG at a chosen DPI, or as PDF.** It is re-rendered through the same drawing
code rather than screen-grabbed — the PNG at that resolution — so the labels and hairlines are drawn
rather than enlarged, and the framing — pan and zoom included — is what is on screen. The PDF is one
page written by the app, its size in points derived from the CSS size, and only the matrix on it is
an image: the cells as the screen draws them, in one lossless raster, with every axis, tick, label,
lane, key and caption round them written as paths and text on the same vector page the 1D browser's
PDF is (`ui/vector.ts`). The page is drawn at 1:1 and has no resolution, so the DPI beside the
format is the PNG's alone and is **absent while PDF is chosen**, as it is on the browser's card —
the copy's tooltip then names the resolution its PNG takes. The resolution is in a PNG's file name
and not in a PDF's. Either is named after the window as its caption prints it, 1-based (§26.1), with
the grouping dropped rather than turned into underscores — `IV_1000001-1400000-<stamp>.pdf` for
`IV:1,000,001-1,400,000` — and so is any other file named after a locus (`exportBaseName`).

Both cards label the format **PDF (vector)**, and so does the 3D model's (§25.7): a biologist who
saved a map as `PDF` for a figure and opened it in Illustrator expecting paths had been told which
they were getting by one card and nothing at all by the other — and on a map there are paths to
restyle, everything but the cells.

**The 1D browser's PDF is vector throughout**, and the map's matrix is the one raster either PDF
holds. A contact map is a raster honestly — twelve thousand bins are pixels and writing them as a
million rectangles would be a larger, slower file of the same picture — but nothing in a genome
browser is: every mark there is a rectangle, a polyline or a word. So the browser's PDF carries only
paths and text, and a figure dropped into a manuscript can be restyled, recoloured and scaled by
whoever receives it. It is produced by handing the *same renderers* a context that emits PDF
operators instead of pixels, so there is no second drawing of the view to keep in step; text is
Helvetica, one of the fourteen fonts every reader has, so nothing is embedded. A vector page has no
resolution, so the DPI control is *absent* while one is chosen rather than greyed out — which is also
what puts the format's full name and the button on one line. The clipboard button in the same row
takes a PNG whatever the format beside it says, so while the select is away **its tooltip names the
resolution it will use**: a slide-maker was pasting a raster rasterised at a number they could no
longer see or change.

**The page keeps its path as a canvas does.** The context is the same drawing only if it answers
every call as a canvas would, and the path is where a canvas and a PDF part: a canvas's `fill`,
`stroke` and `clip` each read the current path and leave it for the next, until `beginPath` empties
it, while in a PDF the operator that paints a path ends it. So the page holds the path itself and
writes it out again in front of every operator that paints it — its points where the transform put
them as they were added, a stroke's width as the transform scales it when it is stroked, as on a
canvas — and `fillRect` and `strokeRect` paint a rectangle of their own without disturbing it. Each
cell of a deck's figure (§16.5) starts on an empty path, as its own canvas does on screen. An empty
path paints nothing, and a clip to it clips everything away. The page used to write a path once and
let it go, so a shape filled and then stroked was printed as its fill and a stroke of nothing: every
exported box plot lost its outline, whiskers and median, the reader's arrowheads came out as white
halos with nothing inside, and a bar track's outline and the 1D browser's chips lost their borders.

**The caption under a figure is quiet, and can be left off.** A saved map figure says under itself
what it shows: the region on the first line, then the file, the bins, the score, the colour range
and when it was made; a 1D browser figure names its genome, its window and the date on one line.
A map drawn to another total than its file's (§6.5) says so after the file's name —
`subsampled to 10,000,000 contacts (of 179,175,551)`, or `oversampled to … (of …, Boost-HiC)` —
because a figure travels without the box that drew it, and a subsample, an inference and the file
itself are three different claims; a map read as stored says nothing, as it always has.
Both are set in the axis labels' grey — the region at 11 px and weight 600, the rest at 10 px,
before the text size is applied — because at 15 px and semibold in the page's ink the region was the
largest type on the page and drew the eye away from the picture it names. Both Export cards carry a
**caption** switch on the save row, after the download and the clipboard it qualifies, on by default, for the reader who lays figures out with a
legend of their own; off, the figure ends at its lowest track and keeps no room for the line. It is
one preference, kept with the overlays' kind (`localStorage`), and shared: off beside the map is
off in the 1D browser, and in the deck's figure, whose cells each read it (§16.5). The tracks'
own names and ranges are the picture's and are saved as they are on screen, whatever the switch
says.

**Copy this: the object under the pointer, and nothing round it.** The right-click menu on the map,
on a lane beside it and on a lane of the 1D browser — and a right click that does not drag on a 3D
model (§25.3) — carries **Copy this**, first on the map's and the model's menus and first under the
track's name on a lane's. It puts that one object on the clipboard as a PNG, as it is drawn on
screen and at the screen's own density: the map's **cells** in the part of the plot they fill, with
no axis, tick, divider, key or frame, no loop, domain or mark drawn over them, and no guide line or
pointer; the **lane** alone, the strip of its stack or of the browser it is drawn in, with no name
or range, no handle, no name column, no hairline and no mark carried off the map — a gene's name
under its body is the track's own and stays, as the overlays switch has it; the **model** as the
renderer draws it, its names on it as the overlays have them, with no centre of rotation, key,
buttons or frame. White goes under the ink, so a cell or a stretch the data leaves clear pastes as
paper rather than as a hole — white in the dark theme too, as every export is. The Export card's copy is a *figure* — labelled,
captioned, at the card's resolution — and this is the object, for a reader assembling a figure of
their own in another program. Each is drawn by the same pass the screen is, stopped before
everything round the data, rather than cut out of the screen's canvas, which carries all of that
over it. The menu closes on the press, so what happened is said in the corner (`ui/toast.ts`): the
size of what was copied, in pixels, or why the browser would not take it.

### 7.3 Genome × genome overview — gated, not default

Available, but never automatic, because it costs a full pixel scan (§4):

- **Local files:** explicit user action, progress indicator, cancellable.
- **Remote files:** **warned above a byte threshold, with the download offered** — the scan streams
  in bounded windows, so only the bytes are large, and the reader knows their connection where this
  page does not. A caution with a way through takes `--warn` and not the colour of a refusal
  (§26.5): red over a button that proceeds is a reader told no by the picture and yes by the words.
  A full scan means downloading the file.
  Offered when a sidecar edge list is advertised in the catalog. **`metacooler network --level genome`
  is the right producer** — it emits a `node1 / node2 / value` TSV (optionally with `--header`) to a
  file or stdout, which for a few hundred MAGs is a few KB of text: no HDF5, no range requests, one
  `fetch`. Prefer it over `aggregate --level genome`, which produces a whole `.cool` for the same
  information. While the maps are drawn to a total (§6.5) the edge list is not read, since it counts
  the file as stored: the same press scans the drawn map instead.

Both remain opportunistic: a plain `.metacool` with no sidecar behaves identically, minus the
overview.

Opportunistic in exactly the same way as the mmetacool ladder: used when present, never required.

**Three levels, one control.** The whole-file view offers `bin × bin`, `contig × contig` and
`genome × genome` in a single picker — at the head of the Genomes card in the General column (§5.8) —
and `level` in the hash selects between them and the shell mounts whichever view draws the answer.
The view is the **whole metagenome**, in its crumb, its heading and its gate's button: *whole
genome* is a cooler's. Only the last two are accumulations over unit pairs — `bin × bin`
is the pooled whole-file read (§9), and on a metagenome it is the same picture as selecting every
row of the genomes table.

**`bin × bin` is the default.** A contig cell sums a rectangle of `length × length`, and a
metagenome's contigs span several orders of magnitude in length, so the contig axis spends its width
on the shortest sequences and its colour range on the longest: a block is as wide as a genome is
*fragmented* rather than as long as it is. Measured on the 48-MAG mock community, 62% of the contig
axis goes to contigs under 5 kb holding 4% of the sequence, one badly-assembled MAG takes 28% of it
for 4.5% of the assembly, and a third of the diagonal comes out empty. Bin cells are all the same
area, so one scale fits the whole picture — and landing on the legible level is worth more than
landing on the one that contains the others. The contig level stays, because "is this bin one
organism?" is a question only it answers. Where a sidecar edge list is advertised the default gives
way to `genome × genome`: that one is a small download rather than a pass over the file, so it is
the cheapest thing to land on.

**The bin level costs what the other two cost, and gives way when it cannot be had.** Its block is
the raster's size whatever the file — up to 4,096² cells — and it used to be summed into a full
`Float64` square and copied to `Float32` for the wire: 12 B a cell, 200 MB at the peak, which is the
allocation a browser refuses first. On the diagonal it now sums the upper triangle in `Float64` and
finishes straight into the `Float32` square, 8 B a cell — the contig and genome levels' own cost. A
tab that still cannot allocate it (Chrome's *Array buffer allocation failed*) is not shown an error
screen: the view goes to `contig × contig` (`chromosome × chromosome` on a cooler) and starts that
read at once, since *compute* was already pressed for a pass over every pixel, and `bin × bin` stays
greyed out in the level select for the rest of the session with one line saying why. A link or the
back button asking for it lands one level up. It is not predicted in advance: `navigator.deviceMemory`
is coarse and capped, reports gigabytes the tab cannot necessarily have, and would refuse the level on
machines that draw it fine.

**All three ask first, and all three are read by genome.** Being the default makes the gate
mandatory rather than optional: the rule is not "warn when it looks expensive" but that a pass over
every pixel never starts on its own, and a threshold would make it hold on large files and lapse on
small ones. So the bin level is gated whatever the file declares `nnz` to be, behind the same
sentence, the same two figures and the same button as the scans: `compute whole metagenome` over one
sentence naming the stored pixels it will read, the cells it will sum them into, and the bytes it
will read or download. Both figures on every gate, because the pixels are what a local read costs
and the bytes are what a remote one costs, and a gate cannot know which of the two a reader is
paying. One gate said `compute overview` — a word that appeared nowhere else on screen, under a
toolbar button reading *whole genome* — and priced itself in bytes alone while its sibling priced
itself in pixels alone. It is also labelled and divided by **genome** rather than
by contig — the axis is the whole metagenome at every level, 2,082 contig hairlines over 48 blocks
are a grey wash, and an axis label that names a genome opens that genome. A *selection* follows the
same rule one level down, because it is the same rule: its axis names **what was ticked**. Tick
several genomes and it is divided and labelled by genome, exactly as the three levels above it are —
four ticked MAGs are four blocks, and the two thousand contig hairlines across them are the same
grey wash hiding the same structure. Tick contigs, or one genome, and the contigs keep the lines:
there the ticked names *are* the contigs, and a single genome has nothing coarser inside it than its
own. Where the axis is pooled the cells are held inside one genome for it, so a boundary drawn on it
is the boundary and not a cell past it — and an axis label, being a genome name wherever the axis is
divided by one, opens that genome from a selection exactly as it does from the three levels above.
The dispatch is on what the axis *is* (`WholeView.labelTarget`) and not on which view is asking,
which is how the two came to disagree: a genome name is a legal range (§5.4), so the selection's
label opened a region view of the genome — one screen short of where the gesture meant to go rather
than a broken click, and correspondingly easy to miss.

**And a click on a cell opens a genome at all three levels.** "Read by genome" is a claim about the
picture, and it has to be a claim about the gestures on it or it is only a claim about the ink: the
two accumulating levels resolved a cell to one MAG's map on the diagonal and to the pair off it,
while `bin × bin` — the *default*, the level a reader lands on — resolved to the contig under the
pointer and opened a region view of two `NODE_` sequences nobody had asked about. The same gesture
on the same file went somewhere else depending on which of three levels was chosen. All three now
dispatch on one rule (`overviewTarget`): same genome on both axes opens that genome, two genomes
open the block between them, and a file with no genome layer falls through to the sequence, which is
what a cooler's whole-genome view has always done. The contig is one click further in, from the
genome's own map, which is where a question about a contig is actually asked.

### 7.4 `__unbinned__` — never displayable

Reserved, holding every contig that binning failed to assign. It breaks the small-MAG assumption
outright — potentially thousands of contigs and a large share of all pixels — and it is **not a
genome**, so there is nothing coherent to display.

**Identify it by name, never by index.** `create` takes a `drop_unassigned` flag; when set, there is
no `__unbinned__` row at all and genome index 0 is an ordinary MAG. Matching on index 0 would hide a
real genome in exactly the files that were binned most cleanly. Match the literal name `__unbinned__`,
and treat its absence as normal.

The rule is absolute, not a default:

- absent from the genomes table, with no toggle to reveal it
- not selectable, in any view, as either axis of a pair
- rejected as a range label with a specific message (§10), not treated as an unknown name
- excluded from the genome × genome overview (§7.3), which incidentally makes that view far more
  readable, since `__unbinned__` normally dominates its own row and column

**Index integrity still matters.** It occupies genome index 0 and its contigs still occupy bins and
pixels. Nothing may be renumbered or compacted to make it disappear — `genome_id` values, the
`genome_offset` array and every bin index remain exactly as written. Exclusion happens at selection
and display time only. Silently reindexing to hide it would corrupt every downstream lookup.

**One retained number — confirmed.** The fraction of contigs and bins that are unassigned is shown
once, as a read-only statistic in the **Binning QC card** of the General column. It is a direct
diagnostic of binning quality, a metagenomics reader will look for it, and a reviewer will expect it.
It is a number, not a view: it opens nothing, selects nothing, and is not a row in any table. Label it
as a QC statistic — "unassigned: 1,204 contigs (30.1%) · 830 bins (8.3%)", each quantity whole, since
a count of contigs beside a percentage of bins leaves a reader to assemble either one from two
sentences — and not as a genome, with one clause under it saying it is never drawn. This is the sole
exception to the rule above and does not weaken it — no code path reaches `__unbinned__` through this
statistic.

It is also the only place it is **counted**. The File card's `genomes` row leaves it out, because the
genomes table a hand's width below that card does: two numbers for one fact on one screen is what
sends a reader hunting for a forty-ninth organism in a list of forty-eight.

---

### 7.5 Derived values — computed here, never read

A cooler stores one number per pixel and, if somebody ran `cooler balance`, one weight per bin.
Everything else a reader wants is arithmetic over numbers that are already on screen, and none of it
requires a companion file, a preprocessing step or a server — so C1, C2 and C3 permit all of it.

Five families, in `render/derive.ts`, `render/smooth.ts` and `render/compare.ts`, the correlation's
arithmetic in `analysis/compartments.ts`:

| Family | Offered as | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Normalisation** — VC, VC √, ICE | entries in the score picker (§7.1's control) | one to a few dozen passes over the block |
| **Baseline** — observed / expected | a toggle of its own, and `e` | two passes |
| **Baseline** — observed / expected along a bacterial chromosome's two arms | `arms`, a toggle beside it (§8.15) | two passes |
| **Baseline** — the expected itself | an entry in the score picker | two passes |
| **Baseline** — the expected along both arms, on one sequence declared circular | `arm decay`, an entry in the score picker (§8.15) | two passes |
| **Smoothing** — a despeckle, fixed or self-sizing | the `smooth` picker | one pass at a fixed radius; three cumulative passes and a bounded search per cell when it sizes itself |
| **Correlation** — Pearson's r between the rows of the O/E | an entry in the score picker, on a file with weights | one matrix product, on the analysis thread and its helpers; square blocks up to 4,096 bins a side |
| **Comparison** — ratio, difference | the `compare` control, beside the split | one pass over two blocks |

**Why this is honest here and would not be in HiGlass.** Every one of them measures a statistic
*from the block*, and that is a genome-wide statement only if the block is the genome — which §2 is
precisely the claim that it is. One block, so one answer. A tile server computing coverage from the
tile under the pointer produces a different normalisation at every zoom level and every pan; there
the same feature would need a precomputed weight column, which is why HiGlass reads one. Where the
assumption does not hold — a windowed region of a whole cooler chromosome — the number is a
statement about the window, and the caption says so rather than leaving the label to imply otherwise.

**Juicer's `KR` is not offered, and its absence is not a gap.** Knight–Ruiz and iterative correction
solve the same problem — the unique diagonal scaling that makes a symmetric non-negative matrix
doubly stochastic — and converge to the same weights; KR is a Newton solver that reaches it in fewer
passes. At §2's scale the fixed point converges in milliseconds, so the faster solver would buy a
name in a menu and nothing a reader could see. A file balanced with `KR` elsewhere and read here
under `ICE` shows the same picture.

**The baseline can be looked at as well as divided by**, and it is in the picker rather than beside
the toggle because it answers "what are these numbers" and not "compared to what". Every cell becomes
the mean the ratio would have divided it by — a banded triangle fading from the diagonal, with a flat
plate over every off-diagonal pair of sequences, and nothing else in it. The reason to offer it is
that an O/E is only as good as its denominator: at long separations the curve is a mean over few
cells and moves, and a ratio that swings there is swinging in the model rather than in the biology.
It **overrides** the toggle rather than composing with it — O/E of the baseline is 1 wherever it is
anything — so the toggle greys and says why, and it is drawn on a sequential ramp with no neutral,
because a mean of counts is count-like and a diverging scale centred at 1 would be centred where
nothing in the picture lives.

**A ratio of two maps is not divided by the expected either.** The ratio is itself a comparison
against a baseline — the second map — and the decay with distance the two share divides out with
it; the O/E of each map first would divide out each library's own decay as well, which is another
figure from the one asked for. So while the comparison is a ratio the O/E toggle greys, unlit, and
says why, and `arms`, which says which decay the O/E divides by, greys with it; `e` and the
palette's entry stand down with the button. The setting is the reader's and is left as it was: `oe`
stays in the address, and a split or a difference built with it on draws it. It used to be applied
to each map before the division, so a ratio drawn with the toggle on was the ratio of two O/E maps.

**On a bacterial chromosome the baseline can be taken along both arms.** Where the
two arms are held side by side the map has two diagonals, and the decay curve
knows only one: it averages each diagonal of the map, every one of them crosses
the secondary diagonal through the origin, so the ratio keeps an X — brightest
along the secondary diagonal, darker than it should be everywhere else — and a
correlation of it draws the X and nothing under it. The arms toggle
(`analysis/arms.ts`) places each bin by its offset from the declared origin, the
short way round on a circle, and compares a cell with the cells of **its own
kind** — the same arm, or across the two — the **same distance apart along the
arms**, `||uᵢ| − |uⱼ||`, and within a window of its own position along them, 50
bins by default and the whole sequence at `0`. The window is what lets the
expectation follow what changes slowly from origin to terminus — the arms are held
tightest near the origin — and not what changes quickly, which is the plaid left
behind for the eye and for the correlation. It replaces the decay wherever the O/E
or the baseline would use it and turns the O/E on with it. It is measured in the
cells of the block on screen, whatever grid that was read on: a pooled read or
one from a sibling rung is placed by base pairs, with the window carried over to
its cells. It is named `arm O/E` in the key, which is one line two numbers wide,
and `O/E along the arms` in the caption. The score picker's correlation is then
of that ratio, and it is the picture the compartment call of §18.8 makes along
the arms. **It is weakest where
the two diagonals cross**, at the origin and at the terminus, where a pair close
along the DNA is averaged with pairs that are not; that is stated rather than
modelled, because the model would be of two small stretches of a chromosome.

**On a circle it is an entry in the picker as well.** Taken along the arms the baseline is an X —
the main diagonal's decay down each arm, and the inter-arm decay either side of the secondary
diagonal through the origin — where `expected` has the main diagonal alone and averages the
secondary one into it. **`arm decay`**, the score picker's entry right under `expected`, is that
baseline drawn: the picture `expected` draws while `arms` is on, offered as one choice so that
looking at both diagonals does not take a score and a toggle. It is read along the arms whether or
not `arms` is on — at its window, or the 50 bins it turns on at — so `arms` greys while it is drawn,
and says why, as the O/E does under any baseline; `ori` stays, and frames it best, the secondary
diagonal then the square's antidiagonal. It is offered **on a view of one sequence declared circular
and nowhere else** — the one view with two arms to read it along — including on a companion of a
deck whose first map is one (§16), and a circle ticked or unticked under the view offers it or takes
it away without rebuilding the view. It is a baseline and computed from the counts, as `expected` is.
The key calls it `Arm decay` — the picker's own word, since `arm expected` does not fit the dropdown
and `decay` is the `arms` toggle's word for what it divides by — and the caption `expected along the
arms`. A link carries it as `score=armbaseline`, and lands on counts on a view it is not offered on,
as one naming a column the file lacks does.

**Normalisation and baseline compose, and their order is fixed.** Normalise first: the decay curve is
an average over cells, so measuring it before the coverage bias is out means measuring it partly on
the bias, and every cell of a badly-covered bin is then compared against a baseline its own
under-coverage helped set. This is cooltools' order, for the same reason.

**The despeckle runs before every division, and one of its two shapes sizes itself.** Each cell
becomes the mean of the cells around it, **itself included**, and it is applied *per file, before two
are combined and before the O/E*, which is what makes it useful on a ratio rather than merely
cosmetic: `smooth(A) / smooth(B)` never has to average the `Infinity` that `x / 0` produces, because
a zero cell with contacts around it is no longer zero.

**The centre is in the mean, and it did not use to be.** The kernel began as `terra::focal` with a
zero centre weight, on the argument that a cell disagreeing with all eight of its neighbours is
evidence about the neighbourhood rather than about itself. That is right about rejecting outliers and
wrong about a sparse map, where a lone contact is not an outlier but the only measurement there is:
the zero-centre kernel replaced it with the mean of the eight zeros around it while spreading it into
those eight, so every isolated count rendered as a **hollow square with a hole where the contact
was**, and away from the diagonal most of the picture was made of those. It is also the wrong
estimator for what the filter now feeds — a local rate that the O/E divides — since discarding the
one cell being estimated at is both biased and needlessly noisy. Despeckling survives the change in
all but the narrowest window: a wild pixel is diluted to a ninth of its excess at `3 × 3` and to a few
hundredths at the widths the adaptive settings reach.

**The order changed with it, and the reason is the same one that puts the filter ahead of a
two-file ratio.** `observedOverExpected` draws a cell where nothing was observed as paper rather than
as the strongest depletion on the ramp — see below — and away from the diagonal *most* cells are that
cell: 98% of them at 200 bins out on a yeast map at 500 bp. An O/E computed first therefore handed the
filter a field that was almost entirely `NaN`, which no despeckle will touch, and every setting drew
the same picture. Smoothed first, a zero cell with contacts around it is never blanked and the map
fills in: that 98% falls to 1% under the adaptive settings and to 39% at `7 × 7`.

**The baseline is averaged over the same windows as the map**, and that is not optional. Dividing a
smoothed map by an unsmoothed curve is a biased operation: near the diagonal the decay is steep, so a
window spanning it averages cells whose baselines differ several-fold and the ratio comes out
systematically high — a measured 24–32% enrichment at radii 3 to 7 that is an artefact of the filter
and of nothing in the file. Averaged over the same cells with the same divisor the bias sits in both
halves of the ratio and cancels, and the mean returns to 1 where an O/E belongs.

**The curve is still estimated from the unsmoothed block.** That is the half of the old ordering worth
keeping: a decay curve is an average over cells, and fitting it to pre-averaged ones would let each
cell's neighbours count twice toward the baseline it is then compared against. Estimating before and
dividing after keeps the estimator honest and still lets the filter do its work.

A **fixed** window is the wrong tool away from the diagonal, and the reason is that the precision of a
box mean depends on the counts it covers rather than on the cells it covers. Near the diagonal a
7 × 7 box holds thousands of contacts; at 300 kb separation the same 48 cells are almost all zero, so
the mean is still noise and widening the box does not help, because what is in it grows in proportion
to nearly nothing. That is the observation
[serpentine](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa249) (Baudry *et al.*, 2020) is built on, and
its answer is to hold the counts constant instead of the window.

The **adaptive** setting takes that criterion and keeps this filter's locality. Each cell's window
grows until it covers a target multiple of the block's mean cell, floored at `3 × 3` and capped at a
radius of 192. Three things about it are deliberate:

- **It is a kernel, not a binning.** serpentine grows *regions* by random agglomeration and averages
  each, which makes the result a partition — right for a differential analysis, wrong for a viewer,
  because the partition is global and stochastic, so panning by one bin redraws every boundary and
  the map reshuffles under the reader. Here windows overlap and no partition is formed: a cell reads
  the same whether it sits in the middle of the viewport or at its edge, which is what lets a reader
  pan a smoothed map and believe what moves. That is the whole reason this viewer takes serpentine's
  *criterion* and not serpentine's *algorithm*.
- **The width is measured on the values as read, and the mean is taken over the derived ones.** That
  is serpentine's own separation — it thresholds on counts and reports a ratio — and here it is what
  makes the setting work at all under the O/E, whose values are near 1 everywhere by construction and
  would size every window the same.
- **The target is a multiple of the block's mean, not an absolute count**, because the cells reaching
  this stage are not always counts: `score` may have put balanced values in them (§6.4). Against the
  block's own mean the criterion means the same thing on both, and reduces to serpentine's threshold
  on counts when the cells are counts. A cell that cannot reach its target inside the cap keeps the
  cap and stays noisy, which is the honest outcome — a window that grew without limit would end up
  averaging the map into its own mean, and a flat field is not a better picture of thin data.

**Picking it turns the O/E on**, exactly as clicking the toggle would, and everything that follows —
`log2`, a symmetric range, a diverging ramp — follows from the neutral of 1 the O/E gives the result.
That is not a shortcut but the picture the setting is for: the window is sized on the counts and
divided by a baseline averaged over that same window, and on raw counts all it can denoise is a
picture of the distance decay that was never in question. Turning the O/E off again is left to the
reader, who may want exactly that.

**One setting rather than a ladder of strengths.** Three of them were three ways of asking one
question a reader has no way to answer, and the one kept is the one that preserves the most detail:
`3 × 3` where the data is rich, and much wider where it is not.

**One wild cell must not become a rectangle, and that takes two things.** A mean
has no defence against a single extreme value, and a box kernel's impulse response *is* a box — so
before this, one hot pixel raised every window that could reach it by the same amount and none of the
next ones along, drawing a hard-edged saturated block that reads as structure. Measured: one cell at
400× its neighbourhood produced a 20 × 20 bin block peaking at 5.3 in `log2` O/E, on a scale that
clips at 0.84.

The first of the two is a **cap on leverage**, applied in a pass before the averaging. Not a multiple
of the local mean, which is the obvious rule and is wrong here: away from the diagonal the map is
Poisson-sparse, so the window mean is 0.05 while the occupied cells hold 1, and *every* honest count
is twenty times the local mean. No fixed multiple both spares those and controls a spike. What the
artefact is, is leverage — a cell shifts the mean of every window reaching it by `(value − mean) / n`
— so the cap is written on that directly: no cell may add more than half again to the mean of a window
its own size, `cap = mean_without_it × (1 + ½ n)`. That scales itself, tight in a 3 × 3 near the
diagonal and two hundredfold in a sparse 21 × 21. The mean is taken **without the cell**, which is the
one thing the old zero-centre kernel had right: excluding the centre is correct for deciding whether a
cell is an outlier and wrong for estimating what to draw there, and the two passes do one each.

The second is a **shoulder on the kernel**. The mean is taken over three nested windows — `r/2`, `r`
and `3r/2` — and averaged, which puts a step in the weights instead of a cliff: the outermost shell
carries about 8% of the weight the centre does, so what remains of an outlier fades rather than
ending at a straight edge. The radii are chosen so this costs nothing in noise — the effective sample
is 3.90·r² against the plain box's 4·r², the same estimate over half again as much ground. With both,
a synthetic spike of 2000× no longer reaches the clip and the O/E mean stays at 1.00 in every band.

**Both of these reduce the artefact rather than removing it.** The cap bounds a flagged cell by
construction — the rule permits it to inflate its window by half, `log2 0.58` against a clip at 0.84 —
and on a real map the residual is still visible. Two stricter responses were implemented and dropped:
trimming the flagged cell out of the sum and the divisor, and replacing it with its eight neighbours'
mean. Both improved the synthetic case and neither removed the artefact reproducibly on real data,
which points at **the detector rather than the response** as the part still wrong, and at the
synthetic used to develop it as not reproducing whatever the real one is. Anyone picking this up
should start by reproducing the artefact from a real block rather than from a planted spike.

Blocks are capped at **16 M cells**, which was the 4096² raster cap. A block read at its own bins may
now be wider (§7.2) — yeast IV at 100 bp is 235 M cells, which at this rate would be two minutes — and
there the choice is honoured at its floor and the caption says so; anything pooled to the picture
still fits. The cumulative tables are built for a **band of rows** at
a time rather than for the block, so what is resident is about 128 MB whatever the block's size;
without that a 16 M block would allocate over half a gigabyte on the thread drawing frames. What the
cap costs instead is time, and it is roughly linear — and about twice what it was before the
winsorising pass, which reads the block again: 78 ms at 353², 300 ms at 841², 574 ms at 1,200², 1.5 s
at 4 M and **7.4 s at 16 M**.

**Above 1 M cells it runs on the analysis thread** (§18.3). Below that it is a hitch on a dropdown and
is done inline, which keeps the map from flashing unsmoothed on the way to being smoothed; above it
the cost climbs past a second and would be a frozen window. So `deriveBlock` runs the pipeline to the
point the smoothing would happen, hands the caller the arrays it would have used, and carries on with
the **unsmoothed** field — and **the caption says `counts`, not `smoothed`**, because a figure exported
mid-wait must not claim a filter it does not have. When the answer lands the caller derives again and
the step is a lookup. That is the correlation's arrangement, for the correlation's reason: every other
step in that module is synchronous, and a promise for the sake of one of them would make every caller
wait on arithmetic already finished. The fixed radii never defer at any size — one incremental pass is
not worth a round trip. Neither does a compared pair, where two blocks would need two jobs and a
half-finished pair would put a smoothed map over an unsmoothed one and call it a ratio. The last is a real freeze and the honest price of the cap being where it is;
everything short of a whole chromosome at a fine bin size is a fraction of a second. Should that need
fixing, the answer is the analysis thread rather than a lower cap — the work is a pure function of
two arrays.

Above the cap the fixed radius the setting is floored at is used instead, and **the refusal is said
twice**: in the export caption, which is all a figure carries once it leaves the app, and in the view
note under the heading, which is what a reader has while deciding what they are looking at. A refused
adaptive window draws a fixed one, and a fixed one looks like a map — this is §7.3's refusal shape and
the correlation's, with the note added because a caption nobody reads until they export is no use to
somebody looking at the screen.

**The two ends of a ratio are paper, not colour.** A cell where nothing was observed is `0`, and on a
scale centred at 1 that is the strongest depletion the ramp can draw — so an O/E map of a sparse
block came out as a wall of "maximally depleted" over every empty pixel, which is the loudest
possible statement of the one thing the file does not say. Zero is *nothing seen here*, which is what
paper means on every other map this viewer draws. An infinite ratio goes the same way, being a fact
about a baseline too small to divide by rather than a measurement of anything, and both are then out
of the auto range they would otherwise drag. A **negative** ratio stays: an extra `/pixels` column may
legitimately hold negative numbers, and blanking those would be this rule deciding what a file is
allowed to contain.

**The correlation reads an empty pixel as zero.** Paper is a rule for the eye, and the score picker's
correlation is not drawn from the ratio but computed from it: there an empty pixel is an observation
of no contacts, and the compartment call correlates it as one (§18.8, as cooltools does).
Blanked, every empty pixel left the correlation, which was then of the cells each pair of rows
happened to share — a different matrix from the one the task solves, though the option's own note
said it was the same — and on a sparse map it was slow for the same reason: *E. coli* at 1 kb had two
hundred and thirty missing cells a row, each pair's arithmetic an exception to correct for, and a
4,096-bin square took fifteen seconds on four cores where its product takes one. The picture under the
veil, while the answer is computed, is the ratio as it is always drawn — paper and all — made from
the same derivation by blanking its zeros, so the block is derived once for both.

**The correlation is one matrix product, on every core.** Pearson's r over the cells two rows share
needs six sums, and only one of them — the products — depends on both rows at every cell; the others
are each row's totals, corrected for the few cells the other row lacks. So the products of every pair
are one matrix product in WebAssembly with SIMD (`analysis/wasm/gram.c`), fused multiply-adds where
the engine has them, and the product is shared out in bands to helper workers the analysis thread
starts and keeps for the next square (`analysis/pearsonThreads.ts`). Measured in Chromium with four
cores, from picking the score to the picture: a thousand bins in under half a second, 2,048 in under
one, 4,096 in two and a half, where it was capped at 1,500 and took three seconds at 929. So the map
correlates any square block it can read, up to 4,096 cells a side — a whole bacterial
genome at 1 kb, a human chromosome at 50 kb — and the Compartments task, which correlates with the
same arithmetic, is no longer the slow half of its own method.

**A score that reads the same cells reads nothing.** `VC`, `ICE`, the baseline and the correlation are
arithmetic over the block on screen exactly as the O/E is, so picking one of them repaints rather than
rebuilding the view; only a score that names another `/pixels` column, or the balancing, is a new
read. Picking the correlation re-read the whole block first — two of the six seconds a 4,096-bin
square took, spent fetching the numbers already on screen.

**Diverging values need three things to change together**, and changing fewer produces a plausible
picture of the wrong thing:

1. `log2` joins the transform list (§7.1's three are still frozen by the parity requirement — this one
   is the viewer's own, for values the CLI cannot produce). Twice and half then sit the same distance
   either side of neutral.
2. The auto range becomes **symmetric about neutral**. Otherwise the colour meaning "these agree"
   lands at an arbitrary point in the ramp, and a map of two identical files comes out uniformly
   coloured rather than uniformly neutral.
3. The colormap becomes **diverging** (`RdBu_r`, red is more). A ratio on a sequential ramp hides the
   only thing it is for.

The panel takes the transform, the colormap and the clip when a derivation is switched on and gives
all three back when it is switched off, because none of them means the same thing about a ratio as
about a count — a `vmax` of 8 is a sensible ceiling on `log1p` counts and nonsense on `log2` of a
ratio.

**The give-back outlives the panel that took them.** A change of comparison — split, ratio,
difference — and the second map's eye rebuild the map rather than repaint it, and the hash a rebuilt
map is seeded from holds what the derivation drew with, so the split after a ratio stayed on the
ratio's `log2` and diverging ramp. What the derivation took over is carried to the map built in its
place, which gives it back if it derives nothing and keeps it to give back later if it still does —
so ratio → difference → split ends on the count map's own scale, and a diverging ramp the reader
chose under the ratio stays through the difference. A derivation that arrived already drawn — a link,
a reload or Back landing on a ratio — never saw the scale before it, and gives back the file's
defaults (§7.1). Closing the first file of a comparison, and *swap sides*, reopen rather than rebuild,
and carry the scale from before the derivation to the file that takes the first triangle.

**Pooling changes too.** A contact map is pooled by its brightest cell, because its signal *is* the
bright cell. A ratio pooled that way shows only the arm above neutral, so every region where the
second file is the stronger one vanishes at fit zoom — half of what a difference map exists for.
A diverging field is pooled by departure from neutral instead.

**A ratio of two maps is made only where both have contacts.** A cell that is zero in either map
is no ratio, and is missing — `NaN`, as two zeros and an unbalanced bin always were
(`render/compare.ts`). `4 / 0` was `Infinity`, the top of the scale, and `0 / 4` zero, the bottom:
on a sparse pair, where a cell empty in one library is a matter of depth far more than of biology,
the two saturated colours covered most of the picture and said the loudest thing the scale can say
about the cells that held the least. **A missing cell on a ratio of two maps is drawn in the
colormap's middle** — white on `RdBu_r`, the colour a ratio of exactly one is — rather than as
paper (`ColorScale.missing`): the map is read as departures from its middle, and a cell with no
ratio departs from nothing. The readout under the pointer says there is no value there. A
difference keeps its zeros, which it can subtract, and an O/E keeps paper for a cell where nothing
was observed (above).

**Tracks get the same two operations**, ratio and difference (`annotations/derived.ts`), combined on
the **common refinement** of the two interval lists rather than on a grid: two bigWigs' intervals do
not line up, and evaluating both onto a uniform grid smears every boundary that falls inside a cell,
so a sharp edge in a control becomes a ramp and the ratio against it spikes at exactly the position
that mattered. A derived lane fetches nothing of its own — both operands go through the ordinary sample
cache — so it inherits §8.4's pan-and-zoom-free rule from the two it is made of.

**What a link carries.** The normalisation is a `score` and needs no key of its own, and so is the
baseline drawn instead of divided by, plain or along the arms (`score=baseline`,
`score=armbaseline`); the baseline divided by is
`oe`, and `arms` its window along the arms in bins where it is taken along them (`arms=50`); the
comparison is `op`, and the despeckle is `smooth` — one key with two vocabularies, a fixed
radius (`smooth=2` is 5 × 5) or the adaptive window (`smooth=a50`). All of them are part of *what is
being looked at* rather than how it is shaded, so §5.5's rule applies: a recipient sees the numbers the
sender saw. A smoothed map matters most here, because it *looks like a map*: a link that dropped the
key would send a recipient a picture whose single-cell features had been averaged away with nothing
on screen saying so.

---

## 8. Tracks and annotations

A contact map is read against what is on the sequence: genes, peaks, coverage, called loops. This
section is the whole of that surface. It is **offered on every container** — see §8.5 — and it is
additive: a file with no annotations loaded behaves exactly as it did before this section existed.

### 8.1 The three cards

Three cards in the Annotations column: **Tracks**, **Manual annotations** and **Metadata
annotations**. Each is absent — not disabled, not empty — on a file that cannot carry them. A
fourth, **Bookmarks** (§8.10), sits under them and is not in this list because nothing in it is an
annotation: it holds places rather than things drawn at them.

The column reads, top to bottom: Contact maps, **Tracks**, Structures, **Manual annotations**,
**Metadata annotations** and **Bookmarks** — the last two **folded** when they are built, since each
is opened when a reader wants it rather than scanned past on the way to a track. The fold is the
card's own (§26.6), is not remembered, and a view saved from the button beside `go` opens the
Bookmarks card so the row it adds is seen.

**Linear annotations** — headed **Tracks** on screen, which is also what its rows, its tooltips and
every other surface call them; *annotation* survives as the column's name and in the two card names
below. One load zone, *Load a track*, names the formats it reads, and the card around it takes a
file dropped anywhere on it; what the bytes turn out to be decides the rest (§8.3), so there is no
zone to choose. Its lanes are drawn *beside* the map, never on it: **gene models** (GTF, GFF,
genePred — any number, since comparing two annotations of one genome is a thing people do; the star
on a feature set's row says which one the feature search reads), **tracks** (bigWig, bedGraph, wig,
bedMethyl and — for its coverage — BAM (§8.13), any number, drawn in one of six styles, §8.8), and
**bed-like files** (any number, resolved as genomic segments), with a FASTA's sequence lane (§8.8)
and the formats of §8.13–§8.23 beside them. Every synthetic row — what a task computed, a comparison
of two tracks — is in the same list (§18.5), and so is every overlay (below). Each lane is placed on
any of the map's four edges — above, below, or down either side — or on several at once; each
carries its own limits, style, colour and value scaling; and any set of tracks may share one
autoscale group.

Where the open map has tracks published beside it — the demo's own, or a shelf a store row or a hub
registered for that file (§24.1, §24.10) — the card offers them as one button under the zone, *load
the N tracks published with this map* (*this genome* in the 1D browser). Not to a session bringing
its own tracks back, which would be offered the same files a second time, and not where the map was
opened *with its tracks*: that road loads them, and shows no button.

The row's **location** is four marks rather than four words: the map as a dashed square with one edge
drawn solid — Lucide's `square-dashed-top-solid`, and the same square turned for the other three
(`scripts/build-icons.mjs`) — each a switch, lit where the track is drawn, named for its edge to a
screen reader. With one map they sit beside the label like any other field. In a deck they sit at the
end of each map's own line, the map's name before them, under the label: the four words were as wide
as the card and took a line of their own under every name, so a deck of four maps spent eight lines
saying where one track is.

**Ticking rows edits them together.** Each row of the Tracks card has a tick box (shift-click takes
the rows between it and the last one clicked), and two or more ticked open a box above the list: the
count and what can be done to them — *combine…* for a pair of tracks (§7.5), *hide* or *show*,
*remove*, *clear* — over **a row's settings**, in a row's shapes and words: colour, height, style
(and its colours under a heatmap), scale, flip, limits, group, location and, for overlays, opacity
and maps. Each control **shows what the ticked rows share**, and *mixed* where they differ — an
empty box saying so, a `mixed` entry heading a picker, a hatched edge or flip, a dashed ring round
the swatch — and nothing is written until the reader picks. A pick is written to **every ticked row
it means something to and no other**: a gene model and two bigWigs ticked together get one style
picker, the pick lands on the two bigWigs, and the control's tooltip says how many of the ticked
rows it reaches. Limits take both bounds before they are written, since a batch has no one range to
seed the other from, and *auto* keeps each row's own manual pair for when it leaves auto again. Every
setting but the location and the maps, which place lanes one row at a time, is one change to the
store however many rows it reaches. A new group named from the box clears the ticks, since the set
now exists as a group.

A fourth kind of lane used to belong to no card at all: the **virtual 4C profile**, a reading of the
matrix rather than a file loaded against it, with no row to be listed in and nothing to remember
across a reload. It is gone (§8.9): the 4C *task* (§18.8) asks the same question of the file, and its
profile is a row of the Tracks card like any other.

**Map overlays.** Annotations drawn *on* the matrix, listed as rows of the Tracks card rather than on
a card of their own: whether a file is a lane or an overlay is a fact about its format, which the
bytes settle (§8.3), and not a shelf the reader has to put it on. Pairs — a BEDPE, an interact or a
longrange file (§8.18), a loop set a task called — mark off-diagonal pairs as circles; an interval
set a task called (§18.5) marks places on the diagonal as points or short markers across it, and
extents as the corners of the squares they claim (§18.7); a BED the reader loads is a lane. **A set of
pairs opens on the map and offers the other display too**, as a called set does: *arcs (1D track)*
draws every pair as an arc from one anchor to the other along an edge of the map — the 1D browser's
own picture of a BEDPE, on any edge, rising the way a signal grows and hung from the other edge when
flipped — and *map overlay* puts the rings back. The row's card holds the choice (`linear` for a
loaded file's track), so a reload keeps it. A loaded set of pairs exports one file, its **anchors**:
both ends of every pair as a BED, each exact place once however many pairs share it.
These answer a different question from a lane — not "what is on the sequence here" but "this pixel
is a feature" — so every one is an outline, a rule or a glyph beside what it points at: an overlay
must not hide the pixel it is about. A place's point is the one dot, and it sits on the diagonal, over
the one pixel a boundary is not about — what it claims is that little crosses there, which is read off
the map either side of it.
A set a task *called* is the one thing wanted in either role, since a peak set is checked against its
coverage and a domain against its map: it is **one row**, and its *display* puts it on the map or
beside it as a 1D track, one or the other (§18.7).

An overlay is **placed per map**, as a track is, and a map draws only the overlays placed on it. It
used to be drawn on every map of a deck: a loop set called on one of six maps was circled on all
six, and a batch of insulation over five drew five sets of boundaries on each, with nothing on the row
to say otherwise. Imported, an overlay is on the session's own map; dropped on a companion's edge, on
that companion; called by a task, on the map it was called from. In a deck its row has a **maps**
field in the location field's shape: a line per contact map — its name, then one mark, the map's grid
from the Contact maps card's head, lit where the overlay is drawn — and under them *every map*, *no
map* and *on N of M*. One mark rather than four because an overlay is drawn on the map's face and
not beside an edge of it, and `maps` rather than `location` because a batch of a bigWig and a loop
set shows both fields and they answer differently. A tracks cell is not listed, having no matrix to
draw on, and *no map* leaves an overlay placed in one where it is. With one map the field is not
shown — the eye on the head already hides the overlay there — unless the overlay is drawn on no map,
which a deck closed after *no map* leaves it, and then it is the one mark that puts it back.

**It is dropped on a map as a track is dropped on an edge.** The middle of every map is a fifth
rectangle, *on this map*, lit with the four strips at its edges while a file or a row is dragged —
and **alone** while an overlay's row is, since the strips name stacks and an overlay has none. A
file dropped there opens onto that map only, an overlay on its face and a track on its usual edge,
where a file dropped in the middle of a companion used to land on the first map — and so does one
let go anywhere else on a companion's cell, its strips aside (§16.9); a row of the Tracks
card dropped there is drawn on that map **as well** as wherever it was, as the marks put it. An
overlay's row let go on a strip is taken the same way, and given no edge. A lane carried by its
grip is not offered the face: that gesture is about an edge.

**Metadata annotations** (§8.12). The columns the open file already carries about its own genomes,
sequences and bins — completeness, contamination, an MGE call, a balancing weight — drawn against the
map's own cells. Discovered rather than loaded, so it is the one card whose contents nobody had to
find, and the one card a `.metacool` got before the gate was lifted (§8.5). It sits **under the
marks, folded**, with Bookmarks after it: what a reader loaded and drew comes first, and a column of
the open map's own tables is reached for on purpose.

**Manual annotations.** Marks the reader draws themselves: any number of lines (vertical, horizontal
or both), arrowheads (on- or off-diagonal) and rectangles (on- or off-diagonal, at any ratio), each
entered as coordinates or picked on the map. This is the card that makes a figure, and
nothing in it comes from a file. They leave through the app's one export row (§26.6) with no
resolution and no clipboard, since a BED is not a picture, and its two options are named for the
marks they write in the card's own words — *lines (BED)* and *arrowheads & rectangles (BEDPE)*, not
*loops & boxes*, which named neither the sub-heads above them nor anything else on screen.

**A mark is moved where it is listed.** Its row reads as the mark's place in the display form,
1-based and grouped (§26.1) — `formatPosition` for a line's or an arrowhead's base, `formatLocus` for
a rectangle's sides, and a side of no width as the one base its BEDPE row is written as — and a
press on it turns that text into the boxes the adding forms use — one for a line, with its axis
select beside it; rows and columns for an arrowhead or a rectangle, the second left empty meaning the
same place on both — taking what those forms take. Enter, or a click away, or a Tab past the row's
last box — which opens the next mark's row, as Shift+Tab past its first opens the one before (§26.8)
— moves the mark **in place**:
its id, its colour and its position in the list are kept, so everything that names it — a map, the
3D key, a chord — follows. Escape leaves it where it was, and a box that does not read stays open with
a red edge rather than dropping what was typed. It used to be removed and drawn again, which lost its
colour and sent it to the end of the list.

**Every box on the card reads what it is typed 1-based**, as every locus box does (§26.1): a base is
`typedPosition` of the number written, a side is its first base less one to its last, so Enter on a
row's own text leaves the mark where it was and a coordinate copied off the map's readout lands on
the base it names. What is kept is the 0-based base a mark names — what a line is drawn at and its
BED row written from — so no file changes. The forms and the rows both used to be the stored
numbers as written: the card agreed with itself, and a locus pasted from anywhere else landed one
base to the right. The map's *Copy coordinates* puts a cell's two bases on the clipboard in the copy
form, 1-based and ungrouped, under menu rows that already named them 1-based; it copied the stored
numbers.

**They come back in by the same card.** An *Import* section above *Export* holds the Tracks card's
load zone, worded *Load marks*: click it to choose files, or drop one anywhere on the card — the zone
lights as soon as a file crosses it, and the drop stops at the card, since the same BED let go over
the map is a lane (§8.16) and this card is where a reader aims when they mean marks. It reads what
the export writes, and any other BED or BEDPE, row by row rather than by extension: a BED row is a
**line** on the axis its name column says (`vertical`, `horizontal`, `both`), and a crosshair at the
interval's start when the name is anything else; a BEDPE row is an **arrowhead** when both anchors
are one base wide, as the export writes one, and a **rectangle** otherwise. Each mark takes the next
colour of the palette, since neither file carries one, and a mark already at the same place is not
added twice — re-importing what was just exported is the accident this rule is for. A line under
the zone says, per file, how many were added, already there, or skipped — tersely, as
`marks.bed: 2 added, 1 skipped.`

The three are three sentences — *this coordinate*, *this cell*, *this block of contacts* — and the
third is two intervals rather than one interval and a shape, because the boxes people draw are not
one shape: a domain is a square on the diagonal, a corner peak is a small square off it, and a locus
against a whole arm is neither. An on-diagonal rectangle is drawn as the same triangle a BED domain
is on a turned map, since that is what it is.

**One word for the mark: an arrowhead.** It is what this card's own section is called and what the
glyph is — a mark stood off a cell along its 45° axis — and it can be put at any off-diagonal point
rather than only at a loop. So the map's right-click menu offers *Arrowhead*, with *a loop at r × c*
as its hint, where it used to offer *Loop* and send a reader looking for their mark under a heading
called Arrowheads; the structure card's chord source is *manual annotations* for the same reason (§25.5).

**Each kind asks the map for the gesture that suits it.** A line and an arrowhead each name a place,
and the gesture for a place is a click. A rectangle names an extent, and the gesture for an extent is
a **drag**: press at one corner, let go at the other, with the map's own marquee and its coordinate
chips showing what is about to exist. The marquee follows the hand on both axes — a selection is
squared because it *resolves* to one range, and a mark does not — and it snaps out to the edges of the
cells the two ends are in, which is what commits. Holding Shift locks the box to the diagonal, so a
domain is one gesture. All three modes stay on for as many marks as the reader wants, and a click
while the map is waiting for a drag places nothing rather than navigating. Beside the 1D browser
(§5.8) — opened on a genome, or the one a closed map falls back to, which keeps the card and the
marks the map had — the buttons read *pick on track* and *draw on track*: a track has one axis, so
what they place lands on the diagonal — a line as a crosshair, an arrowhead on the diagonal, a
rectangle as the square on it — which is the mark a map opened afterwards already shows.

**On the tracks a mark is drawn the same beside a map as in the browser.** A track has one axis,
so what it shows of a mark is the places the mark names along it: a **line** a rule across every
lane — beside a map, on the stacks that measure its axis, or every stack under a turned map — an
**arrowhead** a small triangle at each of its two ends, pointing into the picture past the last
lane, and a **rectangle** its extent **washed over every lane** at a tenth of its colour: one wash
for a box on the diagonal, and both of its stretches where they differ, since a box off the diagonal
is two stretches of a sequence. Beside a map a box used to be two triangles at its edges, past the
last lane, so a stretch boxed in the browser came back from opening the map as two small arrowheads
under the tracks; it is the browser's wash on both surfaces now, on every stack whose axis carries
the stretch, and in every figure saved from either.

**A box drawn on a turned map is a box of the square underneath it.** Both ends of the drag are taken
back to the square they were rotated out of, exactly as a click is, so pressing over one contact and
releasing over another names the rectangle those two contacts span — which may be off the diagonal,
and is the one thing a band selection there cannot say. Shift collapses each end onto its own midpoint
instead of snapping the pointer, which gives the on-diagonal square through the two places the drag
ran between. What is *drawn* while the hand moves is the mark itself rather than a rubber band: a
rectangle of rows against columns leans at 45° on a turned map and folds where it crosses the
diagonal, so a box on screen would be a box drawn around a shape that is not one.

A hand-drawn mark never sits on the pixel it is about (§8.1's rule for overlays generally). For the
arrowhead that means the glyph is stood off the cell along its own 45° axis **and** by a pixel square
to the axes: the mark is anchored at the cell's centre, so a diagonal gap alone clears the centre and
not the corner, and at any zoom where a bin is a handful of pixels the tip landed on the last row and
column of the cell it was pointing at.

**A mark is put away without being removed.** Every row carries an **eye**, between its place and
its ×, as a track's row does: pressed, the mark leaves every picture at once — the map, square or
turned, the lanes beside it and the band their anchors take, a tracks cell, the 1D browser, and the
model, whose bead, chord or colouring it was — and stays on the card, its eye shut, to be pressed
back. A figure saved with a mark hidden is the figure with no such mark. Over the rows the list has
a heading, `MARKS`, which says how many are hidden, and **one eye for all of them**, standing at the
head of the column the rows' eyes stand in, so which eyes it speaks for is read off the card rather
than off a label. `A` is that eye from the keyboard, and the palette lists it as a switch, *Manual
annotations*, wearing its state (§26.4). It is lit while **any** mark is drawn, as a group's eye is
on the Groups card, so a press then hides every mark, and with none drawn a press brings them back.

**What the eye over the list brings back is what it hid.** A mark carries why it is hidden — **on
its own**, from its row, its row on the model's key or a picture's menu; or **with the rest**, from
that eye, `A` or *Hide every mark* — so a reader who put one mark away for a figure and then hid
everything to look at the pixels under them gets the figure back, and not every mark; where nothing
was hidden together, *show* is every mark. A **double-click** on a row's eye shows that mark alone,
the others put away together, and a second brings back exactly those: the sequence key's gesture on
the model (§25.5), and its row-by-row twin. A mark placed while the rest are hidden is drawn, since
what a reader places is what they are looking at, and a mark imported is drawn. Kept on the mark,
the reason travels wherever the mark does — the tab's memory, a saved workspace, a link, a reopen at
another resolution — and one this build does not know reads as drawn rather than as a mark nobody
can show. Hiding is about what is drawn, not about what the marks are: the BED and BEDPE the card
writes carry every mark, and the button's tooltip says how many of them are hidden.

**Every picture's right-click menu names the marks under the pointer.** The map's, a lane's beside
it, the 1D browser's — and so a tracks cell's — and the model's carry a *Marks* group: *Hide this
line*, *Hide this arrowhead* or *Hide this rectangle* for each drawn mark the pointer is on, nearest
first and at most three, the hint naming it as its row does; then *Hide every mark*, or *Show the
marks* once none is drawn, with `A` in the hint column where every menu on a reader's machine prints
its key. On the map what the pointer is on is measured **on the ink**: each mark is drawn again,
alone, into a context that keeps the path rather than painting it, so a rule within six pixels, an
arrowhead's glyph and the cell it names, a box's outline — and its inside, after any mark whose line
the pointer is on, the smaller of two boxes first — are found on a turned map exactly as on a square
one, on the V, the triangle and the leaning lobes the turn draws them as. Beside the map and in
the browser alike it is the rule, the anchor or the wash along the stack — a box found anywhere
inside its wash, after a rule or an anchor within reach and the narrower of two boxes first; on the model
a line at the bead's place, an arrowhead with an end there or a box over it. A hidden mark is under
no pointer, so the rows only hide. Off the browser's lanes — on the ruler, or in the room under the
last track the marks run down to — the group is the whole menu where there are marks, and the page's
own menu where there are none.

### 8.2 bigWig

bigWig via `@gmod/bbi` v10 (the JBrowse 2 parser, MIT). Local files take a `generic-filehandle2`
`BlobFile`; remote files take its `RemoteFile`, which uses the global `fetch`, subclassed as
`annotations/worker/cachedFile.ts`'s `CachedRemoteFile` to read 256 KiB chunks and keep them, one
handle per address — so local and remote differ only in the handle, exactly as with HDF5, and
neither path uploads a byte (§11).

Values are requested through `getFeaturesAsArraysMulti` at the view's pixel resolution: one call per
track per view covers every visible contig at once, `basesPerSpan` selects the file's own zoom level,
and the result is typed arrays rather than a million feature objects. That is what makes a
whole-genome view of ten tracks affordable, and it is the same "averaging when zoomed out" a genome
browser does — read out of the file rather than computed here.

**Contig-naming contract.** bigWig is keyed on chromosome names, which here are **contig** names from
`/contigs`, not genome names. On load, rename the bigWig's chrom list into the map's spelling (§5.9),
intersect it with `chromnames` and report any shortfall explicitly — `10 of 16 sequences matched;
nothing is drawn on XI, XII, XIII, XIV…`, or `No sequence in this file matches the map (0 of 16)` —
where a full match says nothing. Silent zero-overlap is the most likely support question and must be
impossible.

**On a file with a genome layer the report is about genomes** (§8.5). The same arithmetic that is
informative on a cooler is alarming on a metagenome: a coverage track over four MAGs matches `794 of
20,566` sequences, which is true, and is also what a track about another organism entirely would
say. So where the map has genomes the sentence counts them — *794 of 20,566 sequences, in 4 of 48
genomes: metator_00001_00000, …* — and it is a **note rather than a warning**, because partial
coverage is the expected shape of a track over a co-assembly and painting it yellow would make the
ordinary case read as a fault. The two failures that *are* faults keep their voice: no overlap at
all, and a cross-convention match whose lengths disagree (§5.9).

### 8.3 Text formats

Parsed in full, in the annotations worker, never on the main thread — a 9.5 MB GTF is a tenth of a
second of parsing and that is a tenth of a second of frozen UI.

| Format | Accepted as | Coordinates |
|---|---|---|
| GTF / GFF | a gene model | 1-based, inclusive; converted on parse |
| BED 3/4/5/6/9/12, narrowPeak, broadPeak, gappedPeak, and a headed TSV whose first three columns are a contig, a start and an end | segments | 0-based, half-open |
| BEDPE, and a headed TSV carrying `chrom1/start1/end1/chrom2/start2/end2` | pairs | 0-based, half-open |

Detection is by content, not by extension: a `.tsv` of loop calls with a header row is the shape the
demo data has, and refusing it because of its suffix would be pedantry. The name is consulted only
where the columns cannot decide — which peak format a BED-shaped file is, say. Every other text
format has a section of its own and a sniffer asked *before* this one, which answers `bed` for
whatever it does not know: FASTA (§8.8), bedGraph and wig (§8.11), VCF (§8.14), barChart (§8.17),
interact and longrange (§8.18), genePred (§8.19), bedMethyl (§8.20), cytoBand (§8.22), splice
junctions (§8.23) and a 3D model's g3d (§25.2). A file whose contigs do not intersect the map's is
reported with the overlap count, as a bigWig is, rather than silently drawing nothing.

**A GFF row that names no parent is a feature, not a fragment.** GTF and an Ensembl-flavoured GFF3
are a hierarchy — gene, transcript, and the exons and CDS underneath — and a glyph is drawn per
*transcript*, assembled from whichever rows name it through `Parent` or `transcript_id`. A bacterial
annotation has none of that: Prokka, Bakta and DFAST write one row per feature with its own `ID` and
`locus_tag` and not a single `Parent` in the file, because a bacterial gene is one uninterrupted CDS
and a gene row above it would be a second copy of the same span. So a row that names no parent is
read as the whole feature it is, keyed on its own `ID` — two rows sharing one `ID` being GFF3's way
of writing a feature with a gap in it, and a row with no `ID` being one nothing can point at, drawn
keyless. The accession comes from `locus_tag` where the file writes one, which is per-gene by
definition; the symbol from `gene` or `Name`; and `product` joins `biotype` and `source` in the
detail string, because it is the whole of what a bacterial annotation has to say and the colour
picker (§8.16) can only offer what is written there.

The rows that describe the **sequence** rather than something on it — NCBI's per-contig `region`,
GenBank's `source` — are dropped by name. They were dropped by accident before, as rows with no
parent to place them, and drawn they would each be a box the width of the chromosome.

### 8.4 Geometry, and why nothing can drift

One rule: **the heatmap and every annotation share the axis `Scale` objects** (`render/scale.ts`),
which are owned by the view and written by the heatmap's own pan and zoom. Nothing here computes a
second coordinate mapping, so a track and the matrix column above it cannot disagree by a pixel.

What a `Scale` speaks is *matrix coordinates* — fractional cell indices along one axis of the
rendered block — and what an annotation speaks is (contig, base pair). The bridge is a **locus axis**
built from the block's own `AxisGroup`s: a piecewise-linear map, one piece per contig run, derived
from `unitStart`, `unitLength` and the bin size. It is the same arithmetic the hover readout already
does, from the same two numbers, so a tick, a tooltip and a track cannot disagree either. It covers
every view without a special case: one contig, two different contigs, or all sixteen at once.

Annotations are meaningful at bin and contig level. At genome level they are hidden — a cell is a
whole genome there and a position inside one would be an invention — all but a metadata lane, which
is indexed by the map's own cells rather than by base pairs (§8.12).

**Pan and zoom stay I/O-free**, as §2 requires of everything else. A track fetches a window wider
than the view — half the view again on either side — at a resolution rounded to a power of two, and
keeps it (`annotations/samples.ts`); panning and zooming redraw from that cache. A refetch happens
only when the view leaves the window or the required resolution crosses a factor of two — not once
per frame — and until it lands the samples in hand stay on screen.

This paragraph is older than §2's fourth clause and it is what that clause now says too: the matrix
refines by the same rule, from the same three ideas — a window wider than the view, a resolution
quantised so a small zoom asks for nothing new, and the picture in hand left on screen until the
better one arrives.

### 8.5 Every container, and genomes with no map

**This section used to be a gate, and the gate is gone.** It read: every card, every lane and every
overlay is offered only where the file has no genome layer — which is exactly "this is a cooler"
(§9) — and on a `.metacool` none of them are rendered at all. The argument was that a metacool's
