The refusal names the version and the two commands that convert it. A file declaring more than
100,000 sequences is refused as well — opening one reads a record header per sequence, and a count
that large is likelier a truncated file than an assembly — and one that ends inside its index or a
record says it is truncated. So is a record whose gap or mask count it could not hold — a run covers
at least a base and costs eight bytes — before that count decides a read (§10): a flipped
`nBlockCount` asked for thirty-four gigabytes of gap list, which a ranged read answers with the rest
of the file.

The assembly is `origin: 'twobit'` and **exact** — every `dnaSize` is in the index — so an 800 MB
genome declares its chromosomes in a few hundred kilobytes without reading a base. The store is the
shape `IndexedSequences` has, and for the same reason: both are "an assembly in memory and a way to
turn a window into a byte range", and every caller above them wants exactly that. What differs is two
lines of arithmetic. The CLI reads one the same way (`cli/tracks.ts` under `--tracks`,
`cli/reference.ts` under `--sequence`), through the same pure functions, so a metaplot over ten
thousand windows of hg38 reads a few megabytes rather than unpacking 3.1 GB.

### 8.22 Chromosome ideograms: cytoBand

UCSC's `cytoBand` is five columns — `chrom chromStart chromEnd name gieStain` — and the fifth is the
whole of the format: the Giemsa stain a metaphase chromosome takes over that stretch. `gneg` is a
light band, `gpos25` to `gpos100` dark ones by how dark, `acen` the centromere, `gvar` variable
heterochromatin and `stalk` the narrow stalk of an acrocentric's short arm, which is where its rDNA
is. Every UCSC assembly publishes one and IGV draws its ideogram from the same file. `cytoBandIdeo`
is the same five columns with a row for each unplaced sequence as well, its band name left empty.

**It is a `FeatureSet`, one band per row**, for §8.14's reason, which is stronger here than anywhere:
a band is an interval with a name, and the search, the export, the hit test and every task that
reads intervals are the code a peak set already uses. What it has of its own is a **kind**,
`ideogram`, because of the glyph. A band is not a box on a row: it is a stretch of *one* shape, the
chromosome, whose outline pinches at the centromere and narrows at a stalk, and the packing, the
strand bands, the colour picker and the arrowheads a gene model's lane has are questions a
karyotype is never asked.

**It is recognised by its last column.** Every row the sniffer reads must end in a stain, a word no
format of the BED family puts in its fifth column — a BED5's is a score, a number — so the test
cannot capture a BED, and nothing that is a cytoBand fails it. A whitespace-separated
`cytoBandIdeo` whose empty names have collapsed away leaves four columns with the stain in the
fourth, and is read as well. It is asked before `sniffFormat`, for §8.17's reason: that function's
last line is `return 'bed'`, and a cytoBand read as a BED is a lane of grey boxes whose one column
anybody opened the file for was never read. The file's *name* decides nothing about its contents;
it only routes a bare link to the door it opens from (`cytoBand.txt.gz` opens a browser, like a
`chrom.sizes`) — in the plural as well, which is what a file named for its bands is called, the
yeast demo's `Yeast_cytobands.txt` among them.

**The stain is kept twice.** In the detail, as `stain gpos50`, so the card and the tooltip say it the
way the file does; and in the **score**, as the darkness it names: `gneg` 0, `gposN` N, a bare `gpos`
100. That is a number the file states rather than one this invents, and it is what lets a task read
the bands as light and dark — *Signal by group* split by score is a track read over G-light against
G-dark bands, with no code of its own. `acen`, `gvar` and `stalk` are not a darkness and score
`NaN`. The CLI reads the file the same way, so a task run from the
command line gets the scores too.

**A cytoBand declares the genome.** UCSC's bands tile each chromosome, from its first base to its
last, so the end of the last band is the chromosome's length and the file is a `chrom.sizes` with a
picture on it. That is checked rather than assumed: bands that start at 0 and leave no gap or
overlap on every sequence give exact lengths, `origin: 'cytoband'`, and the Genome card's `lengths`
row says `the cytoBand's bands`; one sequence that does not tile and the whole file gives the lower
bound every other feature file gives (§5.8), because a file that tiles some chromosomes and not
others is not making the claim it would be read as making. So `hg19_cytoBand.txt` alone opens a
browser over hg19's 24 sequences at their exact lengths, which is how the human demo opens.

**One outline per chromosome, and the bands inside it.** Each sequence in view is traced once, along
its top edge and back along its bottom: **rounded at a telomere** — only where the chromosome's own
end is in view, since the edge of a window is not a telomere — **pinched to a waist at the
centromere**, where the first `acen` band named on the q arm begins (the middle of the run where the
names do not say), to a fifth of the body's half-height rather than to a point, so the outline
never crosses itself; and **narrowed to half along a stalk**. The bands are filled inside it as plain
rectangles clipped to it, and it is edged once in the plot's ink. A centromere's two triangles are
not drawn as triangles: they are what two `acen` rectangles look like inside a waist. The body is at
most 22 pixels tall and centred in the lane, which opens at 40 — room for it, for a band's name
inside it, and for the two lines of its label in the browser's column.

**A yeast centromere is widened to be seen.** A human centromere is megabases and draws itself; a
budding yeast's CEN is 118 bases, a hairline at any zoom where its chromosome is on screen. So a
centromere is drawn at least six pixels wide, centred on itself and over the bands either side — the
reason a variant is widened to three pixels (§8.14): a mark too narrow to see is not a mark.

**The stains are physical, and the same in both themes.** `gposN` is N % of the way from the
unstained near-white to a near-black, which is how UCSC and IGV read the number; turning the ramp
over for a dark page would draw every G-light band dark to a reader who knows ideograms. The
centromere is the red every ideogram gives it, `gvar` is **hatched** because it is variable rather
than a darkness — in strokes at 45°, not a pattern fill, which the vector export cannot carry
(`ui/vector.ts`) — and a stalk is a paler grey, where there is little to stain. The ink is therefore
not a choice, and the card offers no `colour by`, no arrowheads and no `rows` (§8.16's three modes
pack rows a karyotype does not have): it shows the **key**, the stains this file has in UCSC's legend
order, and chips the row in the centromere's red (in the darkest stain's, where a file has no
centromere).

**One axis.** The bands are drawn where they are, on the lane's own axis (§8.4). This is not IGV's
thumbnail of the whole chromosome with the window boxed in red, which is a second coordinate system
beside the one every other lane shares. Zoomed out the lane is the karyotype — every band drawn,
whatever §8.16's density rule would say, since bands tile rather than overlap and a genome's worth of
them a pixel apiece is still the picture a reader zoomed out that far is looking for. Zoomed in it is
the bands under the window, each **named inside itself** where the name fits, in the stain's
contrasting ink. The line under the lane's name says which bands the window is in, in ISCN — `Xq28`,
`Xq27.3 – q28`, `1p36.33 – Yq12` across the whole genome — which is the one fact the picture cannot
carry once a band is wider than the screen. Beside a map the drawing is the same on all four edges.

**A click names the band as a cytogeneticist does**: chromosome first and `chr` dropped — `Xq28`,
where the file writes `q28` and the chromosome in another column — then its position, its length
and its stain. The card has no score row, because the score is the stain restated.

**Bands are searched by name, beside the genes and never instead of them.** The locus box offers
every band of every ready ideogram whose ISCN name begins with what was typed, `chr` or not — `Xq13`
lists `Xq13.1`, `Xq13.2` and `Xq13.3` with their spans — alongside the gene model's hits, and its
placeholder says `a band` when there is one to find. What a karyotype never is, is the starred set
the gene search reads (`searchesByName`): a cytoBand loaded before the GTF would otherwise have
become the search source, and turned a search for `GAL4` into a search of `p11` and `q12`.

**The demos.** `demo/human/hg19_cytoBand.txt` is UCSC's hg19 file — 862 bands over chr1–22, X and
Y — and is the human demo's genome. `demo/yeast/Yeast_cytobands.txt` is the demo assembly as a
cytoBand, which yeast has no G-banding for, so none is invented: each arm is one unstained band, the
centromere is the CEN element found in the demo FASTA by its CDEI–CDEII–CDEIII architecture, and
chromosome XII's rDNA is a stalk, which is what the stalk of a human acrocentric *is* — its
nucleolar organiser. `scripts/make_ideogram_junction_demo.py` writes both and says where each came
from.

### 8.23 Splice junctions and sashimi arcs

A junction is an **intron a read was seen to skip**: the last base of one exon joined to the first
base of the next, and a count of the reads that said so. It is drawn as the arc every reader of
RNA-seq has learnt alternative splicing from — Katz et al.'s sashimi plot — from one exon's end to
the next one's start, as tall as its count against the lane's ceiling and labelled with that count
at its apex. Two arcs leaving one exon are two isoforms, and the numbers on them say which is used
how much.

Every aligner that splices writes them, in one of three shapes:

| Shape | Written by | Coordinates | Count |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SJ.out.tab`, nine integer columns | STAR | the intron, 1-based, inclusive | uniquely mapping reads (column 7) |
| BED12 of two blocks | regtools, TopHat, Portcullis, IGV | the two anchors and the gap between them | the score column |
| BED6 `.junc` | leafcutter | the intron, 0-based, half-open | the score column |

All three become one `FeatureSet` whose features are the **introns** — donor to acceptor, 0-based
and half-open — with the read count as the score. The intron, and not the anchors-and-intron a
junctions BED spans, because the intron is the fact: the arc is drawn between its ends, the card
gives its length, and a metaplot over splice sites wants the splice sites. Everything else a row says
goes into the detail, keyed, so the card lists it and the colour picker offers it (§8.16): `multi`,
STAR's multi-mapping reads; `motif`, spelled on the strand the intron is transcribed from — STAR
numbers each motif once per genomic strand, and its code 2 is `GT/AG` read backwards, which is
`GT/AG` to the reader and not `CT/AC`; `annotated`, `yes` where the junction is in the GTF STAR was
given, which is what makes *colour by annotated* a map of novel splicing; `overhang`, the longest
anchor any read had; and, from a BED, `anchors`, the two flanks, which are the one thing a BED says
that the intron does not. A BED's score is read as the count it is rather than clamped to BED's
nominal thousand, which any expressed gene passes.

**STAR's table is recognised by its columns; the two BEDs have to say what they are.** Nine integers
with STAR's small codes in the strand, motif and annotated columns are a statement no other file
makes. But a BED12 of two blocks is also a two-exon transcript, so it is read as junctions only
where the file says so — a name with `junc` or `sj` in it (`junctions.bed`, `SJ.bed`), a TopHat
`track` line naming junctions, or regtools' and TopHat's own `JUNC…` names on every row — and a
six-column BED is a peak set as often as not, so only a file called `.junc` is leafcutter's. All of it
is asked before `sniffFormat`: a STAR table read as a BED is intervals one base short of their
introns with no count on them, and a junctions BED is a lane of two-exon "genes" that are all
intron. The CLI reads all three the same way, so a task run from the command line gets the introns
and their counts too.

**The lane is a baseline, and a file with both strands splits it.** Arcs stand on one baseline and
grow the way every value in this application grows (`laneGrowsInward`). A file with junctions on
**both** strands moves the baseline to the middle, as IGV's junction track does: forward arcs rise
from it and reverse arcs hang from it, so the two strands of a bidirectional locus read as two
families rather than one tangle. A junction with no strand stands with the forward ones. The
colouring is §8.16's, strand by default — forward in the lane's colour, reverse in the turned hue,
unstranded in the grey that means *no answer*. An arc is stroked thicker the stronger it is; it is
never lower than an eighth of its side's height, because a one-read arc against a ceiling of three
hundred is otherwise a line along the baseline; and an intron narrower than two pixels is drawn as
a **spike** of the same height at its middle, so a whole chromosome is a map of where splicing is and
how much of it, rather than a fringe of sub-pixel humps. Past four thousand arcs the strongest are
drawn and the caption says how many that was. The lane opens at 72 pixels.

**Each count at its apex, strongest first, and none over another count or another arc.** A count
that sits on two arcs is a count for neither, and one a digit's width from its neighbour is read with
it — `13` beside `1` three pixels away is `131`, a count no junction there has. So a count is not
written where a count already stands, nor where another drawn arc's line runs through it: DDX3X's
alternative acceptors, three bases apart, are three arcs on one span, and the one-read arc's `1`
written at its apex landed on the six-read arc's line and was read as its count. A count left out is
still on the card a click on its arc opens. A count wider than its arc is still written, at the arc's
apex: EFB1's 659 over a 366-base intron beside a yeast map is the arc a reader is looking for.

**The axis is the lane's limits** — §8.17's third reading, for §8.17's reason: two samples' arcs can
only be compared against one ceiling. A typed pair holds across windows and lanes, and the batch box
sets one pair on several rows at once. The floor is also a **filter**, which is what a sashimi plot's
*minimum junction coverage* is: a junction under it is not drawn, and the caption counts what was
(`9 of 10 · 1–400 reads`). Over the ceiling an arc draws full height rather than out of the lane.
**Under `auto` the axis is zero to the largest count in view**, and this is the one feature lane
fitted to the window rather than to its file, against the rule §8.17 keeps for a barChart. Junction
counts are heavier-tailed than expression: in the GBR sample's chrX, TMSB4X's second intron carries
2,800 reads, 23 junctions of 2,967 reach a hundred and half have two or fewer, so against the file
every gene but a handful is a row of flat humps. What makes the window safe here, where it is not
for a chart, is what makes a track's autoscale safe: every arc carries its count, and the caption
restates the ceiling on every frame (`20 junctions · to 23 reads`). A ceiling drag, a ⌘-scroll and
the right-click menu's range reach the lane (`hasAMovableAxis`) and start from the axis on screen;
the map's autoscale button, which says *every track*, now sets `auto` on a junction lane and on a
barChart's as well, where it used to reach only the lanes drawn as a profile.

**A click is tested against the curves on screen**: the nearest drawn arc within four pixels, the
taller of two within half a pixel of each other. Not against boxes the size of each intron, because
nested arcs share their span and a box test would name the last one drawn wherever the pointer was.
The card says `intron` and `intron length` where every other card says position and length, and
`reads` where it says score, then the file's own fields — multi-mapped, motif, annotated, max
overhang, or a BED's anchors. A junction with no name is titled *Splice junction*.

**A junction file is never the search source.** A junction has no name a reader looks for —
regtools' `JUNC00000001` is a row number — and a sample's junctions are not where anybody looks a gene
up, so one loaded before the GTF does not take the locus box's gene search from it.

**A spliced BAM draws its own arcs.** The depth row of an alignment file (§8.13) counts the introns
its reads skip on the pass that counts its depth — the CIGAR `N` that §8.13 declines to cover is
counted here instead, and its span is exactly the intron's — and draws them over the curve. That is
the sashimi plot proper: the curve says how much of each exon was read, the arcs say how the exons
were joined, and no junction file is needed. They are counted under the depth's own filter, the
mapping-quality floor, the duplicate switch and the exclusion of secondary and supplementary records,
so an arc never stands on reads the curve under it did not count. A read with too many operations for
its record carries its CIGAR in a `CG` tag and a placeholder `N` the length of the whole read in the
record, and it is read from the tag: counted from the placeholder, every such read would be an arc
over itself. The strand is the aligner's `XS`, or minimap2's `ts` turned over for a reverse read,
since `ts` is the read's own strand; a read with neither is unstranded. A junction that reaches into
two of a view's padded windows is counted in each and kept once, with the larger count.

The arcs over a depth stand on its baseline and are never split — the depth has one baseline, and a
reverse arc hanging below it would hang out of the lane — and a flipped lane carries them with it.
They are drawn in the plot's ink rather than the lane's colour, which is already the colour of the
filled curve under them. Their ceiling is the strongest junction in view, since the depth under them
is autoscaled to the window too, and their floor is the row's own `junction arcs from N reads`, two
by default, because a junction one read long is as often an aligner's guess as a splice and in a deep
file those guesses are most of the arcs. The switch and the floor are on the depth row's card and
stored with the session; they are not written through to the pile, because they are about how the
depth is drawn rather than which reads count, and the pile draws each read's gap itself. **On by
default**, because it costs nothing where there is nothing to draw: a DNA library's reads skip no
intron, so its lane is unchanged. On both surfaces — in the browser and beside a map.

**A BAM's arcs count records, as regtools does, and STAR's table counts pairs.** A pair whose two
mates both cross an intron is two records, and two arcs' worth of evidence to a reader of the BAM;
STAR's column 7 counts the pair once. So the strongest junction of RPL10 reads 350 over the GBR
sample's depth and in regtools' BED of the same alignments, and 338 in STAR's table for the same
library. Both are right about what they count, and neither is converted into the other: the BAM's
number is the one its own depth curve agrees with.

**The demos.** `demo/human/` is four Geuvadis lymphoblastoid samples, two GBR and two YRI, as
nf-core/test-datasets subsamples them to chromosome X for nf-core/rnasplice: their `SJ.out.tab`s
from STAR, run in **one pass** — a two-pass run inserts the first pass's junctions into the genome
and then reports every one of them as annotated, which empties the one column that tells a novel
junction from a known one — one sample's alignments and index for a depth with its own arcs, the same
sample's junctions as the BED12 regtools writes, and the Ensembl chrX GTF they were aligned against.
The workspace opens the browser from the hg19 cytoBand alone at RPL10 in Xq28, with the GBR and YRI
samples' junctions against one typed axis of 1 to 400 reads. `demo/yeast/Yeast_RNA_junctions.SJ.out.tab`
is STAR's junctions for the chromosome I subset of GSE110004 that nf-core keeps for its RNA-seq
tests, which puts EFB1's arc beside the yeast map. `scripts/make_ideogram_junction_demo.py` writes
all of them and records the commands, versions and commits; nothing in them is generated.

## 9. cool and mcool

Supported natively, and still not as a parallel implementation. A cooler is opened as itself: its
`/chroms` is the contig table, `MetaCooler.genomes` is `null`, and every genome accessor answers
`0`, `[]` or `null`. No downstream path branches, because none of them were genome-specific in the
first place — coordinates, the matrix read, aggregation to contig level and the pixel scan are all
bin arithmetic over `indexes/chrom_offset` and contig lengths, which both formats carry.

*This replaces the earlier synthesis design* (a one-row `/genomes` table named from the assembly,
every contig at `genome_id = 0`, `genome_offset = [0, n_contigs]`). Synthesis was the same work done
dishonestly: it put a row in the UI that is not in the file, it had to bypass the `/chroms`
soft-link check anyway, and it left a `synthesised` flag every view had to special-case. The absence
of a genome layer is a fact about the file, and the reader says so.

**Whole-genome where it fits, measured rather than assumed.** The old rule was *region level only*,
on the grounds that a eukaryotic cooler reintroduces the streaming problem §2 avoids. That is true of
a human cooler and false of the genomes this viewer is most often pointed at: yeast is 12.1 Mb, which
at 1 kb bins is 12,100 bins — one bounded read, about 2.3 GB on screen drawn a bin to a pixel, and the single most useful
picture of the file. Refusing it would be refusing the case cool support is *for*.

So the size question is asked instead. `readDenseMatrix` estimates what a block costs — its cells,
and a raster pooled to a fixed ceiling — and compares that to a budget derived from
`navigator.deviceMemory`, refusing with the numbers a block that does not fit; contig level always
fits and is one control away in the same view. A whole genome no longer meets that question: a block
wider than the picture arrives already coarsened, once, in the reader (§7.2), so what is left to
weigh is the pass over its pixels, which is asked about first above ten million stored pixels — a
hundred thousand bins, for a file that states no count — unless a coarser rung draws it (below).
Concretely:

- the entry point is the **contigs table**, not the genomes table, because there are no genomes;
  the genomes table and the genome × genome overview (§7.3) are not offered at all for these files
- a region selection (`chrom` or `chrom:start-end`) loads and renders normally, using the same
  bounded-read path as a MAG
- the whole matrix is a view of its own (`view=whole`), offered in the root menu beside the
  chromosomes table. It is one bounded read, not a scan: the genome-wide view of a *metagenome*
  (§7.3) still costs a full pixel pass, because summing genome pairs has no index to shortcut
- the vocabulary follows the file: a cooler's sequences are **chromosomes**, and the genomes table is
  shown greyed out with the reason rather than hidden, so "does this viewer have one" is answered
  rather than raised — while the multi-genome format is a dev feature that is **on** (§29). Off, the
  row is absent: the question is not one that page raises, and a greyed row would raise it
- a link naming a view of genomes lands on what the file has: `genomes` on its landing table,
  `genome` and `pair` on the chromosomes table, `overview` on `whole`, and a region or a selection
  carrying a genome name is the same view without it. A locus naming no sequence of such a file is
  refused as *not a sequence of this file*, listing its sequences (§10)
- a block read at its own bins is size-guarded. Three guards, in order:
  `DENSE_MATRIX_BIN_LIMIT` with the CLI's own wording; the 2 GiB a browser serves in one typed
  array — about 23,170 bins a side — which no budget and no "load anyway" can lift; and then a
  browser-side *estimate against a budget* — the dense values at 4 B per cell, the raster at 12 B
  per pooled pixel (pooled values, RGBA and canvas; a ceiling, since it is pooled at
  `RASTER_MAX_DIM`), and one bounded read window. The auto-range buffer is not charged: it holds only
  the finite contacts and is garbage before the RGBA is allocated, and charging it as a fourth 4 B
  estimated yeast IV at 100 bp at 4.7 GB where the tab measured 2.9. There is no per-`nnz` term,
  because the pixel read is windowed rather than whole. The budget is **three quarters** of
  `navigator.deviceMemory` — 6.4 GB on a machine reporting 8, where the half it was refused that
  chromosome — and the widest window the reader reads at its own bins is derived from the same
  budget (`denseCellCap`, §7.2), so a view never meets this refusal where a pooled read would have
  drawn. `navigator.deviceMemory` is Chromium-only and a coarse floor rather
  than a measurement — it was capped at 8, and some machines now answer 16 — so it is a *warning*
  threshold rather than a wall: a browser-side refusal offers "load anyway" with the number, and the
  allocation itself is what actually decides, translating a `RangeError` into the same typed
  refusal. Human chr1 at 5 kb (49,792 bins, 2.5e9 cells, ~10 GB) is the case the budget was written
  for, and a whole yeast genome at 500 bp (24,322 bins, ~2.7 GB) the case it must *not* refuse on a
  machine that can hold it; at their own bins both are now past the single array, and both are drawn
  coarsened to the picture instead (§7.2)
- `.mcool` resolution levels are each fixed-bin, so §3.3's arithmetic applies unchanged; the levels
  drive the zoom control exactly as mmetacool entries do — a refine (§2) reads from the coarsest
  rung whose bins still fill a cell, which is fewer stored pixels for the same picture *and* the
  only honest way to draw a balanced map at a coarse grid, since `zoomify --balance` re-balances
  each level from raw counts and summing a fine level does not (§6.4). Bin indices are not
  comparable between levels, so windows cross through base pairs, per contig. The reader still holds
  one map *open*; the rungs a zoom touches are opened beside it over the same mounted bytes and
  released with the session. An `.mcool` addressed at its **root** is
  refused with `mcool-root`, naming its resolutions — the mirror of `mmetacool-root` — and the app
  opens **a third of the way up them from the finest** (`landingRung`): the third of six or seven,
  the second of four or five, the finest of one or two. The same rung is where a zoomify ladder of
  an `.mmetacool` lands, and where a `.hic` opened with no resolution named opens (§3.6). Not the
  finest, whose every read is the largest the file has — its index, its weights, a whole chromosome's
  block — so that landing there made the first wait of every large file its longest. A reader who
  wants the finest level picks it, and it is then the floor of every zoom (§16.2); a rung a comparison
  or a deck asks for by bin size is still opened as asked
- **the whole genome of a laddered file is read at a coarse rung**, not pooled from the open one:
  the coarsest rung whose bins still fit one drawn cell draws the same cells from a fraction of the
  pixels, balanced at its own resolution. On a 5 GB `.mcool` opened at 25 kb that is the 500 kb
  rung's few million pixels in seconds, where the open rung was a gate asking to download the whole
  file; the open rung is left as it is, and a zoom inside the picture still refines to it. A file
  with no rung that fits, a selection and a second file in the square keep the pooled read and its
  gate
- **so is the first picture of a region wider than the reader draws at the open rung** — a whole
  chromosome, most often. A window wider than the reader reads at its own bins (`denseCellCap`, §7.2)
  is pooled into cells of several bins, so mouse chr1 at 10 kb is a 50 kb picture summed from every
  10 kb pixel; where the ladder stores a rung
  whose bins divide that cell, the first read comes from it: the same cells, balanced at their own
  resolution, from a fraction of the pixels (`poolingRung`). Never coarser than the pooled grid, so
  the picture is the one it was and the refine takes it as it stands; a zoom then reads the open
  rung as before. On a 1 GB `.hic` from S3, chr1's read took 1.3 s where it took 4.3. That chr1 was
  at 25 kb, 7,849 bins, which is now read at its own bins: the open rung's 4.3 s, for a picture
  twice as fine on each axis. A declared
  resolution (§3.4) and a second file keep the open rung. A `.hic` opened with no rung named stands
  the resolution picker on the rung it opened at, not on its finest

The app is therefore not a HiGlass replacement for standard Hi-C. Say so in the paper rather than let
a reviewer discover it: the claim is zero-install regional inspection of any cooler, plus a genome
hierarchy that HiGlass has no concept of.

---

## 10. Refusals and errors

Every refusal names the file's actual state and the concrete fix — **and its title names the
subject**: *Nothing to share*, *Too many tabs*, *That workspace could not be read*. A dialog headed
the same way for every refusal makes a reader read the paragraph to find out what was declined, and
read it again later to remember which of them they had seen. Where a refusal can be avoided
altogether it is: a control that has nothing to act on is unavailable, with the reason in its
tooltip, rather than live and answering with a dialog (§8.5).

| Condition | Message |
|---|---|
| `contig-ordering != genome-then-length` | Name the actual ordering; state that the viewer requires genome-grouped layout; point to re-creating the file. **Known cost:** files built from a cooler (`cool` ordering) or a FASTA-ordered assembly are excluded, and those are plausible things for a user to have. |
| mmetacool opened at root | List available entries and the `::` syntax. The app opens an entry instead of showing it (§3.4) |
| `.mcool` opened at root | `mcool-root`: list its resolutions and the `::` syntax, the mirror of the row above. The app opens the landing rung instead (§9) |
| `bin-type == "variable"` or `bin-size` null/missing | State that the viewer supports fixed-bin files only, and name the file's bin type. Fragment-level and contig-level metacools land here, and so does a fragment-level HiC-Pro map, named by its config key (§3.9). Point to `metacooler binnify` as the route to a fixed-bin file — or, with the multi-genome format switched off (§29), to binning the contacts at a fixed size with `cooler cload pairs`. |
| Range or selection names `__unbinned__` | State that unassigned contigs are not a genome and cannot be displayed — distinct from the "unknown label" error, so the user learns the reason rather than doubting the name |
| `metacooler-format-version != 1` | State both versions |
| Dense selection too large | Enforce the same limit as Python: `DENSE_MATRIX_BIN_LIMIT = 50_000`, counted as `50_000²` cells rather than per axis, as `_check_dense_size` counts it. Reuse the CLI's own hint wording ("use contig level", "narrow the range"). The browser's own two guards follow it (§9) |
| bigWig contigs don't match | Report the overlap count |
| Not HDF5 / HDF5 but not cooler | Distinguish the two. A gzip that is not a `.pairs` is told to decompress first, and a file without HDF5's signature is refused by its first bytes, before HDF5 is asked anything (§3.1) |
| Range refers to unknown label | List genomes and contigs, truncated — on a file with no genome layer, *not a sequence of this file*, listing its sequences |
| Coordinate suffix on a genome name | State that genome ranges are whole-genome |
| Range that does not parse, or falls outside its sequence | `bad-range`, in cooler's own words — *End cannot be less than start*, *Genomic region out of bounds* |
| A group, an entry or a cell the file does not carry | Name it and list what the file does carry (`entry-not-found`, `cell-not-found`); a set of cells is refused rather than summed short of what it named (§3.8) |
| HiC-Pro matrix with no bin file | Name the bin file it looked for, and the three ways to supply one (§3.9) |
| A `.pairs` with no bin size, a remote `.scool`, a HiC-Pro matrix over 200 MB | Not shown as refusals: each is a question the app asks — a bin size (§3.7), which cost to pay (§3.8), whether to read it whole (§3.9) — and the open is made again with the answer |
| Remote: ranges unsupported / CORS blocked | Distinguish the two; name the host |
| Remote: the host compresses the file in transit | `remote-compressed`, naming the host and the encoding: ranges would address the compressed stream. Up to 128 MiB as sent, the object is downloaded whole instead and opens; above that it is refused as too much to download (`remote-too-large`). The desktop build asks for an uncompressed transfer and meets neither (§15) |
| BAM with no index beside it | Not a refusal: read by search (§8.13), and the row's summary says so and names the index it did not find. Refused only where the file's length cannot be learnt, since a search needs one — and then name the `#index=<url>` convention |
| BAM whose index cannot be read | Read by search, the summary naming the index that did not read and what went wrong with it |
| BAM not sorted by coordinate | Name the order it *is* in, state that reads are drawn by region, and give `samtools sort -o sorted.bam <file>`. Where the header claimed otherwise or said nothing and the search found the reads out of order, name the two places that show it, give `samtools sort` then `samtools index`, and say that a Hi-C pipeline's alignment file is in read-pair order and not made for browsing |
| CRAM | Refused for its own reason, not as collateral: it needs the exact reference its records were compressed against, which this viewer will not fetch from a third party (C1, C5). Give `samtools view -b`. **Today this row is only true of the folder listing**, which routes by name, **and of a track hub's `cram` track** (§24.10); a dropped `.cram` still falls down the text path and is refused as unreadable bytes |
| A count, length or offset a binary file declares that the file could not hold — a `.hic` block's record count, a normalisation vector's length, an index entry past the end of the file, a BAI's linear-index size, a CSI deeper than ten levels, a `.2bit` record's gap count, a MessagePack array longer than its bytes | `format`, naming the format, the field and the value — *The record count of a block of this .hic reads 50,000,000, and the 2 bytes after it could hold at most 0* — and ending *the file is truncated, corrupt, or not the format its first bytes claim*. Refused **before** anything is read, allocated or walked on its strength; see below |
| Compressed data that inflates past its cap | `format`, naming the format, the field and the cap. The inflate is stopped as soon as the cap is passed, not after the bomb has gone off; see below |

**A number a file declares is a claim, not a size.** Every binary reader sizes its reads, its typed
arrays and its loops by counts read out of the same bytes as the data, so a truncated download, a
flipped bit and a file written to hurt are all the same thirty-two bits read as a count — and
trusted, a sixteen-byte `.hic` block declaring fifty million records allocated 572 MiB, one negative
vector length in a footer read 341 MiB of a 256 MiB file, and a twenty-four-byte `.csi` would hold
the annotations worker for some twenty minutes a query. So each count passes three questions in
`sources/untrusted.ts` before it sizes anything: **is it a count** (a non-negative safe integer),
**is it under the format's ceiling**, and **could the bytes left hold it** at the fewest bytes one
item takes. The third does the work: it makes every allocation and every loop proportional to bytes
that are actually there. An offset and length pair must also name bytes inside the file, and entries
a writer lays end to end — a `.hic`'s matrix records, a resolution's blocks, its normalisation
vectors — must between them fit in it, since overlapping entries that each lie inside the file would
read it once per entry.

**The ceilings are the formats' own maxima, set generously**, because a ceiling that refuses a real
file is a bug in the ceiling and not a protection. Each is argued where it is set: a `.hic` block
holds at most 2^26 records (Juicer and `hictk` cut a matrix into blocks of about a thousand bins a side,
or a fixed 500 kb or 5 Mb of genome below 500 bp and 5 kb, so a mammalian block holds about a
million; tens of millions are reachable only on a small genome sequenced to saturation at 100 bp or
finer); a BAI reference at most 2^16 linear-index slots (BAI cannot address past 2^29 bp, so the
format's own maximum is 32,768); a CSI at most ten levels (its bins are `uint32`, and an eleventh
level could not be numbered). Two counts are read leniently, as they always were: a `.hic`
normalisation index no file could hold opens the file with no weights, since what follows the
expected values may be no index at all, and a BAM record whose name, CIGAR and sequence overrun its
own length stops the walk as a non-positive length does.

**An inflate is capped in proportion to what went in.** A fixed cap cannot be both safe and
generous: one small enough to hold a thousand-to-one bomb refuses a large real file. So the cap is a
ratio well above the format's real one, with a floor under which a small file may compress as well
as it likes and a ceiling the reader could not use past: a `.hic` block and a g3d model block at
64 times their compressed size (`straw`, the C++ reader `hicstraw` is built on, sizes its buffer at
ten and records three as the most it has seen), never under 16 and 64 MiB; a HiC-Pro matrix or a
FASTA the command line keeps as bytes the same, never under 512 MiB; a share link's workspace the
same, never under 16 MiB. A BGZF member is held to the format's own 64 KiB, which htslib refuses to
exceed, and text to 2^29 bytes, past which no engine can decode a string anyway. The decompressor is
fed 64 KiB at a time and stopped the moment its output passes the cap, so the overshoot is one
slice's worth and never the bomb. A plain-gzip `.pairs` is a stream with no total to cap — its
records are walked as they arrive — so it is fed the same way, and a line in it is refused past
64 MiB rather than carried to the end of the inflate.

## 11. Hosting and privacy

**Public files:** static objects on S3-compatible storage (Cloudflare R2 preferred for egress).
Requirements: `Accept-Ranges: bytes`; CORS permitting `GET` and `HEAD` and the `Range` header while
exposing `Content-Length` and `Content-Range`; `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`, served
without a `Content-Encoding` (§10); long TTLs on immutable versioned objects. A catalog JSON — a
store (§24) — lists available files with the metadata needed to browse without opening any of them.

**GEO and SRA cannot be hosts** — their download endpoints serve attachments without range or CORS
support. Such files are inputs to publication, never live sources.

**Remote HDF5** reads through an FS node shaped like Emscripten's `FS.createLazyFile`, in a worker
(`sources/RemoteRangeSource.ts`; h5wasm's `lazyFileLRU` demo is the reference) — not the built-in,
which probes with a `HEAD` of its own, caches without bound and counts nothing. The open probes
with a `HEAD` before its `GET` to test range support, and that `HEAD` is skipped for a URL carrying
its own signature — `X-Amz-Signature`, `X-Goog-Signature`, or `sig=` beside `sv=` — since such a
URL is signed for a single method. A presigned link therefore opens and goes on working until it
expires (§24.6); a public bucket URL is still what a citation should point at, because a signature
has a date on it.

**Private files:** a local file — dropped, picked, or in a connected folder (§20) — or the reader's
own private bucket, Drive or Dropbox, read from the browser with their own credentials (§20.3,
§24.7, §24.9). Identical code path, different byte source. Nothing is uploaded, so there are no
accounts, no storage, no hosting cost and no GDPR review. Stated prominently in the UI and in the
paper.

**Every web build carries a Content-Security-Policy, in its page.** The site, every archived pin and
the package (§22) write one string (`scripts/csp.mjs`) into `index.html` as a `<meta>` right after
the charset, ahead of everything it governs, and their builds check the page they emit against it. A
meta because GitHub Pages, a registry CDN and a lab's static server send no header anybody here
chooses; the desktop sends the same policy as a header and records what a meta costs (§15), and
both costs are taken knowingly: **it does not reach the workers**, which are files and take their
policy from their own responses, so what it polices is the document — everything parsed into it,
every script it loads and every request it makes itself, a `?config=` workspace, a store's catalog, a
folder listing; and **it cannot say `frame-ancestors`**, which these builds must not say anyway,
since an embed is a frame in somebody else's page (§21). It allows what the app does and nothing
else: scripts from its own origin, with `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` for h5wasm and the correlation kernel;
styles from its own origin, with no `'unsafe-inline'`, because nothing in the tree writes `style=` —
the chart tooltips, which showed the library's styled markup, now carry markup of their own (§18.13);
images from itself, `data:` and `blob:`; connections to itself, to any `https:` host — remote files
are the remote half of the app — and over plain HTTP to `localhost`, where a dev server or a local
object store answers, and to `data:`, which reaches nothing and keeps this the desktop's policy:
its header reaches the worker that fetches the bigWig reader's wasm from a `data:` URL (§15), and
this meta does not; workers, the service worker and the manifest from itself; and Google Identity
Services by exactly the sources Google documents — its client script, fetched on a sign-in click
and never on load (§24.7), its stylesheet, its frames and its endpoints. When that script loads it
writes an inline `<style>` of button styles, which the policy refuses with one console line and
loses nothing by refusing: the token client this app uses draws no button. Everything else falls to
`default-src 'none'`, and no plugin, `<base>` or form submission is allowed. The dev server carries
no policy, since it injects every stylesheet as a `<style>` and talks to the page over a websocket;
`vite preview` serves a build, policy and all. `scripts/ui-csp.mjs` drives a built page under it
— a map, a figure hovered, the 1D browser from a second origin — and fails on any refusal the page
did not ask for, and on a map or a lane left without its data.

**The site describes itself to crawlers and to language models, in files beside the app.** Its
`public/` puts three at the root. `llms.txt` is a summary in the shape llmstxt.org gives one: what
the app is, the formats it opens, how to write a link that opens a file at a place — the hash of
§5.5, with a map's `region` in the machine form and the browser's `locus` in the display form
(§26.1) — how to embed one (§21), how to run the command line (§23), and links to the README, the
validation and timing notebooks, the changelog and this specification. `robots.txt` lets every
crawler in, those of language models included, keeps the archived pins and the pull-request
previews (`/v/`, `/pr/`) out of search — each is a copy of the app at the root, kept for links that
must not change — and names `sitemap.xml`, which lists the app and its two notebooks. The site
build adds a fourth, `llms-full.txt`: the README as one file, its repository-relative links made
absolute (`scripts/llms.mjs`), for a tool that reads a single document rather than following links.
**`llms.txt` is written by hand and held to the app by a test**, because a model acts on it — writes
a link from it, runs a command from it — and nothing reading it can tell a summary that has drifted:
each example link goes through the hash's own reader, each value it lists through the list it is
drawn from, each task through the registry and each store through the shelf. None of these four
files is in the pinned, desktop or package builds.

**The page is written for a search engine too, which reads it after the app has run.** Its title,
*chromosomix – genome browser for Hi-C, tracks and 3D models*, and its description name what the
app is searched by — Hi-C and Micro-C, a genome browser, `.cool`, `.mcool` and `.hic` — inside the
sixty and the hundred and sixty characters a results page prints whole, and the description is the
one a pasted link unfurls with, beside the Open Graph tags. **On the web the app leaves that title
alone while nothing is open** (`App.landingTitle`): a search engine indexes the page as it stands
once the script has run, and the app used to write its bare name over the title the moment it
mounted, so none of the words in it reached an index. A tab with a file open is still
`<file> — chromosomix`, and the desktop window and the single file, which no search finds, say the
name alone. A `<link rel="canonical">` names `https://chromosomix.app/` as the page's one address,
whatever query a link to it carries — `?store=`, `?config=`, `?embed=1` — so that a link to any of
them counts for the root; a pinned copy carries it too, behind `robots.txt`. The `<noscript>` says
what the app is, the formats it reads and where its source and `llms.txt` are, for a reader without
JavaScript and for a crawler that runs none, which reads nothing else of the page. It comes ahead of
`#app`, which is a window tall even empty: after it, the line it used to hold was a screen's height
down a blank page. The package's description and keywords say the same to npm's search (§22).

## 12. Performance budgets

Instrumented from the first commit and surfaced on the status bar — *read*, whose panel gives the
requests and bytes in total and for the last view; these are also paper figures.

| Operation | Budget |
|---|---|
| Open + render genomes table (remote) | ≤ 20 range requests |
| Load one MAG's matrix (remote) | ≤ 5 range requests |
| Pan/zoom within the block in hand | 0 requests, 60 fps |
| Refine, on crossing the block's grid (§2) | ≤ 5 range requests, one bounded read |
| Pan to the edge of the block in hand | one read, **at the same resolution** |
| Zoom out to a block already read | 0 requests |
| A place visited again — the same window, grid and settings of the same map | **0 requests** and no read: answered from memory, its pooled display with it, so only the colouring is redone |
| A place asked for again while its first read is under way | **0** more requests: that read, waited on |
| Genome-pair block | ≤ 5 range requests |
| Time to interactive, cold, remote | ≤ 3 s on a typical connection |
| A region read chunk after chunk (remote) | from the third near miss, one request a stretch growing to 16 MiB — thirty-two sequential chunks in ≤ 8 requests (§6.1) |
| Reads scattered across a file (remote) | exactly the chunk each asks for — no read-ahead (§6.1) |

And for a `.hic` (§3.6), whose one expensive shape is a read across every chromosome pair — a
whole-genome picture, and the census §6.5 takes on every open:

| Operation | Budget |
|---|---|
| A read across chromosome pairs (remote), at a rung inside a record's first 4 KiB | ≤ 2 exact range requests a pair — its record's head, its blocks — and one for many where they lie within 64 KiB of one another, the blocks just past a record read with its head; no chunk of the cache spent on any; six in flight for a picture, four for the census |
| The census, started beside an open | **0** reads before a request already queued has been answered |
| The census or the circularity check, while a view is reading | **0** steps started until no view request has run for 250 ms; at most the one step already in flight |

**A view's reads go first.** One worker reads for everything, and over a network each of its reads
is a round trip that holds the thread — so work nobody is looking at, taking turns with a view,
makes the view wait for its round trips as well as its own. The census (§6.5) and the circularity
check (§8.15) are that work. Every other request counts itself in while it runs, and they wait until
none has run for 250 ms, which covers the hop to the main thread between a view's `range` and its
`matrix`. On a 1 GB `.hic` from S3 (4DNFIYUR29KO), chromosome 1 clicked from the Chromosomes table
while both ran was on screen in 10 s; it is now under 4, of which the read is 1.3 s.

**A place already seen is answered from memory.** Every navigation builds its view afresh, and every
view used to read its block afresh. `scripts/ui-revisit.mjs` walks the lab's 689 MB
`demo/mouse/progenitors.mcool` at 10 kb — chr1, chr2, chr1 again, a window of chr1, chr1 again — and
the same walk on a 940 MB chicken `.hic`, timing each step from the link to the picture. In headless
Chromium against a server answering as S3 does, at 40 ms a round trip and 25 MiB/s, the second chr1
took 3.6 s and the third 3.7 s with every byte already in memory: most of it the worker decompressing
and pooling the same pixels again, the rest the page pooling, ranging and colouring the same block
again — and where another read had pushed the chromosome's chunks out of the source's cache, the
round trips again as well. The answers are now kept on the page by question and by the map the
worker holds (§2, `worker/answers.ts`), each with its pooled display (§7.2), and both come back in
under 0.4 s without a request, most of it the colouring; on the `.hic`, 1.7 s and 3.1 s became 0.3.
A window first asked for is still a read, since nothing kept answers it (§2).

What is kept is bounded by one budget for the page: a sixteenth of the memory the device reports,
512 MiB where it reports none, a gibibyte at most, least recently used out first, each picture
counted twice for the display kept beside it. Every reader on the page shares it — a deck's cells
and a comparison's second file included (§16.7) — and a reader put down takes its answers with it.
An `open` names the map it opens, by its file, entry, source, edit and import, so a resolution left
and come back to finds its answers, and two files of one name dropped from two folders are two maps.
A total drawn to (§6.5), a cell set (§3.8), a `close`, a failed open and any request the cache has no
word for start a name nothing is filed under; an answer asked before such a change and arriving after
it is handed to its caller and not kept. A failed read is never kept. The status bar's *read* panel
says what a view answered from memory cost — no request and no byte — where the worker, which never
sees it, would go on naming the read before; a view that waited on a read already under way is that
read's cost, and says so.

And for an alignment lane (§8.13), where the open cost is separated from the window cost for the same
reason the table above separates opening a file from loading one MAG's matrix — a `.bai` for a human
WGS file is single-digit megabytes read once, and folding that into a per-window budget would hide
the cost it exists to police:

| Operation | Budget |
|---|---|
| Open a BAM: header + index | ≤ 3 range requests, **once for both rows** — the depth and the pile share one open handle and one parsed index — identify, header, index — and the index read is additionally reported in **bytes**, because a request count says nothing useful about a whole-file read. Three and not two: *is this a BAM* and *what is in its header* are one read (they are the same bytes, and asking twice was the first thing measuring this found), but the file's length is a request of its own on a source that must ask for it, and the index is a request of its own by construction |
| One alignment window | ≤ 5 coalesced range requests |
| Pan inside the window already fetched | 0 requests |
| Change a lane control | one window's reads again, and **0** for the depth row beside it — unless the change was the mapping-quality floor or the duplicate switch, which are the only two that alter a count and the only two written through to both rows. Joining mates costs **nothing**: it is drawn from columns the pile already carries. Depth is a count and does not care how the reads were coloured, which is why the two caches watch keys of different widths (§8.13) |
| A window above the byte cap | **0 data requests** — refused from the index alone, which is the whole point of forecasting before fetching |
| Colour the depth by variant | **0 extra requests** — the residues are read from a FASTA already open in the same worker, and never fetched for. It is bounded in CPU instead, by the sixteen-bases-per-pixel gate (§8.13) |

And for the analysis tasks (§18), where the first row is the one the whole threading design exists to
satisfy and is therefore the one that is tested first:

| Operation | Budget |
|---|---|
| **Any analysis task, effect on the view** | **0 dropped frames, 0 blocked reader requests** — pan and zoom stay live for the whole run, however long it is |
| Insulation / coverage / P(s), block already loaded | 0 range requests |
| Insulation, block not loaded (remote) | ≤ 5 range requests per contig |
| 4C, cis (remote) | ≤ 5 range requests |
| 4C, with trans | one streaming pass over pixels with `bin1 < anchor_end`; progress, cancel, and a pre-flight estimate before it starts |
| APA, k windows, local file | 0 network; ≤ k bounded reads after coalescing |
| APA, k windows, remote | ≤ 2 range requests per *coalesced* window, with the estimate shown before **Run** |
| APA over the expected | the windows, and one band per sequence the anchors sit on, read in tiles as deep as its farthest window reaches and never held whole; the estimate says so in words, since the depth is the loop set's |
| Metaplot, k features | 0 matrix reads; ≤ 1 `sample` request per contig touched |
| Correlation / eigenvectors | 0 range requests beyond the block; refused above the bin-count gate (§18.6) |
| Adaptive smoothing of a block | 0 range requests; the arrays go over and back. Inline below 1 M cells (78 ms at 353²); on the analysis thread above it — 1.5 s at 4 M, 7.4 s at the 16 M cap. The map draws **unsmoothed** meanwhile, never blank and never captioned as smoothed |
| Analysis worker mount | opened on first use, never at session open |

And for a `.pairs` import (§3.7), an open with a denominator and a real wait — everything but it
and the two exempt opens below is a bounded read costing a handful of range requests, and this walks
a whole file:

| Operation | Budget |
|---|---|
| Probe a `.pairs`: header, and the index if there is one | ≤ 3 range requests. One BGZF member for the format check — cut *exactly*, from the member's own header — then the preamble, then the `.px2` whole, which is small by construction |
| The binning pass | **one sequential read of the file**, and no second pass ever. Measured on `demo/ecoli/SRR19500734.pairs.gz` (17.7 M records, 238 MB): **0.69 M records/s** at the 64 KiB BGZF framing `bgzip` writes, and **0.12 M records/s** at the ~1.4 KB framing that file actually has. The 5.7× is decompression, not parsing — see below. Progress in records where a `.px2` gave an exact count, in compressed bytes otherwise; cancellable throughout |
| Every rung above the base | 0 reads. Derived from the base pixel table, which is smaller than the record stream by the ratio of records to stored pixels — thirteen to one on `demo/yeast/` |
| Every view, afterwards | **0 reads, ever.** The map is in memory; a rung switch, a pan, a zoom, the deck and every §18 task cost no I/O at all |
| Writing the `.mcool` | 0 reads. Runs beside the open map, with its own bar and its own cancel; the int64 conversion buffer is capped at one chunk rather than one column |

If metadata reads explode, the known cause is walking HDF5's object hierarchy;
`hdf5-indexed-reader` addresses it with a pre-built path → offset index and was built for `.cndb`
chromatin files. Held in reserve — adopting it would not change any file format, only the reader.

**One open is exempt: an `.scool` over the network** (§3.8). Listing a
container's cells reads link records the writer interleaved with the cells' own data, so it is not a
bounded read and no chunk size makes it one — measured on a 3,882-cell file as 1,015 reads averaging
512 bytes spread uniformly across 327 MB, and reproduced on a container `cooler.create_scool` wrote.
The budget is not quietly widened for it. The reader is **asked**, before anything is read, which of
the two costs to pay:

| Operation | Budget |
|---|---|
| Open an `.scool`, local | unchanged — a file on disk seeks for free and is never asked |
| Open an `.scool`, remote | a **gate**, with both costs quoted: one `GET` of the whole object, or ~1,000 small range requests for ~5% of its bytes |
| The cells table, after that listing | **0** further chunks — every cell's attributes are in metadata already fetched |
| One cell's map | as any cooler's: a bounded read (2,802 stored pixels on the Nagano file) |
| Summing *k* cells | *k* bounded reads, linear in *k* and in nothing else — 12.7 s for all 3,882 of them, gated above §7.3's pixel threshold like any other whole-file read |
| What the reader sees while it happens | `summing 1,204 of 3,882 cells…`, counted in cells because cells are what the work is |

This is the case `hdf5-indexed-reader` above was held in reserve for, and it remains the way out:
a pre-built path → offset index would turn the gate into an ordinary bounded open.

**A second open is exempt, and for a blunter reason: a HiC-Pro pair is two text files with no index
at all** (§3.9). There is nothing to hold in reserve here — the format cannot be indexed without
being rewritten — so the whole matrix is read once, at open, and every read after it is bounded and
in memory. The gate is on **bytes rather than on being remote**, because the cost is parsing and
memory rather than round trips and a local file pays it in full:

| Operation | Budget |
|---|---|
| Open a HiC-Pro pair under 200 MB | read whole, ungated — about two seconds at 100 MB/s |
| Open one over 200 MB | a **gate** quoting the size, the estimated pixel count and that the cost is paid once |
| Every read afterwards | **0 requests** — the map is typed arrays; pan and zoom are free |
| Find the bin file beside a URL | ≤ 2 `HEAD` requests — 4 for a matrix under `iced/`, whose bed is looked for under `raw/` too — and none for a signed URL; then the refusal names all three ways to supply it |
| What the reader sees while it happens | bytes, then pixels, on a labelled bar with a cancel — 258 MB in ≈4 s, three of them download |

The way out here is not an index but a conversion, and the gate says so: `cooler load -f coo` turns
the same two files into a `.cool` that opens in a handful of requests at any size.

**Every budget above assumes a file that is what it says it is. One that is not is held to its own
size** (§10). A corrupt or hostile file is either read or refused, and either way the cost is bounded
by its bytes rather than by what its counts claim:

| Operation | Budget |
|---|---|
| Open and read a binary file whose counts, offsets or compressed data are corrupt — `.hic`, BAM with BAI or CSI, `.2bit`, binary g3d | an answer or a refusal; **never more than 16× the file's size read** in one open, never one typed array past 64 MiB, never 1.5 s. `test/unit/fuzz-readers.test.ts` holds every reader to this over 1,140 seeded corruptions of files the repository's own writers made; the worst reads 4× its file and allocates 30 KB, and the slowest takes a tenth of a second |
| An inflate of any kind | stopped as soon as its output passes its cap, at most one 64 KiB slice of input later (§10) |

**A picture says when it is finished** (`perf/rendered.ts`). A view mounting, its map's first paint
and the picture being finished are three moments: the lanes ask for their windows once the map is
laid out, a track still opening asks for its own when it lands, and a smoothing replaces the map it
was computed from. Nothing outside the page could tell them apart. A script timing the app waited
for the network to go quiet, which it never does here while the census and the circularity check
read behind a view (§6.5, §8.15), and a screenshot taken on the first paint had lanes reading
*fetching…*. So everything that can still change the picture says so while it can — a navigation
being routed, a file, a workspace or a shared link being opened, a map's veil (a read, a smoothing,
a correlation), a paint asked for and not yet made, a lane's window, residues or pile in flight, a
track on screen still opening, a finer block being read for a frozen map — and once the last of it
has ended and a frame has passed with nothing new begun, the window says so, once:

| Where | What |
|---|---|
| `performance.getEntriesByName('chromosomix:rendered')` | a mark whose `startTime` is the moment the last wait ended — the end of the frame the picture was finished in — on the clock the page's own navigation timing is on |
| `window`, event `chromosomix:rendered` | the same report, as the event's `detail` |
| the host of an embed, message `chromosomix:rendered` | the same report, under §21.4's rules |

The report carries `seq`, counting from 1; `at`, the mark's time; `status` — `drawn`, `gated` for a
whole-genome read waiting for its button (§7.3), or `error` for a refusal on screen in place of the
picture, with the refusal as `note`; `state`, the view state as the address bar carries it; `maps`,
one per map on screen, every cell of a deck, each with its title, the bin size of the rung its block
was read from, the bins pooled into one cell, and their product as `resolution`; and `lanes`, the
track lanes drawn. **It says what was drawn, not what was asked for.** A whole-genome view reads the
coarsest rung that fits (§7.3) and a wide window may pool its cells (§7.2), so a link naming 5 kb can
be on screen at 25 kb, and a script holding viewers to one resolution has to be told so rather than
time a different picture.

**A repaint alone is not a new picture.** Pointing at the map repaints it once a frame, and a report
per frame would bury the one a script is waiting for: a paint keeps a picture unfinished but never
starts one. A report follows every navigation — a colour change is one — and every read a picture
waits on, a pan past the lanes' padding included. **What it does not wait for**: the side columns,
the status bar and the console, which describe the picture rather than being it; an analysis task,
whose result is waited for when it arrives as a track; the census and the circularity check, which
change nothing on screen; and anything that has left the page — a tab in the background, a view torn
down without saying so — which is looked for four times a second while something waits, and dropped.

---

## 13. Explicit non-features

Stated so they are decisions rather than omissions: tile server; user accounts; file upload; server-side
computation of any kind; required companion files **for a contact map** (§1 states the scope, and
§8.13 the one format that falls outside it: where an index is a format's only bounded read, its
absence is refused by name); required preprocessing; support for orderings other
than `genome-then-length`; whole-genome views that do not fit in memory (§9 — the limit is measured,
not a category); write access of any kind, in either target; an auto-update service; and a desktop
build with a feature set of its own — the package is a delivery mechanism, and the formats, views
and operations are the same in both targets.

**"Write access" means the app never modifies a file it opened**, and §18 makes that worth spelling
out rather than leaving to be inferred. The viewer has always *produced* files — a PNG, a PDF, a BED
of hand-drawn marks, a saved session — and §18 adds a bigWig to that list. All of them are new bytes
handed to the browser to save (§26.6); none of them touches the thing that was opened, and nothing about
them needs a server. The distinction is between authoring an output and editing an input, and only the
second is refused.

Four further non-features arrive with §18, for reasons given at §18.9: ~~no loop or dot calling~~ —
**narrowed**, see §18.9: no caller of this app's own invention, where a port of a published one,
checked against that method's own output, is admitted (chromosight);
~~no contact-based contig reordering or scaffolding~~ — **reversed**, see §18.9 and §27: an edit of
the reference is a lens over the opened file, and what it produces is new files; ~~no writing of
`.cool`, `.mcool` or `.metacool`~~ — **narrowed**, see §18.9, §3.7 and §27.8: writing a matrix
*derived from an opened map* is still refused, and writing the **primary reduction of a `.pairs`
file**, or a **rearrangement** of an opened map's stored counts through a declared edit, is not; and
no differential APA.

Five more arrive with §8.13, each with its own reason rather than one shared one: no **mate
fetching** (one uncoalescable request per visible read, with no locality to coalesce on); no
**`SA` walk** — a split read's other pieces are drawn where the window already holds them, and
following the tag out of the window is the mate problem again under another name; no **variant
calling** (§18.9's argument about a half-good caller, which applies here with more force);
no **contact matrix derived from alignments** (the second application the original refusal was
drawing a line against); and no **CRAM** — which is refused on stronger ground than the others,
since it cannot be decoded without the exact reference its records name, fetched from a third-party
registry (C1, C5) or supplied as a second required file.

There is exactly **one** observable difference between them, and it is a host-compatibility
difference rather than a feature: the desktop build can ask a host not to compress, which a page is
forbidden from doing, so a file served with `Content-Encoding: gzip` is read there by range like any
other, where the website has to download it whole — and refuses it past 128 MiB as sent (§10). See
§15, whose native menu holds nothing the page does not already offer.

---

## 14. Resolved decisions

All three previously open questions are settled. Each removes code rather than adding it, which is
why the spec got shorter as it got more specific.

| Decision | Resolution | What it deletes |
|---|---|---|
| Variable-bin files | **Not supported.** Fixed-bin only (§3.3, §10) | The variable-width coordinate path throughout — and, as a second-order effect, every read of `/bins` |
| `__unbinned__` | **Never displayable** (§7.4) | The toggle, the guarded-open path, and the largest counter-example to §2's small-MAG assumption |
| cool / mcool | **Native; whole-genome where it fits** (§9) | The tiling architecture §2 exists to avoid — a block is one bounded read or it is refused, and it is never assembled from parts — and, since the reader went native, the synthesised one-genome table and the `synthesised` flag every view carried |

This row used to end *"a block either fits in one read or is refused, and there is no third path"*.
There is now a third path and it is worth naming, because it is not the one that was being refused:
a block that does not fit is read **coarser** (§7.2) and then read again, narrower and finer, as the
reader zooms into it (§2). Every one of those reads is a whole bounded block. What §2 deleted was
*assembling a picture out of tiles*, and that is still deleted.

The through-line: each answer protects the assumption in §2 that a unit of display fits in memory in
one bounded read. Variable bins broke the arithmetic, `__unbinned__` broke the size bound, and
whole-genome coolers broke both. With all three excluded, the invariant holds for every view the app
can reach — which is what makes a viewer with no tile server, no eviction from under a picture and no
progressive rendering a defensible design rather than a compromise. The answers §12 keeps for a place
visited again are evicted, but whole and only from memory: what is let go is a picture nobody is
looking at, and it costs a read the next time it is asked for and nothing before.

### Remaining judgement calls

Not blocking, but worth revisiting once something is on screen:

1. **The `genome-then-length` refusal (§10).** Clean, but it excludes files built via
   `create cool` (`cool` ordering) or from FASTA-ordered assemblies — plausible things for a user to
   have. Whether the error message alone is sufficient is a question for first users, not for now.
2. **The genome × genome overview (§7.3).** Gated rather than removed. If it turns out nobody waits
   for the scan, dropping it entirely would simplify the state model further.

## 15. Desktop target

The same bundle, packaged with Electron for machines that cannot reach the website. It is a second
invocation of the same bundler over the same source, never a change to the first: the web build is
what §1 constrains, and nothing here is allowed to alter it.

**The origin is frozen at `app://viewer`.** Everything the browser keys on an origin is keyed on
that string — `localStorage` (theme, per-file table state), the hash router's `history` entries, the
`Origin` header sent to remote hosts. Change it in a later release and every user's remembered
preferences disappear on upgrade with no error and no way to get them back.

**The renderer is served by a privileged standard scheme, never `file://`.** `app` is registered
before `whenReady` with `standard`, `secure`, `supportFetchAPI`, `stream` and `codeCache` (compiled
JS kept between launches). `standard: true` is what gives the page a real, non-opaque origin:
without it `history.pushState` throws `SecurityError`
and the router dies on the first navigation into a genome. `file://` fails earlier and more quietly
— the module worker never constructs, so the app hangs on "Opening…" with nothing on the console.

**`allowServiceWorkers` is deliberately absent.** The desktop build has no offline story to tell,
because it is already on disk; §11's caching bargain buys nothing and costs a stale-build failure
mode. Three independent guards keep it out: the plugin is not in the desktop config so `sw.js` is
never emitted, `registerServiceWorker()` returns early off the web target, and Chromium refuses the
registration on an `app://` origin outright.

**`contextIsolation` and `sandbox` are on; `nodeIntegration` and `nodeIntegrationInWorker` are
off.** Not only for the usual reasons. `isNodeRuntime()` (`h5/bootstrap.ts`) decides, in the reader
worker, which h5wasm filesystem path to take purely by whether `process` exists, so leaking Node
into the worker sends every open down the wrong path and it fails with a generic `not-hdf5` error,
hundreds of frames from the cause — and `mountTarget()` starts writing tens of megabytes into
`TMPDIR` on the way.

**The CSP is delivered as a response header**, not a `<meta>` tag: a meta CSP does not reach a module
worker at all, and cannot express `frame-ancestors`. It keeps `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` — verified in both
directions; without it h5wasm fails to instantiate in both document and worker — and needs no
`'unsafe-inline'` for styles, because `el()` assigns through the CSSOM and the tree contains no
`innerHTML`, no `<style>` creation and no `style=` attribute. The one markup it hands a library is a
chart's tooltip, which ECharts parses with `innerHTML`, and it carries classes rather than `style=`
(§18.13) — the library's own tooltip markup did not, so under this policy every hover over a figure had
its styling refused until the charts had formatters of their own. And `connect-src` takes `data:`,
for a worker: the bigWig and bigBed reader carries its inflate wasm as a `data:` URL and fetches it
before its first read, and this header reaches the annotations worker, where a meta would not.
Without `data:` the fetch was refused inside that worker, where the page hears nothing, and every
bigWig lane said *fetching…* for good while the interval lanes beside it drew. A `data:` URL has no
host behind it, so the clause reaches nothing.

**One request header is rewritten, and it is the target's only capability.** `Accept-Encoding` is a
forbidden header name in Fetch, so no page may set it; the main process may. Every http(s) request
goes out asking for `identity`. Measured: this changes nothing for ranged reads — Chromium already
sends `identity` whenever a `Range` header is present, because it cannot inflate a partial response
— and everything for the `HEAD` that `RemoteRangeSource.open()` probes with, which carries no range
and is otherwise answered compressed. The refusal that follows a compressed probe (§10,
`remote-compressed`) is correct and stays — the website answers it by downloading the object whole,
up to 128 MiB as sent — and the desktop build simply stops provoking it. No response header is ever
injected, and in particular no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`: it could not make a
server produce partial content, and the `?edges=` sidecar fetch takes a user-supplied URL, which a
blanket injection would turn into a read-anything primitive.

**No path→bytes route.** Local files are read exactly as in the browser: a `File` from the drop, a
`Blob`, `FileReaderSync` in the worker. Routing the bytes through an IPC protocol handler was
measured at ~15× slower per read with a fixed ~3 ms floor per call, which is precisely what HDF5's
many-small-reads metadata walk punishes. If a local path is ever wanted, it is wanted as a *string*
for addressing, and the bytes stay on the Blob.

**A native menu, and nothing on it the page does not already do.** Beside the platform's own items
— editing, full screen, the window list — and a link to the source, every entry mirrors a page
command (`electron/menu.cts`) and shows its key without taking it, `Open…`'s ⌘O apart, so the
shortcuts dialog stays the one list of what is bound. A static menu cannot follow the dev-features
switch (§29.5), so its words are true of every file: *Landing table*, *Previous* and *Next sequence*.
Reload and page zoom are left off it — a reload loses a dropped file, and page zoom changes the
canvas size a figure's dpi is computed from.

---

## 16. N maps side by side

Several contact maps on screen at once, navigating together — HiGlass's multi-view, arrived at from
this app's own constraints rather than ported from its architecture. There is no tile server and no
pyramid here (§2), so a panel is not a viewport onto a stream: it is a whole bounded block, held
whole, exactly as the single map already is. What N panels add is a **shared coordinate**, not a
shared cache.

The viewer already had two answers to "two files", and this is a third because neither of them
generalises. A **tab** (§5.6) is a whole second session with its own worker, tables, tracks and
address-bar entry, and only one is on screen at a time — it answers *open*, not *compare*. The
**lower-left triangle** (§5.7) is two files in one square, which is the strongest comparison
available and is why it is gated on a matching bin size and a matching chromosome list. Both survive
untouched, and a session may hold a blended square *and* a deck: they are different claims, and both
can be true of one screen.

### 16.1 The panel model

A deck is a **lead** and its **companions**.

The lead is the session's own file. It owns the breadcrumb, the genomes and contigs tables, the
tracks, the record card and, where there is one, the second file blended into its lower triangle. It
is not in the companion list, and "which file is this session of" is not a thing that changes by
dragging. **Its cell is a cell like the others** all the same: it moves by its grip and closes with
its × (§16.9), and neither changes which file the session is of — only where its picture stands, and
whether it is on screen. It used to be cell 0 for good, with no grip and no ×, and a figure of a model
beside its map, or of the model alone, could not be drawn with a deck whose first cell could do
neither.

A companion is the smallest thing that is still a map: its own `ReaderClient` — so its own worker, its
own h5wasm instance, its own I/O — its own colour scale, its own block, and a heading with its name
on it. It has no level toggle and no second file. Each of those is a control over something the
deck *shares*, and five copies of a shared control are five ways to put the deck out of step with
itself. The score and the tracks used to be on that list and are not: a companion's score is its
own, picked on its *Map* card (§16.2), and the session's tracks can be drawn on it (§16.8).

The lead's element is **re-parented** into a cell of the grid — the first, until the reader moves it —
rather than rebuilt, so a session with companions costs the session it would have been, plus the
companions.

### 16.2 What is shared, and what is not

| | Shared | Per panel |
|---|---|---|
| Which region, genome, pair or selection | yes | |
| Aggregation level (`bin` / `contig`) | yes | |
| The 45° turn (§17) | yes | |
| Pan and zoom | yes (§16.3) | opt out |
| Which rung of a collection (§3.4) | seeded from the lead, then the zoom's | yes |
| Score column and balancing | seeded from the lead | yes |
| Derived values — O/E, the smoothing and the arms (§7.5, §8.15) | seeded from the lead | yes |
| Transform and colormap | seeded from the lead | yes |
| `vmin` / `vmax` | one press (§16.5) | yes |

The rule is: **what is being looked at** is shared, **how it is drawn** is not — and every row of
the second kind is set on the *Map* card of the **starred** map, or on every map at once while none
is starred (§16.5).

A rung is now *also* what a zoom reads from (§2), which does not change the row above but sharpens
it: the picker still names the map a panel is **addressed** as, the link still carries it, and a
reader who touches it has said something the zoom does not overrule. Concretely, **the rung that is
open is the finest one a zoom may use.** Somebody who opened the 2 kb level of a
`100/200/500/1000/2000/5000` file has said *2 kb*; a zoom that fetched the 100 bp level would be
overruling them with their own file. Coarser rungs are still the zoom's to choose, that being the
direction the picker did not rule on. What the zoom chooses is which level
answers one bounded read, and that is a fact about a picture rather than about an address.

**Resolution is the one thing on the shared side of that line that cannot be shared**, and it is why
the lock's currency is base pairs (§16.3). That is also what lets panels refine independently: five
maps each reading their own window at their own grid stay in step, because the lock was never
counting cells. Two files rarely have the same ladder, so a deck lands an `.mcool` on the lead's
bin size where that rung exists and otherwise on the rung a collection opened at its root lands on, a
third of the way up from its finest (§9) — the right guess, and only a guess: the rung that makes a
comparison legible is not always the one that matches a number. So the entry is a picker, as the
`::1000` beside the companion's name, and the choice is written into that panel's own address rather
than held beside it. That is what makes it stick: the map reopens at the rung the reader chose after
