every navigation, every change of chromosome, and through the link.

A change of the **first map's** rung is the deck's, though — from the breadcrumb's picker, a link or
*match all resolutions* — and every companion follows it there, exactly or not at all: a file without
that level stays where it is and says so in a line under its own heading, rather than being moved to
the nearest rung and leaving the deck at two resolutions with nothing said.

**The turn sits on the shared side, and it is the one setting of the Map card that does.** A lead
drawn as a band along its diagonal beside four squares is five pictures in two coordinate systems
under a bar claiming one navigation: the lock's rows are separation on a band and position on a
square (§16.3), so there is no per-map turn to offer. The turn on a companion's card is the deck's
turn, and pressing it turns every map.

**The score and the derivations moved to the other side.** They used to be shared — one panel
drawing O/E beside four drawing raw counts was argued to be four wrong comparisons rather than a
choice — and each was applied by every panel and offered by the lead alone. What that cost was the
reader's own comparison: *this replicate normalised, that one raw* had no control anywhere, and the
Map card said *every map* about half its rows and *the first map* about the other half without
saying which were which. Each map now **opens on the lead's** score, O/E, smoothing and arms, so a deck
nobody has touched is exactly the deck it was, and from then on each is **that map's own** — set on
its card while it is starred, remembered with its clip (`deck:looks`), and read by every picture,
export and analysis of it. A normalisation, a correlation and the baseline are answers to *what are
these cells*, which is the score, so a companion draws them off **its own** score: picking `VC` on a
companion used to label it VC and draw it however the lead was normalised.

The selection has to be shared, or a deck showing four files at four regions is four unrelated
pictures that happen to be adjacent. It is shared **by name** — `chrI:20,000-80,000`, a list
of ticked sequences — and each companion resolves the name through its own reader. That is what makes
the feature affordable, and it is also what makes its failures well worded: a file with no `chrI` is
refused by `parse_metacooler_range`'s own error, listing its own sequences (§5.4). No gate had to be
written for that case and none could have phrased it better.

The score a companion is **seeded with** is the lead's **resolved choice**, not the hash key that
named it. The resolution runs through the *file's* default as every view's own picker does — read
straight from the state it said `count` for a map whose picker said `balanced`. A companion is told
whether its score is balanced as well as which it is: under `log10` a balanced cell is negative, and
the automatic range keeps negatives only when it is told the matrix is balanced — a companion that
was not drew a blank rectangle over perfectly good data. A file somebody balanced opens balanced
and that default is nowhere in the URL, so two panels each applying their own default would
disagree silently; the seed is what stops that. Each panel still resolves the id against its *own*
columns, so a file that cannot serve it falls back to counts rather than to a read it has no answer
for. A companion's score, O/E and smoothing are not in the hash — the hash carries the lead's —
and travel as its clip does, in the session's memory, the workspace and the durable record — and in a
share link for a companion the recipient can open, a local one's look being keyed on a filename off
the sender's own disk and left out.

A companion **opens on the lead's scale, clip included**: a map put beside another is put there to
be compared with it. The exception is that fallback — a panel drawing counts because it has no
weights must not inherit a clip measured in balanced units, which would draw a perfectly good map as
a black rectangle. There it takes the transform and the ramp and finds its own bounds.

The clip is still the panel's own from then on. `vmax` is a number of contacts, and two libraries sequenced to
different depths do not have the same one — one clip across a deck draws the shallower file as an
empty rectangle. This is §5.7's argument reached from the other side: there, one grid forces one
scale, and a second file of another depth is drawn to the first's total (§6.5) rather than rescaled;
here, two grids allow two scales. Drawing every map to one total, with the chevrons after the
breadcrumb's *contacts* box, puts the libraries themselves at one depth; a reader who knows they are
comparable as stored presses **match all scales**, which copies the starred map's clip onto every
panel once (§16.5). A press rather than a setting, because a setting
could not keep its promise: left on, every later nudge of any panel's clip either had to be undone
or left the deck claiming a shared scale it no longer had. After the press each clip is honestly its
panel's own again, which is the stronger claim made only where it is true.

### 16.3 The navigation lock

The currency is **base pairs**, measured from each block's own start, and not matrix cells.

That is the whole of why panels can be honestly locked where triangles cannot. A 1 kb file and a 5 kb
file both answer `chrI:20,000-80,000`; the answers are 60 cells and 12. A lock in cells moves the
coarse panel five times too far, and would have to be gated on a matching bin size — which is exactly
§5.7's refusal, reintroduced for no reason. A lock in base pairs is one division and one
multiplication per axis at each end.

**Above bin level the currency is the cell index** (`panels/lock.ts`'s `LockUnit`). A cell there is a
whole sequence and has no width in base pairs — the number a panel answers for it is the file's bin
size — and a window converted through it put chromosomes 10–14 of a 1 kb roll-up on chromosomes 2–3
of the 5 kb roll-up beside it. Cell `i` is sequence `i` in both, so the index is what the two grids
share and what a contig-level deck navigates by, while the two roll-ups have the same cells (§16.4).
A panel still drawing the other level is moved to no window at all, and the pointer's echoes say
*nothing here* between two maps at two levels, as they do off the end of a shorter block.

Conversion **rounds outward**: a window landing between two coarse cells becomes the smallest cell
window containing it, so a coarse panel shows at least what was asked for and never less. A window
running off the end of a shorter block is **slid back inside it, keeping its span**, not truncated to
whatever overlaps — truncating would answer a 40 kb view with a one-bin view, which is a wildly
different zoom in a deck whose whole promise is that the panels are showing the same thing. It is the
rule `HeatmapView.clampView` already follows for a pan against the edge of one map.

Both ends of the conversion read the grid **actually drawn**, which on a turned map (§16.2) is the
band and not the square it was rotated out of. A rotated cell is half a bin on both axes, and the
band is `2n − 1` columns wide; answering with the square's bin size and the square's column count
while reporting the band's window converts a whole-band view into twice the base pairs it covers and
then clamps it back to half the columns at the far end — every turned panel of a deck showing half of
what the one beside it shows. Up the side a turned panel's cells are half-bins of *separation*, so
two turned panels lock to each other in distance from the diagonal, which is the only thing they
could honestly share there.

There is one owner. Panels never speak to each other: each reports where it is and the lock decides.
With N panels each echoing to N−1 others there are N² conversations and no frame in which the deck is
in one state.

The feedback loop is real and is guarded three ways, because an echo has three shapes. A panel moved
programmatically redraws, and redrawing is how a panel reports — so every push returns as a report
one frame later, quantised to the receiving panel's grid and possibly slid inside its block.

1. The **synchronous** echo is swallowed by a flag held for the length of one broadcast.
2. A pushed panel is owed exactly **one** report and that report is thrown away. This is what stops a
   panel that *slid* from becoming the driver — without it, panning the lead past the end of the
   shortest companion's contig drags the lead back to where that companion stopped, which turns "pan
   past the end of the short one" into "you cannot pan past the end of the short one", in a deck
   assembled precisely because the files are not identical.
3. Anything arriving later at what is, to within **half a cell of the reporting panel**, the window
   already broadcast is swallowed as the same window seen through that panel's quantisation — a
   resize, a re-fit, a second frame of one gesture.

Without (3) a two-resolution deck drifts one coarse cell per frame until it hits a wall.

Any panel may be taken off the lead individually, the lead included.

**A companion off the lead reads its own window.** A box drawn on it with Option held (§5.4's
marquee, Option+Shift to hold it square on the diagonal) is a read of **that window, for that map**,
as finely as the rung it is open at (§16.2) and its share of the budget (§16.7) allow — not a
magnification of the block it already held. The same file open in three cells can then be a whole
196 Mb chromosome at 640 kb, a 35 Mb stretch of it at 80 kb and 6 Mb at 10 kb — before, the third
cell's box only enlarged a block read over the whole chromosome, which that budget capped at 50 kb,
and scrolling out gave back the chromosome it had never stopped holding. The window is shown as a
pill in the cell's heading, the locus it read, with **widen 3×** — the zoom step's own factor —
and **×**, which gives the map back to the deck's window. It is held by name, like the deck's own
selection (§16.2), resolved through the map's own reader, and remembered with its looks
(`deck:looks`); relinking the chain drops it, since a chained map shows the lead's window by
definition.

**Every map cell's heading names the sequence its map is on**, and is the road to another one. A
quiet picker beside the name — the rung's own idiom (`::1000`) — lists the cell's **own** file's
sequences in its order and in its names, and stands on the one the block it read is of; a block between
two says `IV × V`, one over several says how many, neither of which is a place to go. On a companion a
pick is a window of its own, the **whole** of that sequence: the map leaves the chain where it was on
it (a chained map shows the lead's window by definition), reads it at its own rung, and the others stay
where they are — so micro-C can stay on IV while Hi-C beside it shows V. It is the box's window in
every other respect: the pill says the map reads its own window (without repeating the name the picker
beside it says), its `×` gives it back to the deck's, and it is remembered with the map's looks. On the
first map a pick is the session's own navigation — the locus box's, the view as it is on another
sequence — so every map on the deck's window goes with it. A file of one sequence has nothing to pick
from, and one of more than a thousand has a table rather than a menu (a metagenome's contigs): there
the picker is not offered, and the box drawn on the cell is the road.

On a companion **still on the lead**, the same box navigates the deck — it is forwarded to the first
map's own marquee, so every chained map moves to it, which is what drawing a box on one of several
maps locked together can only mean. The pointer's echo between two maps that are not showing the
same window goes through the locus under it rather than through their cells, and the lanes'
echo is not drawn at all there: a lane position on one map is a different place on the other.

### 16.4 The compatibility gate, and why it is weaker

`compareRefusal` (§5.7) refuses a genome layer, a different bin size and a different chromosome list.
Each names a way the *blended* picture would be a lie. Side by side, two of the three objections
evaporate: two grids may be two resolutions, and each panel indexes its own list of sequences. The
third stands, and more strongly: a file with a genome layer holds no deck at all (§16.8).

What is left is the one claim panels actually make — *these two pictures are of the same place* — and
it is checked against the **blocks that came back**, not against the files. Two panels that resolved
one name to spans of different length resolved it against different sequences, whatever the name
says, and a shared window between them would be two places. The tolerance is one cell of the coarser
panel **per sequence on the axis**, because the last bin of a contig may be short (§3.3) and a
stricter test would refuse every honest pair whose bin size does not divide the contig — and a cell
never straddles two sequences, so an axis of sixteen chromosomes rounds sixteen last cells, not one.

Above bin level, where the window is carried as a cell index (§16.3), two axes that agree about how
much sequence they hold must also roll up into the same number of cells, or cell `i` is not the same
sequence on both; a pair that does not is refused in those words, and back at bin level it follows. A
panel still drawing the level the deck has just left is *not following yet*, and says so, until its
own read of the new level lands.

A **turned** deck (§16.2) has a second way to disagree, and it is a different fact. Up the side of a
band is distance from the diagonal, and two bands cut to different depths — each a whole number of
its own bins — would make one row window two distances. That refusal is about the *bands* and not
about the sequences, and it is worded as such: borrowing the sentence above would tell a reader their
files resolved one name against different sequences when they did not, which is a claim they may act
on. It goes away when the deck is turned back off. The deck cuts every turned companion to the first
map's reach, in base pairs (§17.3), so two bands agree by construction wherever both blocks hold that
much, and the refusal says the one way left for them not to: the band was cut to the first map's
reach, and this map's block does not hold that much. Each used to be cut to its own box, and boxes
measured while the grid was still settling made two depths out of a layout race, which this refusal
then blamed on the files' resolutions — and went on blaming them, *each map opens on a fraction of
its own block*, after the deck had stopped cutting that way.

A panel the gate refuses is **still shown**, still readable and still exportable. Only the lock is
off, and the panel says so in a line under its own heading rather than only in a tooltip on a chain
icon — a lock that claims to be closed while the deck skips it is the one way this can be quietly
wrong, and a still map reads as data.

### 16.5 Layout, and the side panels

The panels are a CSS grid of equal columns, as many across as the reader asked for — with a `+` on an
edge (§16.9) or with the picker in the deck's bar. Equal always: a comparison whose halves are
different sizes is one the eye has to correct for.

**The session's heading leaves the first cell.** The view's title, its locus box, its zoom steps and
its block summary answer *what am I looking at*, which is one question however many pictures are on
screen — so in a deck they are hoisted above the grid and the lead's cell holds the map and its file
name, exactly as every other cell does, wherever it stands. Left inside, they made the first cell a head taller than the
others and the first map was drawn smaller than the maps it is there to be compared with. The
element is **moved**, not rebuilt, so the box keeps its caret and the summary keeps the numbers the
last read wrote into it; it goes back when the deck is put down.

The deck's own count rides on the end of that summary — `113 × 113 bins · … · 3 maps`, and
`2 maps · 1 empty cell` while a cell stands empty — because how
many maps is a fact about what is being looked at, and the line that already says that is where a
reader is looking. Not in the bar, which is controls.

**The maps are aligned to the pixel, tracks or no tracks.** The room the deepest stack on each edge
takes, whichever map it is on, is *reserved* on every panel (§16.8), and each panel's
picture is pushed to the foot of its cell — the cells being equal, the plots are then the same size
at the same height whatever heading sits above them. Without it a map inset by a stack of tracks
stood beside a map that was not, which is a comparison the eye has to correct for before it can
begin, in the one widget whose entire purpose is that adjacent pictures are comparable.

**And a cell's lanes stay in its cell.** Three or four across, the first map's stacks — spatial
tracks down its left edge, genes and a signal or two down its right — can be wider than the cell
before the map has had a pixel, and the grid used to spill them over the next cell's heading and
locus box: a picture drawn across another picture. Inside a deck the map's column gives way down to
10rem, the floor the map's own size has, rather than the 20rem a whole column affords; what still
does not fit **scrolls sideways inside the cell** instead of being painted over its neighbour or cut
off out of reach, and the scroll starts with the map in the middle of the cell — left at its start,
a cell with a stack down its left edge showed that stack and no map at all.

**Rearranging is a drag, not a pair of arrows.** Every cell but an empty one has a grip before its
name, **the first map's included** — an empty cell is where the others are dragged *to*; taking hold
of one shows the tiling, and dropping it on a cell **exchanges** the two. `◀` `▶` could only say
*one place along a list*, which describes a 2 × 2 poorly: moving the
bottom-left map to the top-right was three presses, each shuffling everything in between. The first
map used to have a name and no grip, on the argument that it is the session's own view and which file
a session is of is not a thing a drag should change. Nor does the drag change it — the breadcrumb,
the tables and the tracks are the same file's afterwards — and a deck with one cell that could not be
moved was a deck whose first picture was wherever it happened to start. Where the lead stands is kept
in the session's memory beside the column count (§8.6), with whether it is shown and its chain
(§16.6), and not in `maps`, which lists the companions:
it is arrangement, like the columns, and a link that moved only the lead would say nothing new. A cell
closing before it moves it up with the rest of the grid, and a `+` re-seats it with every other cell,
in the row and column it had.

**Every cell's chain sits in its own heading, the lead's included.** Taking a cell off the shared
navigation (§16.3) is a statement about that cell, so the control for it belongs on it, beside the
star. The lead's used to be in the bar, which put one glyph at two heights meaning the same
per-cell thing — and the one in the bar, among controls that act on every cell, read as a lock over
the whole deck rather than as the first map's own. It is drawn like every other toggle in the
application: lit while the cell is following, plain while it is not, and dimmed never (§26.3).

The deck's bar holds what is shared, in the order the work is done: **add a cell…**, which opens the
row that takes a file, a published URL, the session's 3D structure or a stack of tracks (§16.11);
**match all scales** and **match all resolutions**, two presses that each copy the starred map's
clip or bin size onto every panel once — greyed, with that reason on them, while no map is starred,
there being nothing to match *to*; how many across; and the whole deck as one figure — saved, or
copied to the clipboard, which is what `⌘C` reaches while a deck is on.

The deck's figure is **one arrangement written two ways**: a PNG at a resolution — the bar's 300
dpi, or the Export card's — and a PDF that is a vector page, each cell drawn on it as its own PDF
draws it: a map's cells the one image of that map, its axes, lanes, key and caption round them
paths and text; the tracks, the browser as lead and a model paths and text throughout. One
composition lays both out (`panels/deckFigure.ts`) — every cell the size of the largest, the same
air between — so the two files cannot disagree about where a cell stands; the PNG rasterises each
cell and places it, the page places each cell's own drawing. The deck adds nothing of its own but the
page under them, which is white in either theme (§7.2): each cell carries its own caption, key and
frame, as on screen, and an empty cell stays empty. The PDF used to be the PNG on a page, so six panels' axes and track names left as
pixels in the one file meant to be a drawing. A PDF's file name carries no resolution; a PNG's
does.

The Aesthetics column's **Export** card saves and copies that same figure whenever any cell beside
the first map has a picture of its own — a map, a structure, a stack of tracks — and the first map's
own figure only while every other cell is empty. The figure is the cells as
they stand on screen: the first map where it was moved to, and not at all while it is hidden (§16.9). It used to ask for another
*map*, so a deck of a map beside its 3D model exported the map alone from the card, while the bar's
button beside it wrote both: two exports of one screen disagreeing about what was on it.

Rearranging is the grip and is not a button here. **Adding is**, and that is the one thing the bar
repeats: a `+` on an edge draws an *empty* cell for something to be dropped on, and a published
cooler has nothing to drop — the URL box is the only road it can take (§11) — while the tracks cell
has no other road on screen at all. The toggle is named for what the row opens, a *cell*, rather
than for the map that is only one of the four things in it.

It is **read from the left**, in one run, with exactly one control across the gap at the far right:
**close deck**, a bordered word like every other control in the bar (§5.4). Everything else in the
bar adjusts a deck that is staying, and a destructive control in among them is one a hand reaches by
accident; a window's close has been at that end for thirty years. It was the same bare × a cell's
own close is, on the argument that the two would read as one gesture at two scales — and what they
read as is two identical marks a finger's width apart, one taking a cell and the other taking every
companion and the lanes drawn on them, which is the accidental reach this placement exists to
prevent. What it closes is every cell but the first map's, and **never a track**: a bigWig dropped
on a companion's edge is an import into the session's one track list, and closing the maps it was
drawn on is a statement about layout, not about what the reader loaded. A lane that was only on the
companions is moved onto the first map, at the edge it was on, and noted against the companion's
file, so it goes back where it was when that file is in a cell again; it used to be deleted with the
maps, so a reader who gave four replicates a bigWig each lost three imports to a gesture about how
many pictures were on screen. A track that is also on the first map is being read against a picture
that is staying, so it keeps its lane there and loses only the companions'. The first map stays — on
screen again if it was hidden (§16.9) — and the companions are **put away, not let go**: each is held
on the Contact maps card, hidden, as the × on its own cell holds it (§16.9) — the card's × is where a
map is let go, and the eye there opens a cell for it again.

**The Aesthetics column's *Map* card is the starred map's**, as its *3D structure* card is the
starred structure cell's (§25.3). Every map of a deck has a card — the score, the smoothing, the
picture row with its O/E, the transform, the ramp, the clip, the overlays — and the column shows
**one**: the first map's while it is starred, a companion's while the star is on that companion,
swapped in the first map's place so the cards around it stay where they were. Moving the star
moves the card; a setting changed on it changes **that map and no other**. A line under the card's
title names the map it sets, with the star it was starred by, so a reader never has to infer from
the numbers which picture the card is about — and a companion starred before its map is drawn, or
one that could not open, gets a card that names it and says its settings arrive with the map,
never the first map's card standing in for it. The one row on it that reaches further is the turn,
which is the deck's (§16.2) and is on every map's card for that reason — and `ori` beside it, which
frames the window every map reads (§8.15); the overlays are preferences about every picture in the
app, as they always were.

**The General column's *File* card follows the star too.** It describes the starred map's file — a
companion's bin size, format, pixel count and the rest once its panel has opened the file, and a line
saying they arrive then until it has — under the same line the *Map* card carries: the map's name,
with the star. With the star on the first map, or on none (the star shown dark), it is the session's
own file, and a comparison's *File 1* and *File 2* are the first map's two triangles, so they stand
aside while a companion is starred. It used to describe the first map whatever was starred, under a
heading that did not say which file it was: a reader who starred a Hi-C map beside a micro-C one read
the micro-C file's bin size as the map they had just chosen.

**The star can be on no map.** A filled star is live — pressed, it leaves none filled — and then the
column shows the first map's card with *every map — all N* under its title, in the warn colour: a
setting changed there is made to **every map of the deck at once**, one moved setting at a time, so
picking a ramp does not also flatten each map's clip onto the first one's. That is also the state in
which no task that reads a map can run, and the 1D tasks, which read none, still do (§18.1). *None*
holds for as long as the deck does, and a deck put down leaves the next one starred on its first
map, which is where every deck starts.

A companion's settings used to ride **on its picture**: a button in the bottom-left corner of the map
opening a menu upward over it, with the score, the transform, the ramp and the clip, while the Map
card in the column set the first map — so a deck had two places that set a map, a card that said
nothing about which map it set, and half its rows (the turn, the O/E, the smoothing) reaching every
map from a card that looked like the first map's. The menu is gone; nothing is drawn on a
companion's picture but the picture.

**A card that cannot act is absent** (§8.5). The Map, Tracks and Export cards arrive with the block
and not before: behind the whole-genome gate — a heading, what the read would cost, and the button
that starts it — the column used to show the whole Map card over an empty canvas, clip and all, and a
reader who nudged the clip there and saw nothing happen concluded the card was broken. The **overlays**
row holds only the marks that light: the refit, which is an action, stands with the turn and the
diagonal lock in the *picture* row, where it used to be the one unlit mark in a row of seven lit ones —
read as an overlay that was off, and turned on by a press that threw the reader's pan away.

The deck's controls ride **above the grid**, and are deliberately not another card in the side
columns. Those columns are the *session's* furniture. The argument used to add that one of them —
Annotations — did not exist at all on a file with a genome layer, the kind of file a deck was
expected to be most useful for; its cards are offered on every container now (§8.5), and a file with
a genome layer holds no deck at all (§16.8). A **map's** settings are in the Aesthetics column all
the same, because that column is present on every file a map can be drawn from, and it is where the
first map's always were: the star says which map's.

The grid is inside `.content`, which pins the light palette **while it holds a picture** — a deck's
grid, a map's heatmap or a browser's stage — so the maps do not change colour in the dark theme and
no rule had to be written to keep them from it. The furniture framing a picture is pinned with it,
since a locus box in dark chrome beside a light map belongs to neither. The pin used to be on
`.content` itself, and every view mounts there: a reader who chose dark got the landing page, the
Genomes and Chromosomes tables, the whole-genome gate and the error view as a white sheet inside a
dark frame. A drop zone and a table of chromosome lengths are not figures that will be exported, and
the argument for pinning was only ever about the ones that are.

### 16.6 Links

One key, `maps`, holding the companions in order.

Pipe-separated, not comma-separated like `genomes` and `regions`. A comma is legal in a URI path, so
`maps=a,b` resolves — to two maps that are neither of the ones that were sent — the first time
somebody publishes `sample,rep1.cool`. RFC 3986 excludes `|` from every part of a URI, so the split
cannot be wrong. It is left unescaped in the hash for the reason the comma is: `maps=a.cool|b.cool`
is a list at a glance and `maps=a.cool%7Cb.cool` is not.

A **local** companion is written as `~`, not omitted. `uri2` omits its local second file, which is
right when there is one slot: its absence says *nothing here*, which is true. With N slots omission
moves every companion after it one place to the left, so a deck of `[remote, local, remote]` arrives
as a deck of two with nothing anywhere saying a map is missing. The placeholder keeps the count and
the order, and the recipient gets a drop rectangle where the sender's file was. A cell the sender
drew empty (§16.9) is the same `~` and travels the same way, so an arrangement nobody has filled yet
is a link like any other.

`maps` **survives a navigation within one file**, and so does `uri2`. A navigation builds a fresh
state — `{ uri, view: 'contigs' }` and nothing else — which is right for the region, the genome, the
level and the pair, and wrong for the two keys that name what is on screen *beside* the view.
Without carrying them, clicking Chromosomes and then a contig, the plainest way there is to look at
another chromosome, arrived with no `maps`: the deck reconciled itself to nothing and released its
workers on the way past a table. Same file **by path**, so changing the resolution keeps the deck
and opening a different file does not. The carrying is the session's and not the store's — the
address bar is obeyed exactly as written, or a pasted link would show a deck nobody sent.

Nothing else is in the hash. The lock and the drawn column count live in the per-file session
memory (§8.6) beside the table filters, on the same grounds: the hash has never carried a pan or a
zoom, so there is nothing there for a lock to be consistent with, and how many
columns the grid has is furniture in the sense the width of a side panel is. Which cells are empty is
*not* furniture and is in the hash, because it is part of the list of maps rather than part of how
they are arranged — a deck of three with a gap in the middle is a different deck from a deck of
three.

The lock is kept a chain at a time: a companion's with its look (`deck:looks`), the first map's
beside its place (`deck:lead`, written only while it is open). So a reload, a restored workspace and
a deck built again all bring back every map that was moving on its own, the first included — whose
chain used to come back closed, driving the deck, whatever the reader had left it.

The lanes drawn on companions are kept the same way, each against its companion's file
(`deck:lanes`, a workspace's `lanes`), and come back as the maps do: parked until a cell opens that
file, then put under it at the edge they were on. Two things decide that they do come back. The
record is **read before the tracks are restored**, because restoring a track writes the session's
lanes — none yet — over it; and a lane waits **for its track as well as for its map**, since a cell
can open before the track it carries has been read. Either wrong, and a workspace whose MNase was
drawn under each of three maps opened with every companion bare and the track on the first map only.

### 16.7 Cost

`checkBrowserDenseSize` budgets **one** block against a share of what the device reports, and has no
idea how many blocks are about to be live. Five whole-genome coolers are five dense blocks, five
rasters and five pooled buffers, all resident, each passing a guard that was asked about one.

So the deck divides. Every panel is read with `budgetBytes` set to the deck's whole allowance — one
panel's — divided by the number of panels. Two consequences, both wanted: a deck can never cost more
than the single map it replaced, and **every map added shrinks every panel's share**, so an
over-large deck is refused by arithmetic rather than by a limit somebody had to guess. The refusal is
`checkBrowserDenseSize`'s own, with its own numbers in it, printed beside the panel it is about. The share
also sets how wide a window the panel reads bin for bin (`denseCellCap`, §7.2) — a deck of four reads
a whole chromosome a panel cannot afford pooled rather than refused — and the panel's zoom judges its
blocks against that same share, so it never waits for a finer block its reads will not return.

The answers kept so that a place visited again costs nothing (§12) are not divided: they are one
budget for the page however many panels it holds, so a deck of eight keeps fewer places per panel
than one map does, and never more memory. A panel's answers go with its worker.

Above that sits a backstop of **64 cells including the lead**, an 8 × 8 grid (`MAX_PANELS`). It was
a hard ceiling of six, for the reason `MAX_SESSIONS` has one: a panel is a worker and an h5wasm
instance whether or not its block is large. But six was a judgement about how many maps are useful
rather than about the machine, and a figure is however many panels it has — a row of eight replicates
is a legitimate thing to want. The share above is the limit, measured in bytes on the machine in
front of the reader; the backstop is there so that a hand-edited hash asking for thousands of cells is
cut to it before thousands of workers are started. Reaching it is said in the deck's bar, and on a
`+` edge that would pass it, which is greyed with the reason rather than removed — never on an error
screen.

### 16.8 What is not offered

A companion answers views that name a **place** — a region, a genome, a pair, a selection, the whole
file. The two tables and the whole-metagenome scan (§7.3) are pictures of a *file*, and a second
file's genomes table is not this one with more rows in it. "Add a map" is disabled there rather than
hidden, so the answer to "can this viewer do that" is *yes, from a map*.

**Nor is there a deck on a file with a genome layer** (§8.5), which is why a genome and a pair,
places as they are, never reach a companion. A deck's panels must share a coordinate system, and two
metagenomes have none: their axes are contigs from two independent assemblies, so a region that names
a place in one names nothing in the other, and the lock would move the maps to different places. The
`+` edges are absent there, "Add a map" is greyed, a `maps=` in a link builds nothing, and a cooler
dropped on the session opens as its map rather than beside it.

A companion **does** carry tracks, and that is a change from what this section used to say. §8's
contig-naming contract is between a track and one file's `/contigs`, and the reason a lane beside a
companion looked like a fourth thing keyed on a third assembly is that the *track* and the *lane*
were one object. They are two now (§8.1): a track is the import and the style true of it
everywhere, a lane is one placement of it on one map. There is still exactly one list of tracks and
one contig contract; what a deck adds is where each of them is drawn.

Which forces one rule on the layout. **Every map leaves room for the deepest stack on each edge**,
whichever map has it, and pads out the difference between that and its own. Without it a map with a
strip above it stands lower than a map without one, and two pictures of one place have to be
corrected for before they can be read against each other — which is the whole thing a deck is for.
The figure is asked of every panel at the moment it is used rather than accumulated as the panels
report: they announce their stacks in whatever order they finish reading, and a running maximum is a
maximum over whoever has spoken so far.

### 16.9 Drawing the deck

A `+` down the right-hand edge of the map, and another along the bottom. Pressing one opens a
**cell**, not a map: what comes back is the arrangement the reader asked for, with their own map in
the first of it and every other cell standing empty as a drop target. The empty cells are filled in
any order, from a drop, a file chooser or a URL, or never.

**An empty cell takes anything a deck can hold**, not a map alone. It reads *drop a map, a track or a
structure*: a contact map dropped on it opens there as a map; a **track** — a file, or a row dragged
from the Tracks card — opens a *tracks cell* there drawing it, the file loaded into the session's one
list of tracks and placed on that cell, the row placed on it while staying on every map it was
already drawn on; and a **structure** — a file, or a row of the Structures card — opens its model.
A row dragged out of the Files panel is routed the same way, by the name of the file it names. It
used to say *drop a map here*, which was true of the one kind it then took and hid the other two:
a tracks cell had no road on screen but the bar's row. Where the session carries no tracks (§8.5)
it does not promise one.

It **answers a drag with an effect the drag allows**. A drop target's effect has to be one the
source's `effectAllowed` includes, or the browser refuses the drop with no event at all: the Tracks
card's rows allowed only a *move*, the cell answered a *copy*, and a row dropped there slid back to the
card while a test that dispatched the `drop` itself saw it land. The rows allow either now — moved up
and down the card and onto a map's edge, placed on a cell — and an empty cell answers with what the
drag allows (`ui/dom.ts`'s `dropEffectFor`).

This is the first entry point a reader can *find*, and until there is a deck it is the only one on
screen — once there is, its bar offers *add a cell…* beside it (§16.5). Before either, the first
companion was reachable only through the command palette, so nothing on screen said several maps side
by side was a thing this viewer did. The one gesture a reader would try, dropping a second cooler on
the map, now builds a deck too: a contact map dropped on an open session opens **beside** what is
there, as a companion in the first empty cell or a new one at the end — the road the bar's URL box
takes — and several dropped at once fill a deck (§16.11). Replacing the open file is a deliberate act
elsewhere: *Open a different file*, or a new tab.

**Cells before maps, and that is the design rather than an ordering.** Adding maps one at a time
makes the arrangement a consequence of the order the files arrived in, and the arrangement is what
somebody assembling a figure is composing: two conditions across and two timepoints down is a
statement about the experiment, and reaching it by dropping four files into a row and then pressing
`◀` twice is repairing a layout rather than drawing one. So the shape is drawn first and is a thing
the reader states, not a thing that happens to them.

**The shape is a rectangle, filled in reading order.** `+` beside adds a column, `+` below adds a
row, and both add the whole edge — a single extra cell on the right of a two-row grid is not
expressible without pushing every map after it one place along, and a press must never move a map
that has already been placed. A ragged last row, which is what closing a map out of the middle
leaves, is squared up by the next press for the same reason: the holes are drop targets and the
rectangle is the shape that was drawn.

The column count a `+` sets is remembered per file (§8.6), and the bar's **N across** picker is the
other way to set it. The two write the same number, so the grid and the picker cannot disagree.
There are no layout presets to override any more: a row of lit presets arranged however many maps
happened to be open, which is not a shape a reader states, and a deck that reflowed into a row the
moment a map was closed was not an arrangement at all. The picker is the honest replacement, and it
is also the only way a deck that arrived in a link can be reshaped — a `+` only ever grows one.

**An empty cell is a real cell.** It takes a slot in `maps`, travels through a link as `~`, counts
towards the 64-cell backstop (§16.7), and can be closed like any other — and moved, by dropping
another cell on it, having no grip of its own (§16.5). It does **not** count towards the memory
budget (§16.7): an empty card has no worker and no block, and dividing the allowance by it would read
the two maps of a 2 × 2 deck at a quarter each while half went to rectangles.

The `~` it is written with is the same one §16.6 introduced for a local companion, and the two are
deliberately not told apart in the hash: to the recipient they are the same thing, a position with
no file in it and a rectangle where the map goes. Within the session that drew them they are told
apart in words only — a cell a reader drew offers to take a map, a track or a structure, and one a
link left says a map was here — because telling somebody a map used to be in a cell they drew
empty a moment ago is a small lie about their own deck.

A **collection** dropped into a cell opens one of its maps rather than refusing. An `.mcool` is a
ladder of complete coolers and is not a map at its root (§3.4), so opening one by name is an error
about `::` syntax the reader never typed, standing where their picture should be. The rung to land
on is the **lead's bin size**: two files with the same ladder are comparable at any of them, and the
finest-regardless rule would put a 1 kb map beside a 16 kb one and call it a comparison. What was
opened is written back into `maps`, so the link names the map rather than the collection — resolved
against a recipient's own lead it could otherwise be a different rung.

A file **dropped on an edge** opens the cell that edge names and fills it in one movement, which is
the gesture a reader tries first. It goes into the cell that press opened **nearest the edge** — the
top of a new column, the left of a new row — rather than the first empty cell in the deck: the two
differ only when the deck already had a hole somewhere, and there the aim is the tie-breaker. Not
the first cell the press opened, either: a press below a short last row squares that row up too
(above), and the first of its new cells sits in a row above the one the reader pressed for. A map
arriving by any other road — the bar's URL box, the file chooser, the command palette — takes the
first empty cell instead, because those name no position and the empty cells are the reader's own
instruction about where the next map goes.

**A file let go on a filled cell is that cell's too, wherever on it the hand lets go**
(`PanelDeck`'s `watchFileDrops`). On a companion's map it means what the rectangle in the map's
middle means, *on this map* (§8.1): a track drawn on that map on its usual edge, an overlay on its
face. On a tracks cell it is a track drawn in that cell, at its foot, where every track on one is
drawn. A row dragged out of the Files column or out of a store (§20.5, §24.2) is aimed the same way
as a file off the disk. What a file *is* is still decided by its name, where every drop's is: a
contact map let go on a map is a map, beside it — the first empty cell, or a new one — and a
structure opens a cell of its own (§25.3), which a structure cell, answering for itself, does too.
The map's own rectangles keep their drop, being aimed more finely, and so does an empty cell. While
the file is in the air the cell that will take it is outlined, as a cell a map is carried to is, and
the outline goes while the hand is over one of the map's rectangles, which then say where. A
companion used to take a file on its rectangles alone and a tracks cell on nothing, so a track let go
on the lanes under the second map, on its heading or anywhere on a tracks cell was loaded under the
first map — the content area's answer to a drop nothing else took, and still the answer on the first
map's own cell, which is the session's.

**Rows of the Tracks and Structures cards take the edges too.** A Tracks card row dropped on a `+`
opens the cells with a tracks cell drawing that track in the one nearest the edge — *placed*, as on
an empty cell, so it stays on every map it was drawn on. A Structures card row opens its model there
and **moves** it: a cell that was drawing it is left **empty where it stands** rather than closed.
Closing it closed the grid up in reading order, and the new cell slid into the place the model had
just left, so the drop read as two empty cells and nothing else.

**A lane carried by its grip goes anywhere a track can be drawn, and it is a move**: drawn where it
is let go, and taken off the edge it came from. Onto a rectangle round **another map** — they light
on every map while a lane is in the air, not only on the map it is leaving — it is drawn on that edge
of that map. Onto a `+`, it opens the cells with a tracks cell drawing it in the one nearest the edge;
onto an **empty cell**, that cell becomes a tracks cell — the 1D browser of it; onto a **tracks
cell**, that cell draws it. **A lane in a tracks cell is carried the same way**, by the same grip
that reorders the cell's stack: over the cell itself it goes on moving up and down the stack, and
past the cell's border it is a carry like any other, lighting every map's rectangles, the `+` edges
and the other cells. It used to reorder and nothing else, so a track sent to a cell of its own could
not be carried on from there. The cells show their tiling while a lane is carried, as they do while a
cell is. An overlay group travels as the one lane it is on screen; a lane arriving on a map it was not
on is turned for the edge it lands on (§8.9); and what it held of its own on the map it left — a
ceiling, set on that library's depth — stays behind with that map. **The lane is one edge's**: a
track drawn along two sides of a map, one of them carried away, is still drawn along the other — the
carry used to take it off the map altogether — and a grip let go on another of the same map's
rectangles moves that lane there and leaves the track's lane on a third side where it is. Whatever
stays behind is turned for the edge it is left on before the lane lands, so the lane that left is not
turned with it. The Tracks card is where a track is put somewhere *as well*. The grip drag is a
pointer drag captured by the lane it began on, so nothing else on the page hears it as a drag: the
places a lane can land answer where the pointer is through one registry instead (`ui/laneCarry.ts`).

**A `+` that fills the cell it opens writes the deck once, filled.** The deck is written into the
link and the session reads the link back a moment later, so two writes in one gesture — the empty
cell, then the filled one — came back as two states, the first of them no longer what the deck held,
and the deck rebuilt its cells from it: a lane let go on a `+` went back to the map it had left, and
the new cell stood empty.

**Every map the session holds is a row of the Contact maps card**, in the order the grid holds
them — the first map where its cell stands, with the one in its lower triangle (§5.7) under it, which
is the one square, and each companion under the name its cell's heading gives it — then the maps held
hidden, which have no cell to be in the order of. The card used to list the first two only, so a
deck of four maps showed a card of one and the other three were named nowhere in the column; and
then it listed the first map first wherever its cell had been moved to.

Each companion's row has an **eye** and an **×**, and they are two acts, as on a track's row. The
eye is the Structures card's (§25.3): lit, the map is in a cell, and pressing it takes the map out
and keeps it on the card, dimmed, with its eye dark; pressed again, the map opens in the first
empty cell, or in a new one at the end of the grid — the road every map that names no position takes
— drawn as it was, its looks being remembered by its file.

**The × on a map's own cell is that eye, not a let-go.** Closing a contact map in the deck hides
it: the map is kept on the card, eye dark, exactly as the eye would keep it — it used to be dropped
from the session altogether, so a map closed to make room was a file to be found and opened again.
The **cell** goes only where the map was all it held. A track dropped on a companion's edge is
drawn in that cell and nowhere else, so a cell with tracks in it stays, as the tracks cell those
tracks make, under the same id they are placed by — rather than closing and parking them on the
first map, where the reader had not put them. The star cannot stand on a cell that is no longer a
map, and goes back to the first map. The card's own × is the one that **lets go**, with the same
rule for the cell; a map still on screen elsewhere — another cell of the same file, the first map,
the lower triangle — is not listed twice, and one already hidden is not listed again. A hidden map is held by the session
rather than by the deck, since a deck left with only the first map puts itself down, and it is let
go by its × or when the session's own file closes; it is not in the link, which carries cells. Its
eye is greyed in a view no deck frames (§16.8), which has nowhere to open it. The compared map's eye
keeps its meaning, the lower triangle taken away (§5.7), and so does the first map's where there is
no deck: the 1D browser. **In a deck the first map's eye is its cell's**, as every other map's is —
it used to put the map down for the browser there too, which re-read the state with no map to lead,
and a deck of maps cannot stand beside a browser (§25.3): the companions went with it.

**The first cell closes like any other.** Its × is on its heading, after its star and chain, while
another cell is beside it — a × on the one cell of a deck would leave nothing on screen. What it does
is the eye's: the cell leaves the screen, and it is **parked, not closed**. Its view stays mounted
behind the grid, at a column's width and out of sight, because it is what the rest of the deck
follows — the maps' lock, the window a structure or tracks cell lights, the locus box above the grid,
which goes on steering the deck — and a view taken out of the page would measure nothing and report
nothing. The session is still of its file, and its tables and tracks are what they were; a track
dropped while it is hidden is on it, as ever. It comes back **where it stood**: from the eye on its
row, now dimmed, and from a `show …` in the deck's bar — the only road for the 1D browser as lead,
which has no row on the card, and which it names as `show the 1D browser` rather than by the genome's
name, which for a model that opened the session is the model's own file. It comes back by itself
when the last cell beside it goes, since the deck is then put down and the view goes back to its own
frame, which it must not reach hidden; *close deck* is that too. While it is hidden the star cannot
stand on a map nobody can see — the *Map* card would be setting a picture off the screen — and moves
to the first map still on screen, where there is one; the deck's count says the maps on screen, and
its figure, its copy and the Export card's save are of the cells on screen. Hidden or not, it is
remembered with its place, in this session's memory and in a saved workspace (§8.6) — which brings
both back whether it is dropped on the window or opened from its address, a published figure or a
`?config=` link, whose names are resolved against it on the way in (§21.1). The second road used to
lose them: resolving rebuilt the deck from the fields it knew, and the lead's was not among them.

Every row has a **grip**, the Tracks card's own, and a row dragged onto a cell **puts that map
there**: a companion's row onto another cell exchanges the two, exactly as its cell's own grip
would, and onto a `+` edge moves it into the cell nearest the edge, leaving an empty one where it
stood; a hidden map's row onto an empty cell, or onto a `+` edge, opens it there; the first map's or
the compared map's row, the same way, opens that file there as a new companion — the plainest way to
read one file at two windows or two colour scales. The first map's row onto a cell that holds
something moves the first map there, as its own grip would (§16.5), and a companion's row onto the
first map's cell exchanges the two. Taking hold of a row shows the tiling, as a cell's grip does.

**A row dragged up or down the card moves its map's cell**: let go above the middle of another map's
row, it goes before that map; below it, after — and the arrow keys on a focused grip move it one map
up or down, as on the Tracks card. It is an **insertion among the maps**, where a cell's grip
exchanges two cells: a list is reordered by insertion, and a reader carrying the eighth map to the top
of the card means *first*, not *swap with the first*. Only the seats maps stand in are dealt again,
so a tracks cell, a model and an empty cell keep their places while the maps move round them. The
first map moves the same way, its square with it; the compared map, being that square's lower
triangle, has no place of its own, and a hidden map has no cell to move. A move of the companions is
written into `maps`, and one of the first map alone into this session's memory, where its place is
kept (§16.5). Everything that follows the grid's order follows the move: the card, the deck's figure,
and the analysis — a batch's runs, the drawer's tabs, and the all-maps overlays and tables (§18.7).

### 16.10 Naming the maps

A map is labelled by its file, which is the right default and a poor name for the work: four
replicates of one experiment are four labels differing in a digit, and two conditions being compared
are `mat_G1.mcool::1000` and `mat_G2M.mcool::1000`, whose two informative characters are the last
thing anybody reads. So **any map a session is holding can be called something** — the one it is of,
the one it is compared against (§5.7), and every companion of a deck. The control is the Tracks
card's own, in both places it appears: an `<input>` that looks like text until it has the caret, on
the **Contact maps** card and on a deck cell's heading. Enter commits, Escape abandons, and an empty
box hands the map back to its file name, which is what makes a rename undoable. Tab commits and puts
the caret in the next name — the next row's on the card, the next cell's heading on a deck, which is
four replicates named in one go (§26.8).

The name is used **everywhere the map is named**, through one function: the card that lists it, the
heading over its cell, the two bands of a turned comparison (§17.2), the readout and the tooltip
under the pointer, the derived label on a ratio, and the caption on an exported figure. A rename is
not a rebuild — it changes what the picture is called and nothing about what is in it, and rebuilding
the view would put a gated whole-genome scan (§7.3) back behind its button.

**What a task makes of a map is named by it too** (§18). A run names the map it measured — the
drawer's tab for it, its line in the all-maps overlay and its rows in the all-maps tables (§18.7),
the lane or the model it adds (`<output> · <map>` on any map but the first, whose are the output's
name alone), a reproducibility run's matrix, tables and lines, and the console — by what the map is
called when the run is made, and never by its file:
`dparAB`, where the legend used to read `Bsubtilis_dparAB^mapped_PY79^NT9IOH.mcool::10000`. The
drawer's tabs, overlays and stacked tables are named afresh on every refresh, so a result computed
before a rename follows it; a lane, a model or a comparison's own figure is named when it is made
and keeps that name, which is then the reader's to change like any other row's. A track and a model
are the same: a run takes each chosen row's name as it is dispatched, and a task's form open over a
rename lists the row under its new name.

Three things about where the name lives:

- **One record per session, not one note per file.** Every name sits under the session's own memory
  key, keyed by the file each one is for — `deck:looks`'s arrangement, and for its reason: a
  workspace is gathered from one key, so a name filed under a companion's own key would be a name
  the saved session did not contain. It travels in the workspace, in the durable record and in a
  share link, beside the tab's own name — the link carrying only the names of maps a recipient can
  open, since a local map's is keyed on a filename off the sender's own disk. *Can open* is one test
  for every field of a link keyed on a file, the lanes' and the session's own included: an
  `https:`, `s3:` or `gs:` address (§24.5).
- **Keyed by the file, never by the rung**, so a name survives a change of resolution the way every
  other per-file fact does (§5.5). One consequence, which the deck's saved looks already had: one
  file open twice in a session has one name.
- **An empty name is not a name.** It is dropped rather than stored, so a map with no name is a map
  the record says nothing about — and a config that says nothing leaves the importing tab's names
  alone.

### 16.11 Cells that are not maps

A deck was *N maps*; it is now *N cells*, of which the maps are the kind the lock drives. Two
kinds hold no file: a **structure** cell drawing the session's 3D model, and a **tracks** cell
drawing the session's tracks alone (§25). Both answer the same short contract (`panels/cell.ts`):
adopt the view, be told the lead's window as loci, remeasure, repaint, export a canvas, be
destroyed. Everything the deck says to a *map* by name — a lock member, a lane floor, a bin size,
a colour scale, the star — it goes on saying to the maps only. A cell holds no file, so it takes no
share of the read budget (§16.7) and is not an empty card either; the bar counts it as neither.

Both are opened from the deck's add row — *add a 3D structure*, which opens one more structure cell
at every press, drawing the first model no other cell draws where there is one (§25.3), where it used
to be greyed with its reason once the deck had one; and *add a tracks cell*. Each leads with a verb,
like the rest of that row: labelled `3D structure` and `tracks`, as they were, two nouns at the end
of a row opened by a button saying *add* read as kinds of thing the URL box takes rather than as two
more cells to open.

In the link a structure cell is `3d` and a tracks cell `tracks`, in the `maps=` list where the
maps and the `~` of a vacancy are. A deck holds **as many structure cells as the reader asks for** —
a second `3d` opens a second cell, and two cells of one model are two views of it (§25.3) — and as
many tracks cells as the reader opens, named apart in the location control: by the name the reader
gave the cell (§25.3), or numbered where they gave none.

**A `~` is resolved against the cells the deck is already holding, before the record.** The hash can
say no more than `~` about a local map (§16.6), and what it is resolved against was the *stored*
record, re-opened through a filesystem grant. A file that arrived by **drag and drop** may have no
grant: outside Chromium the browser hands over a `File` rather than a handle, and nothing can ask for
one afterwards, and Chromium's handle is written down only once the file is opened
(`ui/chooseFiles.ts`). So
dropping four coolers opened four live panels, published, came back round, resolved none of them,
and replaced all four with vacancies reading *this cell held that file and it could not be
re-opened* — about files the deck still had in hand. A live cell is the best possible answer for its
own index and is asked first; the record answers for the rest; and both only ever over a `~`, so a
list naming a remote map or a structure cell at that index still wins.

**Only the state still in force is reconciled.** Asking the record for a grant is asynchronous, and
several coolers dropped at once are added one after another, each add a publish and each publish a
render of its own — `~`, then `~|~`, and so on. Every one of those renders waited for its grants and
came back after the last map had been added, so the render of `~` shrank the deck to one companion
and the renders after it grew it back from the record, which cannot re-open a dropped file: eight
coolers dropped on a new tab opened two or three maps and five or six vacancies. A render whose state
the store has since moved past reconciles nothing; the state that replaced it has a render of its
own, and that one says what the deck is.

## 17. The turn: 45°, distance up the side

A contact map is symmetric about its diagonal, and the diagonal is where all the signal is. So a
square map spends most of its area on the far corners, which are empty, and draws the part anybody
is reading as a thin bright band across the middle. Turning it puts that band along the bottom of a
rectangle and gives the whole picture to it.

Two things follow, and the second is the real reason to do it. A domain becomes a **triangle
standing on the axis** and a loop becomes a **dot at the height of its own span**, both far easier
to see than a square-cornered block and a dot off the diagonal. And the x axis becomes *genomic
position* — the same axis a track is drawn against. A coverage profile under a square map lines up
with one edge of it; under a turned map it lines up with the picture. That is what every published
Hi-C figure is doing, and it is what §8.4's one coordinate model was already built for.

### 17.1 The geometry, and what it fixes

A cell `(b1, b2)` goes to `x = (b1 + b2) / 2` and `y = (b2 - b1) / 2`, both in bins, both drawn at
the same bases per pixel. A **true rotation**: nothing is stretched, a domain's two edges meet at a
right angle over its midpoint, and a base pair measured up the side is the same length as one
measured along the bottom.

**The window reported is the same window either way.** The rotated lattice counts in half bins, so
the right half of the last bin has no column to be measured to and the summary line under a turned
map read `400 × 400 bins · 1.0 kb · IV:1,000,001-1,399,500 · 399.5 kb` — an arithmetic a reader
checks and does not get. Every window this view reports — the line under the picture, the framing an
analysis runs on, a bookmark, what the 1D browser opens at — is snapped to the file's own bin edges,
which changes nothing on a square map and restores the missing half bin on a band. The turn is a
presentation (§17.2), and a presentation that moved the window would not be one.

The consequence to hold on to is that **height is half of separation**. A contact between two bins
100 kb apart sits 50 kb above the axis. The y axis is therefore *labelled* in separation, which is
the question a reader is asking, while the coordinate underneath it is half that. Stretching the
picture to make the two agree is the alternative and it is worse: it would put a domain's edges at
63° and make a base pair up the side shorter than one along the bottom, so nothing could be measured
off the plot with one ruler.

**The lattice is half-bin.** `b1 + b2` and `b2 - b1` always share parity, so the rotated grid is a
checkerboard with half its positions empty. Filling only those and interpolating blurs; drawing each
source cell as a diamond costs a path per cell. Instead each source cell fills **two adjacent
columns**, which makes the output dense, uniform, square-celled and exact to within the half bin it
is drawn at — and an ordinary uniform matrix, so pooling, colouring, pan, zoom, clip, the colourbar
and export are all the code they always were.

**The corners are empty, and that is honest.** A cell at the far left of the window and high up
needs a partner off the left-hand end of the block, which was never read. Those two corner triangles
come back `NaN` and draw as paper. Reading wider than the window would fill them and is the obvious
later improvement; nothing pretends they are zeros.

### 17.2 Where it is offered, and the box it is drawn in

Only on a block that **has a diagonal**: the two axes must cover the same bins, it must be one
sequence, and it must be at bin level. Each is the same condition from a different side — distance
from the diagonal is the whole of the y axis, so a block without one has no picture to make, and
"the distance across a boundary between two sequences" is not a distance. The toggle is **greyed
rather than hidden** where this is false, so a reader looking at a whole metagenome can see that the
control exists and find out what it wants of them.

**And wherever it is offered it is off until it is asked for**, which is `flip` being absent meaning
square and only an explicit `true` meaning turned (§11).

It was the other way round, on the argument that a block with a diagonal is a band along a genomic
axis with tracks under it — that being what a contact map is *for* at this scale, and what every
published figure of one looks like. The argument is sound about the *figure* and wrong about the
*arrival*, and the reason is the paragraph above: the conditions that make a block turnable admit one
sequence against itself and nothing else, so every map the default reached was a single chromosome —
and a reader who clicks a chromosome in the table is asking to see that chromosome, not to have it
rotated on the way in. The picture changing shape as you arrive is a worse first frame than a square,
however good the band is once you have chosen it.

So the turn is a reading, like `O/E` and the smoothing beside it: one press, and then it is written
down. The hash of an ordinary view stays short because only the reader's "yes" is in it, and a link
with no `flip` in it opens the way this viewer opens.

A block with no diagonal draws square and **writes nothing back**. Recording the refusal would let a
metagenome a reader passed through switch the turn off for every map after it, which is a preference
edited by a navigation.

**The turn survives a navigation**, and that is the other half of it being a preference rather than a
fact about the block. Opening a region by dragging a box on the map, or clicking through Chromosomes
to another sequence, builds a fresh state; left to that, the band a reader had just shaped came back
as a square every time they went to look at something in it — which is the gesture a turned map is
for. It is carried across a navigation of the same file exactly as the deck and the second file are
(`READING_KEYS`, beside §16's `COMPANION_KEYS`), with the same exception: a state that has said
`false` is believed.

**A turned map is a rectangle of a size the reader chose.** Its height and its width are set by
dragging its own edges — a bar along the top, and one at each end — and neither moves when the map is
zoomed. What the zoom changes is what is *inside* the box: more or less genome across, more or less
distance up.

That is the whole of what the turn is for, and the alternative is what this used to do. A band was
fitted like any other matrix, on whichever axis was tighter, so its height was `depth × zoom` and
zooming in grew it until it filled the panel — at which point the picture is a square map again, with
the far corners the turn exists to throw away back on screen. A band that stops being a band as soon
as anybody looks closely is not a presentation, it is a starting position.

So **how far from the diagonal the band reaches follows the zoom** rather than being the number the
reader sets. The box is so many pixels tall, a cell is so many pixels, and the deepest contact on
screen is the quotient — which is also the honest reading: zoom in and you are looking at a shorter
stretch of genome, so the distances that fit above it are shorter too.

**A band deeper than the box is the same picture**, and that is what the re-cut costs almost nothing.
The band stands on the box's floor at every zoom, so rows past the top edge are clipped by the rule
that already clips the columns past either end: the rows on screen are the same rows either way. So
the band is re-cut only when it is too *shallow* — which is to say only on the way out. Zooming in
asks for less distance at every notch and is answered by the picture already drawn, where re-cutting
per notch is a rotation and a fresh pooling of the whole band per wheel event. It holds for a mirrored
pair too, and only because that pair is pinned by its middle rather than by an edge: the surplus is
then clipped equally from both, so the two bands show the same depth at every zoom.

And when it is too shallow it is cut **deeper than asked**, twice over, bounded by the block. Zooming
out is a gesture rather than a step; buying twice the distance the box wants right now is one
rotation instead of the several the rest of the gesture would have asked for. Not on a mirrored pair,
where the spare rows are not spare: one band stands on the box's floor and the rows past the top edge
are clipped, while two stand on the fold between them, so buying twice the depth pushes that fold —
and the whole of the first file with it — off the top of the picture.

The **colour scale is not re-measured** by a re-cut, and this is the other half of the same
sentence. The range is the square block's (§17.6) and measuring it is a pooling and a percentile
selection over that whole block — the most expensive thing the renderer does. The block a band is cut
from does not change when the cut does, so the measurement survives the reshape. Dropping it on every
re-cut, which is what a general-purpose "the matrix changed" invalidation does, spent four fifths of
every zoom on a turned map proving the colours were the colours they already were.

The box opens **as wide as the panel allows and a quarter as tall**, which is the shape of the
figures this is a viewer for. A whole triangle is exactly twice as wide as it is tall — that is what
the half-bin lattice makes it — so a quarter shows half the separation the block holds at the fitted
zoom: enough band for a domain to be a triangle rather than a smear, and short enough that the
picture still reads as one strip along the genome rather than as a map. A fraction of the width rather than a
distance in base pairs, deliberately: a default of "500 kb" is most of a bacterial chromosome and a
rounding error on a human one, and this viewer opens on both.

**The box is the reader's, not the panel's**, and it outlives every navigation. A change of
resolution, a click on another chromosome, a zoom that opens a region — each of those destroys the
panel and builds another, so a box held as a field on one is a box the reader loses the first time
they go and look at something in it, which is the gesture shaping a band is *for*. It is a store
(`ui/turnBox.ts`), kept in this browser's storage on `ui/plotOptions.ts`'s rule — how tall somebody
likes their bands is a preference, not what is being looked at (§5.5) — so it is the same in every
tab and survives a reload. Shared as well as remembered: the turn is the deck's rather than one
map's (§17.3), and a deck of bands at four heights is not a comparison.

What is stored is what the reader dragged, and it is fitted to each panel **on the way out** rather
than clamped on the way in. The panels drawing from it need not have the same room — a deck of four
is four narrower panels — and a window can be made narrow and wide again; a box clamped into storage
would lose the reader's number the first time it did not fit, where one clamped on the way out comes
back with the room. An untouched axis is stored as *nothing*, not as a number, because its default is
a rule — the panel's own width, and a quarter of it — and "as wide as there is room for" cannot be
written down as a width.

**What bounds the box is the room the panel has**, and it is measured against the panel rather than
against the grid the box sits in. The grid is sized by its contents, so a box narrowed by a drag
narrows the grid with it, and a ceiling read from there is a ceiling that follows the box down: every
drag inwards lowers the limit to wherever the edge has just got to, and the width can be given away
and never taken back. The room is the panel's own width less the stacks of tracks beside the map, and
the height a square map would have claimed — both facts that do not move when the box does.

**Both ends widen the box about its middle.** Two handles rather than one, because the box is
centred: with a single handle the reader has to know which end the app decided to grow from, and
either answer is wrong half the time. The edge under the pointer stays under it and the far one goes
out by the same amount — and the tracks follow, since a stack takes its width from the map's canvas
and a box that narrowed only the map would leave every track pointing at the wrong base pair.

**No height is reserved for the square**, and that is a decision that changed with the default. The
panel used to be held open at the height a square map would have taken so that flipping did not
resize it; a turned map was then what a block with a diagonal opened as, so reserving a square's
height meant every ordinary view carried a screenful of paper above a band a quarter as tall — room
kept for the exception. The default has since gone back to the square (above), and still nothing is
reserved: the panel is as tall as its picture, so turning the map shortens it and *squaring* the map
grows it. The assembly is still centred across the column, where the box really can be narrower than
the room.

There is nothing to align to the bottom either: a band fills its box by construction, so the diagonal
is on the box's own floor at every zoom — and there is no vertical pan at all, because a band dragged
off its own diagonal has lost the axis it is measured from.

**A two-file split is turned into two bands, not one** (§5.7). The square holds the first file above
the matrix diagonal and the second below it, and a turn that kept only the upper triangle would throw
away the entire reason the picture is split. Mirrored, the pair meets at **one shared genomic axis**:
the same position is the same column in both, the first file grows upward from the line and the second
downward, and the two are read against each other at every place without the eye having to reflect one
of them through a diagonal first. It is the same block read twice — `[i][j]` into the first band and
`[j][i]` into the second — so nothing is rotated twice and no second square is kept, and the diagonal
is drawn in both because it is the row the two files share.

The box is one box whether it holds one band or two, so a mirrored pair gets **half of it each**, and
its two horizontal edges are both far edges — the diagonal being in the middle of the picture, there
is no idle one. It is pinned by its **middle** for the same reason, which is where the paragraph above
about a band standing on its floor stops applying: a pair deeper than its box, which is what a zoom in
leaves, has a surplus to lose, and anchoring it by an edge takes the whole of that surplus off *one* of
the two files. What a reader saw was a sliver of the first map above a whole one of the second — and,
far enough in, the shared axis off the picture altogether and neither map identifiable. The ruler up the side runs outwards from the shared axis in both directions (§17.5),
so a separation is written twice and neither band is labelled with a negative distance; a pointer in the
lower band reads the lower band's file; and each band carries its map's name (§16.10) on its own side
of the line, the four corners being spoken for by the two rulers and the colour key. A **ratio or a
difference** stays one band: there is one derived field over the whole square there, so its two
triangles are the same numbers twice.

### 17.3 The turn is the deck's, not one map's

The turn is a property of the **session** and reaches every map in a deck — where the derivations of
§7.5, which it used to be grouped with, are now each map's own (§16.2). A bar claiming one navigation
over a band and four squares is not a comparison. The navigation lock (§16.3) measures a turned
map's window in the same base pairs it measures a square one's, remembering that a rotated cell is
half a bin — without which every turned panel drew half of what the one beside it drew.

**The band's reach is the deck's too.** Each turned companion is cut to reach as far from the
diagonal as the first map does, in base pairs converted to its own bins, rather than as far as its
own box has rows for, and is not cut deeper on the way out as a lone band is (§17.2). A grid lays its
cells out over several frames, so two panels asking their own boxes at their own moments got two
answers: two bands of visibly different depths, which the lock then refused to move together (§16.4).

### 17.4 Tracks under a turned map, and marks on one

**Every track falls into the stack below the rectangle**, whichever edge it was put on, and a track
placed on two edges arrives there once. There is nothing for a vertical lane to be drawn against:
up the side is a distance, not a place.

This is a *presentation* of the placement and not a rewrite of it. The turn is something a reader
switches on and off, and a track that came back from it on the bottom edge because it happened to be
turned when they pressed the button would be the picture editing their settings behind them — so
"back where it came from on the way home" costs nothing, the store never having moved.

Marks are placed by the **pair of loci they were always about**, since there is no row axis to ask
where a locus is:

- a **line** becomes the **V** its place makes: the two 45° rays of contacts that place anchors,
  standing on the axis at its position and opening to the far edge of the band — one V in each band of
  a mirrored pair — and it carries on **straight down the lanes** from the V's apex, where the x axis
  is the tracks' own. Drawn straight up the band, as it was, it crossed contacts between two *other*
  places the whole height of it, a column of a turned picture not being a place; the V is what a
  pointer on a track draws there too. A mark stored as horizontal is the same V, and continues down the
  lanes too, the axis it was drawn against being gone but the locus it names not; and a place just off
  the side of the picture still draws the arm that reaches into it;
- a **domain** becomes a triangle standing on the axis, apex over its own midpoint at the height of
  its own span;
- a **loop** becomes one dot at that height — the pair and its mirror rotate to the same point, so
  the square map's "which half do I ring" question does not arise;
- an **arrowhead** stands over the dot it names with its tip pointing back at it, square to the axis
  rather than at 45°, and on the far side from the diagonal so the cell is never under the glyph —
