`HiContacts::distanceLaw()`'s `norm_p` down to that package's gap distance and its break table, with one
correction to its denominator that §18.10 sets out — and the **expected**, which is
`cooltools expected-cis`: contacts over the bin pairs that could have held one, the polymer-physics
reading, and the number most published scaling exponents refer to. `density / expected = pairs(s) /
constant`, so they are the same picture while the separation is short against the sequences and diverge
as it approaches the longest one: on the yeast demo, within 1 % below 10 kb, 13 % apart at 100 kb, a
factor of fifty apart at 1.2 Mb — and on a mammalian map, whose chromosomes are two orders of magnitude
longer, indistinguishable over everything anybody fits. The second is also what a 4C profile over
expected, the compartment chain, inter-arm alignment and the pileups **divide by**, and they reach it
through `expectedAt` rather than through the panel: the plotted curve is a figure and the denominator
is a denominator, and changing what is on screen must not change what an O/E is taken against.
**The first two diagonals are left out unless the reader asks for them** — *minimum separation*, in
bins, is 2 by default. The diagonal and the one beside it hold what ligation could not separate,
self-ligation and unligated fragments, and say nothing about the polymer, which is why cooltools'
`expected_cis` leaves them out by default (`ignore_diags=2`). Under the density the floor is also the
floor of the total every point is a share of, so 0 puts the diagonal back in the first break, where
`distanceLaw` has it. It was 0: the density's first break held the diagonal and the one beside it — on
a 1 kb map, two thirds of every cis contact — and every other point was a share of a total they
dominated.

**And the four orientations beside it, wherever there are records to count them from.** Not a
property of the matrix at all: it is counted from the records, in log-spaced base-pair bins, because
binning sums the four together and destroys exactly the thing they are read for. The separation at
which `++`, `+−`, `−+` and `−−` converge is the shortest one the library can be believed at, it is
usually *below* whatever grid the reader chose, and the run reports it as a number under the plot. All
four are normalised by **one shared denominator** rather than each by its own: ligation does not know
which way a fragment pointed, so at long range the four are equally abundant and lie on top of each
other, and scaling each by its own total would divide the short-range excess back out and take the
convergence point with it.
**Drawn on the edges they were counted on.** The records are counted at a fine factor of 1.05 and
drawn at *log bins per step*, and every drawn edge is a counted one, each point divided by the width it
actually covers — the correction the matrix's own curve makes (§18.10). Built on its own, the drawing
axis beat against the counting one: at 1.1 over 1.05 every twenty-second drawn bin held one counted bin
and was divided by the width of two, and all four curves fell by half there, together, every 0.9 of a
decade. **No point is drawn empty or from a handful of records.** A bin with no record has no density
on a log axis and broke the line, and a filtered library has runs of them at short range; a run of
sparse bins is pooled into points of at least sixteen records — a counting error of a quarter, which is
the tenth of a decade the convergence is read at — each over the whole stretch it spans, while a bin
holding sixteen on its own is never widened, so a real spike is not averaged into the sparse bins beside
it. The line runs from the first record to the last, whatever the minimum separation says: that trims
the matrix's near-diagonal, a fact about its grid, and the separation the four converge at is usually
shorter than one bin of it.
**Where the records are.** A map **binned from a `.pairs`** had them counted in the import's own pass
(§3.7), and the form asks for no file: *four orientations* is the only question, and the price beside
**Run** says where the curves come from. On a map opened as a matrix, or binned from a file with no
strand columns, the form asks for a `.pairs` — dropped on it, chosen through it, or named by its address
(§18.2) — which is read for its records alone: no map changes and nothing is binned. A `.pairs`
dropped on the app rather than on the form is *opened*, as a map. Absent, with a sentence, where there
is nothing to count them from.

*Scalogram*, which is P(s) with one summation left undone, and sits directly after it for that reason.
The decay curve averages every bin of a sequence into one line and answers *how does this genome fold*;
the scalogram keeps the bins apart and answers *where does this genome fold differently from itself*.
At each bin it accumulates the cumulative distribution of its contacts over separation — the two cells
either side of it at each distance, which on a circular sequence are the two ways round — and reports
the separation at which that cumulative reaches each of a set of quantiles. Cournac et al. (2012)'s
reading, and `HiContacts::scalogram()`'s quantity. It is a **distribution** and not a mean, because
contact probability has a heavy tail by construction: the mean separation of a bin's contacts moves by
a factor of two when the balancer drops a single distant cell, and its median does not. The quantile is
**interpolated** between the two separations the cumulative crosses the threshold between, because
rounding to the bin would quantise five smooth bands onto multiples of the bin size and step all five
in the same places.
Its reach is what it costs, it is a number of **bins** — it is the depth of the band the run reads,
and asked in base pairs it was divided by the bin size before it meant anything — and the default is
**0, the whole sequence**, because that is the only unbounded answer: cut at a thousand bins on a
250,000-bin chromosome and the ninetieth centile is the ninetieth centile *of what is within a
thousand bins*, a different number wearing the same name. The estimate prices the uncut run as the
square it is and says so; a reader who sets a cut is told what it came to in base pairs on this file
and gets the cut in the lane's own label, on every band, so the picture cannot be mistaken for the
unbounded one.

*Coverage and marginals* — total, cis, trans
and the cis fraction, `cis/(cis + trans)` rather than a ratio that is infinite wherever there is no
trans, the total alone ticked by default — as synthetic tracks, which is how a reader sees that a
domain is a coverage artefact. *Cis and trans per sequence* is the same question one level up and
the first number any Hi-C paper quotes: per sequence its cis and trans contacts and the ratio between
them, and beside that the **sequence × sequence** square with a ranked table under it. The
off-diagonal value is, by default (*against indifference*; *raw contacts* and *per bin pair* are the
setting's other two), observed over what the two sequences' own trans coverage predicts under
indifference, `T_a·T_b/2T`, scaled so that the expectation sums to the contacts there actually are —
without that correction the model spends part of the mass on a sequence contacting *itself*, which
is not a trans contact, and every cell comes out uniformly above one so a picture centred on 1 is
centred on nothing. Above 1 is a translocation, a fusion, a centromere cluster or a Rabl
configuration, depending on the organism.
It is the same accumulation the inter-MAG network performs with the group being a contig rather
than a genome, and **it is not a translocation caller**: a ranked table against a stated null is a
summary of the file, and a call would need false-discovery control and a golden built from
`hic_breakfinder`'s own output, which is §18.9's bar and which nothing here attempts. The diagonal
is left out of the square rather than drawn, being one to three orders of magnitude above every
other cell and therefore the whole colour scale.
**And the per-sequence reading is a picture as well as a table**, because it is what the task is
opened for and it was the one output with nothing to look at: one bar per sequence, in the file's own
order, of the cis fraction, of the trans fraction, or of both stacked — which, the two summing to
one, is a full bar split at the cis fraction. A setting says which. **Fractions rather than
counts**, since a bar of a sequence's raw contacts is a picture of how long the sequence is and says
nothing else; the ordinate is a share and is written in per cent while the numbers behind it stay
fractions (§26.2); and a sequence with no contact at all is a gap rather than a bar of height zero,
which is the rule its row in the table already keeps. There is no ceiling on the number of bars as
there is on the square, which is not drawn past 512 sequences: a square becomes a grey band because
its cells shrink in both directions at once, while four thousand bars are a silhouette of the same
shape, read the same way, and one control away from the line that silhouette already is.
*Per-cell contact QC* is offered on an `.scool` and nowhere else, and it is there because the whole
of that container's interaction is a decision nothing was helping anybody make: the Cells table ranks
by `nnz` and `sum`, which is what the *writer* recorded and a statement about the sequencing rather
than about the contacts. Per cell, from its own pixels: total contacts, cis fraction, and the share
of its contacts in each of four separation bands — Nagano et al. (2017)'s, whose *near* against
*mitotic* scatter is the cell cycle drawn as a horseshoe. The edges are typed in base pairs with that
paper's mouse-sized defaults, because a yeast chromosome is inside the near band and the run says so
rather than drawing a column of points on the axis. **Base pairs and not bins**, which is the one
matrix task where that is so: the three edges are a citation, they are what the scatter's own axes and
the table's own column heads print, and nothing in the run ever counts bins with them — the histogram
measures a contact's separation in base pairs and compares it there. It costs exactly what a pseudo-bulk of the same
cells costs — the same reads in the same order, with one accumulator per cell instead of one shared —
and its numbers land back in the **Cells table** as sortable columns, because the gesture they are
for is the one that table already has: sort, tick a run of rows, sum them. It does not assign a
phase: the bands are a measurement with a citation and a cut through the horseshoe is a method with
choices, and §18.9's argument applies to a phase call as it does to a loop call. *Diamond insulation* at any window, or several windows at once, with boundary calling from its
minima — **cooltools' own, to the pixel**. A bin's score is the mean of the valid cells of the
`window × window` square cornered on its own diagonal pixel, `ignore_diags` left out, divided by the
median of those means over its sequence and taken in log2; its boundaries are `find_boundaries`' —
the prominence of each minimum, found over the bins whose diamond holds at least `minValid` of the
fullest diamond's cells, and called at or above the threshold. A mean and not a sum, because a window
that runs off the end of the sequence or over a dropped row then averages what it has, where a sum of
fewer cells is a smaller number that reads exactly as a boundary: so every bin with a cell to average
is scored, and `minValid` is cooltools' `min_frac_valid_pixels`, deciding only which bins the calls are
read from. It never averages across a contig boundary, and never across a MAG boundary on a metacool.
**Both scans on the map read a diagonal rather than a square**, and that is what decides how fine a
resolution either can be run at. A diamond reaches `window` bins each side of the bin it scores and
chromosight correlates inside a band `max_dist` wide; neither has ever needed the `n²` square around
those cells, and reading one put a ceiling on each that belonged to the reader rather than to the
arithmetic — a single `Float32Array` is refused past 23,170 bins on any machine (§9), which is
116 Mb at 5 kb, and loop calling stopped at a hard-coded 8,192 bins, which is 41. Insulation now walks
the sequence as overlapping squares with a `window`-bin halo, filling in each bin's *totals* — the sum
and the count of its diamond, which are local to it — and takes the score, which is a ratio against the
median over the whole sequence, once at the end; the answer is identical cell for cell to the whole
square's rather than merely close, and the boundaries wait for every sequence, the floor they are read
above being a share of the fullest diamond of the run. Loop calling reads the band it was always going to scan, which is
what `analysis/chromosight.ts` had already banded every one of its own objects to. Its gate is
therefore a bound on the **band** — the scan distance times the sequence — and no longer on the
chromosome: the whole mouse genome scans at 5 kb, and what is still refused is a deep scan on a fine
grid, named as the two settings that fix it. **A sequence a gate does skip is named**, which the old
one promised and did not do. Its price beside **Run** is the band's as well — the strips that read
it and the widest band held at a time — where it went on pricing one dense square a sequence after
the square was gone.
**It calls the domains between those boundaries too, and by default**: the span from each call to the
next, as a second called set beside the boundaries. That is not a second algorithm — it is the eight lines of
pairing that every reader was writing by hand — and it is on by default because a boundary set is half
an answer: everything downstream of insulation takes an *interval* rather than a point, and the scaled
pileup over those intervals is the domain APA. Consecutive domains **tile**, so the lane reads as a
segmentation the way the A/B track does, and each carries the **weaker** of its two edges as its score,
because a domain is only as well defined as its worse-supported side. Two boundaries make a domain and
one makes nothing: the two ends of a sequence are left out rather than run to the telomere, which would
assert an edge the data never placed. A run lands as **three rows** (§18.7): the score; the boundaries
as a 1D track of segments one bin wide — the resolution they were called at — under it, where each is
read against the minimum it was called from, or on the map as points or short diagonal markers; and the
domains on the map as the corners of their squares along the diagonal, or as a 1D track of long
segments. Each row's display moves it, and a second run keeps where the reader put it.
*Directionality index* — Dixon et al. (2012)'s signed χ², and the other answer to the question the
diamond asks. Insulation says *little contact crosses here* and finds a boundary whatever is on either
side of it; the index says *this bin looks one way* and finds it from the asymmetry, which also marks
the inside edges of a domain and gives the sign flip the original paper's HMM segmented on. A boundary
both agree about is a boundary. Its window is in **bins, like the diamond's**, because both tasks are
read side by side against the same map and a form that asks for one in bins and the other in base pairs
makes that comparison arithmetic; the default is **50 bins**, which is Dixon's 2 Mb at the 40 kb his
paper worked at, and the run notes what that came to in base pairs on the file actually open, since a
50-bin window on a 1 kb bacterial map is 50 kb and is a different reading of the genome. The statistic
is computed as `sign(B − A)·(A − B)²/(A + B)`, which is the paper's long form collapsed by an identity
the tests check rather than trust, and `ignore_diags` defaults to **0** here where the diamond's is 2:
the index *differences* two sums that both contain the near-diagonal, so it largely cancels, and Dixon's
own numbers were computed with every cell in. `minValid` is a fraction of **each side separately**,
because a bin with a full window one way and an empty one the other is the worst case and would pass a
test on the total.

It calls **borders and domains**, the same two sets the diamond produces, the domains through the
same kernel. The reading the index gives of a domain is a shape rather than a value — the 5′ half looks
downstream and the 3′ half upstream — so a border is the negative-to-positive flip between two domains.
Called flip by flip that is fragile, because a track that stutters across zero has crossings a bin apart
and only one of them is an edge, and the rules that pick it are the rules of prominence written out
badly. So the index is **integrated** first: the running sum climbs through every downstream-biased
block and falls through every upstream-biased one, which makes each border a *local minimum* and each
stutter a dimple on the flank of the real trough — exactly the distinction `callBoundaries` draws, with
tests, by each minimum's prominence, which is what the diamond's own calls are read by since they became
cooltools' (`insulationBoundaries`). Both sets filter on that column and tile the same way, and the
call lands **one bin past the minimum**, which is the first
bin that looks downstream again and therefore the opening bin of the new domain rather than the closing
bin of the old one.

The curve is standardised by the **median absolute index** before it is integrated, so the prominence is
in *bins of ordinary directional bias* rather than in χ². A χ² grows with how deep the library was
sequenced, so a threshold in the index's own units is a different threshold on every file; this one is a
property of the structure, and it is what makes a prominence a reader found on one map worth typing into
the next. The gaps the index leaves stay gaps — the sum carries across them but emits nothing, so a
dropped stretch cannot be the floor of a trough — and Dixon's own HMM differs from this in one visible
way worth knowing before comparing against a published set: the HMM leaves stretches it calls
unorganised in no domain at all, where borders-between-borders tile.
*HiC score* — the **mean** cell value along the bin's own line across the near-diagonal, which is the
reading Bignaud et al. use where the question is not where a domain ends but how tightly a stretch is
folded against itself. Every cell `a[k, k + d]` for `|d| ≤ D − 1`, over `N = 2D − 1`, which is how many
of them there are. The first two are **ratios** and are deliberately blind to depth, which is what makes
them comparable between chromosomes; this is a **mean of cell values** and is not, which is why it is a
third reading rather than a third smoothing of the same one — a region that has lost its local structure
has a smaller mean and an unremarkable insulation score, because the ratio it is measured against fell
with it.

**Half a crosshair, not a whole one.** Drawn on a map the shape is a straight line through the diagonal
— one arm-pair of the cross. The matrix is symmetric, so the row and the column carry the same contacts
under two names, and taking both would count every off-diagonal contact twice against a main diagonal
counted once; one arm-pair counts each contact exactly once. Every cell in it touches bin `k`, which is
what makes this a statement about *that bin* rather than about its neighbourhood: a square window would
also count the self-contact of `k − 1` and the corner joining `k − 1` to `k + 1`, cells that involve `k`
in no way, and on a bacterial map those borrowed cells make consecutive bins share half their score and
turn a single bright bin into a three-bin plateau. This is the shape the R the score comes from computes
and the app is checked against it: on `Bignaud2025_T7.mcool::2000` at `NC_000913.3:3,442,000`, the
kernel returns that script's own sum to the last digit once multiplied by `N`.

**The parameter is a count of diagonals**, counting the main one, defaulting to **3** — the main
diagonal and the one either side, five cells, reaching two bins each way, which is the bacterial reading
at the 2 kb resolution this score is computed on there. It is the R script's `num_diagonals` plus one,
that one counting the diagonals *beside* the main one. In diagonals rather than base pairs for the
reason the diamond's window and the index's are in bins (§18.2): the near-diagonal is a fact about the
grid, and the same typed distance meant three diagonals at one resolution and one at the next. The
runner says what the reach came to in base pairs on the file open and how many cells are behind each
point. The band behind it is read `D − 1` deep and no deeper, which is the shallowest read of the three
banded tasks — at the default, two bins, and on most files one strip with no tiling at all.

**A bin without a whole line through it scores nothing.** Dividing a short sum by a full `N` fades both
ends of every linear sequence towards zero, which reads as *this end is unstructured*; it is the
artefact the diamond avoids by averaging only the cells its window holds, and it arrives here the
moment the reading becomes a mean. A circular sequence has no end to run off and every bin on one is
scored. A cell the balancer dropped *inside* a whole line is a different thing and is counted rather
than guessed at: the mean is genuinely smaller there, is never scaled up to pretend the missing cells
were average, and a bin that has lost more than `minValid` of its line scores nothing at all.

**`ignoreDiags` matters more here than its default suggests.** At three diagonals the main diagonal is
the bulk of the line; it is where self-ligation and undigested fragments land; and on a balanced map it
is the one place the weights were never fitted, since cooler's balancer excludes `ignore_diags`
diagonals from its own solve and then scales them anyway. A score carried by that cell is a score
carried by the protocol — and a peak that is in the weights rather than in the counts looks exactly like
a peak that is in the biology.

*4C profile* from an anchor — a sequence, a stretch of one, or on a metagenome a whole genome — output
as a bigWig. On a cooler it is **cis by default with trans as a stated-cost toggle**, and optionally
**over expected**, where "expected" means the anchor's own sequence's decay in cis and the mean of what
the anchor reaches off it in trans, so that a profile carrying both halves carries one quantity. Per
sequence rather than from P(s)'s genome-wide curve: a small chromosome divided by the average behaviour
of the large ones comes out with a slope that is a property of the set.
**And optionally over coverage, which is the other bias and a different one.** The decay is a property
of *separation*; coverage is a property of the **target bin** — a bin in a repeat, a bin with few
restriction sites, a bin the mapper half-lost is seen less by everything, so it is a dip in every
profile drawn against it whatever the anchor. On a raw map those dips are most of the small-scale
structure a reader would otherwise take for real, and they sit exactly where a spurious interaction is
most tempting to believe. So *Normalisation* is one control with four answers — none, by coverage, by
P(s), by both — rather than two controls or three exclusive options: the two divisions are independent,
a reader wanting a clean profile wants both, and the provenance line then says which of the four the
numbers are. The divisor is each bin's own total contact **centred on one**, so it is a bias correction
and not a change of units: a raw profile stays in contacts and an O/E ratio stays centred on one. The
mean behind that centring is taken over the bins that *have* coverage and not over every bin in the
file, or a cis run — which fills the marginal for one sequence and leaves the rest of the assembly at
zero — would scale the whole track by however much of the file that sequence happens to be. In cis the
divisor is the column sums of the square already in hand and costs nothing; with trans it is a total
over every bin, so the pixel walk **cannot stop at the anchor** the way §18.6 otherwise prices it, and
the estimate says the pass is the whole file rather than half of it. A marginal accumulated from half
the file would correct the bins before the anchor and leave those after it uncorrected — one quantity
by the axis and two by the arithmetic, which is the failure the trans expectation already exists to
prevent.
**Exclude anchor region** leaves the anchor's own bins, and one bin either side, empty (`NaN`, a gap
rather than a zero) — off by default. The anchor against itself is the diagonal and the bin beside it
its shoulder: the brightest cells of the map by orders of magnitude, so in a track they are a spike
that sets the scale every other bin is read on, and on a metagenome the whole of the MAG named. With
it on, the label says *anchor excluded*, and a profile left with nothing — a whole sequence named,
cis only — says so in the job's notes rather than exporting an empty bigWig without a word.
**On a metacool the form asks for the anchor and that, and nothing else**, and the two other switches
are absent because neither question survives contact with the file. An anchor there is one MAG among hundreds
sharing a tube, and the reading wanted is what it touches *everywhere* — a profile restricted to the
anchor's own assembly answers a question about a genome in isolation, which is not why anybody opened a
metagenomic map. And a decay curve accumulated from one MAG's contigs is not an expectation for contact
*between* MAGs, so the ratio it would produce is a number with two meanings in one track. The runner
settles both keys itself on such a file rather than trusting a value a stored session or a form filled
in on a cooler left behind: always trans, and *Normalisation* at *none* — neither over expected nor
by coverage. The arithmetic of both switches is
untouched and still goldened (`run/fourc.ts`); what varies by file is which of it is *offered*, which
is the same stated rule §18.2 already bends by for options that need a `/genomes` table.
*Compartments* — expected → observed/expected, as cooltools prepares it or as the Pearson
correlation of its rows (*method*, below) → eigenvectors by Lanczos iteration, behind the bin-count
gate — with
**phasing from a dropdown** over the loaded gene models, tracks and
FASTAs, a gene model or a FASTA defaulting to the starred one, reporting the correlation it used and
saying so when that correlation is too weak to decide a sign. It is over **several ticked sequences,
every one of them by default**, and under *cis and trans* the square it correlates holds their **cis
and trans blocks together**: two chromosomes in the same compartment touch each other in trans, and
that is where a genome-wide eigenvector's signal comes from, so ticking them all is one answer the
per-chromosome runs cannot give rather than sixteen runs stacked up.
The *expectation* stays per chromosome and that distinction is the
whole of it — a cis cell is divided by its own sequence's decay at that separation, a trans cell has no
separation and is divided by its own pair's block mean. **Which halves it reads is a control** and the
three settings are three computations: *cis only*, the **default**, is **one correlation per sequence**
rather than one across them, because a single square with its trans blocks removed correlates to a
block-diagonal matrix whose leading eigenvector lives on one chromosome and is zero on the rest — and it
is priced and gated per sequence accordingly, which makes it the mode that still runs where the other
two are refused on size; *trans only* is the standard genome-wide call, with no distance decay entering
the answer at all, and needs two sequences. Both it and insulation take cooltools' **`ignore_diags`**
(`|col − row| < n`, default 2), which is what keeps the near-diagonal — self-ligation and unligated
fragments, the largest cells in the matrix and the least structural — from carrying a correlation or a
diamond mean that then reads as structure. It emits **A/B segments** from E1's sign beside the eigenvector,
because the interval is what gets cited and thresholding a bigWig elsewhere is a second tool for one
comparison against zero. *Saddle*, which follows from the two above, is drawn by the same run —
*draw the saddle*, on by default, over 50 *quantile groups* of E1 — with its AA, BB and AB strengths
under it. The task is absent on a metacool: a bacterial MAG has domains and no compartments.

**On a bacterial chromosome the expectation can be taken along both arms** — *decay along both
arms*, the map's own reading of §7.5, within a window along them (50 bins by default, the whole
sequence at 0), read from the origin declared for the sequence (§8.15), and cis only, because the
arms are a fact about one sequence. Divided by the decay alone, a chromosome whose arms are held
together correlates to the X its two diagonals draw, and its leading eigenvector is the arms rather
than its compartments: on the *P. aeruginosa* PAK map at 8 kb, by the default method, it follows
the distance from the origin (Spearman 0.74) and nothing in the sequence (|r| = 0.04 with GC
content), where along the arms the first component carries 28% of the matrix, no longer follows the
origin (0.05) and follows GC content (r = 0.35; 22% of the variance and r = 0.33 by the
correlation). **The
components are ranked by their eigenvalues and by nothing else**: E1 is the component with the
largest, E2 the next — up to three, one by default (*components*). They are found one at a time,
the largest in size first, by Lanczos iteration with every vector orthogonalised against those before
it and the matrix deflated by each pair found — the method ARPACK runs for cooltools — each to a
residual within 10⁻¹² of its eigenvalue: power iteration, which found them before, converges at the
ratio of the two largest, and where two were close in size its five hundred multiplications left them
mixed (chr14's E3 on the validation's mouse map, §18.10) and took seven-tenths of the task's time.
The phasing signal *signs* each one — positive where it rises with the signal, once their
correlation reaches `minR`, the sign the solver gave it otherwise — and never
chooses among them, because a component chosen for following GC content would make any later
comparison of GC content between the compartments it calls a comparison of GC content with itself.
A *components* table says what each one is: its eigenvalue, **how much of the contacts it accounts
for** — *of contacts*, below — and its Pearson r with the phasing signal as drawn. The
phasing signal is a gene model, else **a track** — any loaded or computed lane, chosen and never
assumed (§18.2) — else a FASTA's GC content. Circular sequences are divided by their decay measured
the short way round, which is version 2 of the task; version 3 is ranked by eigenvalue alone,
reports r as drawn and decomposes cooltools' matrix by default.

**What the eigenvectors are taken of is a choice** — *method*, **cooltools' by default**
(`eigs_cis`), which is what the field computes today; the other, *Lieberman-Aiden 2009*
(`--method correlation` in a shell), is the Pearson correlation of observed/expected's rows, as
Lieberman-Aiden et al. (2009) did it and as every version of this task before the third did.
cooltools' matrix is observed/expected itself, clipped at 0 and at its 99.9th percentile (NumPy's, linear
between ranks, of the cells that have a value), one subtracted so that each cell is its departure
from expected, and every gap — a cell with no value, and the `ignore_diags` near-diagonal — zero,
which after the subtraction reads *as expected*; each eigenvector is then scaled by √|λ|, as
cooltools writes it. Everything before the decomposition is shared — the usable bins, the
expectation chosen (the distance decay, both arms, the short way round a circle), the contacts mode
and its gate, the phasing. On the zoo's *P. aeruginosa* PAK, *C. necator* and *E. coli* maps at
8 kb, each read as a line over its distance decay, all three components agree with
`cooltools.eigs_cis` on the same balanced matrix to |r| = 1.000, with eigenvalues within 0.03% and no
bin more than 0.03 apart on a track reaching ±0.74. What remains is cooltools' own expectation, which
averages the diagonals past about the thirtieth in logarithmic groups, and its percentile, which also
counts the dropped rows' zeros and the ignored diagonals' ones. The two methods agree where a
chromosome has compartments to find and part where it has none: E1 against E1, r = 0.94 on PAK and
0.58 on *E. coli*. **Of contacts** is one measure under both: the share of the map's departure from
expected — cooltools' prepared matrix, observed/expected clipped and less one, a gap as expected —
that a component's checkerboard carries, `(vᵀAv)²` over the sum of every cell squared. Under
cooltools `vᵀAv` is the eigenvalue, so this is the share its table has always reported; under the
correlation it is the one number about the map the table lacked, since a correlation matrix's
eigenvalue over its rows — the table's *variance*, kept beside it — is a share of how alike the rows
are rather than of the contacts, and cannot be set beside a cooltools run's. Orthogonal components'
checkerboards are orthogonal, so the shares add up to what several carry together. cooltools' road
skips the correlation, the cubic step, so its estimate prices a decomposition and gives no warning
about the cube — three components of *E. coli* at 1 kb, 4,642 bins, take under two seconds, an
eighth of what power iteration took, where the correlation of the same square is four more on one
core (§7.5). A method the task does not have is
refused rather than read as the default.

*Inter-arm alignment* — how strongly a bacterial chromosome's two arms are held together, as a number
rather than an impression of a picture: the secondary diagonal is the mark SMC leaves when it is loaded
at parS and zips the arms together as it travels (Wang et al. 2017), present in *Bacillus subtilis*,
lost without ParB or SMC, and absent from *Escherichia coli*, whose MukBEF does not align them. It is
the mean `log2` observed/expected within `band` bins of the secondary diagonal, over the sequence's own
decay — the ordinary one, which is what makes the secondary diagonal stand out — read from the declared
origin and round the circle on a declared circle. **Only where the two diagonals are apart**: near the
origin and the terminus they run into each other and a cell there is a pair a few bins apart along the
DNA, whose ratio says how compact the stretch is rather than whether the arms are aligned, so a cell
nearer the main diagonal than `2 × band + 2` bins is left out. Three shapes of one reading: a
**curve** against distance from the origin, the figure the literature draws; a **track**, how much
each locus touches its mirror image; and a **table**, one row per sequence, of its **reach** — outwards
from its peak, how far it holds above a fifth of it on `log2`, four-fifths of the way back to 1, so that it
reads where the alignment ends rather than the middle of its fall — an alignment still spreading out
from parS has an edge tens of bins long, and half the peak sat well behind its last aligned loci —
both read from a running mean over 2% of the arm so that one noisy distance neither sets the peak nor
carries the reach to the terminus of a flat profile — and its **enrichment**, the mean **from the origin out to the
reach**. So the reach says how far the arms are held and the enrichment how strongly where they are,
where a mean over the whole arm said both at once and read an alignment confined round parS like a
weak one that runs to the terminus. **The table is linear** where the curve and the track are `log2`:
the enrichments are folds over expected — how many times as often the mirror images touch
as two loci as far apart along the DNA, 1 being no alignment — two to the mean `log2`, so that
enrichment and depletion still weigh alike in the averaging. Read over the stretch that holds above
a fifth of the peak, a chromosome whose arms are not aligned shows its noise's highest stretch rather than 1;
where nothing reaches, the enrichment is the whole arm's. Beside it is the **enrichment after
detrend**: the same cells over the decay along both arms — the expectation the map's arms and
Compartments divide by (§8.15), within `armWindow` bins along them, 50 as theirs is — which takes the
secondary diagonal into itself, read over the same stretch so that both average the same distances: a
control on that detrending, not a second measure. It is drawn too: the **profile after detrend** is a
curve of its own beside the measurement's, the same cells by distance from the origin over the decay
along both arms, and the two open on **one ordinate** — the range that holds both — since a flat line
read on a window fitted to its own noise looks like a profile, which is the one thing it is there to
show it is not. The peak the reach is read from is not a column, and neither is what each cell was
divided by, since one row says both readings; what each cell was divided by is a figure instead — the
**decay curves**, the two expectations side by side on log–log axes, each log-binned as P(s)'s
`expected (cooltools)` curve is (1.1 a step, from one bin away from its diagonal): the ordinary decay
**along the diagonal**, the short way round a circle, which the enrichment is read over, and the
decay along both arms, **within an arm** by the separation along it and **across the arms** by the
distance from the secondary diagonal, which the control is read over — averaged over the whole of the
arms, the window `0` reading of the expectation `armWindow` follows along them. It separates what it
should: 3.1–3.2× on *P. aeruginosa* PAK from 2 to 16 kb, reaching 3.0 of its 3.2 Mb arms, against 1.20–1.22× on
*E. coli* MG1655 from 2 to 20 kb, whose arms are not aligned; and after detrend PAK's is 0.93–0.97×.
Each square is read whole, so a sequence past Compartments' 8,192-bin gate is left out and named. Absent on a metacool,
whose MAGs have no declared origins.
*Loop calling* — the one question *where are the loops*, which Pattern detection answers as one of
five shapes it can be handed: HiCCUPS (Rao et al. 2014) as `cooltools.dots` computes it, ported with
its Python API's defaults. Every pixel the scan reaches is tested against four **neighbourhoods** of
its own — the donut about it, a bar through it each way and the square below and left of it, out to
the kernel's outer half-width `w` and with the square of half-width `p` about the pixel left out —
whose **locally adjusted expected** is the distance decay at the pixel times what the neighbourhood
holds over what the decay says it should, on the balanced map, scaled back to the pixel's raw count
by its two weights so that a raw count is tested against a Poisson tail. The pixels are put in
**λ-chunks** of like expected, 40 by default, log-spaced by 2^⅓, and Benjamini–Hochberg runs within
each chunk, kernel by kernel, to the count a pixel of that chunk must reach; a pixel that reaches all
four is **enriched**, enriched pixels within the **clustering radius** of each other are one loop,
called at its brightest — clustered by BIRCH, as `dots` clusters them — and the **enrichment
filter** keeps a loop at 1.5× its vertical and horizontal expecteds, 1.75× its donut and lower-left
ones and 2× one of those two, and a cluster of one pixel only at q-values summing to 0.02 or less.
**The kernel is the one setting with no default.** cooltools has kernels for 4 to 28 kb bins —
`w 7, p 4` from 4 kb, `5, 2` from 8 kb, `3, 1` from 18 kb, Rao et al.'s — and refuses any other
resolution unless it is handed one; so the two half-widths are seeded from that table, and on a map
outside it the boxes are empty and the run is refused, saying why, until the reader fills them.
Every other default is `dots()`'s, in the map's bins where it is a distance: 10 Mb from the
diagonal, a 20 kb radius, an FDR of 0.1 — where cooltools' command line has 2 Mb, 39 kb and 0.02 —
and like Base composition's bin size they follow a change of resolution until typed (§18.2). Four
outputs: the **loop set**, a BEDPE that lands on the map as rings the moment the run finishes; a
**table** of every call with its four expecteds and q-values; the **loop spectrum**, each loop's
enrichment over its donut against separation (below); and **the contacts each λ-chunk asked of a
pixel**, kernel by kernel against the line where a pixel merely meets its expected — the
correction drawn, which is where a sparse map shows it was held to thresholds nothing in it could
reach. A balanced map only: the expected is the balanced map's, so a file with no weights waits,
saying to run `cooler balance`. **The task's own words name no package**: its row, its form, its
notes, its figures and its command, `chromosomix loops`, say *loop calling*, and Pattern
detection's row, form and notes name none either; the package each is a port of is named here, in
§18.9 and §18.10, and in the validation notebook, where what is claimed for it is checked.
*Pattern detection*, which is chromosight — loops, borders, hairpins, centromeres and stripes, by
normalised cross-correlation against a template, over a map detrended by its own distance law, with
neighbour suppression and a Benjamini-Hochberg q-value on every call. **The pattern is a parameter
and not five tasks**: they are one computation with different templates, and every threshold under
the picker follows the picker because chromosight tuned each of them per template — a form that
baked one preset's `pearson` into a box would report borders at twice the threshold upstream uses.
A reader who takes the thresholds over types the three distances — the scan band, the floor away
from the diagonal and the gap between two calls — as **counts of bins**, since each is a count of the
grid's own cells and upstream divides its own base-pair config by the bin size before using it. The
presets stay in base pairs, because they are generated from the installed package and must not be
edited, and they are converted in exactly one place. *Refinement passes*, one by default and up to
five, re-scan with the pileup of what the last pass called as the template.
It emits five things and the split is the point: a **loop set** (a bedpe, or a BED for the patterns
that live on the diagonal) that lands on the map as an overlay the moment the run finishes; the
**pileup** of every window it called, drawn on chromosight's own fixed 0–2 seismic scale so it can
be laid beside a published figure; the **spectrum** of the scores behind that pileup, because a
smooth shoulder running down to the threshold says the calling stopped where the threshold was
rather than where the pattern did; the **loop spectrum**, which is those same scores against how far
apart the anchors are; and a table of the strongest calls.

The loop spectrum is the plot the other two cannot give and the reason is that both of them average
the distance away: a pileup is a mean over windows at every separation the scan covered, and a
histogram counts scores with no regard to where they came from — so a set whose 30 kb calls are loops
and whose 2 Mb calls are noise is a plausible dot under a clean unimodal peak. Against distance the
two commonest ways a loop set is wrong are visible at a glance. Scores that **fall away with
separation** are a detector reporting the distance decay it failed to remove; scores **piled against
the minimum-distance cutoff** are calls made on the diagonal's own shoulder, which is where a template
that looks like a blob finds a blob in every map ever sequenced. It is a cloud of points with a median
line through it in log-spaced bands — the points are where the calls are, spread included, and the
line is the trend; bands rather than a fit, because nothing claims the relationship has a shape, and a
median because a tail in the score distribution is exactly what is being looked for. Log-spaced and on
a log axis, for the reason every distance plot here is. Drawn only off the diagonal, where there is a
separation to plot against; thinned by rank in separation past a couple of thousand marks, never
truncated, so it stays the same picture. The same plot comes back from the chromosight **pileup**
(where the scores are per anchor rather than per call) and from the ordinary APA over a loop set,
where the quantity on the ordinate is each anchor's own P2LL, and from *Loop calling*, where it is
each loop's count over its donut's expected. This and *Loop calling* are the two 2D tasks whose
output is a *claim about the data* rather than a summary of it, which is why §18.9's paragraph
against loop calling is answered in that section rather than here, and why each one's golden is its
package's own output rather than a re-derivation (§18.10).
*Reproducibility* is the one task in the catalogue whose unit is a **pair of files**, and it is a
port: HiCRep's stratum-adjusted correlation (Yang et al. 2017), which smooths both maps with a 2D
mean filter (*smoothing half-width*, 1 bin by default), correlates each diagonal **separately** —
where the decay the two share is a constant and contributes no variance — and pools the
per-diagonal coefficients with **variance-stabilised
weights**: `n` times the variance of the ranks of a diagonal's `n` values, which is `(n + 1)/12`, so a
diagonal counts by the positions it compares. Weighting by the variance of the counts instead lets the
few diagonals nearest the main one, where the counts and the correlation are highest, carry the whole
number; on raw counts that alone lifts it by a few tenths. Both halves are load-bearing. Plain Pearson on two matrices comes out
near 0.9 for two *unrelated* maps of the same assembly, because almost all of the variance is in the
one gradient every Hi-C map has; and without the smoothing the coefficient measures depth as much as
structure, which is why two shallow replicates would score worse than two deep ones of different
conditions. It reads a **band** rather than a square, so a mammalian chromosome is a few dozen
bounded reads. How far it compares is a **number of strata**, capped at and defaulting to 500: a
stratum is a diagonal offset — which is the whole reason two maps on different grids cannot be
compared at all — so the 5 Mb this used to be asked in was divided by the bin size in two places, and
reached the cap on every file at 10 kb or finer. It is part of the answer, as the reference's `dBPMax`
is, since a far stratum weighs about as much as a near one.

**The other maps are the deck's**, in the order they are on screen and under the reader's own names
(§16) — there is no second file picker, because a coefficient against a file that is not on screen
is a number with nothing to look at beside it. The map a run is about is named the same way, never
*This map*: run on every map of a deck, each run names every map alike, and the all-maps tab shows
the comparison once (§18.7). The row is offered as soon as the deck holds a second map: a map is one
of the others **once its file has opened**, whichever map is starred, the first map included — its
name, its address and its bin size are all the task asks before a run, and a companion has them when
it draws. The companion is asked for the two tables an analysis reads when the column is priced,
where it used to wait until a batch or a star had asked, and the row said *open a second map* over a
deck of two; a run waits for them as *run on all maps* does, so the first one in a fresh deck finds
every map rather than none. The one thing the deck deliberately does not settle
is the grid: §16's lock is in base pairs precisely so a 1 kb file and a 5 kb one can follow each
other, and a stratum is a diagonal offset in *bins*, so a mismatched map is left out and named in the
run's notes, and a run with no other map on its grid is refused in the estimate, exactly as §5.7's
triangle refuses a mismatched pair. Four outputs: the N×N coefficient matrix on a fixed `[0, 1]`
scale, a table of every pair pooled over every sequence, the per-sequence table, and — the one that
says more than the scalar — the **correlation against separation**, which distinguishes *these
agree near the diagonal and not far from it*, which is a depth difference, from *these disagree
everywhere*, which is two experiments.
The arithmetic is **`hicrep` 0.2.6's**, the Python implementation of the R package,
exactly: the upper triangle, with the main diagonal and every diagonal past the furthest compared set to
zero before the smoothing; the window's mean over the cells it covers inside the sequence, zeros
included; each diagonal from the first compared over the positions where **either** map is non-zero,
one with a constant side pooled as zero with its weight. The reference is defined over raw counts,
which have no missing cells, and a balanced map has them wherever the balancer dropped a bin: such a
cell leaves the window's sum and its count, and a position whose whole window is dropped leaves the
comparison (`analysis/hicrep.ts`). Neither changes a raw map's answer.

*CID* — insulation plus boundary calls plus a pileup over those calls — is **gone**, and its going is
the argument that withheld it carried to its end. Everything it did is reachable and now in one place:
insulation calls the boundaries, calls the domains between them, and an APA over those domains is the
pileup. What it added over that was a composite whose three settings never reached the step they named
— `AnalysisRunner.plan` walks a required task at *that task's* defaults — so its window, its region and
its prominence were controls that changed nothing, and its estimate read a window labelled base pairs
as a count of bins. A task nobody could run, whose settings did not work, duplicating two that do.

**Which settings are settings.** A parameter is a question the reader is *entitled to a different
answer to*; anything with one right answer per file belongs to the file. **Balancing** is the case that
settles the rule: a balanced cooler should be read balanced and a raw one has no weights to apply, so
the tasks that read the matrix derive it from `hasWeights` and show no control (`--no-balance` on a
`chromosomix` line reads the raw counts) — it is still a parameter in every other sense, so the
runners are unchanged and an exported TSV still says what the numbers were computed with.
*Coverage and marginals* is the one exception and keeps *use balancing weights* as a tickbox,
off: a balanced file should have a flat total, so the marginal drawn balanced is how a reader checks
the weights fit the file.
The same reading removes the near-diagonal trim's ambiguity (**bins, not base pairs**: the
near-diagonal is a fact about the grid, and a number typed in base pairs meant three bins at one
resolution and one at the next), takes P(s)'s *sequences to draw* away entirely (a run that leaves out
sequences by default answers a question about a subset the reader did not choose), and settles *which
sequences* on **one shape, the tick boxes** (§18.2) — where a dropdown offering *every sequence* or
one of them could not say *these three*, and where the seeding it used to get from the map's framing
silently narrowed three tasks to whichever chromosome happened to be on screen. Five tasks moved onto
it — P(s), the scalogram, insulation, the directionality index and the HiC score — and each reads
every ticked sequence on its own, which is one lane or one curve apiece. The **estimate** refuses a
run with nothing ticked, and — for the directionality index and the HiC score, whose every bin needs
a whole window or line — refuses one whose ticked sequences are all too short for it rather than
reading them and reporting a column of gaps, where insulation scores even a sequence shorter than its
window, from partial diamonds. **Unanswered** is every sequence, which is what a job that never met
a form means — a stored session, or a `chromosomix` line with no `--sequences`. *Cis and trans
per sequence* and *Reproducibility* take the same list and refuse an empty one in the same words,
though the first reads the whole pixel table whatever is ticked and the list only narrows what it
reports: both used to answer *none* with every sequence, which is the whole-file run nothing ticked
must not become (§18.2). A run that arrives with an empty list anyway says so and reads nothing.

**Over the sequence.** *Find a motif* allows **mismatches**, up to four and never the whole motif,
because a binding site is a consensus and a genome carries variants of it: its sites carry how many
they differ by, and its name says what it was asked. It takes **the sequences to search** as the tick
boxes: every one of the session's ticked is the whole reference, the sequences the map has not got
included, which is what the search was before it had a list; fewer is exactly those, reached by the
map's spelling of them (§5.9) and named in the lane's label — *GATC (both strands) on chr1*, counted
past three — and in its id, so a search run chromosome by chromosome leaves a row per chromosome
rather than each replacing the last. **A reference read by range is searched as well** (§8.8,
§8.21), a FASTA over the whole-read line opened by its `.fai` or a `.2bit`: the run reads it 16 Mb at
a time, each piece carrying one base short of the motif past its end so that a site across a seam
lies whole in exactly one piece, scans it and lets it go, and sees a Stop between two pieces — so
what it holds is a piece whatever the genome, and the sites are the ones a search of the whole file
finds. Its estimate is a **scan** rather than *free*: every base of the ticked sequences times what
the file spends on one (61/60 of a byte in a FASTA wrapped at 60, a quarter in a `.2bit`), and over a
network a request per piece — a whole mouse genome is 2.8 GB, chr1 a fourteenth of it. The site
ceiling stays at 500,000, and a run that reaches it over several sequences says to tick fewer.
*Base composition* — GC content, GC skew
`(G − C)/(G + C)`, AT skew and the cumulative GC skew, per bin and under the map's names, each a lane
like any other and each written as a bigWig. The **bin size** is the open map's resolution unless the
reader asks for another, and 10 kb with no map open: a 1D browser (§5.8) with a FASTA in it is enough
to run it. The lanes, and the files they leave as, are laid out over the same sequences cut at the bin
size read, never over the map's grid at another; a window wider than a bin is an odd number of them
centred on it, named as what was read, and wraps on a circle. *Origin and terminus*, the first step of any analysis of a bacterial
chromosome's folding, since the map is read *from* the origin: the two turning points of the
cumulative GC skew (5 kb windows, 1 kb steps) are the candidates, and which is the terminus is
decided as Bacchus decides it (Lamy-Besnier et al. 2023) — the one nearer the matS cluster where ten
or more matS sites are found, else the one farther from the parS cluster, else the one with the
lower Hi-C coverage. The sites are searched with the motif search above — parS `TGTTNCACGTGNAACA` at
one mismatch, matS `GTGACRNYGTCAC` exactly, both parameters and either skippable — and the coverage,
where a track is chosen, is sampled at 5 kb and smoothed by a cubic spline (*spline knots*, 10 by
default) whose maximum over its minimum is the **ori/ter ratio**, copies of the origin per copy of
the terminus. It leaves the two
loci and the two site sets as interval sets that draw on the map and leave as BED, the smoothed
coverage as a lane, a table of how each call was made, and **the origin itself, declared** on every
sequence the reader has not declared one on (§8.15). A call whose terminus disagrees with where the
skew alone would put it is said, and so is a sequence read as a line, on which an origin at the
first base is split between the two ends.

**Calling peaks on a track.** *Peak calling* is **yapc** (Jänes et al. 2018), ported (§18.9): a peak is a
stretch where the smoothed signal **curves down**. The track — or its mean with a replicate — is
convolved with yapc's composite kernel, the nine-point second difference smoothed three times by a
150 bp rolling mean (456 taps), and every run of bases where that second derivative is below
10⁻¹⁰ is a candidate, summited at its most concave base and scored by each track as minus its mean
second derivative there. Candidates narrower than 75 bp are dropped and the 100,000 strongest by
each track's best rank are kept. With a **replicate**, IDR (Li et al. 2011, in Boley's `idr` 2.0.3,
the implementation ENCODE's pipelines use) fits its copula mixture to the two rankings, and the
peaks at or below the chosen global IDR — one of the six yapc writes, 0.001 to 0.2, 0.05 by default
— are the set. With **one track** there is no test, and the run says so in a note and in the lane's
name: the candidates are ranked by curvature, and a figure of every candidate's curvature on a log
axis, split by what was kept, is how the cut is chosen. On the demo ATAC track the scores are plainly
bimodal, and the 5,000 strongest overlap a MACS2 peak 97 % of the time and recover 89 % of the MACS2
set.

**Why yapc**, and not a threshold. A bigWig is normalised signal rather than reads, so the Poisson
background MACS computes from reads is not there to compute; MACS's `bdgpeakcall` thresholds a score
track at a cutoff that means nothing on normalised coverage, SEACR assumes the sparse background of
CUT&RUN, and LanceOtron is a trained network. A peak found by its **shape** needs no background model
of a signal that has already been normalised, is indifferent to its scale, and splits two summits on
one shoulder into two peaks rather than one wide one — which is what a narrow-peak assay wants.

The port keeps yapc's numbers where they look like oversights. The pooled track and its second
derivative are **float32** where yapc decides on them, since yapc writes both to bigWigs and reads
them back; numpy's `'same'` convolution centres an even kernel half a base right, and on a sequence
shorter than the kernel centres on the sequence; a stretch of constant signal passes the concavity
test, the kernel's float64 sum being a few times 10⁻¹¹ below zero rather than zero; and a sequence
with no rising edge has no regions at all. Where yapc has no answer the port gives one and says which: a sequence ending
on an open concave stretch with no rising edge before it (yapc raises an `IndexError`), a fixed
half-width reaching past a sequence end (yapc writes a negative start; here it is cut at the end),
and a tie — at the truncation cut, or in an IDR ranking — which yapc breaks at random and unseeded,
and which is broken here by position, so that a run is reproducible (§18.4). And with one track only,
a **flat** candidate — one the signal is constant across a whole kernel's width inside, which is a run
of explicit zeros in the bigWigs deepTools writes — is left out, as IDR would leave it out of two
replicates: a structural test, not a threshold on a score.

It reads **every base** of every ticked sequence at the file's own resolution and is priced as a
scan. It reads a window of 256 kb at a time, plus the kernel's reach of 228 bases each side, so
memory is a window's rather than a chromosome's (yapc holds each chromosome of each sample as
float64), and a Stop is read between windows and between IDR's rounds (§18.3). What comes out: the
peaks as an interval set, with each summit as its thick part and a BED on export; a table per
sequence; with a replicate, yapc's six thresholds as rows, each with the peaks its BED file would
hold; and on request a row per peak — its start and summit printed 1-based and saved 0-based, as
§18.7's tables are — with its curvature on each track and its local and global IDR. A fit that ends at the edge of IDR's parameter box — where two tracks that are not
replicates of one experiment put it — is said, naming the parameters that hit it, since its IDRs are
then not a statement about reproducibility.

**What a genome costs, and what that does not change.** Nine-tenths of a genome-wide call is the
convolution — on the validation's mouse ATAC-seq pair, a hundred float64 terms a base, one per constant
piece of signal under the kernel, over 2.7 billion bases for the pooled track and each replicate — and
it is summed **piece by piece**: each piece adds its term to every base whose window it meets, so that
neighbouring bases no longer wait on one another's additions, while each base adds the same terms in
the same order as it did summed a base at a time, and comes out the same in the last place. Each
replicate's own second derivative only scores a region, so it is summed only where the pooled one is
concave — about half the bases. Of the candidates, 6.5 million on that pair, only those that can still
be among the strongest are held from one sequence to the next: a region whose score on every track is
below that track's 100,000th best so far ranks below every region the cut keeps, and the cut over those
held keeps the same regions in the same order as the cut over all (`StrongestRegions` in
`analysis/yapc.ts` has the argument). A score that is not a number — which only an infinite value in a
track can give — leaves no order a subset reproduces, and the scan is then run again holding every
candidate. And IDR's pseudo-values, which depend on the number of peaks and the parameters and not on
which peak holds which rank, are bisected once a round for both replicates, where `idr` bisects once
for each. None of the four moves a number (§18.10). On that pair, genome-wide on a 4-core 2.1 GHz Xeon,
a call took 29 minutes and 1.27 GB and takes 10 minutes and 435 MB.

**Over tracks and feature sets.** *Metaplot over a feature set*, in both **reference-point** (a
point ± a flank) and
**scaled-region** (flank, body resampled to a fixed width, flank) modes, strand-aware, over any number
of bigWig or synthetic tracks, with a bootstrap band and a per-feature heatmap for every curve — because
the mean of a bimodal set is a line that describes nothing. The heatmaps of one run list the features in
one order, by each one's mean over every bin of every track and strongest first, which is how deepTools'
`plotHeatmap` orders several samples: a row is the same feature in each of them, and each has colours of
its own. Only the first curve had one, so over two tracks the second's rows were never seen; the first
keeps its name, and the others are numbered after it. A window several features share — the
transcripts of a gene that start at one TSS, a fifth of the RefSeq set — is asked of each track once
and its row made once, then given to each of them. *Aggregate peak analysis*, likewise in both
**fixed** (centre ± W bins) and **scaled-region** (the domain, or the rectangle between two anchors,
resampled to a fixed grid) modes; on-diagonal from a feature set, off-diagonal from a pair set, and
off-diagonal from **every pair of one feature set** inside a separation range;
normalised by **observed/expected by default**, by distance-matched controls, by **chromosight**, or
not at all; with the P2LL enrichment reported under it and a per-feature score table that can leave
the app.

**A pileup's axes are distances, in base pairs.** `-21 kb`, `0`, `+21 kb` — five labels along each
axis, the ends at the ends, the sign written out on both sides because what a label says is *which
side of the anchor*. They were counts of **bins**, which is a number only a reader holding the
resolution in their head can use and a different number for the same window at every resolution: a
±21 kb pileup reads `±21` at 1 kb and `±21` at 5 kb, two pictures five times apart labelled
identically. The labels are positions along the axis rather than the offsets of the cells they land
on, which is what keeps a symmetric window symmetric — rounding each quarter point to a whole bin
puts `-10 kb` opposite `+11 kb`. A *scaled* window has no such distance, its axis being the feature
from 0 to 1, and keeps its own labels. The rule is one function in `analysis/run/labels.ts` and the
three tasks that draw a pileup — APA, chromosight's own, and the chromosight pileup — all read it,
since two of them rounding differently is how one figure comes to look computed by another tool.

**A pileup is cut about a point of the feature, and which point is the reader's** — *start*, *centre*
or *end*, strand-aware, the same three the metaplot has offered since it existed and spelled the same
way. It took the midpoint and never said so, which on a gene set is a pileup at whatever is half way
along a gene: not the figure anybody draws, which is the one at the transcription start site. Worse,
a metaplot set to *start* and a pileup beside it were then aggregates of two different anchor sets
under one caption. The point the window is cut about is also the point a *generated* pair's separation
is measured between, or the range and the picture would disagree about which pairs they are of. The
axis label says which point it is; *bins from the centre* over a pileup of four thousand TSSs is a
caption for a figure nobody drew. Hidden where there is no point to choose: a loaded loop set brings
its own two anchors, and a domain pileup's window *is* the feature, start to end.

**A pileup's window is cut as coolpuppy cuts one, and its observed/expected is coolpuppy's.**
Nothing is taken from below the diagonal. The map is read whole, both triangles, and a loop window
that crosses the diagonal holds the same contacts twice there — once above it and once mirrored
below — so the cells below it are left out, as coolpuppy, which cuts its windows from the upper
triangle, leaves them out. The main diagonal and the one beside it go too (*diagonals left out*,
coolpuppy's `min_diag`, 2 by default), being mostly what ligation could not separate. A window on
the diagonal is its own mirror and is kept whole but for those diagonals, either side of the main
one, which is coolpuppy's local pileup folded onto its transpose; and a distance-matched control is
cut by the same rule as the window it divides, or the ratio would carry a pattern that is in
neither. Observed/expected divides **each window, cell by cell, by its own sequence's expected at
that cell's own diagonal**, then averages the ratios: coolpuppy's `ooe`, with cooltools'
`balanced.avg` — the mean of each diagonal over the whole sequence — read as a band as deep as the
farthest window reaches. That is the pileup's normalisation and nothing else's: the map's own O/E
(§7.5) divides by the curve it always has. **A loop set leaves out the loops nearest the diagonal**,
as coolpuppy does: every loop whose two anchors' centres are nearer than *nearest loop* bins of the
file, **five by default**, measured as coolpuppy measures it, in base pairs between the centres.
coolpuppy's own default, `mindist='auto'`, is further out — twice the half-width and two, the
separation at which a window stops reaching the two diagonals left out, so that at that floor no loop
window has a gap cut in it — and leaves out 959 of the yeast demo's 1,506 loops at 1 kb; the
validation types it to hold the two to each other (§18.10). The run says how many loops it left out
and how near they were, and 0 piles up every loop; *every pair* of a feature set keeps its own
separation range instead. It used to divide
the finished pileup by an expected looked up at each cell's distance from the *pileup's* centre,
which is a cell's diagonal only for a window on the diagonal, and to take that expected from the
windows' own cells, which over a loop set are the places the set picked, enriched by construction.
On a mouse loop set whose centre coolpuppy puts at 2.9 that said 0.2; read whole, the raw pileup of
the same set was up to ten per cent from coolpuppy's in the cells nearest the diagonal, and more at
coolpuppy's default `min_diag`. Cut this way, every cell agrees to 5e-6, gap for gap (§18.10).

**Tracks aggregate along the pileup's two edges.** Any number of bigWigs or synthetic tracks may be
chosen, the starred one to begin with, and **none is an answer the form keeps**: every box unticked
stays unticked through the next run, where it used to tick the starred track back on. Each is averaged
over the **same windows** the pileup is taken from — the real ones, never the shifted controls,
which are the denominator of the picture rather than the picture — and drawn as a profile above it
and beside it (under every normalisation but chromosight's, which answers with its
own outputs). That is the figure most papers using an APA actually print: the
aggregate contact map with the aggregate signal on its edges, which turns *these places touch* into
*these places touch, and this is what is bound where they do*. Until this a reader had to run the 1D
metaplot separately over anchors they re-derived by hand, and the two aggregates were over different
windows unless every setting happened to agree. Each profile is normalised **against its own extent, not from zero**, with the two
edges of one track sharing a ruler and the range printed in the key: two tracks in two units have no
common axis, a band three lines tall is not an axis either, and what a marginal promises is the
*shape* along the window. Drawn from zero — which is what shipped — a ChIP aggregate running from 45
to 92 is a line across the top of the band with a bump in it, while the same numbers as a metaplot
curve two blocks down the drawer are a peak twice the height of its baseline: two pictures of one
quantity disagreeing about whether anything happened. Each profile is resampled by the window's
**own** grid edges, so a cell of the profile is the cell of the pileup above it by construction
rather than by a second resampling that could land a domain boundary a column out, and it leaves as
numbers with the matrix it belongs to — a second block under the pileup's own table, since contacts
and signal are two units and a spreadsheet that read them as one rectangle would average them
together.
A track dropped between the form being filled in and Run being pressed is left out and said out loud,
rather than drawn as a flat line.

**The two edges show one profile unless the reader says otherwise.** Which anchor of a loop is
written first in a BEDPE is whichever sits further left on the sequence, and nothing else: it is not
upstream in any biological sense, not the cause of the contact, not the end with the factor on it.
Profiled apart, the top edge is every pair's second anchor and the right edge every pair's first, so
the two lines differ by whatever that arbitrary ordering happened to sort — and a reader comparing
them reads a difference between the two ends of a loop that the file never claimed. So each window
contributes **both** of its anchors to **both** edges, which is one mean over twice as many anchors:
better estimated as well as honest. The pooling is done a window at a time rather than by averaging
the two finished profiles, since the accumulators count per cell and a cell one of them never saw
would otherwise be weighted as though it had. A tickbox turns it off, for the file where the ordering
*is* the figure — a BEDPE whose left column is always the promoter, say — and it is offered only off
the diagonal, where both axes cut the same window from the same feature and the two profiles are
already the same numbers.

**The scaled mode on a feature set is the domain pileup**, and it is the picture that sits beside a
loop APA in every paper: TADs — insulation boundaries called, then the span from one to the next —
piled up with the body of every domain resampled onto the same columns and a flank each side. Four
things make it that picture rather than a plausible smear, and each was got wrong before it was got
right. The window is `[start − fL, end + fL]` **on both axes**, so the domain is the square in the
middle; it used to be laid out from the feature's *midpoint*, which is the same width and half a
domain to the right of where it belongs, and produced a figure with the body against one corner and
the whole flank on the far side. The body's two ends are pinned to their **own grid lines** for every
domain whatever its length, rather than the whole window being stretched evenly — otherwise a 20 kb
domain's boundary lands on one column and a 200 kb domain's on another and averaging them softens
both. The distance-matched control is shifted by a **multiple of the window** rather than by a count
of bins, because a control fifty bins from a thousand-bin window is mostly the window and the ratio
comes out at 1 everywhere. And the statistic under it is the **domain's own corner against the same
block across its boundary** rather than P2LL, whose lower-left quadrant here is the domain's two
neighbours and reads well above 1 on a set with no boundaries in it.

**Observed/expected is refused in the scaled mode, in the form rather than at Run.** One cell of a
scaled pileup is fed by windows at a dozen different separations — that is what scaling *is* — so it
has no one diagonal offset for a P(s) to be looked up at, and dividing by one anyway was a plausible
picture of nothing. The distance-matched control is the answer there and is drawn at the same
separations by construction. **Every anchor is piled up and every window is summed**: there is no cap on the anchors read
and no minimum coverage a window must reach — the one floor being a loop set's nearest loop, which is
about where a loop is rather than a sample of the set, is coolpuppy's, and is said in the run's notes.
Both existed and both were quietly a change of subject —
a cap makes the figure a pileup of whichever anchors sorted first, and a coverage floor drops exactly
the windows in sparse regions, which are the ones a weak pileup is weak because of. The accumulator
counts per cell, so a half-empty window contributes what it has and nothing more. The chromosight
normalisation is `chromosight quantify` and is a fourth control rather than
a fourth task: the other three divide the pileup by something computed from the windows, and this one
detrends **the map** by its own distance law before any window is cut, so a cell is
observed-over-expected at that separation on that sequence — which is what chromosight's figures are.
Three things follow and none is optional: the window is the **template's** size rather than the
reader's half-width, since the score under the picture is a correlation against those cells; the scan
distance is the **loop set's own reach**, which is what `cmd_quantify` sets it to, so a short-range
set is detrended against a curve fitted to short ranges; and **every anchor comes back**, scored or
not, because quantification answers about the positions it was given. It reports the same score
spectrum the detector does, over the same templates.
*Track correlation* across any set of tracks, over fixed windows (100 bp by default) or over a
feature set's intervals, by Spearman's rank correlation by default or by Pearson's. A window's value
is the **exact mean over the bases a track has a value for**, each record weighted by how much of the
window it covers — pyBigWig's `stats(…, exact=True)` — so every track is read at its own resolution,
never from a zoom level, a megabase at a time: a zoom record is a mean over a span of its own, and one
17 kb record weighted whole into a 10 kb window took a mouse genome's correlation from 0.88 to 0.81.
Windows are whole windows, kept as a tiling per sequence rather than as an object each. A window any
of the tracks lacks is left out of **every** pair, as deepTools' `plotCorrelation` leaves out a row
with a missing value, so every coefficient is over the same windows: left out of each pair alone,
two mouse ATAC-seq replicates beside an insulation score with gaps read ρ = 0.59 at 100 bp where
deepTools reads 0.54 from the same windows. The run says how many windows it left out, and
*compared*, beside *units* under the matrix, how many are left.
*Fraction of signal in features* — ChIP-seq's FRiP, over whatever is loaded: of everything a track
carries, the share of it inside a chosen interval set, against the share of the assembly that set
covers. The ratio of the two is the column to read, and it is the reason the covered fraction is
beside the FRiP rather than behind it: thirty per cent of the signal in thirty per cent of the
genome is a track with no preference at all, and the same FRiP over half a per cent is a sixtyfold
enrichment. The quantity is an **area**, `Σ value × width`, and not a mean of per-feature means — the
latter weights a 200 bp peak and a 20 kb domain alike, so it moves with the width distribution
rather than with the signal, and every published FRiP is a ratio of sums. The features are merged
before they are measured, or a GTF with one row per transcript counts its shared bases once per row
and reports a fraction above one; the features are read finely and the assembly coarsely, because a
span-weighted sum estimates the same area at any resolution *except at a boundary*, and a peak set is
nothing but boundaries while a genome-wide total has almost none. Both resolutions are reported, and
a row per feature is one toggle away (*score every feature*).
*Signal by group* — one or more tracks compared between groups of the genome, which is the question
behind *is compartment A GC-rich* and *is B transcribed less*. The groups come from **a feature
set**, split by what is written on its features — the name (A and B on a compartment call), the
strand, the score in quantiles, or nothing — with what the set does not cover as a group of its own;
or from **a track**, its bins cut by sign (an eigenvector's two compartments, uncalled) or into
quantiles, and a grouping made that way is written out as intervals named by group. What is compared
is **stretches of at most one bin**: a group's merged intervals cut on the bin grid, a piece shorter
than half a bin joined to its neighbour and a feature shorter than a bin kept whole, so a 30 kb
compartment is three observations and a 300 bp peak one, each the track's mean over the bases it has
a value for; the bin size is seeded as base composition's is (§18.2). Each group is summarised (count,
bases, mean, SD, median, quartiles, and its mean less that of every other stretch) and drawn as a
**violin**, and the groups are tested **by ranks** — Mann–Whitney pairwise, with the rank-biserial
effect and the median difference, and Kruskal–Wallis over three or more — tie-corrected, in the
asymptotic forms SciPy uses and held to its numbers, with every test's q-value (Benjamini–Hochberg)
adjusted together, and P and q written in scientific notation where four decimals would print a zero
(`TableColumn.scientific`) — a P of 10⁻¹³ is not `0.0000` — in the drawer and in the exported TSV
alike, where the TSV keeps six significant digits (`6.5319e-22`). A group with nothing in it — the rest of
the genome, where a compartment call covers every base — is left out and named in a note. A row per
feature, with its mean on every track, is one toggle away.
*Interval set overlap* — counts, Jaccard, intersection and differences — because "how many of my
loops sit on a boundary" is the question that follows every domain call.

**And that question is not answerable from those four numbers**, which is what the shuffle test
under them is for. Every one of them is descriptive and none has a scale: forty per cent of a loop
set on a boundary is either the result the run was made for or exactly what any forty per cent of the
