genome would have given. The null is `bedtools shuffle`'s — one set relocated uniformly at random
**within the sequences it already occupies**, preserving its per-sequence count and its length
distribution exactly, which is what makes the comparison about position rather than about size or
about which chromosomes the set is on. Which of the two moves is a parameter, because the
per-feature statistic is not symmetric and neither is the question: *are my loops on boundaries* and
*are boundaries on my loops* have different nulls. Reported as the observed against the null's mean,
a fold, a z and a permutation p on the tail the observation actually fell on — one tail rather than
both, because a table offering both invites the smaller one to be quoted whichever way the result
went. The p carries Phipson and Smyth's `+1` and therefore has a floor of `1/(iterations+1)`: an
uncorrected permutation p can come out at exactly zero, which claims a significance the number of
shuffles cannot support. A sequence whose length this session does not know is drawn over the
furthest position either set reaches there, which is shorter than the sequence and overstates the
enrichment — so it is named rather than absorbed.

**The third anchor mode is the test a loaded loop set cannot be.** A BEDPE is somebody's claim about
which pairs matter, so a pileup over one measures the claim; every pair of a peak set within a
separation range is not a claim about anything, which is what makes it an answer to *do these places
contact each other more than places like them do*. The pairs are generated by a sliding window over
the set's own order, so the cost is the number of pairs **produced** rather than `n²` — four orders
of magnitude apart on a genome-wide set with a 2 Mb reach — and past a cap they are **sampled with
the run's own seed rather than truncated**, for §18.8's reason about the anchor cap that used to be
here: taking the first two hundred thousand is taking whichever sequences sort first, and a pileup of
chromosome I captioned *200,000 pairs* is a change of subject.

**And either off-diagonal mode may be split by separation**, into log-spaced bands with a pileup and
a control apiece. One pileup over pairs spanning 30 kb to 2 Mb is an average of a strong short-range
contact and a weak long-range one, which is a picture of neither — and the bands are log-spaced on
the observed range rather than by equal counts, because contact falls off with separation as a power
law and equal-count bands over a skewed set give a first band spanning a decade and a last one
spanning a factor of two, which are then not comparable with each other. Splitting by separation and
splitting by rank are two divisions of the same anchors and never both at once: `N × K` panels is a
figure nobody reads, so separation wins where it is asked for. A pair whose two anchors land in one
bin has no separation to band by and goes in the nearest band rather than being dropped, since every
anchor is piled up.

Both aggregation tasks carry a **ranking and subsetting** control: sort the features by any
numeric column and take a top N — or, on the metaplot, a bottom N — or K equal groups aggregated
separately; on the pileup it is offered over a feature set alone, since a pair has two features and
two scores and no one right way to combine them. This is what
turns *here are four hundred calls* into *the strongest fifty look like this and the weakest fifty look
like nothing*, and it is what makes a boundary set or a loop set falsifiable rather than decorative.

**On the metagenome**, and offered only on a `.metacool` with more than one genome — and, like the
format, only while the `metacool` dev feature is on (§29.3) — because these are the tasks nothing
else can do and the reason the panel is not nearly empty on this app's primary format. *MAG contact
QC*: per genome, its bins, its covered bins, its intra- and inter-MAG contacts and the fraction that
stays inside. *MAG purity and contamination*: per contig, the fraction of its contacts landing
outside its own MAG and which MAG they land in, flagging the contigs that send more than a set share
of it elsewhere — half, by default — a direct read on binning quality, exported as a BED and as a
per-contig track. *Split-MAG detection*: the contig-level matrix of one MAG, split
spectrally in two, flagged when the cross-block contacts are too few for it to be one organism.
*Inter-MAG network*: the genome × genome matrix as a ranked edge table, written in the column order
`metacooler network --level genome` uses so the two are interchangeable downstream, and built from
*MAG contact QC*'s own matrix — its *inter-MAG matrix*, on by default — which runs first at its
defaults and is reused where it already has. An edge is ranked by its *edge weight*: by default
*per coverage*, the contacts over the geometric mean of the two MAGs' intra-MAG contacts, so a
deeply sequenced pair and a shallow one rank on one scale; *per bin pair*, the contacts over the
product of the two MAGs' bin counts, since a large MAG touches more of everything for no reason but
its size; or the *raw contacts*. A MAG with nothing to divide by gives its edges no weight rather
than an infinite one.

`__unbinned__` appears in none of them as a row, exactly as §7.4 requires — and its contacts are
dropped from every metagenome accumulation rather than counted as inter-MAG, because counting them
would make every real MAG look leakier in proportion to how badly the *rest* of the file was binned,
which is the opposite of a per-MAG diagnostic.

**Three things about this catalogue are settled differently from how they are described above**, and
the reasons are worth recording where the descriptions are:

- **Aggregate peak analysis is not a composite**, despite needing an expected curve for one of its
  four normalisations. `requires` is resolved before every run, so declaring it would compute a
  whole-file P(s) on every pileup, under the three normalisations that never read it too — and the
  expected a pileup needs is narrower than the task that produces one: the diagonals its own
  windows reach, on the sequences its anchors sit on, read as one band per sequence and never
  deeper than the farthest window. **The inter-MAG network is** a
  genuine composite, for the mirror-image reason: its upstream is the whole input, unconditionally.
- **Multi-scale insulation is a doubling ladder from a settable base**, not a list of widths. A list
  needs a free-text control the parameter model does not have, and a parser with failure modes of its
  own, to express what a base and a count express exactly. A genuinely irregular set of widths is two
  runs, which leaves two provenance lines rather than one.
- **Compartment phasing by GC content is built, and it is built through `TaskInputs`.** The sequence
  is held by the annotations worker and the task runs in the analysis one, so the main thread asks
  that worker to `sample` the FASTA at `basesPerPixel = binsize` — the same request its GC *lane* is
  drawn from, so this is one implementation and not a second GC path — maps the intervals onto the
  bin grid area-weighted, and ships the vector under the parameter's own key. A `sequence` parameter
  and a `track` parameter are therefore resolved identically, and `run/compartments.ts` never learns
  that a FASTA was involved. The vector is fetched for the **analysis venue only**: a task running in
  the annotations worker is holding the file it would be sent a copy of.

### 18.9 Explicitly not built

In the spirit of §13, and for reasons rather than for lack of time.

**No loop or dot caller of this app's own invention.** ~~No loop or dot calling.~~ The original rule
was the second sentence, and its reason still stands: a HiCCUPS-class caller needs false-discovery
control across several local backgrounds, and a half-good one inside a viewer is a liability
*precisely because its output looks like a result*. What that argument is against is **writing** a
caller. It is not an argument against **porting** one, and the distinction is the whole of the
reversal: `analysis/chromosight.ts` is chromosight — a published, benchmarked method that arrives
with the two things the objection demands, a background model (the distance law the map is detrended
by) and false-discovery control (Benjamini-Hochberg over Fisher-transformed correlations) — and its
golden is that package's **own output** over `demo/yeast/`, compared call for call rather than in
spirit (§18.10). A number a reader can reproduce by running `chromosight detect` on the same file is
the opposite of the failure mode this paragraph names; the alternative was a viewer that displays a
loop set it can neither produce nor check.

Two consequences are worth stating so the rule keeps its teeth. **A second caller needs a second
upstream**: anything added here must be a port of a published method with a golden built from that
method's own implementation, not a variation on this one that seemed reasonable. And **the port does
not get to improve on it** — the `>= 10 → 1` clamp, the `half = size // 2 + 1` window, the asymmetric
frame rules and the sub-diagonal band of `NaN` are all reproduced, including where a first reading
takes them for oversights, because changing one is changing what the score means and the agreement is
the entire value of having it.

**Peak calling is the second caller, admitted on exactly those terms.** *Peak calling* is yapc 0.1 with
the IDR 2.0.3 it thresholds by, both ported rather than approximated, and its goldens are those
programs' own output, over `demo/yeast/` and over a pair drawn from IDR's own model — yapc's
functions and its `main()` loaded as they are, IDR's fit at the commit yapc cites — compared region
for region, summit for summit and cut for cut (§18.10). A cut of this app's own devising is still
refused: a single track is reported as a ranked candidate list with no significance claimed, rather
than cut at a valley in its histogram or at a score that looked about right, because yapc's cut is
IDR and nobody published another. A port of either is a translation of GPL code — yapc is GPL-3.0,
IDR GPL-2.0 or later — and is why chromosomix itself is under the GPL, version 3 or later (§22.4).

**Loop calling is the third, and the one the original rule named.** *Loop calling* is HiCCUPS as
`cooltools.dots` 0.7.1 computes it — the Python API's defaults, a kernel from cooltools' own table
or the reader's — and its golden is that package's own output over `demo/yeast/`, stage by stage, in
two configurations, the API's and the command line's (`test/golden/analysis/hiccups.json`). The port
does not improve on it here either. The λ-chunk labels pandas rounds to three decimals are the λ the
Poisson test and the q-values are taken at, and a pixel a hair past the last rounded label is
dropped, as `dots` drops it; the tail is SciPy's `pdtrc`, Temme's asymptotic series included; and the
clusters are sklearn's BIRCH down to the roundings the BLAS beneath it fuses, without which a pixel
equidistant from two subclusters joins the other one.

**Contact-based reordering and scaffolding: the reference editor (§27).** ~~No contact-based contig
reordering or scaffolding. It would only be useful if the reordering could be written back into a
file, and it cannot — see the next paragraph — so it would produce an ordering with nowhere to go.~~
The argument was right about its premise and is overtaken by it: an ordering now has three places to
go, and none of them is back into the file. It is a **lens** the whole session is drawn through
(§27.2), so an edit is useful the moment it is made — the map, the tracks and every task after it are
in its coordinates. It is **written as new files** — an AGP, a Juicebox `.assembly`, a chain, a
FASTA, lifted tracks — each of which is authoring an output, which §13 never refused. And it is
**re-applied** from the AGP or the `.assembly` to the same library's other files. What stays refused
is what the rule was protecting: the file that was opened is never modified. The editor is a dev
feature (§29.3), drawn only while the dev features are on.

**No writing of a `.cool`, `.mcool` or `.metacool` this app derived.** ~~No writing of `.cool`,
`.mcool` or `.metacool`.~~ The original rule was the second sentence, and its reason still stands: a
derived contact matrix is a format contract, and owning one means owning every question about what
its provenance, its balancing and its bin table mean. §13's rule is therefore read as covering files
the app *derives* and not only the file it opened.

What that argument is against is writing a matrix **derived from an opened map** — smoothed,
balanced, transformed, a rung the file did not carry — where every one of those questions is a
choice this app would be making on the reader's behalf and then sealing into a file that outlives
the session. That is still refused, and the reason is stronger than it looks: a picture drawn wrong
is wrong in one figure that somebody is looking at, and a `.cool` written wrong opens perfectly in
cooler, HiGlass and Juicebox, lands in supplementary data, and is re-binned by people who will never
see this app.

It does **not** reach the one case §3.7 adds, and the distinction is the whole of the reversal. An
`.mcool` written from an imported `.pairs` is not derived from anything: it is the **primary
reduction of a primary file**, and the three questions the paragraph above names are answered by the
input rather than by us.

- **The bin table** comes from `#chromsize:` and a bin size the reader chose in a dialog. Nothing is
  inferred and nothing is negotiated.
- **Provenance** is the source file's name, its preamble carried verbatim, the record count, and
  what the import skipped, clamped or had to merge — in named attributes and in `metadata`, so a
  file handed to somebody else says exactly what this session says.
- **Balancing** does not exist. No weights are written, none are implied, and `generated-by` says
  `unbalanced` so that a reader who wants them runs `cooler balance`.

And what is written is *what is on screen*: `sum` and `nnz` are the numbers the info panel is
showing, off the arrays the map is being drawn from. There is no second computation that could
disagree with the first — which was the other half of the original worry, and is the half that
would have applied to a derived matrix and does not apply here.

**The price of the reversal, and it is paid rather than argued away.** §18.9's own rule for a port
is that it arrives with a golden built from the reference implementation's output, and a written
format is held to the same bar. `cooler cload pairs` is the reference and is already in this
repository's own workflow (`data/README.md`), so the comparison is available rather than
hypothetical — and it is made: `test/unit/pairs-cload-oracle.test.ts` holds the importer's pixel
table, bin table, `nnz` and `sum`, at every resolution, exactly and in order, to cooler's own output
over a fixture with records placed on bin edges (`npm run fixtures:pairs`; skipped by name where that
golden has not been built). Two more checks stand beside it: the written file is read back through
this app's own reader and matched against the in-memory table, **and** compared cell for cell
against an independent binning of the same records written the slow obvious way in
`test/support/pairs.ts`. The round trip alone would only prove the reader and the writer
agree — which is exactly what they did about `.hic` endianness (§3.6), and why it is not the whole
of the check.

One structural difference from `cooler cload` is stated rather than left to be discovered:
`bins/chrom` is written as plain `int32` codes rather than as an HDF5 enum, because h5wasm exposes
no way to construct an enum type. cooler reads it, and `Cooler.bins()` returns integer codes where a
file from `cooler cload` returns a categorical of chromosome names. Everything numeric is identical.

**A rearrangement is not a derivation, and the lifted contacts of §27.8 are the second case this
admits.** A map moved through an edit of the reference computes no count. Every stored count — a
stored map's, or the table a `.pairs` import binned, rung by rung — is moved, whole, to the bin the
edit puts it in: nothing is smoothed, balanced or re-binned, and what is approximate is the bin a
junction falls in, which holds the contacts of a stored bin beside it, or of one twice — at most one
bin a junction (`metacooler/lens.ts`). The three questions are answered as they are answered above:
**the bin table** from the edited assembly's lengths and the opened map's bin size; **provenance** as
the source file, the steps of the edit and the contacts written, with a note that a stretch set aside
is left out and a duplicated one written at each copy; **balancing** none, `generated-by` saying
*unbalanced*. The checks are not the same two: the file is read back through this app's own
reader, its total held to the opened map's less exactly what a stretch set aside held, and a contact
in a turned stretch followed to where it lands (`test/unit/edit-lifted-contacts.test.ts`) — but
nothing re-bins the same records through the same edit independently.

**No differential APA**, and **no differential insulation task**. Two insulation tracks from two files
are two synthetic tracks, and comparing tracks is something the app already does; a task that only
subtracts one from the other would be a worse version of a picture the reader can already make.

**This does not reach a *statistic* about two maps, and the distinction is the whole of why
reproducibility is built.** The argument above is that a subtraction is a worse version of an
existing picture. A stratum-adjusted correlation is not a subtraction, derives nothing from two
figures, and is not a picture at all — there is no arrangement of this app's outputs that produces
it, which is the opposite of the case the paragraph refuses. `analysis/combine.ts` made the same
distinction for overlaying N curves on one axis and it holds here with more force, because a curve
at least *looks* like something the deck could draw and a coefficient does not. It is also a port
rather than an invention, with the two things §18.9's rule for a port demands — a published,
benchmarked method (`hicrep`, `hicreppy`) and the reference's own definition reproduced including
where it is inconvenient.

**No phase call on a single cell, and no clustering of cells.** Per-cell QC reports four band
fractions per cell and draws the scatter they make; where to cut the horseshoe is a method with
choices in it, and the paragraph at the top of this section applies to a phase label exactly as it
applies to a loop. The reader ticks the cells, which is what they would be doing in the paper's own
figure.

**No translocation or structural-variant calling.** *Cis and trans per sequence* ranks sequence
pairs against a stated null, which is a summary of the file in the sense the inter-MAG network is
one. A **call** needs false-discovery control and a golden built from `hic_breakfinder`'s or
`EagleC`'s own output, which is the bar the first paragraph of this section sets for any second
caller, and neither is attempted.

**The reference editor's suggestions are the one method this section admits without a port, and the
exception is stated rather than slipped in.** §27.5 is the app's own — designed here, to be published
as a method of its own, and different in parts from everything it was weighed against — so there is
no upstream whose output could be its golden, and *the port does not get to improve on it* has nothing
to bind. What the first paragraph fears is a half-good caller whose output *looks like a result*.
Three things keep §27 on the right side of that line. **A suggestion is an offer, not a result**: in
manual and review mode nothing enters the reference without a press, on a mark drawn over the very
contacts it is about. **What auto mode applies is written down**: every step with the evidence it was
taken on, undoable, in the history the AGP, the chain and the lifted contacts quote. **And it is held
to a truth known by construction** (§27.11): scrambles of good assemblies whose inverse is known
exactly — a bar a port does not meet, since a port is held to another program's answer rather than
to the right one. So far that is a fixed few, of the demo map and of simulated ones, put back in the
unit tests; the seeded grid that would report every scramble recovered or not is not yet built. It
reports no variant, and the paragraph above stands for anything that would.

**And, restating C1 because this is the section most likely to erode it:** no analysis runs anywhere but
on the reader's own machine — in their browser, or in `chromosomix` from their own shell, which
runs the same tasks' own code. There is no compute service, no offloading of the expensive cases, and
no "upload it and we'll do the scan". A task that could only be done on a server is a task this app
does not have.

### 18.10 Correctness

This is the largest cost in §18 and the one that decides whether any of it should be believed. An
insulation score three per cent away from cooltools is worse than no insulation score, because somebody
will put it in a figure.

The bar the reader is held to — goldens exported from a reference implementation, compared cell by
cell (`scripts/make_golden.py`) — carries over, and only its arithmetic changes, since these outputs
are floats rather than counts:

- **`scripts/make_golden.py` gains an analysis section**, guarded so that a machine without the extra
  packages still produces every existing golden. The new developer-side Python dependencies are
  **cooltools** (expected, insulation, eigenvectors, saddle, dots), **scikit-learn** (the clustering
  `dots` calls), **coolpuppy** (pileups), **chromosight** (detection and quantification),
  **deeptools** (`computeMatrix`, for the 1D metaplots) and **pyBigWig** (the writer cross-check).
- **The tolerance is recorded per task in the golden file**, not written into the test, so it is data
  that can be tightened: relative `1e-6` for anything that is a sum or a ratio of sums, `2e-6` where
  numpy's float64 is held to arithmetic over the `Float32Array` a block reaches a task as, `1e-4` for
  eigenvectors, where solvers legitimately differ, and exact for counts, bin indices and interval
  bounds.
- **An eigenvector is compared up to a sign**, since phasing is the step that makes the sign mean
  anything: to `numpy.linalg.eigh`'s over the same correlation matrix, at a correlation above 0.999
  either way round. No golden holds a phased one — cooltools' `eigs_cis` is held only to the
  correlation the golden recorded, above 0.8 on one chromosome at least, because budding yeast at
  1 kb has no compartments worth the name.
- **The fixture is the published demo data.** `demo/yeast/` already carries a real 1 kb micro-C cooler,
  a real loop table, a real anchor set, a real GTF, a FASTA and six real bigWigs, which is every input
  every task above needs — so the goldens are against real data and cost no new fixtures.
- **Determinism is tested directly**: the same seed and the same parameters, twice, byte for byte.
- **Every writer round-trips**: a bigWig back through `@gmod/bbi`, a BED back through this app's own
  parser.
- **The remote reads get a budget test**, in the shape `test/budgets/` already has:
  `test/budgets/analysis.test.ts` holds insulation, coverage, P(s), 4C, APA and the eigenvectors to
  their rows of §12. §12's first analysis row is not among them, because no count of range requests
  can say that the reader worker served the view while a scan ran: it holds by construction — the
  analysis worker mounts the file itself and the reader worker is never given analysis work
  (`analysis/worker/protocol.ts`).

**Two of these were settled differently once the goldens were actually built**, and the record is here
rather than left to be inferred from the code.

**It is a second script, `scripts/make_analysis_golden.py`, not a section of the first.** The two prove
different layers, against different references, to different bars, on different inputs — the reader
against metacooler and cooler on the synthetic fixtures, the analysis against cooltools and friends on
the published demo data. Folded together they would produce a run that half-succeeds on a machine
missing one package and a manifest that has to say which half. `npm run fixtures:analysis` invokes it,
and every golden it cannot build is *named* in its manifest, because an absent golden and an unwritten
one look identical from the JS side. `deeptools` is not among the dependencies after all: the metaplot
oracle is pyBigWig, which reads the same file the app reads with `@gmod/bbi` and therefore proves the
two readers agree as well as proving the kernel. It is not the writer's cross-check — the bigWig the
app writes is read back through `@gmod/bbi` instead — and no saddle is goldened.

**Each golden carries two oracles rather than one, and the distinction is load-bearing.** `direct` is
this repo's own definition recomputed in numpy from the same file, compared to equality; `reference` is
the other tool's number under *its* definition, compared to whatever relation actually holds. Writing
only the second would force a choice between a tolerance loose enough to cover a difference of
definition and a test that fails on a difference that is correct. `direct` asks whether the code
computes what it says; `reference` asks whether what it says is the quantity the field means by that
name. Four of the relations are exact — P(s) against `expected_cis`, coverage against `coverage` up to
the diagonal being counted once here and twice there, APA against coolpuppy — raw, over the expected
and on the diagonal, at coolpuppy's own floor on how near a loop may be and with every loop, the
windows that cross the diagonal included, through the task's own runner — and
**insulation against `cooltools.insulation`**, bin for bin: the score, the
cells each diamond counted and the boundary strength, at three windows, with the calls at the threshold.
It was once only correlated — the diamond here was a sum, half a bin along, over the contig's mean —
and the golden recorded the correlation and asserted it had not degraded; the diamond is now cooltools'
own, so the golden asserts what is true. **HiCRep** is held to `hicrep` 0.2.6's own coefficient, through
its `trimDiags`, `meanFilterSparse` and `sccByDiag`, on a pair of maps with zeros scattered through both,
at three smoothings — to twelve decimals, its three answers written into a unit test
(`test/unit/analysis-new-kernels.test.ts`) rather than into a golden file.

**And one golden has no `direct` half at all, deliberately.** There is no second definition of *what
chromosight detects* to recompute in numpy: the algorithm is the definition, so the oracle is the
package's own output at each stage — the detrended map it scans, the correlation map it thresholds,
every call that survives its filters with its score, p-value and q-value, and the pileup it plots.
Those are five separate comparisons rather than one end-to-end check, because a single failure would
say only "different loops" while these say whether the disagreement is in the distance law, the
convolution, the focus picking, the window filters or the multiple-testing correction — five bugs
with nothing in common but their symptom. The chromosomes are part of the answer rather than a sample
of it: neighbour suppression and the FDR are global, so a q-value over two chromosomes is not the
q-value of the same call over sixteen, and the golden fixes the set. What survives the comparison at
`1e-6` is everything a reader sees — the calls, the scores, the p-values, the q-values, the pileup —
and the one place a **relative** bound does not describe the difference is the correlation map itself:
a dense block reaches a task as `Float32Array` while chromosight works in float64 from the same
pixels, the distance law is a mean of those values so the error does not stay where it started, and
the residue lands as `3.2e-8` **absolute** on coefficients of a few ten-thousandths. That is four
orders below the 0.15–0.3 a call has to reach, which is why the calls compare exactly and the map
compares against an absolute floor.

**The loop caller's golden is staged the same way, for the same reason.** `dots` is the definition of
what it calls, so its golden is its own functions called in its own order over the demo cooler — the
expected `expected_cis` hands it, the kernels, the λ-chunk edges and the labels pandas cuts by, the
chunk every scored pixel of a tile falls in and its four expecteds, the four histograms whole, the
thresholds, every enriched pixel with its expecteds and q-values, the clusters with their centroids,
and the calls — and then `dots()` itself, asserted equal to the staged calls before anything is
written, in two configurations: the API's defaults at `w 5, p 2`, and the command line's at `w 3,
p 1`. The thresholds, the histograms, the clusters and the calls compare exactly; the expecteds to
`1e-13` and the q-values to `1e-11`, relative, since the expected is summed in a different order and
the tail is a series. Beside it, the tail at 2,950 points over fifty λ against SciPy's own, exactly
zero where SciPy's is, and BIRCH on two point sets whose nodes split and whose distances tie, chosen
because a plain rounding of them clusters otherwise.

**And one golden is against R rather than Python, for the curve the panel actually draws.**
`HiContacts::distanceLaw()` is P(s) as a *probability density* — the share of all cis contacts at a
separation, per base pair — where cooltools' `expected-cis`, goldened above, is P(s) as a *mean per bin
pair*. The catalogue entry says why the app plots the first and divides by the second; this golden is
what makes the first reproducible rather than merely similar. What it compares is the **numerator,
break for break**, because that is where every way of getting this wrong shows: the gap distance off
by one bin, the break table regenerated wrongly, the mirrored square not folded. It is exact at three
places a near-miss would be invisible on a log-log plot. The
**separation** is HiContacts' gap distance, `pairdist(type = 'gap')` over bins that HiCExperiment
builds as `IRanges(start + 1, end)`, so two bins *k* apart are `(k − 1)·binsize` apart and the
diagonal and the first off-diagonal share the first break — a one-bin shift, which is a factor of two
at the left edge. The **bins** are that package's 205 hard-coded breaks, which are exactly
`unique(round(1.1^n))`, so `logRoundedBreaks` regenerates them and the test compares all 205 rather
than trusting the identity. And each unordered pair of bins counts **once**: the accumulator is fed
mirrored dense squares, harmless to a mean and fatal to a share of a total, since the diagonal arrives
once among off-diagonals that arrive twice.

**The denominator is deliberately not HiContacts', and this is the one place the app disagrees with
it.** That break table was built for a *pairs* file, where a distance is continuous and the counts in
a break really are spread across its whole width. A contact matrix is not like that: its separations
sit on a lattice of `binsize`, and the breaks near ten kilobases are about a kilobase wide — so on a
1 kb map one break holds two lattice points and the next holds one, and dividing both by their
nominal widths makes the first almost twice as dense as the second. The result is a sawtooth of a
factor of two, alternating bin by bin, straight through the decade the cohesin shoulder is read in.
On `demo/yeast/Yeast_microC_G2M_1kb.cool` the log-log slope of the nominal-width curve moves by
**0.83 between neighbouring points** and swings between +1.7 and −2.9; the shoulder it is hiding is a
change of about **0.26**. Dividing instead by the separation the bin actually covers —
`offsets × binsize` — is the same quantity estimated on the lattice the data are on, moves the slope
by **0.087** between neighbours, and agrees with the nominal width wherever a break is wide enough to
hold several offsets, which is everywhere past about 50 kb at 1 kb bins. HiContacts says as much
itself: its matrix branch prints *"the P(s) curve will be an approximation"* and its pairs branch does
not. A test in the suite asserts both roughness figures from the golden's own numbers, so the
sawtooth cannot come back unnoticed.

The oracle is `scripts/hicontacts_ps.R`, which is HiContacts' own pipeline copied line for line with
one substitution — the two lines that read the map — rather than a transcription into numpy. Two of
that function's output columns are left out because nothing here computes them: `slope`, which it
loess-smooths where `logLogSlope` draws the raw central difference, and `norm_p_unity`, which is a
rescaling of the goldened column rather than a second curve. That is
the same rule the chromosight golden follows for the same reason: reproducing R's `findInterval(...,
all.inside = TRUE)`, its `left_join` and its group semantics in another language would make the oracle
a second implementation of the thing it checks. It is the first golden whose dependency is a program
rather than an importable module, which is what the `bin:` prefix in the generator's `have()` is for,
and like every other it is *named* in the manifest when it is skipped. One test in the suite is not a
comparison at all: it drives the kernel with the mirror fold switched off and records what that
produces, because what it produces still looks like a P(s).

**And three goldens are built in an environment of their own.** yapc's last release passes
`dtype=np.int`, which numpy removed in 1.24, and IDR 2.0.3's Cython types its ranks `np.int_t`, which
numpy 2 and Cython 3 do not have; neither is patched, since a golden from a modified reference is a
golden from something else. `scripts/make_analysis_golden.py --only yapc yapc_idr idr` rebuilds them
under numpy 1.23 and Cython 0.29, leaves every other golden and its manifest entry as it was, and
records its environment's versions on the three entries it writes. They compare **exactly** where the
answer is an integer decided by a comparison — a region's ends, its summit, which peaks each of yapc's
six BED files holds — and to a tolerance where it is a float: a curvature to 10⁻⁶ relative, a global
IDR to 10⁻⁴. The IDR port is held to the reference's **path** as well as its destination: on a pair
drawn from IDR's own model it converges in the same 227 rounds to the same parameters in the last
place, and on the demo pair — ATAC against a Pol II ChIP, which drives the EM out of its box — it
takes the same coordinate-ascent fallback, with SciPy's bounded Brent ported beside it, and passes
the same 1,615 to 1,630 peaks at the six thresholds.

**What makes peak calling cheaper is held bit for bit, not to a tolerance** (§18.8). The convolution
summed piece by piece is compared value for value, `NaN` for `NaN`, with the sum taken a base at a time
— over pieces one base wide and wider than the kernel, zeros and gaps, at both ends of a sequence and
on one shorter than the kernel — and so is its flat mask; a replicate summed only where asked is the
whole convolution there; the cut made as candidates arrive keeps what the cut over all of them keeps,
over ties at the cut and tracks that score −∞, with one track or two, and leaves the one-track figure
the same values below it; and the pseudo-values shared by two replicates are each replicate's own.

**And beside the goldens, two notebooks at full size.** `notebooks/validation.qmd`, rendered with
Quarto, runs nineteen analyses twice over public data, each file named by its accession and fetched
from where it was published (4DN's; GEO's yeast Micro-C; and UCSC's mm10 sequence and RefSeq genes
as Illumina iGenomes distributes them) — once through `chromosomix`, once through the package each
reproduces, called as it is meant to be called and never re-implemented — and lines the two up bin
by bin or call by call: insulation, compartments, P(s), coverage and virtual 4C against cooltools;
the directionality index against `domaincaller`; peak calling with IDR on two replicates against
yapc 0.1; loops against chromosight 1.6.3, and the pileup's chromosight score against `chromosight
quantify`; loop calling, genome-wide on a mouse map at 10 kb, against `cooltools.dots`; pileups — raw, over the expected and over distance-matched controls, off the diagonal and
on it — against coolpuppy; reproducibility against `hicrep` 0.2.6; the 3D model against pastis;
Boost-HiC against its own Python, through `chromosomix boost` (§6.5); the metaplot against
deepTools, over one track and over two, its heatmaps in `plotHeatmap`'s order; interval overlap and its shuffled null against bedtools; base composition against
bioframe and Biopython; the motif search against seqkit; and the track correlation, on two ATAC-seq
replicates and a Hi-C insulation score cut to chr19, against pyBigWig's exact window means with
SciPy, a window any track lacks left out of every pair as deepTools leaves it, and against
deepTools, whose zoom-level means are measured apart. Where a reference draws at random — a pileup's
controls, an overlap's shuffles, IDR's ties — two distributions are compared, the reference's own
spread from seed to seed the yardstick. **Every number its figures draw is a line of one table**,
`notebooks/work/validation/validation.txt`, read off each figure as it is shown rather than gathered
beside it, so that the table and the picture cannot disagree and any figure can be drawn again from
the table alone: a row a mark — a point, a vertex of a line, a hexagon of a density with its count, a
cell of a picture, a bar, a band or a line across a panel, a tick that names something, a text — with
the figure's label, the panel's letter and axes, what the mark stands for and where it is drawn, to
ten significant digits. A density is the hexagons it draws, not the millions of values behind it,
which are the outputs of the commands it prints; a symmetric map's numbers are written once, its
upper triangle; and the metaplot's heatmaps, tens of thousands of transcripts in a picture a few
hundred pixels high, draw each line as the mean of a hundred, which is what the table holds. It
writes every command it ran to
`notebooks/work/validation/commands.json`, and `notebooks/timing.qmd` runs them again, four times
round robin, each a fresh process — all but the ones that would time a job twice or two different
jobs: one seed of the shifted controls, the *Sox2* viewpoint of virtual 4C, Boost-HiC on chr1, and
APA raw and over controls but not over the expected, where coolpuppy is handed an expected computed
beforehand. **The two sides of a pair take turns to go first**: the even rounds run each analysis's
references before its `chromosomix` commands, because the side that goes first is the one that reads
from the disk what the page cache let go since the round before, and in one order that wait was
always `chromosomix`'s. Every run is one line of the tidy table
`notebooks/work/validation/timings.tsv` — CPU and wall-clock seconds and peak memory, with the machine
and every version — and each `chromosomix` command's speed is a fold over the reference commands it is
paired with, a side's commands summed where there are several (deepTools' `computeMatrix` and then
`plotProfile` against one metaplot, and `plotHeatmap` as well against one over two tracks).

**The timings open on the time to a picture.** Before the analyses, `notebooks/timing.qmd` times
chromosomix against the two viewers most used for the same thing — juicebox.js on a `.hic`, and
HiGlass on an `.mcool`, served by higlass-python's own tile server, at the versions
`notebooks/viewers/package.json` and `notebooks/requirements-higlass.txt` pin — and chromosomix on both
formats. Every picture is one map and one track: yeast, chicken and mouse (4DN's 7 GB mouse map), each
seen whole, one chromosome, a region and a locus, every view at one resolution the plan names, of a
window of three to five hundred bins on a side. **No viewer chooses the resolution**: chromosomix is
handed a workspace naming the map's rung, juicebox.js an explicit state, HiGlass the window and the
rung as its `maxZoom`; each answers with the resolution it drew, and a picture drawn at another
resolution, or of part of the window, is kept as what it was, never as a time for the one asked for. A
view a viewer cannot draw at that resolution — a rung its file does not store, or a whole genome in
juicebox.js, which draws one only from the `.hic`'s own whole-genome matrix — is not run but reported,
with why. Each picture is read from disk, the page cache emptied first where the runner allows, and
from the bucket it is published in, and timed in a fresh browser context, the viewer's empty page
loaded first and kept apart, then left two seconds as a reader's is while they find their file, from
the moment the viewer is handed the files to the moment it says the picture is finished: chromosomix by its own report (§12, *A picture says when it is finished*),
juicebox.js by its last repaint covering the state asked for and its track's tiles, HiGlass by every
tile in view fetched and drawn. Four rounds, the viewers taking turns to go first; every run, and
every cell refused, is one line of `notebooks/work/validation/viewers.tsv`, with the requests and
bytes the page asked for, the machine and every version.
They are documents, not tests: they need the data (about 6 GB for the analyses and 15 GB for the
viewers), the reference packages, yapc's own environment and higlass-python's, and the two viewers, and
nothing in the suite runs them.

**They are published with every release.** `.github/workflows/notebooks.yml` installs all of it on a
fresh runner — the reference environment pinned package by package in `notebooks/requirements.txt`,
yapc's in `requirements-yapc.txt` with IDR and yapc built at the commits the notebook cites,
Boost-HiC's checkout, Ubuntu's bedtools and seqkit, the app's build, the two viewers with Playwright's
Chromium, and higlass-python's environment with libfuse — renders both notebooks, and publishes them at
`<site>/validation/` and `<site>/timings/`, each a self-contained page with its tables beside it
(`commands.json`, `summary.tsv` and `validation.txt`, every command, every verdict and every number its
figures draw; `timings.tsv` and `viewers.tsv`); a release keeps its own copies of both pages and of the
four tables as assets, and every run keeps
what it rendered as an artifact for 90 days, the validation alone, with the timing rounds it finished,
when the timings fail. It runs when a release is published and on demand. Each page opens on a block
saying when it was rendered, from which version, commit and release, by which run or by hand, and on
what machine, and closes on how long it took; the two link to each other there and on a reader's disk
alike. The pages are no build of the app, so the service worker leaves those two addresses to the
network, as it does `v/` and `pr/`, and the app, from this version on, finding itself at either
unregisters its worker and reloads once (`recoverPinnedNavigation`), as at `v/`; a worker from before
answers there with its own app until its reader takes the update it offers.

### 18.11 A set of scales is one picture

Some tasks produce a *set* of profiles that are one reading at several settings, and diamond
insulation at several windows is the case that forced this: the same score computed over diamonds of
10, 20, 40 and 80 bins. Adopted as four ordinary tracks that is four lanes, four autoscaled axes and
four curves crossing each other — and a reader comparing scales holds four pictures against each other
by eye. **A value per bin per window is a matrix**, and one line per window is what a matrix looks like
drawn as a bundle of curves.

So a lane gets a fourth drawing style, `heatmap`, where the value is a **colour** rather than a
position. It costs no height, which is the whole point: several of them fit where one track fitted.
Everything else about the lane is unchanged and deliberately so — the same limits, the same autoscale
group, the same ceiling drag, the same flip (which reverses the ramp, because that is what flipping an
axis means), the same `NaN`-is-a-gap rule, the same export. It is a mode of `drawTrack`, not a second
renderer.

**Heatmaps stack; everything else overlays.** Two translucent lines in one lane are legible because ink
adds and a reader can follow either. Two translucent colour maps are a third colour that means
neither — so a lane whose members *all* draw as heatmaps divides its own thickness between them
instead, and the height the reader set stays the height of the group. All of them and not most: a line
among three heatmaps has nowhere to be drawn but across the whole lane, over the colours, and dividing
the lane under it would leave it a fraction of the height its axis is labelled for. A mixed lane
overlays, and the reader who wanted the stack sets the odd one out. The rule is one function in
`annotations/types.ts` because both lane renderers ask it, and a rule about what a lane *is* that lives
in one renderer is one the other drifts from.

**The colours are chosen by the data unless the reader chooses.** *Auto* is a reading and not a
fallback: values that straddle zero are a departure from something and get a diverging map with its
middle on the zero, values that do not are an amount and get a ramp — the same reading the value axis
already makes when it decides where to put its baseline. Insulation is the first kind, and a log2 ratio
drawn on `viridis` puts "no change" at an arbitrary green. The per-lane picker sits beside the style
and **appears only under a heatmap**, because on a line the colour is the chip on the row's head and a
second colour control there is two answers to one question. It is built together with the style
control rather than by the card, so it appears on the pick that asks for it: a `<select>` keeps focus
after a pick, and every card defers its rebuild while a control holds a value the reader may still be
giving.

**A task may say how its set reads, once.** A `ProfileOutput` can carry a group, a drawing style and a
mode for that group, and multi-scale insulation carries all three: one group, in overlay, drawn as
heatmaps. They are written into the row's style on the way in and are the reader's from that moment —
renaming the group, breaking it up or switching a row back to a line are ordinary edits to an ordinary
track (§18.5), and nothing re-asserts the suggestion on the next repaint. The group's *mode* is the one
that is not the row's own, so it goes through `knowsMode`: a suggestion applies to a group nobody has
decided about, and a reader who pulled the stack apart and ran the task again gets it back the way they
left it. The group name is made specific to the map for the same reason the label is (§16.10) — a batch
over a deck would otherwise stack five replicates' rows into one lane.

The scales are emitted **widest first**, because lanes are laid out in the order they are adopted and
every published version of this figure sharpens downwards: the widest window on top, so a boundary that
survives every scale reads as a column through the whole stack. A single-scale run is untouched — an
ordinary ungrouped track — because there is no set for it to be part of, and a heatmap of one row is a
worse picture of one track than the track.

A computed row is a row of the Tracks card (§18.5), so it carries the style control every loaded track
carries — the one control this section needed a computed lane to have, since a mode offered to one kind
of row only would be a mode the four insulation scales could never be drawn in.

### 18.12 A set of quantiles is one shape

The scalogram needs something the heatmap stack cannot give it, and the difference is worth stating
because both look at first like "several profiles in one lane". Multi-scale insulation is several
*independent readings* of the same quantity, stacked so they can be compared; the scalogram's bands are
the **edges of one picture**, and what a reader is meant to see is a single shaded shape rising and
falling along the genome — not five lines to be matched against a legend.

So a lane gets a fifth drawing style, `ribbon`, and it is the only one whose picture depends on a track
that is not itself: a ribbon fills the band between its own curve and the curve of the member **below it
in the same lane**. Four filled areas in one lane cannot express that — they paint over each other in
the order they were drawn, and the reader sees the topmost one and four edges. Everything else about the
lane is unchanged for §18.11's reason: the same limits, the same autoscale group, the same ceiling drag,
the same `NaN`-is-a-gap rule, the same export, and it is a mode of `drawTrack` rather than a second
renderer.

**Ribbons tile; they do not overlay.** They do not overlap, so they are not dimmed — the dimming is what
makes two *overlapping* tracks both visible — and the rule is one function in `annotations/types.ts`
beside the heatmap one, because both lane renderers ask it. Two consequences follow. The **order
matters**, since each fills down to the one before it, and a lane whose members have been reordered
draws a different picture, which is correct: the reader has said the bands go in a different order. And
the band exists only where **both** curves do; a slot either of them is missing is a hole, because
drawing across it would invent an edge from the last value measured to the next one, over a stretch the
run deliberately said nothing about. Only the **top** edge of each band is stroked: the lower edge is
the neighbour's curve and is drawn by the neighbour, so stroking the closed path would draw every
interior hairline twice and darken every join.

The bands are emitted **innermost first** — ascending quantile — which is the opposite of §18.11's
widest-first and for the opposite reason: those are independent readings laid out by convention, and
these are the edges of one shape, so the order they are produced in *is* the order they nest in.

A `ProfileOutput` may also carry a **display scale**, and the scalogram is what that is for. Its values
are genomic separations, which run from one bin to a whole chromosome; on a linear axis the bands a
reader is comparing are squashed into the bottom tenth of the lane and the picture is carried entirely
by whichever bin reached furthest. A suggestion like the group and the style, written into the row's
style on the way in and the reader's from that moment, and a display scale and nothing else — the
numbers behind the lane and every number that leaves it as a file stay as they were computed.

**A `log2` lane is read in what it measures.** Its values are logarithms, so its label wrote exponents
— `0 – 16.7` on a scalogram's lane, which is a range nobody reads a distance from — and its autoscale
anchored it at zero as a linear lane is, which on a logarithm is *one*: one base pair, a bin below the
nearest band, so the lower half of every lane was a stretch no value could reach. An output says what
its values measure as well as how they are drawn, and the scalogram's are **base pairs** (`unit: 'bp'`,
written into the row's style beside the scale, and carried by the output into a workspace). On such a
lane the autoscaled floor is the **power of ten below the data** — `1 kb` under a 1 kb run — and on a
`log2` lane with no unit the power of two below it; a limit the reader typed is theirs, as everywhere.
The ends of the range are written as the quantity: `1 kb – 104 kb`. And the lane carries **its own
axis**: a faint dashed rule at every power of ten inside it — the 1–2–5 steps, or every whole step,
where the lane spans less than two of them; the powers of two on a lane with no unit — none on the
lane's own edges, which are the edges, and each rule's distance written at the end of the lane its name
is not at, set in from the edge by half its height rather than cut by it, with the label's halo behind
it. The words are written **after** the label and left out where they would land on its block —
on a scalogram's lane five names can run its length, and the range in the block already says where the
lane ends. The axis is drawn wherever the lane is — beside a map, in the browser, in a saved figure.

### 18.13 A figure is a spec, a style and a renderer

Every picture a task produces is now **restylable**, and the whole of how is one separation: what a
figure is *of* is not what it *looks like*.

- A **`FigureSpec`** (`src/figures/spec.ts`) is the output as the plainest thing that can be
  plotted — numbers, names, axis titles, and the task's *suggestions* about scale, window, mark and
  colour. It carries no colour of the reader's, no line width, no legend and no hidden series. Three
  shapes, because there are three genuinely different pictures: `xy` (one or more series over shared
  axes — a curve, a profile, a scatter, a histogram and a box plot are all this), `matrix` (a small
  dense grid, which keeps the `MatrixOutput` itself), and `table`.
- A **`FigureStyle`** (`src/figures/style.ts`) is everything the reader has decided. One flat
  record for every kind of figure, deliberately: a matrix has no line width and a curve has no
  colormap, and a union would cost a migration on every new control and would stop a table that
  became a scatter from carrying its own axis choice across.
- A **renderer** turns the pair into a picture, and which renderer depends on the kind.

**Contact maps are not drawn by a chart library, and never will be.** A contact map is a raster of
up to sixteen million cells behind a reader that pools on the way (§7), with its own gestures, its
own overlays and its own export path, and a heatmap series of one rectangle per cell is not a thing
it could ever be.

**A result matrix is, up to a size.** A saddle, a pileup, a cis/trans square and a
track-correlation heatmap are *small grids of labelled cells*, and the thing a reader wants from one
is the number under the pointer: which two sequences, how strong, is that cell the one the statistic
under the picture is about. A painted picture has no answer, and the colour bar is a caption rather
than a control. So a `matrix` whose cells number at most `MATRIX_CHART_CELLS` (20,000, about a
hundred and forty a side) is built as a heatmap by `figures/matrixOption.ts` and drawn by the same
chart every curve is; above that the painter draws it exactly as before — five hundred thousand
rectangles in an SVG is not a picture anybody can point at, so the interaction it would buy does not
exist at that size either. The colour scale is this application's own (`render/colormaps.ts`) and
the painter's rule restated — a task's fixed range, else symmetric about a declared centre, else
fitted, with what the reader typed above all three.

**The cells are square unless the rows are a list.** `MatrixOutput.aspect` says which, and both
renderers obey it. Square is the default and is what everything with a diagonal needs: a saddle is
read by comparing its two corners, and a corner stretched 40% along one axis looks stronger than the
one opposite it, so the aspect of such a picture must not be decided by how wide the drawer was
dragged. The exception is a picture whose rows are a **list** — the metaplot's per-feature heatmap,
three thousand features down against distance across — which has no diagonal, nothing to compare
across one, and which square cells turn into a ribbon a fifth of the card wide. It takes the whole
box, under the profile it shares an abscissa with, which is the figure every metaplot tool draws.
**And it is one picture, not a grid of squares.** Its rows are features read as a density — where the
signal sits across thousands of them — and drawn as a chart's rectangles, one per cell, below twenty
thousand cells, it was a grid with a seam at every edge, a border lit on the cell under the pointer
and a card naming it, none of which a reader of a metaplot asks for. So a list is never charted: the
painter colours it once, onto a canvas of its own, averaging neighbouring rows where there are more
than two thousand, and places that image across the plot with smoothing at high quality — a bilinear
stretch on screen and in the PNG, and in the PDF one image marked `/Interpolate true`, which every
viewer smooths. Nothing answers the pointer over it, so the figure's settings offer no switch for a
readout it does not have; and it has the frame every plot has (below).
**A picture read like a map** — a dot plot's two assemblies end to end (§28), `MatrixOutput.large` —
is square and as large as the drawer lets it be, its cells a fraction of a pixel wider than whole where
that is what fills it, each cell's edges on whole pixels; and it is always painted, however few its
cells, since its axes are its sequences end to end, which the painter marks and a category axis cannot.
In the drawer, though, a dot plot is not drawn from its cells at all: every run gives it its streaks,
and on screen — and in the PNG and PDF beside it — it is a view of its own, the streaks drawn as lines
(§28.2), with no colours in its strip, since the lines are red and blue whatever a colormap would say.
A chart's grid is stated as four insets and stretches to whatever it is put in, so a square aspect
means the builder is told the size of the box and answers with a grid in pixels — and the colour bar
stands beside the picture at the picture's own height rather than against the far edge at a fixed
one.

**Everything else is ECharts, drawn as SVG, and the PDF is still a true vector page.** That last
clause is the constraint the whole design was built to meet. Every figure meets the `PlotFigure`
contract — an element, a `draw(ctx, box)` that paints into *any* canvas context, a `destroy` — and
that contract is why the PNG is a redraw and the PDF is paths and text rather than a photograph
(§18.7). A charting library paints into a canvas of its own and hands back an image, which would
have cost exactly that. So the library is asked for **SVG**: on screen the SVG *is* the live chart,
and for an export the same option is rendered once more, offscreen, at the size being exported to,
and `figures/svgPaint.ts` replays it as canvas calls onto whatever context the caller passed —
paths and text into a `VectorPage`, pixels onto a canvas. One implementation, two destinations,
and no way for them to differ. `VectorPage` gained `bezierCurveTo` (a chart's curves are cubics),
`transform` (a `<g transform>` composes with the caller's placement rather than replacing it) and
`lineCap` for this. It keeps a path through a fill and the stroke after it, as a canvas does (§7.2),
which a chart needs as much as any track: `zrender` draws a box plot's box, whiskers and median as
one path, filled and then stroked.

Three limits of the replay are stated rather than hidden: a **linear gradient fill is drawn as
bands** — a hundred strips across its line, each the colour the gradient has at its middle, clipped
to the shape — because a page's `fillStyle` is a colour string, and a radial gradient or a gradient
stroke, which nothing here draws, stands as its middle stop; `<image>` is skipped, because nothing
these charts draw is a raster; and `<style>` is ignored, because what the renderer puts there is
`:hover` rules. The gradient was flattened to its middle stop until a matrix chart's continuous colour
bar was found to be one: every exported pileup's key was a single orange rectangle beside a picture
in a hundred colours.

**What an export leaves out is the hidden series' names.** On screen a hidden series stays in the
legend, greyed, because that entry is the control that brings it back; on paper there is nothing to
click, and a grey name beside no line is a series the figure says it has and does not show. So the
offscreen option drops them from the legend (`paperOption`) and draws everything else as the screen
does. **A hidden series stays hidden with the legend off**, on screen and on paper: the chart hides a
series through its legend's selection, so a legend switched off still carries that selection and
draws nothing — without it, every series the reader had hidden came back the moment the legend went.

**The library arrives in a chunk of its own**, fetched when the first figure is built, exactly as
three.js is for the 3D cell (§25.3) — a reader who never runs an analysis never downloads a chart
library. Only the charts these figures draw are registered, named statically in one module so the
bundler can leave the rest out.

**Controls are in two places, and the split is the point.** A **slim strip** sits over every figure
with the two or three controls that are reached for constantly — the mark, the two log axes, the
legend, *fit*; a colormap for a matrix; a filter box for a table. Its toggles are bordered buttons in both
states, because §26.3's *lit means on, plain means off* has no third state where a toggle stops
looking like a control, and so are the figure's exports in the strip above it: `TSV`, `PNG` and `PDF`
in a bar beside a bordered icon read as buttons or as captions of the title, and they are buttons.
**`Copy` sits beside them, on every figure that has a PNG**: the PNG's own picture — the same redraw
at 300 dpi — put on the clipboard instead of in a file, for a slide or a message, with a line in the
corner naming the figure and its size in pixels (§7.2's *copy this*). The redraw happens inside the
press, because a browser takes an image for its clipboard only there. Everything else is one button
away, in the **same dialog the 3D model opens in**: the figure at the size of the window, every
control in a resizable column beside it, the grip and the hide toggle behaving as they do there.
That shell is `ui/StageDialog.ts` and the two are callers of it rather than two implementations of
it. The figure's element is **moved** into the dialog and moved back, never copied, so the window a
reader zoomed to is the window the export draws.

**Every plot is drawn in a frame, in the ink.** A chart's plot is boxed on all four sides by the
grid's own border in the text colour — black on paper — drawn over the data, as the painter has
always drawn its own last, so it closes over the end of a curve that starts on it. The two axes are
two of its sides, in the same ink, and they stay on it whatever the other axis holds: the library
puts an axis through the other's zero by default, which across a profile that changes sign is a
line through the middle of the picture carrying the ticks with it. **Every line in a plot is solid**
— the gridlines, the crosshair — and a gridline is half the frame's width, a guide for the eye
rather than a mark of anything; the gridlines stop short of the two ends of an axis, where the frame
is — a dashed grey line along each edge was the whole of a plot's border before, and read as no
border at all. A matrix chart is framed the same
way, over its cells, and so is everything the painter draws: a curve, a matrix too large to chart,
the metaplot's per-feature heatmap, the colour bar beside a painted matrix, and a dot plot. A
pileup's two marginal bands are its margins rather than plots of their own, and are not.

**An axis on auto fits what is drawn**, not the library's *nice* extent, which on a log axis is a
whole decade past the data at each end: a P(s) from 5 kb to 2 Mb was drawn from 1 kb to 10 Mb, most
of a decade empty on either side. **Along a curve the abscissa runs from the first sample to the
last** — those ends are the data's, and the painter's curve has always been drawn that way
(`padSpan`). **Every other fitted axis keeps a twentieth of its span past the data at each end**, in
decades on a log axis, which is what matplotlib and ggplot2 keep, because a maximum drawn on the
frame is a maximum nobody can see: the ordinate, the abscissa under points (a marker centred on the
frame is half a marker), a histogram's abscissa past its outer bins, and a box's or a violin's
ordinate past its whiskers, its outliers or its whole support (`option.figureFit`). A bar's
ordinate still starts at zero, and a bar chart's abscissa is still the library's, which measures the
bars' widths. **The ordinate fits what is drawn in the abscissa's window**: a P(s) a task opens
from 4 kb kept room above it for the first separations, off the picture to its left; a line that
crosses an edge of the window counts where it meets the frame, interpolated as the axes draw it. A
wheel or a drag along the abscissa refits the ordinate as it goes — its bounds alone, so the gesture
under way is not dropped — and an export, drawn from the style, draws the same. The ends of a
fitted axis are rarely round, and are left bare (below). **A log axis is labelled where the
library's labels fail it** (`option.logTicks`): at ten decades or more on whole decades every few
of them, about six to the axis — the library's own step there is ten decades, one label on a P(s)
drawn as violins, and a step handed to it is counted from the axis's end, which on a fitted axis
is no decade (`1.2e-10`, `1.2e-8`); and with fewer than three decades inside, where the library
labels only decades, at 1, 2 and 5 of each, then at every digit, then on a linear ladder — a P(s)
zoomed to 221 kb – 783 kb had no label at all. **And every one of those ticks is drawn**: the library
hides the first and the last of the ticks it is handed where an axis's end label is left bare, wherever
they fall, so a loop spectrum fitted from 10.9 kb lost its 20 kb tick, and the grid line with it; an
end's label is left bare only where the first or the last tick is that end.

**A legend down the right is beside the plot, never over it.** Its room was a fixed 132 pixels, and
a series named after its file — `T4dNDD-infection.10min.mcool::5000`, as a map in a deck is — ran
the legend out over the curves. The names are measured in the figure's type, the room is the
longest one plus the swatch, the padding and a gap, and the plot is drawn in what is left. Past
about a third of the figure's width a name goes onto more lines rather than taking the plot's room
(`option.wrapName`), broken after its own dots, dashes, underscores and colons: the library breaks
only at a space and a few marks, and cut a file name, which has none, at whichever letter filled the
line. A figure whose legend is on the right is laid out again when it is resized, since what fits
on one line is a question of its width.

**The window lives in the style, not in a zoom transform.** A wheel gesture and a number typed into
the sidebar are the same change to the same place, and the export draws whichever happened last —
which is what §18.7's *what you export is what you see* means once a figure can be panned. The wheel
zooms the abscissa and a drag pans it; with shift held, the wheel zooms the ordinate — each gesture
the window of the axis it moved and of no other: both used to be taken as the library reported
them, so a wheel along the abscissa stored the ordinate's whole extent as two typed numbers and an
ordinate on auto stopped fitting anything. **A window
wider than the data is honoured**: the chart's zoom lives inside its axis and clamps a window to what
is drawn, so where a window reaches past the data — a range typed to match another figure, or two
figures a task opens on one ordinate (§18.8's inter-arm control) — the axis is stretched to it on
that side, and nowhere else. **One end typed is a window**: on an axis still fitting the data, the end
not typed is the one the axis had on that side — its fit, room and all (above), and on a histogram's
ordinate the count, from zero — so typing one end moves that end alone; it used to wait for the
other, the number kept in its box over a picture that had not moved. **An end of a window is
labelled only when it is round** — a whole
tenth of the decade its span is in on a linear axis (`10`, `-2`, `0.15`), a power of ten on a log
one: an end is a tick of the axis, printed as the end itself, which after a box drawn by hand is
`8.00215` over the `10` beside it, inside the data or past it. Where an end is not round it is left
bare and the ticks inside it carry the axis. **Tick labels that would print over each other are
thinned**, on either axis — a list too long to name, and as much a distance spelled `300.0 kb` once
the type size is raised for print, which ran each label into the next.

**A box drawn on a figure is how a reader arrives somewhere.** Hold ⌘ (or Ctrl, the same key on the
other platforms) and drag a marquee over any chart, and the axes come back holding what was in it.
**Which axes** is read off the shape of the drag, with no mode to be in: an axis is set when the
drag covered at least a twelfth of *that axis's* length on screen, so a flick across the picture
sets the abscissa alone, a flick down it sets the ordinate, and a box sets both. Proportional rather
than a pixel count, so the rule reads the same in a folded drawer and in a full window; below it on
both axes the gesture is a click and nothing moves. A **double click** puts both axes back to the
windows a *control* last set — the numbers the reader typed, or the whole of the data where they
typed none — which is a second bookmark and not a second window: the single source above still
holds. The gesture is taken in the capture phase, because the chart pans on a drag and a picture
sliding under the box being drawn on it is the one thing this must not do; ECharts' own brush is not
used, since it arrives with a toolbox of buttons over the picture and zooms both axes always.

**What the pointer says is the file's words as text, in this application's markup.** ECharts writes a
tooltip with `innerHTML`, and what a tooltip names comes out of the file: a cis/trans square's ticks are
its sequences' names, a track correlation's are its tracks', a curve is named after either. So every
chart has a formatter of its own, and every name, number and colour reaches its markup through one
escape (`figures/tooltip.ts`) — interpolated as it came, a sequence named `<img src=x onerror=…>` ran
its script on hover. The library's own markup, which a chart with no formatter shows, escapes its text
but styles every margin and swatch with `style=` attributes, which a policy without `'unsafe-inline'`
refuses (§11, §15): one pass of the pointer over P(s) raised seven hundred violations and left a box
of bare text with its swatches gone. The formatters' markup carries classes instead, and a series'
swatch is an SVG `fill`. **Each coordinate is spelled as its axis spells it** — a sequence's name
over its bar and `84.3 kb` along a P(s), where the library printed the raw number under the pointer,
`6.00` and `84,281.00`; per cent where the axis is; and `2.24e-7` under ticks of `1e-7` rather than a
run of zeros. The crosshair's two numbers on the axes are spelled the same way, where the library
printed `387,269.00` along a P(s) in kb and `0.00` up its ordinate. Over a point, a histogram's
bar, a box or a violin the series comes first, then the
pair, the count, the five numbers the box is drawn from, or, for a violin, nothing more: the shape is
the answer. Tick labels, legends and titles are not markup — the SVG draws them as text — and are not
escaped.

**A boolean is one of two shapes, and a tick box is neither.** A *named parameter* — smooth, fill
under, the grid, the tooltip — is a label and an `on`/`off` button on one row, which is what every
settings column in this app already draws. A *compact set of named things* — the two axis scales, a
table's columns — is a row of buttons each carrying its own name and lighting when it is on, which is
what the overlay marks already draw. Both are `btn-toggle` with `aria-pressed`, so one stylesheet rule
lights them (§26.3), and the figure's settings had a third idiom that was neither.

**A column head is aligned with its column**, left for text and right for numbers. A `<th>` centres
itself by default, which put every head over the middle of a column of left-aligned cells; and a head
is a button that sorts, so it has a name — a blank one is a control whose tooltip reads *Sort by* and
whose column the reader has to infer from its rows.

**New marks.** Line, area, step, points and bars over a pair of axes; histogram, box and violin as
summaries of the ordinate. **An area, and a line with *fill under* on, is shaded down to zero** and
no further — a profile dipping below zero is shaded up to zero there, so above and below read as two
sides of one line — and to the axis's edge only where zero is not on it: a log axis, or a window that
leaves it out. The last three are rules with parameters rather than plots of the data,
so the rules are in `figures/stats.ts` where they can be read: Freedman–Diaconis for a bin width
unless one is typed, Tukey's whiskers stopping at the furthest *observed* value within 1.5 IQR, and
a Gaussian kernel density at Silverman's bandwidth for the violin — every violin on a figure scaled
by the same peak, because two violins each normalised to their own width say the two samples are
equally concentrated. A table can be drawn as any of them: one numeric column as a distribution, or
one against another as a scatter.

**A column of names can be the abscissa, read at the number each name writes.** A time course is
named rather than numbered — a deck's maps are `+parB 15 min` and `+parB 30 min`, and the all-maps
table (§18.7) carries those names in its `Map` column — so a text column is offered beside the
number columns once two of its rows carry a number, each row placed at the **first number in its
cell**, unsigned, since a hyphen in a name is a separator far more often than a minus (`rep-2`). A
row whose name writes none — `WT` beside the time points — is left out, as a row with no number in
a number column is. The axis says what it is: `number in Map`. A name can be changed to be the
number meant (§16.10). **And a scatter can carry its least-squares line** — *least squares* in the
table's rows card, under the abscissa — drawn from the first abscissa to the last as a series of
its own, named by its equation, r² and n (`least squares: y = 2·x + 5 · r² = 1.000 · n = 3`), so
its legend, which opens over the picture once there are two series, carries the numbers into
the PNG and the PDF; its id is `least-squares`, hidden or recoloured like any other series. **The
line is fitted to the points in the abscissa's window** where it has one, and refitted when the
window moves: a box drawn across the time points whose alignment is under way, leaving out the one
taken before anything started, is the fit of those points — the line is what is drawn, as the
export is. **A table drawn as a scatter has a curve's axes card**, read off the scatter it becomes:
its scales, its windows and its names, the columns' (`number in Map`) as the placeholders a reader
replaces with what the axes are — *Time after induction (min)*. And the chart it is drawn as keeps
the plot's mark and its legend through a change made in place — a title, a type size — which
used to hand it the table's own style: a line where the points were, the fitted line's legend
moved to the side. A task whose every series is a sample rather than a function says
so (`CurveSeries.mark = 'violin'`), and its figure opens as violins, one per series — *Signal by
group*'s groups — which the mark control turns into boxes or a histogram like any other. A box or a
violin names its series along the abscissa, so it has **no legend and keeps no room for one**, whatever
the legend switch says; and a violin is **cut at the grid**, because its density runs three bandwidths
past the sample and an ordinate the task or the reader set cuts through it — uncut, the tail was drawn
on over the names under the axis.

**Bars stack where the series are parts of one whole.** A sequence's cis and trans fractions sum to
one, and the reading is one bar split in two rather than two bars side by side whose sum the reader
performs. The task says which series share a stack; **only bars** honour it, because the same
declaration on a pair of lines would draw an upper line that is the sum of two quantities under an
axis claiming it is one of them — so a stacked bar chart restyled to lines is two lines again. The
all-maps overlay keeps the stacks **per map** (`analysis/combine.ts`), since four libraries in one
stack would be a single bar four libraries tall with each one's fraction standing on the sum of the
ones before it.

**A table is a view, not a printing.** Filter, sort and choose columns, which for four thousand MAGs
is the difference between a record and a tool. The filter is a substring over each cell's *text*,
because that is the search a reader means; a row missing a value sorts last whichever way the column
runs, because a row with no value is not a row with the smallest one.

**Every decision is remembered**, per file, per task and per output, in the `UiMemory` scope beside
the task's parameters (§18.2) and carried in an exported session (§5.6). The argument is §18.2's one
step further on: if the recipe is worth keeping then so is the picture the recipe was read from, and
a session that came back with the parameters but with every log axis, hidden series and colour
thrown away would reproduce the numbers and not the figure. What is stored is untrusted input like
everything else that outlives the build that wrote it, and every field is validated against the spec
it is about to be applied to.

---

## 19. Standalone target: one HTML file

A fifth build of the same source, after the site, the archived pin, the desktop shell and the CLI.
It emits exactly one file, `dist-standalone/index.html`, with every script, stylesheet, worker and
icon inlined, and it is meant to be opened by double-clicking it out of a downloads directory. As
with §15 it is a second invocation of the same bundler over the same source and never a change to
the first: `npm run build` is what the deploy workflow runs and must keep producing the same bytes.

**What it is for is three machines the other four targets do not reach.** An air-gapped or HPC
login node with no route to the website; a reviewer who will not install an unsigned binary and
should not have to; a laptop holding unpublished patient-derived data, which is the reader §11 was
written for. §11's promise — nothing is uploaded — holds in every build, but only in this one is it
structural rather than a claim, because there is no origin to upload to.

A remote file cannot be opened here at all — there is no origin to read one from — which is a
property of the target and not a bug in any format. It matters most for a `.bam`, since a dropped
one and its index are the *only* way to get alignments into this build, so the interface says so
rather than failing at it: the URL box is what is absent, and a dropped pair works exactly as it
does everywhere else.

**Four things a `file://` page cannot do.** Each was measured in Chromium before the config was
written, and each is absolute rather than a degradation:

1. **A module worker cannot be constructed.** This is the same failure §15 records against
   `file://` for the desktop renderer, and it is why that target registers a privileged scheme
   instead. Here there is no main process to register one, so the workers change shape:
   `worker.format: 'iife'` plus `?worker&inline` in `src/worker/spawn.standalone.ts` — and in
   `src/analysis/worker/spawnGram.standalone.ts` for the correlation's helpers, which the analysis
   worker starts itself — gives classic workers over blob URLs, which do construct.
