2. **A sibling `.js` cannot be fetched** — the same refusal that blocks a dynamic import.
   `inlineDynamicImports` collapses the graph to one chunk, at both the app and the worker level,
   and the build's own plugin folds that chunk into the HTML.
3. **No network at all.** The origin is opaque, so every remote read fails before it is sent — and
   the page's own policy says so, so that it is a rule rather than a circumstance (below).
4. **No service worker.** Registration is refused. `pwa.ts` needs no change: it already treats a
   refusal as "this page has no cache", and the `TARGET !== 'web'` guard excludes this build anyway.

**The interface is honest about (3) rather than failing at it.** `IS_STANDALONE` removes the remote
URL box, the store tiles (the version picker is gone already, as it is from every target that is
not the web) and the store drawer with everything that opens it — the header's button, the
backslash, the palette's *Stores* (absent there rather than greyed, since no state of this build
opens a store) and a `?store=` link, which reads nothing (§24.2); leaves the landing page's folder
row with the one
place this build can reach — under *Connect a folder*, since a heading naming two kinds over a row
holding one is the same false promise in smaller type, and the Files column's button and the
palette's command say *connect a folder* with it rather than offering a remote half there is not —
and says under the drop zone that this copy opens local files only and where to go for the rest. A
build that offered a URL field
which could never succeed would be a worse artefact than one that does not offer it.

**It is about 14 MB and more than half of that is h5wasm.** The runtime ships its wasm
base64-inlined in its own JavaScript, which is the reason this target is possible at all — there is
no `.wasm` to fetch — and the reason it is this size. It appears twice, in the reader worker and in
the analysis worker, because a `file://` page has no shared chunk to give them; the app chunk itself
carries none. The rest is the app, with three.js (§25.3) and the charting library (§18.13) folded in
where the site loads each as a chunk of its own. Most of the size is the price of HDF5 and is not
reducible without dropping it. It gzips to about a quarter in transit and costs roughly a second of
parsing on each open, with no HTTP cache behind it.

**It carries a policy of its own, computed over itself.** A file can be sent no header, and the
site's `'self'` policy (§11) would refuse every script and stylesheet this build inlines, so the
build writes a `<meta>` CSP after inlining them: `script-src` and `style-src` name the SHA-256 of each
inline element and nothing else — over the text as the parser hands it over, CR LF folded to LF —
`'wasm-unsafe-eval'` keeps h5wasm, workers come only from `blob:`, which is how they are built here,
and images only from `data:` and `blob:`. `connect-src` names `data:` alone, which makes (3) a rule
the browser enforces rather than a property of an opaque origin, and a worker built from a blob
inherits its page's policy, so here — unlike on the site — the workers are policed too: a fetch to
any host is refused in the page and in a worker alike. `data:` is there for a worker and reaches
nothing: the bigWig and bigBed reader carries its inflate wasm as a `data:` URL and fetches it before
its first read, and under `'none'` that was refused inside the annotations worker, where the page
hears nothing of it — every bigWig lane said *fetching…* for good. The hashes are written last,
because any edit to the page after them names a script it no longer holds, and the browser answers
that by refusing the app's one script.

**Every way this build can fail is silent, so the shape is a rule the build enforces.** A page that
kept one `<script src>` paints its shell and stops, with nothing on a console nobody is looking at;
a page that kept the module worker format looks completely normal until a file is dropped on it.
`scripts/standalone-shape.mjs` holds the rules — one file, within a size band (4 MB to 24 MB), no
external script or stylesheet, no root-absolute reference, no PWA tag, no `{type:"module"}` worker
construction, the blob-URL construction present, the target's own name in the page, a policy
naming exactly the scripts and stylesheet the page holds, recomputed over the file it reads, and
the third-party notices every other build writes beside its page, which this one carries as a
comment ahead of `</html>` because it may not be two files (§22.4) — and
`check-standalone-build.mjs` runs them over the directory as the last step of
`npm run build:standalone`. The lower size bound is as load-bearing as the upper: a build whose
inlining silently did nothing produces a small, tidy, entirely broken file.

**And the rules can all pass on a page that does not run**, so `scripts/smoke-standalone.mjs` drives
a real Chromium at a real `file://` URL, mounts the app and opens the contact map named on its
command line through a real worker. It skips with a named message where the browser or
`playwright-core` is absent, in the same way the fixture-dependent tests do. `scripts/ui-csp.mjs
standalone` drives it under its policy — the yeast map and a bigWig dropped on it, two tasks run and
every chart hovered — and fails on a lane or a map left without its data, and on any refusal, in the
page or in one of its workers, but the ones it provokes to show the policy is there.

**Every release carries it.** The release workflow's `standalone` job builds it from the tag and
attaches it to the release as `chromosomix-<tag>.html` — a name that says what it is and
which version, in a downloads directory that already holds several `index.html`s.

**Storage is shared with every other `file://` page on the machine**, because they are all one
origin. Saved sessions and preferences are therefore not isolated between standalone copies, which
matters only when somebody opens two, and cannot be fixed from inside the page.

**Verified in Chromium.** Firefox and Safari are untested against this target; the constraints above
are Chromium's, and another engine may impose more.

---

## 20. Connected folders

Every door to a file the app had asked *which file* once and then closed: the landing page, the
file crumb's *Open a file*, a URL box. That is the right shape for opening one thing and the
wrong shape for the way people work with a directory of data, which is to open one, look, open the
next, and keep going. A **connected folder** is a place the window keeps, browsable in a column, for
as long as the reader wants it.

Four things are folders, and the whole point is that they are the same thing here:

- a **directory on the machine**,
- a **key prefix on a bucket**, public or private,
- a **Google Drive folder**, and
- a **Dropbox** (§24.9).

`browse/folder.ts` is the interface — given a path, the sub-folders and the files; given a file, how
to open it — and the backends are the whole of the difference. Nothing above that layer asks which
kind it is holding, so "a local folder or an S3 bucket, read the same way" is a property of that
file being small rather than a feature written twice.

**They are connected from one dialog, drawn as providers** (`ui/ConnectCard.ts`): a row of four
tiles — this machine, a bucket, Google Drive, Dropbox — and the form of the one pressed under it.
The dialog used to stack six sections down one scroll, and two of the six were not places: a Google
API key and a Google account are settings of *one provider*, and a reader meeting them between a
bucket and a Drive folder had to work out which they belonged to. They sit under Google Drive now,
which is the only tile that needs them, in the order a reader meets them — the key, because a
public Drive link fails without it; the account, because a private one fails afterwards with a key
in place; the folder, because it needs the account. Since then the key and the client id have
become the site's (§24.7), and each of the two panes that sign a reader in is **one title, a
`?` and a button** (`ui/connectHead.ts`): *Google Drive* or *Dropbox* on the left of a line, a `?`
at its far right, and one large sign-in button under it. **Every pane is headed by its own tile's
name** — *This machine*, *A bucket*, *Google Drive*, *Dropbox* — because a tab that renames its
subject on being pressed reads as a further step rather than as the thing pressed; two of the four
were imperatives, and *Connect to your Dropbox* under a tile saying *Dropbox* was the dialog asking
twice. What a pane is *for* is the dialog's title. The sign-in button says **sign in to Google** /
**sign in to Dropbox**, in the words the door said one press earlier (§24.2), and the bucket pane's
says **connect this bucket** rather than *save*: it does save the bucket, but what the reader
pressed a door for is the listing, and that is what happens (§20.3).
Everything the pane has to say about the service — what the grant is, where the token lives,
what is kept — is behind the `?`, shown on hover, on focus, or pinned by a click for a screen
with no hover; what is on the pane itself is what a reader acts on: the button, the reason it is
disabled on a site built without the registration, the code box a Dropbox sign-in opens, an
error. On the Drive pane the folder box — a name, a link or id, *connect this folder* — is not on
screen until the sign-in has happened, and appears under the button the moment it has, on the
same pane, under the same title; there is no second heading. A build that cannot offer a provider
does not draw its tile (§8.5): the standalone build offers this machine alone, and the desktop
build's Drive pane keeps its title and its `?` and says under them why there is no button.

**One verb names this door wherever it is.** The dialog is *Connect a folder*; the landing page's
heading, the Files column's button and the command palette all say *connect a local or remote
folder* — and all three say *connect a folder* in the standalone build, which has no remote half
(§19), from the one name in `ui/connectFronts.ts`; the landing page used to say it there alone.
There were three — the landing page said *Mount*, jargon used nowhere else in the app, the
dialog it opened was titled *Open a local/remote folder*, and every button and every sentence about
the result said *connect* — so a reader pressed under one word, landed on a second and was
reassured in a third. A file is opened; a folder is connected (§26.4). The Files column's button
opens the dialog, and so do three of the four buttons in the landing page's row — those carry the
pane to open on, since a reader who pressed *sign in to Dropbox* has already chosen and must not be
asked again.
The fourth, *choose a folder…*, opens **the directory picker itself**: it is one gesture, the
browser draws it, and a dialog in front of it would be asking the reader to press the same words
twice (§24.2). Both screens call `connectDirectory` (`browse/connected.ts`) and take the button's
label from `localVerb` (`ui/connectFronts.ts`), and therefore cannot disagree about which of the two
shapes this browser gets, nor about the label that says so.

### 20.1 One level, never a walk

`list` answers one path with its immediate children. Nothing recurses, and that is a constraint
rather than an omission: on a bucket a recursive listing is one signed request per prefix against a
key that may be allowed some of them and not others, and on a disk it is an unbounded walk of
somebody's home directory to draw a sidebar. The folder view is the folder, not an index of it —
the same rule its own filter states about itself.

All four backends stop at **1,000 entries** and say so. S3's own page is a thousand; a local
directory had no limit at all, which is the wrong asymmetry to leave in, since a `fastq/` directory
of forty thousand files would build forty thousand rows on a gesture the reader cannot undo. "My
file is not here" and "my file is past the cap" look identical otherwise, and only one of them is
actionable.

### 20.2 The local half, in two shapes

**A grant**, where `showDirectoryPicker` exists — Chromium and the desktop build. The page holds a
`FileSystemDirectoryHandle`: a capability, not a path and not a copy. Listings are read through it
when they are asked for, so the folder is live — a file a pipeline writes into it five minutes later
is simply there — and the handle is structured-cloneable, so it can survive in IndexedDB and the
folder be still connected after a reload. **It is kept only by the installed app** (§20.6): the
desktop build, the single-file build, and the site installed as an app. In a browser tab a granted
folder is connected for the visit, as a snapshot is, and the row says so in the same two words. A
grant can lapse — browsers hand a directory back for a while and then ask once more — and the folder
then stays in the column with a *reconnect* button rather than vanishing, since a folder that
vanished reads as one never connected and the fix is one click only the reader can make; a grant the
reader *denied* is forgotten instead of asked for on every reload.

**A snapshot**, everywhere else. Firefox and Safari have no picker; `<input webkitdirectory>` hands
back a flat `File[]` carrying `webkitRelativePath`, from which the tree is rebuilt once. It does not
update and it does not survive a reload, because a `File` is bytes the page was handed rather than
permission to go and get them.

They are not the same feature and the panel says so on the row, in two words — *this visit*.
§8.5's doctrine — a control that cannot keep its promise is absent rather than disabled — does *not*
apply: the gesture works in all four browsers, and what differs is how long the answer lasts.
Hiding it in two of them would take a working feature away to avoid writing one clause.

Asked in `'read'` mode explicitly. §13's "the app never modifies a file it opened" should be true of
the question the reader is shown as well as of the code.

### 20.3 The bucket half, and the one thing a public bucket usually cannot do

A scope may now carry **no credential**, and that is a scope over public data rather than a broken
one. A public bucket costs one field — its URL — instead of six. An unsigned `GET` with no custom
headers is a *simple* CORS request, so it is not preflighted, which means the ordinary public-data
policy (`GET`, `HEAD`, `Range`) answers a listing as it stands and the whole class of preflight
failures the signed path has to explain cannot arise.

What it does need is `s3:ListBucket` granted to `*` in the **bucket policy**, which is a different
grant from the `s3:GetObject` that makes the objects downloadable — and most published buckets grant
the second and not the first. **A public bucket that refuses to be listed is a normal
configuration, not a fault.** With no backend (C1) there is nothing the app can do about it, so the
403 says which of the two grants is missing and says that files under the prefix still open by URL.
`docs/hosting.md` has the policy.

The rule inside a scope is **all three signing fields or none**; a row holding one or two is dropped
rather than downgraded to an unsigned one, because falling back would turn a mistyped secret into a
bucket that 403s on data the reader believes they have a key for.

The stored-data screen (§20.6) lists each as what it is. A scope with no key is *Buckets you
connected*, named, as the folders and the stores are — an address, kept with nothing secret in it —
and *Bucket keys* is there only where some part of a key is on the disk, a dropped row's included.
Every scope used to be *Bucket keys — access keys for private buckets*, which told a reader who had
connected one public bucket that there was a credential to forget.

The form's one button is **connect this bucket**. It was *save*, from when the same form stood in a
credentials dialog where saving was the whole of it; behind a door that said *connect a bucket…*,
beside a Drive pane that says *connect this folder*, *save* promised a stored setting rather than
the listing the reader came for — and the listing is what pressing it produces. There is no *test
connection* button, because that listing **is** the test: the same signature and the same preflight
as every later read, where a separate probe would be a second code path whose passing would mean
nothing about the first.

### 20.4 The fifth column, and the one that is not about the open file

§16.5 says the side columns are the session's furniture and each describes the one file the session
is of. **Files is the exception and is meant to be.** What it holds is the places this window is
connected to, which are the same in every tab and outlive all of them, exactly as the theme is. It
is therefore built once, never re-parented on a tab switch, and — alone among the five — **available
with nothing open at all**: a reader who has connected a folder and opened nothing yet is exactly
the reader it is for.

**It is there while a place is connected, and not otherwise** (`App.refreshFilesPanel`), which is
§8.5's rule as the other four columns already follow it. It used to be there unconditionally,
because its own *connect a local or remote folder* was the only door to a folder and a column
nobody can see is not a door. The landing page now offers the four places itself (§24.2), so what
that rule was buying on the first screen is an empty column beside a row of buttons saying the same
thing.
Connecting one opens the column on it (`reveal`), because the answer to the gesture is in there;
disconnecting the last one takes it away again. A reload opens it on the folder it last showed,
without asking for a permission no gesture is behind. The doors are elsewhere and stay elsewhere: the
landing page — which is what a new tab is — and *Connect a local or remote folder* in the command
palette.

**The key left of `1` folds it** — a backtick on QWERTY, `²` on an AZERTY PC — because it stands
left of General's `1` as the column stands left of General (§26.6). It was `f`, which the `fills`
overlay gave up when the column arrived and has had back since the columns moved to the digit row. The row stays in the command palette, which promises to list everything the
app can do. The key itself is live only while the column is there: with nothing connected it would
fold a column nobody can see, so the palette's *Files panel* row is dimmed and says to connect a
folder first.

### 20.5 Two verbs on a row

Every file row in the application carries the same two marks, and only marks (`ui/rowVerbs.ts`): a
`+` that **adds the file to the session in front** — a second map beside the one that is there,
anything else drawn on top, an empty tab filled rather than added to, which is the routing a
dropped file takes — and a window with a `+` where its corner was that **opens it in a session of
its own**, the empty tab in front or a new one, leaving whatever was open as it is. The words are
in the tooltips, which also say what *add* means for that kind of file. Both are offered whatever
the tab holds: on an empty tab the two land in the same place and the tooltips say so, because a
row with two marks in one store and one in the next is a row a reader has to think about. **An
empty tab is filled by a row of any kind**, as the landing page's drop zone fills it: a folder on
this machine hands its file to the road a drop on the window takes, whose empty seat was a map's
alone, so a bigWig pressed there — its `+` saying it would open in this tab — did nothing and said
nothing. A workspace row has the second alone — it is tabs, not a file, and there is nothing it
could be added to. The same pair stands on a store's rows (§24.2), on a folder's rows here and on
the files under a gallery card, whose own head carries the second mark alone; with words beside the
marks it is the tray under a portal, and the second mark is on a portal group's *open with its
tracks*. Clicking a folder row's name is the first verb.

Dragging a file lets the reader say *where*: onto the map's edge rectangles for a lane in a named
stack (§8.9), onto the rectangle in the middle of a map for that map alone — an overlay's one target
(§8.1) — onto a companion, anywhere on its cell, for a track on that map, and onto a tracks cell for
a track drawn in it (§16.9), onto the Tracks card, onto a deck's edge or an empty cell for a cell of
its own (§16.9), onto a 3D cell for the model it draws (§25.3), onto the Contact maps card's *Load a
map into the lower triangle* for the second file in the square (§5.7), onto an analysis form's file
box as the run's input rather than as anything opened (§18.8), onto the content area, onto the
landing page's drop zone — which replaces, because that is what the landing page has always meant.
**A store's row is dragged the same way, to the same places** (§24.2): every row that is a file,
in the drawer's lists and under its cards, as every file row here is — and not a saved workspace's,
which is tabs rather than a file and has nowhere to be aimed, as a workspace in a folder is a row
that does not drag.

**The Files column is the only door onto a connected place.** Its folder view lists every place the
window is connected to — a directory on this machine included — and a row hands back the file with
the credential the listing used; a row dragged out of it is resolved at the drop, through the folder
it names (`ui/fileDrag.ts`). The same view in a dialog was opened by the *from a connected place…*
buttons below and by nothing else, and went with them.

**The cards that ask for a file keep no second door.** Each of them — Tracks, Contact maps,
Structures, an empty cell of a deck — used to carry a box to paste a URL into, folded away behind
*or open one by URL*, and beside it a *from a connected place…* button onto that dialog. Both are
gone from all of them, and the deck's add row has lost the button too. **Structures** went last and
separately, having arrived with §25's card after the others were cleared: the rule is the card's
shape and not a list of cards, so a new one that asks for a file is a drop zone and nothing under
it. A structure held at an address still opens by every road it did — the landing page's box, a
session, a `#uri`, the Files column — and what is gone is the third of them on the card itself.

The box went first and for the obvious reason: it was the worse half of the pair it was in. A reader
holding a URL can drop the link on the window or paste it into the landing page's own box, which is
where this application says *open a file*; a reader **without** one was being asked to produce
something they have not got — and that is the commonest state in all three places the boxes stood
in. The bigWigs beside a map are keys in a prefix whose names came off a run sheet; a reader
repairing a shared deck is looking at a `~` precisely because the sender's file had no address a
page could fetch by name (§11).

The button went for a different reason, and it is the one worth stating: **browsing a connected place
is a column, not a dialog.** §20 opens by saying that every door to a file this application had asked
*which file* once and then closed, and that the way people work with a directory of data is to open
one, look, open the next, and keep going. A button that opened a one-shot copy of the column from
four different rows was four doors to one room, each of which closed on the first pick — the shape
the connected folder exists to replace. What a card that asks for a file needs is the drop zone and
nothing under it.

A dragged row carries a **folder id and a path**, never bytes: the file behind it is fetched at the
drop, once, by the target that accepted it. The path alone would be ambiguous the moment two folders
are connected. A store's row carries **neither, and not its address either**: it travels under the
same type, so every target that takes a folder's row takes it, and what the type carries is a token
naming the drag, the row's file being held by the page that started it (`writePickedDrag`). An
address in the payload would let any page have this one open any URL by dragging something across
it with the right label on; a token, like a folder id, resolves only to what this window is holding,
and the tracks the row brings (§24.3) are noted when a target takes it, not when the hand picks it
up. Everything ends at `Session.addPicked`, which decides nothing — it hands a local file to the
same door a dropped one takes and a remote one to the door a typed URL takes. A third routing table
is how a `.cool` picked from a folder would come to open somewhere a `.cool` dropped on the window
does not.

**A file the viewer has no route for is drawn, dimmed and inert, with the reason in its tooltip.**
Hiding it would make the folder view disagree with the folder, which is the one thing it is for; a
`.cram` sitting there unhighlighted answers *why is nothing happening when I click it* before it is
asked. An index is one of them, and its tooltip says it is picked up with the file it indexes: a
file picked from a folder on this machine brings its index from beside it (`browse/folder.ts`'s
`PickedFile.index`), so a `.bam` whose `.bai` is one row down opens with it — wherever the row is
let go, the landing page's *Load files* included, which took a row by its address alone and opened
the `.bam` without it (`LoadBox`'s `onPicked`). The one thing a local
listing does leave out is a name beginning with a dot — `.DS_Store`, `.git` — which is somebody's
tooling rather than a file. The route is the name's (`browse/route.ts`), so every name a format of
§8 is published under has to be in it: a `.barChart`, a `.bigBarChart` and a cytoBand in the plural
were drawn dimmed while the loader read all three — and so, until every name each reader takes was
checked against the table (`test/unit/browse-route.test.ts` holds the list), were four kinds more.
A **3D structure** (§25) — `.g3d`, `.3dg`, `.bed3d`, `.pdb` — is the genome door's, and the same
name test makes its row a structure the moment it is begun, so its cell opens before a byte is
read. A **saved workspace** is a `.json`, routed by the test the config road itself uses; its row
carries the new-session mark alone, and pressed, its tabs are appended beside the window's as a
store row's are, with no empty tab opened for them first. A **text table** — `.txt`, `.tsv`,
`.tab`, compressed or not — says nothing by its name and is offered all the same, because it is
what a §8 format is published under when its own suffix is not used (chromosight's `loops.tsv`, a
GEO supplement's `peaks.txt.gz`), and the loader reads it by its bytes (§8.3) as it does a dropped
one; one whose rows no reader takes — a page of notes — is refused as *text, but not a table this
viewer reads*, saying what a table is read as, where it used to reach the contact map's door and be
told it was not an HDF5 file. And **`.bgz`**, which is what `bgzip` is told to write for a file
meant to be indexed — gnomAD's VCFs — is read everywhere a `.gz` is, its `.tbi` found beside it
included.

What stays dimmed says the one thing its reader needs. A track hub's `hub.txt` is a store, opened
from the stores drawer (§24.10), and its `genomes.txt` and `trackDb.txt` are read from it rather
than offered as tables; a CSV is comma-separated, and every table read here is tab- or
space-separated; a `.bz2`, `.xz` or `.zst` is a compression this viewer cannot inflate, and gzip or
bgzip is the way out; a `.gzi` is an index this viewer does not use, a compressed FASTA being read
whole (§8.8); a `.crai` is refused with its CRAM. A name a folder's address does not carry decides
as well: a Drive or Dropbox row is routed by the name the folder handed along (§24.9), a workspace
and a model as well as a map and a track.

### 20.6 What a connected folder is, in privacy terms

Wider than a chosen file, and worth being exact about how. The page can see the **names** of
everything under the directory and read any of them without a further gesture — that is what makes
browsing possible — and, for the durable shape, it can do so again after a restart.

**Kept by the installed app, and by nothing else.** An app the reader installed on their own machine
— the desktop build, the single-file build they saved and open from their disk, or the site installed
as an app, which a browser opens in a window of its own (`installed.ts`: the `standalone`,
`minimal-ui` and `window-controls-overlay` display modes, or Safari's home-screen flag; never
`fullscreen`, which a tab answers too) — is a place they have chosen to keep things. A browser tab is a
page on whatever machine opened it — a shared one, somebody else's, one reached from a link — and a
page that kept a grant to a directory of unpublished data would be keeping it for the next person at
that browser. So in a tab a folder is connected for the visit: held in memory, listed and browsed
like any other, and gone with the page; nothing about it is written down, and the connect button and
the row both say *this visit*. Grants a tab stored before this rule are left in storage for the
installed app on the same origin, which shares it, and are listed — and forgettable — in the
stored-data screen like everything else.

**And it finds a workspace's files there again.** A file opened from a kept folder is remembered by
the folder it was in and its path from that folder's root (`state/locations.ts`), and a workspace
saved by the installed app carries the same (`folders`: each folder by its id and name, and its files
by name with their paths). A session that comes back — after a restart, from the workspace file,
in another window — asks for `rep1.cool` and finds it at `run2/hic/rep1.cool` through the grant on
`run2`, its tracks too, and nobody is asked to find anything. A workspace opened by another
installation knows the folder by a different id or none: there the folder's **name** is what is left,
and then any kept folder the path is found in, and a file found must carry the name asked for, as a
file grant's must (`state/handles.ts`). Where no such folder is connected, the note over the picker
names it and its path, with a button that connects it, after which the session's files are found
there on their own. None of this is written outside the installed app; a share link carries no
`folders`, and a workspace published at a URL has them dropped, since both reach people whose disks
those paths are not about. The desktop build lets its own page re-read what the user chose — a
`fileSystem` permission, read access, its own origin only — and refuses every other permission as
before.

What has not changed is where the bytes go: **nowhere**. §11 holds exactly as it held for a dropped
file. A local folder is read in place, a slice at a time, by code on the reader's own machine; a
bucket is read by the browser from the bucket. There is no server in between because there is no
server. Every connected folder this browser keeps is accounted for in the stored-data screen — *What
this browser is remembering* — beside the file grants and the places of the files opened from them,
and is revocable one at a time by its × in the Files column or all at once by that screen's *forget
everything* — which is the same bargain `state/handles.ts` already struck for a single file, made
visible at the wider grant.

In the standalone build (§19) the bucket half is absent — the origin is opaque, so every remote read
fails before a byte moves — and the local half has no shape of its own: a `file://` page is a secure
context, Chromium exposes the directory picker to it, and `browse/local.ts` asks the browser rather
than the build, so it is a grant where the picker exists and a snapshot where it does not.

## 21. Embedded in another page

Not a sixth build: the same web build, mounted differently. `?embed=1` renders **one view of one
file with no window around it**, so the app can be what it has never been able to be — the figure
*inside* somebody else's page: a portal, a lab's site, a paper's supplementary material, a course
page. `src/embed.ts` is the only module that reads the flag; everything downstream asks it.

**Nothing has to be installed at either end, and that is a consequence of §1 rather than a feature
added on top.** There is no backend to point at and no package to depend on, so an embed is an
`<iframe src=…>` and nothing else. Three properties this app already had are what make that work,
and each is load-bearing:

- **No `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` or `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy`, and no `SharedArrayBuffer`**
  (docs/deploy.md). This is the usual reason a wasm application *cannot* be embedded — cross-origin
  isolation has to be arranged by the *host* page and almost never is. h5wasm 0.10.x is
  single-threaded with the binary inlined, so there is nothing to isolate.
- **Every view state is in the hash** (§5.5), so what to show is sayable in the `src=`.
- **Every push is archived at `…/v/<commit>/`** (docs/deploy.md) — the last twenty of them, and
  every release for ever, by its tag at `…/v/<tag>/` as well — so an embed can name an immutable
  build and go on rendering the same picture in five years. A figure in a paper should be pinned to
  a release; the root is for a page that wants the newest. **The promise outlives the site's
  address.** An archived build is built once, for the address the site had, with that base in every
  asset URL; when the base changes — the site's own domain, `chromosomix.app`, puts it at the root —
  the deploy rewrites each archived build and preview for the new base, once
  (`scripts/archive-rebase.mjs`), and `…/v/<commit>/` goes on opening the same build there.
- **No `frame-ancestors`.** The web builds' policy (§11) is a `<meta>`, which cannot carry the
  directive, and would leave it out if it could: a policy deciding who may frame the viewer is a
  policy against this surface. The desktop's header says `frame-ancestors 'none'`, which is right
  for an application window and is the one clause the two policies do not share.

The data host needs no new CORS entry per embedding site: a frame's requests carry the **frame's**
origin, which is the viewer's, so §11's hosting requirements are exactly as they were.

### 21.1 What decides what an embed shows

Three seeds, in the order they override one another, and each is reached only because the ones above
it said nothing: a **shared session** in the fragment (`#session=`, a workspace of one tab deflated
into the URL); a **view state** in the fragment (`#uri=…`, which is what a navigation leaves behind,
so it has to beat the `src=` or every reload would undo the reader's last click); and
**`?config=<url>`**, a published `.chromosomix.json` fetched and opened through
`Session.openConfigUrl` — the same road the picker's own URL box takes, so a seeded session and a
chosen one differ in nothing after the fetch.
With none of the three, an embed is the file picker — its *Load files* alone (§21.2) — which is a
legitimate thing to embed.

`?config=` is the pointer form of what `#session=` carries as a payload. A payload cannot be changed once
the embed is published and grows the URL by the size of the session; a pointer is a file on a bucket,
editable afterwards, of no length, and — because the names inside it resolve against its own URL
(`state/SessionConfig.ts`'s `resolveConfig`) — self-contained enough to be copied to another bucket with its data. Both are
read by one parser, and the view state in either by the one a `#uri=` link is read by (§5.5).

A relative `?config=` resolves against the page it was named on. Only `http:` and `https:` are kept,
judged after `canonicalUrl` has made an `s3://` or a `gs://` the address it stands for (§24.5): the
value is about to be fetched, and the other schemes are the ones with no server on the other end.

`?store=` is the third mounting parameter and is not a seed: it opens the store drawer over
whatever the window shows (§24.2), carrying the store's view in the rest of the address, and an
embed — which has no drawer — ignores it.

### 21.2 What it keeps and what it drops, and why each one

- **The window furniture.** Header, tab strip, restore slot, status bar — and with the header the two
  surfaces it opens, the store drawer and the console, which are not built at all (§21.1, §23.5).
  The header is controls over a window; the tab strip offers tabs an embed does not keep; the
  restore slot offers *the reader's own* previous workspace, which inside an article would be six of
  their files on a page that never asked for them (§11); the status bar is a byte counter under a
  figure.
- **Three of the five columns.** Files is the places this window has been connected to (§20),
  General is a reference card about the file, and Analysis starts jobs and writes results — all
  three about the window and the work around it. **Annotations and Aesthetics stay**, because they
  are controls over the *picture*: which lanes are drawn, how they are coloured, scaled and clipped.
  A reader looking at somebody else's figure has every reason to reach for those two.

  They arrive **folded**, whatever anything else says, and stand as their own named spines on either
  edge. This one was measured rather than reasoned. A column is open unless it has been folded — a
  fresh browser has nothing stored, and a session may carry a layout of its own — so the first real
  embed of a published figure came up in a 1,200-pixel frame behind five open columns, with
  **thirty-two pixels of map** between them. An embed is a picture first.

  An embed's columns also neither read nor write the stored fold and width. Reading would open a
  column inside somebody's figure because the reader once left it open on the app's own site;
  writing would rearrange the application for a reader who opened a panel in a page they were only
  reading. Same rule as the window's memory above, one level down.

  **The landing page loses the two doors that led to what is gone.** A store tile opens the drawer
  and a place is connected into the Files column, so an embed's picker is *Load files* alone, with
  neither the tiles nor the row of places (§24.2): it had both, and in a frame a tile pressed did
  nothing and a folder chosen was connected into a column nobody could see. The palette keeps its
  shape (§26.6) and greys the same rows — *Connect a folder*, and the folds of the Files, General
  and Analysis columns, as it greys the console's.

  Everything else — the view, the analysis drawer, the content area, dropping a file, every keyboard
  shortcut — is built exactly as it is for a top-level window, so no view knows it is embedded.
- **History entries.** A frame's `pushState` writes into the *joint* session history, so an embed
  that pushed would take over the reader's Back button: clicking a genome and pressing Back would
  step the map instead of leaving the page. Every write replaces. The bar is still written — a
  reload and a copied link both read it — only the stack is left alone.
- **A memory of itself.** Neither the `sessionStorage` tab strip (§5.6) nor the durable record
  under it (`state/workspace.ts`) is written. An embed is one view seeded by its URL and must show what the page says on
  every load; and a third-party frame's storage is partitioned per embedding site, so what it wrote
  would be a store the reader has no interface to and no way to clear.
- **The service worker and the version notice.** An embed is not an app to install, and a bar
  offering "take the newest build" across the top of somebody's figure is chrome by another name —
  and an offer only the page's author could accept, since they pinned the build on purpose.

**The File System Access API is unavailable to a cross-origin frame**, and in the way that is hardest
to see: the pickers are *present* and reject when called. Every gate on a picker that opens
something therefore tests `crossOriginFrame()` as well as `typeof`, and a cross-origin embed takes the
same fallbacks Firefox and Safari have always taken — an `<input type="file">` for files, the
snapshot shape for a directory (§20). The save dialog (§26.6) needs no such test: it tells a refusal
from a cancel by the error it is given, and a refused one becomes the plain download it always was.
**Dropping is untouched**, so "drop your own file on this figure" is an embed a page can offer. A
same-origin frame is deliberately not caught: the pickers work there.

### 21.3 The one bar it has

Not a smaller header: the breadcrumb row with three things added, and what is on it is what a figure
in somebody else's page owes its reader.

**The mark and the name**, left. In a window the brand is the way home — the picker, **in a new tab**,
so the tab in front keeps its file, its tracks and its deck: every page has taught a reader that the
logo is safe to press, and a dropped local file cannot be re-opened without another gesture (§11),
which is the same reason the file crumb stopped navigating to the picker. An empty tab *is* the
picker, so a tab with nothing in it goes straight there rather than opening a second empty one. In a
frame there is no new tab to open and nothing may be thrown away either (§21.2), so it is a link
*out*: this same view in the full application, in a new tab, with `embed` dropped from the query
string and the fragment carried across untouched. Its address is rewritten on every navigation, so
copying it copies where the reader actually is.

**The file and where they are in it**, next: the ordinary breadcrumb (§5.5), in the same slot the
session fills in a window, with its own frame taken off so the row reads as one bar.

**The two panel toggles and About**, right. The toggles are the panels' *own* buttons — the same
objects the header holds in a window, so there is one fold path and not a second written for frames —
and each hides itself when its column has nothing to show. About is the same dialog the header opens,
and it is the answer to every question this bar raises: what this viewer is, that nothing is uploaded
(§11), which build is in the frame, and where the source is. An embedded figure that could not say
those four things would be asking a reader to trust a picture with no provenance.

### 21.4 The channel

An embed that can only be linked to is a picture. `postMessage` is the other half, and it is five
messages (`app/EmbedChannel.ts`). Out: `chromosomix:ready`, once, carrying the protocol version and
the build and **nothing about the session**; `chromosomix:state`, the view state as the hash is
written from; and `chromosomix:rendered`, the report of a finished picture (§12), which is what a
host takes a screenshot on. In: `chromosomix:where`, answered with the state; and `chromosomix:navigate`, a **patch**
laid over what is on screen — `{ locus: … }` moves the browser without the host knowing what else is
in the state, a key sent as `null` is removed, and `state: null` is the picker.

Two rules decide the rest. **Only the window that framed this one is answered**, and only after it
has spoken — `ready` is the single exception and the reason the handshake terminates. Replies and
pushes go to the origin the host spoke from, never to `*`, because a reader can open *their own* file
in an embed and the URL that follows is not the host's to learn unless it asked to be told. An opaque
origin — a `file://` host, a sandboxed frame — cannot be named as a target, and is answered at the
window itself, which is the only address it has.

And a patch is **serialised and parsed back** through §5.5's reader rather than believed. It is an
object from another origin, so it is exactly as untrusted as a hand-edited link, and there is already
one reader that validates every key, clamps what needs clamping and drops what it does not recognise.
A `view` this build has never heard of falls back; a smoothing radius it does not offer is dropped;
an array where a genome name should be is not stringified into one. What the host is told afterwards
is where the view actually **went**, which for a trimmed patch is not always where it asked to go.

## 22. The package: the copy that goes to npm

A sixth build of the same source, after the site, the archived pin, the desktop shell, the CLI and
the standalone page. It emits `dist/` — the ordinary web app — and it is published to a registry as
a **built directory rather than as something to import**. Nothing depends on it; things *serve* it.

**What it is for is one question §21 could not answer.** An embed is an `<iframe>` and a URL, and
until now that URL was this project's GitHub Pages site. A page that frames it takes on a dependency
on somebody else's domain, deployment and lifetime — which is a reasonable thing to decline, and a
thing a figure in a paper should decline. A published version is the alternative: immutable,
checksummed, mirrored, and unpackable into any server the reader's institution already runs.

`package.json` used to say `private: true`, on the argument that this is an application rather than a
library and that a registry has no use for it. The first half is still true and is not what
publishing changes. What a registry is wanted for here is not dependency resolution; it is **hosting
nobody has to trust**, which is a distribution channel beside Pages rather than a claim that anyone
should `import` this.

### 22.1 The relative base, which is the whole of the build

Every other build knows where it will be served from: the site root and `/v/<commit>/` for an
archive (§21), baked into absolute asset URLs, and `app://viewer` for the desktop shell, whose own
protocol handler serves the renderer out of the asar (§15). A tarball knows nothing — it is
unpacked into `/viewer/` on one site, `/npm/<name>@<version>/dist/` on a CDN, a deep path on the
next — so its base is `./`, and one published version serves all of them with no rebuild.

The rule that comes with it is the reader's: **the URL has to end in a slash, or name `index.html`.**
A relative base resolves against the document, so `…/viewer` without the slash looks for the assets
one directory too high. Most servers redirect; a CDN generally does not.

Two absences follow from not knowing where it is, and both are enforced rather than assumed
(`IS_PORTABLE`, `src/versions.ts`):

- **No service worker.** A copy mounted under a path it does not own must not claim a scope there —
  on a registry CDN that scope covers other people's packages.
- **No version manifest.** `SITE_BASE` resolves against the document, so asking for `versions.json`
  would be asking whichever directory the copy was unpacked into for a file only the deployment has.
  The About dialog therefore lists no other builds, which is correct: there is no site to list.

It also carries no source maps and nothing from `public/` — ~20 MB of a ~26 MB site build — because
a tarball is downloaded by everyone who installs it and cached for ever by every mirror. What is left
is ~6 MB unpacked, 1.7 MB compressed.

### 22.2 What is in it, and the one thing that rides along

`files` is `dist/` and `dist-cli/`, and it is the whole of what stands between a publish and 250 MB of
demo data: npm's default is everything not ignored by git. `dist-cli/` is there so the declared `bin`
resolves inside the package — `npx chromosomix` then works against a published version with no
clone, which is what makes `h5wasm`, `@gmod/bbi` and `generic-filehandle2` — the three the CLI's
bundle leaves external — runtime dependencies rather than dev ones. They are the only ones, because
`dependencies` is what every install downloads. Everything a bundle compiles in is a devDependency —
`echarts` and `three` among them, which `dist/` already carries and the command line never loads.
Declared as dependencies, those two and `zrender` under them were 90 MB of the 116 MB an install of
the package put on disk.

npm **force-includes the file `main` names**, ahead of `files` and ahead of a negation. `main` is the
Electron entry point (§15) and cannot be dropped without breaking `electron .`, so a pack run in a
working tree that has built the desktop target carries 18 KB of compiled main process with it. It is
inert — nothing in the package requires it — but it makes the tarball depend on local state, which is
why publishing happens from CI, on a clean checkout, where the directory does not exist.

### 22.3 Why the shape is asserted before it can be packed

`prepack` runs the build, so `npm pack` and `npm publish` both fill `dist/` from source at that
moment rather than shipping whatever was there — and `dist-cli/` too, which `build:package` builds
first. Then `check-package-build.mjs` refuses the result if it is wrong — no `index.html`,
`icon-192.png` or `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt`, no module script under `./assets/`, a root-absolute
reference, a service worker or a web manifest, a source map, a data file, more than 12 MB in all, a
page without the site's policy (§11), which a copy carries in the page because no server it lands on
will send it, or a `dist-cli/` without the command `bin` names or its notices (§22.4) — and the
rules are held by a test (`package-shape.mjs`, `test/unit/package-shape.test.ts`) in the arrangement
§15 and §21's archived build both use.

That check earns its place twice over here. `dist/` is written by **two** builds — the site's and this
one — and only one of them may be published; a tarball packed over a site build would carry absolute
asset URLs that 404 on every mount that is not the site root, plus 20 MB of maps. And unlike every
other artifact in this repository, **a published version cannot be corrected**: an archived build is
rebuilt over on the next push and a deployment is redeployed, while a tarball is on the registry for
ever, mirrored by every CDN that has seen it and pinned in the lockfile of whoever installed it that
week. The pack is the last moment any of it is cheap to notice.

**The version is asserted before the pack, too.** The release workflow publishes on a `v*` tag, and
its first job refuses a tag that is not `v` and the version `package.json` carries, before anything
is built or published: npm takes the number from `package.json`, not from the tag. `v0.14.0` was
made by hand, on a commit still versioned 0.13.0, and the workflow packed `chromosomix@0.13.0` for
it — published, it would have been 0.13.0 for ever with 0.14.0's code in it. Only a tag `npm version`
made has been through the checks (`preversion`) and named its changelog section, and only that tag
agrees with the file. There is no 0.14.0: the next release was 0.15.0.

**And it publishes without a secret.** The workflow publishes by npm's trusted publishing: npm takes
the upload only from this repository's `release.yml`, by the short-lived identity GitHub gives that
run, and publishes it with provenance, so a version on the registry says which commit and which run
built it. There is no token to leak or let expire — 0.15.0, the first version, needed one, because
npm trusts a workflow only with a package that already exists. A run in any other repository, a
fork's, skips the registry rather than being refused by it.

### 22.4 The notices: what every build owes what it carries

chromosomix is under the **GNU General Public License, version 3 or (at your option) any later
version** — `LICENSE`, and `GPL-3.0-or-later` in `package.json`. It was MIT until peak calling was
ported from yapc (GPL-3.0) and IDR (GPL-2.0 or later, §18.9): a translation of GPL code can only be
distributed under the GPL, and version 3 is the one that admits both of them and echarts' Apache-2.0
at once. Everything else it carries is permissive and compatible with it — but each of those licences
is a condition on every copy, and a bundle is a copy. echarts is Apache-2.0, which asks for its licence
and its NOTICE to travel with the work; zrender, and the HDF5 inside h5wasm, are BSD-style and ask
for their notices in any redistribution in binary form; every MIT and ISC licence asks for its
copyright line in all copies or substantial portions. Minifying drops the comments that carried
them: three.js's two were the only notices that reached `dist/`, and a tarball carried chromosomix's
own LICENSE and nobody else's.

So **every build writes `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt` beside what it built** — the site and an archived
pin at their roots, the desktop renderer in its asar, the package in `dist/` and, beside the command,
in `dist-cli/` — listing what it carries and then reproducing each licence in full. The standalone
page may not be two files and carries the same text as a comment ahead of `</html>` (§19).

**What is listed is read off the bundle, not off `package.json`** (`scripts/third-party-notices.mjs`),
because a dependency is not a copy and a copy need not be a dependency: the CLI leaves `h5wasm` and
`@gmod/bbi` external, so npm installs each with its own licence and the command's notices owe them
nothing, while `zrender` is nobody's dependency here but echarts' and is in every page that draws a
figure. Every module that put code into an output is filed under its package by the `node_modules/`
in its path, and the package's licence, copying and notice files are quoted as installed — echarts'
`licenses/` too, which holds the licence of the d3 it embeds. Vite builds each worker with a Rollup
of its own whose plugins the page's never see, and the readers, the kernels and h5wasm are all in
workers, so a collector in `worker.plugins` reports into the same record the page's plugin writes
from.

**Material a generator copied into `src/` is carried too, and named by the file that holds it**: the
interface icons from Lucide (ISC) and the brand marks from Simple Icons (CC0), chromosight's preset
kernels (MIT), matplotlib's colour tables (the Matplotlib licence, which asks a derivative to say
what it changed: sampled at 256 entries and stored as RGB) and ColorBrewer's schemes behind `Reds` and
`RdBu_r` (Apache-2.0). Each licence is the installed devDependency the generator read or, for an
upstream that is not an npm package, a text committed verbatim under `licenses/`; the version is read
off the generated file's own header where it records one, so the notice names what the material came
from rather than what is installed today. A test holds every such file to existing, since renaming
one would drop its upstream's licence without a word.

**So is code ported from a reference implementation.** §18.9 holds an analysis to the numbers its
reference gives, and some of them get there by following that code function for function, in its
order — a translation, which is a copy in another language and owes what a copy owes. Each is named
by the files that hold it, beside the material above: yapc's peak calling (GPL-3.0) and IDR's fit
(GPL-2.0 or later), cooltools' HiCCUPS and peak prominence (MIT),
cooler's region parsing (BSD-3-Clause), chromosight's detection functions (MIT, with its kernels),
the cephes functions SciPy's `xsf` carries and SciPy's `fminbound` (BSD-3-Clause), NumPy's pairwise
sum and its two samplers (BSD-3-Clause, and NCSA or BSD-3-Clause for `numpy.random`), scikit-learn's
BIRCH (BSD-3-Clause), Boost-HiC (MIT) and fdlibm's `erf` (Sun's notice). An implementation written
from a paper and checked against a tool's output owes that tool nothing, and is not listed.

**chromosomix's own licence leads the texts**, because the desktop's asar and the standalone page
carry no `LICENSE` beside them. **A package that ships no licence text** — `generic-filehandle2`,
which declares MIT and has no text of it in its tarball or its repository — has the licence it
declares, naming the author it names, committed under `licenses/` and reproduced in its place.

**About names them too**, under *Licences*: chromosomix's own licence, the GPL, then one line per project —
its name linking to its home, what it does in this viewer, and its licence — with a dependency folded
in beside what pulls it in, and a link to the build's own `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt` (the site's, from
the desktop and the standalone page, which have none a link can open). The list is
`src/licences.ts`, and `test/unit/licences.test.ts` holds it to every package the source imports and
everything those pull in, to every entry the notices name as copied or ported, and to the README's
*Licence* section. Then one line on the marks of the stores and services the interface shows. The
dialog is wider than a plain one for its three columns, and taller, so the build stamp under them is
on screen on a laptop.

Each check asserts the notices are there — the package's (§22.3), the archived pin's (§21), the
desktop renderer's (§15) and the standalone page's (§19) — because a notice that stopped being
written leaves a build that looks exactly like one that succeeded.

## 23. The console: what this window has done

The Analysis drawer carries a **copy CLI command** button under a finished result
(`analysis/cliCommand.ts`), and the argument that button makes is the one this section finishes. A
reader spends twenty minutes moving a window and nudging four numbers until the picture is right;
the moment they have two hundred files rather than one, clicking stops being the interface and the
run has to become a line in a shell. Transcribing that line by eye is the one step in the loop where
the numbers in the figure and the numbers in the table can quietly stop being the same numbers.

The button closed that gap for **the result on screen, while it is on screen**, and that leaves two
holes which are not small:

- **A batch is one command out of six.** *Run on all maps* over a deck of six is six runs against
  six files, and the drawer shows one result at a time. Five of those commands were never offered.
- **A day is not a result.** Change a parameter and run again, and the command that produced the
  figure from an hour ago no longer exists anywhere. So the reader who assembles a methods section
  at five o'clock is reconstructing it from memory — which is transcription again, with the numbers
  no longer in front of them.

So the command is written **when the run happens** rather than when a result is looked at, into a
log that outlives the result, the tab and the browser session. That log is the console.

### 23.1 One line per job, not per press

The record is written by `AnalysisRunner.execute`, which is the one place that knows a **job** from
a button: `runAll` queues one job per map, so a batch over six maps is six lines, each naming its
own file and each carrying its own command — and a 1D task, which reads no map, is one job and one
line however many maps there are (§18.1). Nothing else can produce that — the drawer holds one
result, the panel row holds one state per task, and both are per session.

It is also the only place that sees a run which produced nothing. A **failure** and a **Stop** leave
no `TaskResult` and therefore no `Provenance`, and a failure is precisely when a reader wants the
parameters back. So the line is opened when the job is dispatched, from a provenance composed out of
the job (`analysis/record.ts`), and the result's own replaces it the moment there is one — never
beside it, because two accounts of one run is how they come to disagree. A press of *run* that never
became a job — nothing open, or no contact map in view to run against — leaves a line too, once
however many maps it was aimed at: a sentence with the refusal under it rather than a command, since
a command is written from a framing and the missing framing is the refusal.

The command itself is `cliCommandFor`, called with the same `Provenance` the drawer's button passes
it. One function, two callers: a line in the console and a line on the clipboard cannot drift.

**Every run is a command, and the shell takes every task.** For a while the CLI refused by name — the
three tasks that read a bigWig, whose reader lived in the annotations worker alone; the one that reads
a second map, which the deck supplies and a shell has no concept of; and any run made in a session
with **no contact map**, since `chromosomix` opened its first argument as one and a 1D browser
(§5.8) has none to name. Each refusal was honest, and each was recorded here as a sentence with the
refusal under it, which is a record with holes in it exactly where the reader is least likely to
look. So the shell gained what it was said not to have, each as the code the worker already runs:
`src/cli/tracks.ts` opens a bigWig, a bedGraph, a wig or a FASTA under `--tracks` and answers `sample`
in the worker's own shape — a bigWig, and a `.2bit`, through one descriptor held open and read
synchronously, ahead of a walk forward (`src/cli/heldFile.ts`), where `generic-filehandle2`'s
`LocalFile` opened and closed the file at every read: sixteen thousand times for a metaplot over the
RefSeq TSS, half of the time it spent sampling, and on a disk that had not cached the file a seek for
each; a reference under `--sequence` is opened as the browser opens one
(`src/cli/reference.ts`) — a `.2bit`, or a FASTA with `samtools faidx`'s `.fai` beside it, by range,
and anything else whole, where `readFile`'s 2 GiB ceiling used to refuse every mammalian FASTA before
a byte of it was parsed and now refuses only one with no index, naming the command that makes one;
a file under `--features` or `--pairs` is read by the loader's own
sniffers and parsers, in its order — a BED or a peak file, a GTF, a genePred, a VCF, a cytoBand, a
barChart, junctions, a model, a bedpe, an interact or a longrange — so it reaches a task as the
browser draws it, where everything past the first few was read as a BED and came out empty or
wrong; `--against` names the maps `hicrep` compares with, mounted through the
same `peer`; a track task with no positional runs over the assembly the tracks declare, framed exactly
as the session frames it; a FASTA named for compartment phasing becomes the per-bin GC vector the
session would have shipped; and a `.pairs` named for its orientation curves is read from disk. There
is no refusal left for `cliCommandFor` to write. What the record does not hold arrives as a `#` note
above the line rather than as a silent omission — the maps `hicrep` ran against are the deck's and not
the result's, so they are read off the session and, with no session to ask, the note says to add them.

**The framing is written, not only the parameters.** Six facts a session sets from the picture are
inputs to the arithmetic and parameters of no task: the score column the map is drawn from (§3.5),
the sequences declared circular and the origins declared on them (§8.15), the ticked cells of an
`.scool` (§3.8), the number of contacts the map is drawn to (§6.5), and the resolution the reader
added that it is drawn at (§3.4). A line without them repeats a different run, so each is a reserved
flag of the command's own — `--value`, `--circular`, `--origin NAME:POS` (1-based, as the table
prints it, digits grouped or not), `--cell`, `--contacts N`, `--coarsen BP` — written whenever it
differs from the shell's default and refused before the run when the file cannot answer it. A run
summed to `--coarsen` names its outputs for it, `sample_1000_coarsen3000.…`, so that beside a run on
the file's own rung in one `--out` the two are two sets of numbers.

**Balanced is the shell's default, as it is the form's.** *Use balancing weights* is answered from
the file and never shown in a form (`paramDerived`), and a shell answers it the same way: a map is
read balanced wherever the file carries weights — the framing and every such parameter alike — and
`--no-balance` reads the raw counts. So a balanced run's line says nothing about it and an
unbalanced one says `--no-balance`. `--balance` itself is refused by name rather than taken as a
no-op: it asked for what is now the default, and a command that forgot it ran on raw counts under a
framing line that said *balanced*, which is the failure the default exists to prevent. It survives
only as coverage's own parameter, which is not the file's to answer and is off, since raw coverage
is the point of it. The two about the molecules are written for a run with
no map as well: an origin call from the Chromosomes table reads the circle, and so must its line. The window is *not* one of them: no runner reads the framing's
extent, which decides only whether the block on screen can be reused, so `--window` is written for
the record's label and the numbers are the same either way. An imported `.pairs` writes the
`--bin-size` it was framed at, since a contact list declares no resolution of its own (§3.7).

**Every locus on the line is the display form**, because the shell reads every locus as a reader's
box does (§26.1). `--window` is the framing through `formatLocus` — `--window chrIV:100,001-200,000`,
the window the breadcrumb named — and the shell takes it back through `typedLocusToRegion` to the
bins the framing was; a whole sequence or a genome is its name. A locus parameter — 4C's `--anchor`,
the structure tasks' `--region` and `--locus` — is written as its record holds it, the typed form the
form held (§18.2), grouped digits and all. `quote` leaves both bare, since a comma, a colon and a
hyphen are nothing to a shell, and quotes a list of loci, which has a space in it. The window was
cooler's 0-based numbers, `chrIV:100000-200000`, which the shell read as written: right in the shell,
and the one locus in the console a base away from the same window everywhere else on the screen.

**The line is read by what the command takes.** A task's descriptor says which of its parameters
are switches, and the shell's own flags are known — `--quiet`, `--no-balance`, `--help` and
`--version` are switches, and `--out`, `--window`, `--features` and the rest take a value. So a switch never takes
the word after it: `--stranded` turns one on, and `--stranded=false` or `--no-stranded` turns it off
(`--no-balance` stays the shell's own, the raw counts, and is never coverage's `--balance=false`). A
flag took the next word unless that word began with `--`, so `coverage a.cool --no-balance b.hic` ran
over `a.cool` alone with exit 0, `coverage --quiet a.cool` refused itself for want of a file, and
`--out --quiet` wrote into a directory called `true`. Where a task's parameter shares a name with
one of the shell's own flags the task has it — apa's `--window` is its half-width and never a locus,
coverage's `--balance` its own switch — with one exception, because both meanings are needed on one
line: `--contacts` is the total a map is drawn to (§6.5) on every task and also Compartments' own
choice of contacts, and the console writes both, `--contacts cis --contacts 10000000`. A choice is
one of a few words and a total a number, so the words among the task's options are the task's and
every other is the shell's; given wholly to the shell, `cis` was read as a total and every
compartments line the console had written was refused. A word a switch's value used to be written as,
`--stranded false`, is refused rather than read as a file of that name, and the refusal says what to
write; a flag that takes a value is refused without one; only the shell's own flags may come before
the task; and a flag the command does not take is refused by name, for `replay` and `circular` as for
a task. `replay` takes the files named after the workspace as it takes those after `--over`, so
`--over data/*.hic` as a shell expands it replays every file rather than the first alone. The console
writes a switch as itself or as `--key=false`, the one spelling read alike before and after, and a
test reads every task's line back through the parser.

**`--version` names the build, and what it runs on.** The first line is `chromosomix` and the
version, with the commit the bundle was built from where it was built in a repository —
`chromosomix 0.13.0 (7a6fea2)` — the words every file the command writes opens with
(`# chromosomix 0.13.0 cli`), so `head -1` is the line a pipeline records. The lines after it are
what a version does not fix: the Node it runs on, with the platform, and the `h5wasm` and
`@gmod/bbi` that every map and track is read through. Those two are ranges in `package.json`,
settled when the package is installed and not when it was built, so two installs of one version can
read a file through two builds of either; their numbers are read off the copies installed beside the
command for that reason, never baked in. npm is not listed: it installs the command and takes no
part in a run. Like `--help` it is answered wherever on the line it is written, before anything else
is checked, with exit 0. `chromosomix --version` printed the usage until now — an answer to a
question nobody had asked, and none to the one a pipeline's record of its tools asks.

**A reader that stops reading is no failure of the command.** `chromosomix tasks | head -1` closes
the pipe under the command, and Node reports the next write as an error on the stream — `EPIPE`, or
`EOF` on Windows — which, unheard, killed the command with a stack trace and exit 1 the moment `head`
had its line, and killed a task piped as `insulation map.cool 2>&1 | head -1` before it had written a
single file. Both streams now let the reader go: what was left to print is dropped, and the command
finishes what it was doing and exits with the status it would have had. It does not exit on the
spot, which is the usual answer, because progress and notes go to stderr: that task would have
stopped with its files half written under an exit code that said nothing was wrong. Any other error
on a stream is thrown, as before (`ignoreClosedPipe`).

**A value is one the form could have held.** A choice is one of the options its descriptor lists, a
switch is on or off — `true`, `yes`, `on` or `1`, or their opposites, after an `=` — and a number is
digits, a point and an exponent. Anything else is refused before a file is opened, with exit 2 — the
shell's code for a fault in the command, against 1 for a file that failed — and a sentence naming the
values there are: *There is no --quantity “expectd”. It is density or expected.* The runners read a
choice with a fallback, so that a stored session from a later build cannot change what the numbers on
screen mean, and the form never reaches it: it moves a held value onto an option it offers before any
run (`resolveChoiceDefaults`). The shell did reach it. `expected --quantity expectd` ran the density
and wrote `# param quantity: expectd` above it — a provenance naming a computation nobody performed —
`--factor=` ran at nought, and `--rungs abc` built one rung. What a workspace recorded is checked the
same way before `replay` opens a file. Which options a *file* is offered — a per-genome P(s) needs a `/genomes` table — is the
runner's to refuse, by name, once the file is open.

**Each input of a command is written under a name of its own.** An output is
`<stem>.<task>.<output>.<format>`, and the stem is the file's name up to its first dot with a group's
last segment after it — `sample` for `sample.mcool`, `sample_1000` for
`sample.mcool::/resolutions/1000` — as it always was, so a command over one file names its outputs as
it did and a script that reads them keeps working. Where two inputs of one command would share a
stem, those two keep more of their names, a step at a time, until they differ: the name less its
format extension and a `.gz` (`HCT116.rep1`, `HCT116.rep2`), the whole name (`sample.cool`,
`sample.hic`), then the directories they are in, nearest first (`dirA_sample`, `dirB_sample`); one
file named twice, or two names a Mac's disk holds as one, is numbered (`sample_2`). Nothing a command
has written is written over by the same command. `coverage HCT116.rep1.cool HCT116.rep2.cool` wrote
`HCT116.coverage.*` twice, the second run's files over the first's, with exit 0.

**An address is fetched first, whole.** The app reads a remote file by range, through a reader that
is synchronous (§11), which a worker has and Node does not, so a shell cannot read one that way. An
http or https address — the map, an `--against`, a `--sequence`, `--tracks`, `--features` or
`--pairs`, a `.pairs` named for P(s)'s orientations, the workspace `replay` reads — is downloaded
instead, streamed to disk with its progress on stderr unless `--quiet`, into one directory per
command under `$TMPDIR` that is removed when the command ends, Ctrl-C included; and with the sidecar
its format reads beside itself, where the server has one: a FASTA's `.fai`, a HiC-Pro matrix's bin
file. A batch lets each map go once its run is done, so it holds one at a time. What every run reads
— a `--sequence`, `--tracks`, `--features`, `--pairs`, `--against` or the workspace — is fetched
before the first, so an address there that cannot be had is exit 2; a map that cannot be is that
file's failure, named, and the batch goes on; and a `.pairs` a parameter names is fetched when the
task asks for it, and noted by the task where it cannot be, as a file on disk is. The map is opened *as* its address, so the
framing, the provenance and every sentence about it name the URL that was typed, and its outputs are
named after its file, the query left off. Any other scheme is refused by name: an `s3://` address
needs credentials the command has not got. An address went to `stat` as a path until now — *cannot
stat /cwd/https:/example.org/x.cool* — under a README that said it was fetched, and the console said a
shell reads local files only; its note now says what the line costs instead (§23.3).

### 23.2 What else is on it, and what is not

A day is not only its runs, so three more things are recorded — each at the one place every road to
it already converges, which is the arrangement `AnnotationLoader.onFilesAdded` already uses:

- **A file opened**, in `Session.open` and `Session.openGenome`, *after* the read succeeds: a
  `.pairs` and an `.mmetacool` both reach that door twice, and a line written on the way in would
  name a URI the reader never got to look at.
- **A track loaded**, in `AnnotationLoader.addFiles` and `addUrl` — the two doors a *reader* drives.
  Not `restore`, `carry` or `reattach`, which are the app bringing back what it already had; a
  console that opened with nine lines after every reload is a console nobody reads.
- **A file written**, in `chooseSaveTarget`'s write, through which every export in the application
  passes, under the name it was written as — the reader's own where the save dialog let them change
  it (§26.6), and nothing at all for a dialog they cancelled, which wrote nothing. A
  reader whose figure was recorded because they exported it from the drawer but not when they
  exported the same figure from the map would be looking at a difference nobody can see the rule
  behind.

**Navigation is not recorded.** A pan is a reading of a file rather than an operation over one
(§18's opening paragraph draws that line), a minute of it would write dozens of lines, and the view
a result belongs to is already in that result's framing.

### 23.3 A script, not a transcript

What the panel hands over — one row, one day, or the lot — is **a shell script**: commands bare,
everything else commented. The day headings are `#`, the opens, the tracks and the exports are `#`,
a failure is `# failed: …`, and a press of *run* that never became a job (§23.1) is `#` too. So a day
pasted into a file runs, in the order it ran the first time, with the afternoon around it left in as
the context saying what the commands were for. The **save** button writes exactly that as `.sh`,
under a `#!/bin/sh` line and through the save dialog every export opens (§26.6), and — being a file
leaving the app — records itself.

The **provenance** toggle is the choice between a script and an archive. Off, a row is its command
and the caveats that qualify it; on, each row is preceded by the full provenance block — the build,
the task and its version, the framing in words, every parameter one per line — which is the header
every exported file already opens with (§18.4). It is off by default, because eleven `#` lines per
row is a log nobody scans, and it governs the clipboard as well as the screen: a reader who turned
it off to paste clean commands must not find the provenance on their clipboard anyway. It is named
for what it shows, in the word the Analysis drawer's *copy provenance* already uses for the same
block: it read *output*, which beside a column of commands names the one thing it is not — what the
runs produced. And it is a toggle rather than a ticked box (§26.3), which leaves the header's
controls one shape each: three word buttons, a toggle, and the cross. With nothing recorded the three
words are dimmed, on §26.3's rule from the other side: a copy and a save of nothing wrote an empty
file, and a clear forgot nothing.

The caveats are **not** part of what the toggle hides. They are `cliCommandFor`'s notes about what a
shell cannot be told — a window across several sequences or off the diagonal, a parameter naming a
set with no file behind it, an `.scool`'s cells or the maps `hicrep` compared against where the
record does not name them, a map drawn balanced and read raw or the reverse, which the one
`--no-balance` cannot say, a map drawn through an edit of its reference (§27.7) — and a command that
runs and answers a slightly different question is worse than one that says what it left out. And
about the one thing a shell is told at a price: a remote file, which the line names and the shell
downloads whole before reading it (§23.1), where the app reads only what it draws — so the note says
so, and that a reader running several lines over one file should fetch it once and name the copy.

They sit **above a command and below anything else**, which is one rule read twice: a caveat
qualifies a line the reader is about to run, so it comes first; a refusal explains a line that is
not a command at all, so it comes after the thing it is about. Written the other way round, every
run the CLI cannot repeat opened with a paragraph about a command that was never there.

### 23.4 The panel

A drawer along the bottom of the body, and deliberately the **same** drawer §18.1 specifies: it
floats over the content rather than joining the flex row, carries a shadow off the edge that faces
the window, is dragged by that edge with its height remembered, comes back open after a reload if it
was left open, and is dismissed by Escape.

**It is not a modal**, on §18.1's terms exactly: no backdrop, no click-outside, no keyboard taken.
Every shortcut keeps working behind it, so reading back this morning's commands while panning the
map is an ordinary thing to do. Escape is a *dismissal* and not a cancel — closing the console stops
nothing, because the log is not the panel — and it fires in the bubble phase and skips an event
something else has already handled, so a marquee, a caret and an open dropdown all keep the Escape
they answer first.

**Along the bottom rather than beside the map**, because the log is wide and shallow: a command is
one long line and there are a few dozen of them in a day. In a column each wraps four times and six
of them fit; under the map it reads as what it is. It is also what lets the pair be up at once — the
Analysis drawer down the right, the console along the bottom, the map in the corner between them.

The **day is a separator across the list** rather than a column, carrying its own count and its own
copy, because "what did I run on Tuesday" is the question this panel exists to answer and one press
should be the whole of the answer.

The button is in the header, **last of the group after the four panels** (§5.5): back and forward,
then the two other things that take something out of this window — a link, and the workspace as a
