if WashU will not allow a cross-origin GET the front says so in the ordinary way, which is the same
sentence any hub gets and the reason there is nothing special to write here for it. What is written
is whose it is: a 404 or a page of HTML is a shipped store *not published yet* (§24.2), and the
sentence names WashU's VizHub as what publishes it (`StoreRef.publishedBy`) rather than sending a
maintainer to the Stores workflow, which has never written it and could not put it back.

**Its own tile.** A hub gets a door beside the store one on the landing page, and the argument is the
portals': a hub is not a rarer kind of store file, it is the format an enormous amount of published
data is already in, and a reader holding one thinks of it as *the hub*. A door that never says the
word is a door they will not try. Nothing behind it is hub-specific — a hub pasted into the other box
works exactly as well — and a remembered hub keeps the hub mark and the hub's grouping, because both
are facts about the rows rather than about the door they arrived through.

**Pasted, when it cannot be fetched.** A store is fetched by the *page*, so the host has to allow a
cross-origin `GET` — and plenty never will, `genome.ucsc.edu` among them, which puts UCSC's own
example hubs out of reach of every browser-only viewer. Both doors therefore carry a paste box, with
an optional base for relative names. **One box and not three**, even though a hub is three files:
`useOneFile on` is a hub in a single file, and a `hub.txt`, `genomes.txt` and `trackDb.txt`
concatenated are the same thing, since the only keys the concatenation loses are the two saying where
the next file is. `hasGenomeStanzas` is what tells a whole hub from its first file, so a text that is
only a `hub.txt` is refused by name and told what to paste after it. A pasted shelf is not put in the
address bar and not offered for remembering: a store worth keeping is one with an address, and the
honest way to get one is to publish the file. Each box offers a **worked example** that reads — a hub
and a store over the lab store's yeast files, the hub an assembly hub naming R64 as a `.2bit`, two
bigWigs and the micro-C map as a `.hic` — because an example beside a paste box is not there to
show syntax, which this document does better, but to be pressed: the reader's first edit should be to
something that already drew a shelf.

**What CORS costs, measured.** On 2026-09-16 neither `genome.ucsc.edu` nor
`hgdownload.soe.ucsc.edu` answers a cross-origin `GET`, which puts UCSC's own example hubs and the
whole of GenArk out of reach of every browser-only viewer — this one, igv.js, anything without a
server. The failure message says so for a `*.ucsc.edu` host rather than sending a reader to check a
URL that is perfectly correct, and says the part that would otherwise be found out one row at a
time: pasting such a hub's text gets past the header for the *hub*, and its `bigDataUrl`s are on the
same hosts and will not open. Downloading the hub and opening it from a connected folder is the road
that works, and it is the reader's own machine doing the fetching, which is the only place this
project is willing to move that work to. What this does **not** do is proxy the fetch — routing a
reader's traffic through a third party to work around somebody else's header is exactly what C1
refuses.

**A hub to try it on.** `scripts/make_demo_hub.py` writes one over the yeast demo data — a `.2bit`
of its genome, the loop calls as `longrange`, the six bigWigs as a composite and the contact map as
`type hic` — so the whole path is walkable with `npm run dev` and
`http://localhost:5173/demo/yeast/hub.txt`, same origin, with no third-party host and no CORS
question standing between a reader and the answer. It is **strictly valid**, which constrains what
is in it: a hub's tracks are the `big*` formats plus `bam`, `cram`, `vcfTabix`, `hic` and
`longTabix`, so the demo's `.narrowPeak`, `.bed`, `.gtf` and `.barChart` cannot appear without a
`bedToBigBed` this project does not ship, and a hub naming them anyway would open here and fail in
UCSC's browser — the one thing a demo hub must not teach. The same loop calls as `interact` and the
demo's GTF as a `genePredExt` sit beside it as files to drop instead.

The `.2bit` that script writes is checked with `py2bit`, a wrapper around the C in kent's own tree.
That is the only check worth having: a file this repository wrote and this repository read proves
that two implementations share a reading of the format, which is exactly what they would do if the
reading were wrong.

## 25. A 3D structure beside the map

A chromatin model — one chromosome or several, one haplotype or two — read from a file of beads
with a place in space, drawn as a cell of the deck beside the maps and the tracks, linked to them
in both directions, and coloured by whatever the session already knows about the sequence. The
design it was built from, with the alternatives weighed and the sizes measured, is
`docs/structure-3d.md`; this section is what stands.

### 25.1 Words

A **structure** is the file and the row it makes in the Structures card — a row of kind
`structure` on the card `structure`, which is also a feature set: every bead is an interval. A **model** is one set of coordinates; a
**chain** is the beads of one sequence and one haplotype in genomic order; a **bead** is one row
of the file. A **cell** is any occupant of the deck (§16.11).

### 25.2 The formats

**g3d text**, WashU's own and what `g3dtools` takes: `chrom start x y z [haplotype]`, no header,
no end column, rows in any order, the sixth column `m`, `p` or `s` (or `maternal`, `paternal`,
`shared`; any other word is a category of its own, as `g3dtools` allows), and the `chr7(mat)` fold
of a `.3dg` read the same. The **width** of a bead is the
commonest step between consecutive sorted starts, counted across every sequence — the spacing the
file was modelled at, inferred rather than declared, and printed under the row so a reader whose
file was meant to be at 10 kb and reads *1.04 Mb* has been told the one thing this reader could
get wrong. It is independent of the map's bin size: the same file opens the same way beside a 1 kb
map and a 50 kb one.

**bed3d**: the same file with the end written down, `chrom start end x y z [haplotype]`, for a
model whose beads are the bins of a map or of any width a BED can say. Each bead keeps its own
end; the commonest length is the width under the row.

**Binary g3d**, the container `g3dtools` writes: a 64 000-byte msgpack header and one zlib block
per resolution, read by range like a BAM rather than whole like a text, through a reader written
here (`annotations/g3dBinary.ts`, `annotations/msgpack.ts`) rather than a dependency. It opens at
its finest resolution and names the others under the row. A version-1 container is refused by
name, with the way out (`g3dtools` rewrites it).

**PDB**, as this app writes it (§25.7), and no other (`annotations/pdb.ts`). A PDB says where each
atom is in space and nothing about the genome — a residue number is four columns and a chain one
character — so a model written here carries its loci in a table of REMARK 250 lines a viewer skips:
each chain's sequence and haplotype by atom serial, each run of beads laid end to end as its first
serial, count, start and width, and the centre and the factor its coordinates were written with,
which the reader undoes so the model opens in its own units and reads back bead for bead. The first
MODEL of several is read, since a row holds one model (§25.8). **Every other PDB is refused, with
the reason.** pastis writes its beads in bin order — one chain, no residue numbers, no bonds, `nan`
for a bead it could not place — and the other solvers that write a PDB say no more, so the only way
to put such a file on the genome is to number its atoms against some map's bins, which is a guess
drawn as a fact; the refusal says to write the coordinates beside the bins they were modelled at, as
a bed3d. A PDB written here and saved again by PyMOL gets a sentence of its own: PyMOL keeps every
atom and every bond and drops every REMARK, the table with them, so the file to open is the one this
app wrote, or its bed3d. A PDB under a name that does not say so is told by its records — it opens on
one a PDB opens on, and holds an atom — which nothing in the BED family can do.

All five are sniffed by content before the BED family sees them — a five-column g3d read as a BED
would be a lane of boxes whose *end* is a coordinate in space — and **a file that names its format
is not sniffed at all**: `.g3d`, `.3dg`, `.bed3d`, `.pdb`, gzipped or not, local or over HTTP, is
read as the structure it says it is. The name is read **first**, before a single row, and read the way the
drop routing reads it: past any directories, with a `?query` or `#fragment` cut off, so a model
published at a URL is as named as one on disk. A file whose name claims no format is asked two
questions, and each exists to tell a structure from a BED whose columns happen to be numbers: are
the coordinates **fractional**, and do the beads walk like a **chain** rather than scatter. A named
file has been told apart already, by the reader who named it — so a model whose beads *are* a
scatter (a randomised control, a draw from a null, a fragment set nobody has folded) is read as a
structure rather than falling through to BED. A named file that turns out **not** to be one gets
the parser's refusal, in the format's own words and on the card its name sent it to, rather than
being quietly drawn as a lane. The tests pin what a BED5, a BED6, a bedGraph and a narrowPeak are
not.

**A bead the solver could not place is still a bead.** A solver writes `nan` — or `NA`, `n/a`,
`inf`, `None`, `null`, `.`, or an empty field — in all three coordinate columns for a bin it was
given nothing to place: a repeat, a gap in the assembly, a bin nothing mapped to. Such a row is
**passed over** by the sniffer, which counts it neither for the file nor against it, and dropped by
the parser, so a
model of a real map opens at the beads that have places. It is not a disqualification, which it
was: one `nan` row thirty-one rows into a 1,683-bead pastis-NB model answered *not a structure* for
the whole file, so its `.g3d` was refused by the BED parser it fell through to — *all 1,683 lines
failed the "contig, start, end" test* — and the `.bed3d` beside it, whose third column really is an
integer end, was drawn as a lane of 1,683 boxes whose name is an x coordinate. A file where *every*
bead is unplaced says **that** rather than the sentence naming the columns, because its columns are
fine. A coordinate that is neither a number nor one of those spellings is a file that is not a
structure at all, which is what still keeps a BED6 out: a name, a score and a strand are not three
ways of saying *nowhere*.

A structure row is **never a lane**: it is unplaced on import, offered no
location control, and skipped by every stack; its picture is the cell.

**The Structures card.** Every model the session holds — dropped, named by URL, or computed
(§25.6) — is a row of one card under the Tracks card, and of no other: the Tracks card leaves
`structure` rows out, computed or not. Each row carries the head every row has (grip, colour, name,
eye, close), what it holds (`2,412 beads · 5 kb · 16 sequences`), the task and the framing for a
computed one, and **bed3d** and **PDB**, the model out (§25.7), after the word *export* — the PDB
disabled, with the format's reason as its tooltip, for a model past what its columns can number. The **eye** in the row's
head is what shows and hides: it puts the model in **a cell of its own**, opening one beside whatever
is already there, and takes it away again — from every cell drawing it (§25.3). The lit eye is the
whole of the state — the row carried an accent bar down its left gutter as well, which was a second
way of saying what the eye already says. There is no second control for that and no button
labelled with what is already true (§26.3, §26.7) — a *shown in the deck* button beside the eye was
two controls for one act, and a reader who pressed the lit one expecting it to un-show got nothing.
The card's own load zone names what it reads — the three formats, and a PDB this app wrote — and,
like every other zone that asks for a file, says it takes a drop or a click.
A computed row that came back from a reload is detached and offers **recompute**, which opens its
recipe in the drawer, as a synthetic row on the Tracks card does (§18.5).

### 25.3 The deck of cells

**A structure cell** draws **one** structure row — the one the reader chose from the Structures
card, by its eye or by its row dropped on the cell, remembered per file, or the first of the list no
*sibling cell* is already drawing; and **the deck holds as many cells of a model as the reader asks
for**. It was one cell per deck, then one per model, on the reasoning that two cells of one row are
one picture drawn twice — which is only true while the two are the same picture, and they are not:
each cell has its **own camera, its own height and its own turn**, so two cells of one model are two
views of it, which is the ordinary way anybody looks at a fold. The mirrors and the planted axes are
the model's rather than the cell's — set up once for how the model is to be read, on its row — so
every cell drawing it shares them. The eye
on the row still means *is this model on screen*, so it opens one cell and closes every cell drawing
it; the row's **grip, dropped on the cell that is to hold it**, is how a second view is asked for,
and it does not refuse a model a cell already draws. What each cell remembers — the
model it draws, the camera it draws from, its height, whether it turns with the others — is
remembered under its **seat**, its place among the structure cells counting from the left; they all
used to write to one slot, so a deck of two views came back from a reload as the same view twice.
**Every model that arrives opens a cell of its own and is on screen from that moment** — dropped,
named by a URL, or computed, and *every* one of them where several land together, where only the
last of a batch used to get a picture and the others sat on the card as rows with nothing drawn,
which is the one state a reader reads as *it did not work*. It opens beside whatever was there
rather than taking it over, and it opens **one**: a model dropped on a map, named by a URL or
picked from a folder opened two, a cell for the file's name and another for the row's arrival; the
watch on the store that every road ends in is the one that opens it now. It used to be one cell per
deck, which made two models something a reader could only compare by swapping back and forth, and
made a reconstruction landing destroy the model it was to be judged against — the commonest way to
lose a picture in this application.
**A model that opens the session on its own is drawn alone.** A structure file dropped on an empty
window names a genome — its beads are on sequences — so the session it opens is a browser of that
genome, and the browser has nothing to draw: a structure is a row and a cell, never a lane. It used
to stop there, an empty axis and the model nowhere on screen, the row having arrived with the store
and been taken for one already there. The model now gets its cell the moment the browser is mounted,
and the tracks give it the screen — hidden rather than closed (§16.9), so the heading above the deck
still steers which stretch of the model is lit and `show the 1D browser` in the deck's bar puts them
back. With nothing beside it the cell takes the height a map would, where a cell of a row with no map
in it had the 16 rem floor. Where something is already drawn on the tracks they stay on screen, and a
link or a restored session names its own deck: **every model a restore brings back is noted before
the first of them lands**, so none opens a cell the link did not name. The watch used to begin at the
store's first change, which in a restore is the first row back, so every model after it was taken for
an arrival and opened a cell — and publishing those cells wrote them over the maps the link was
putting back, so a tab of five maps and five models came back as five models. **Cells built together
draw the models in the order the session lists them**, each the first no cell before it is drawing:
they used to fall to the first model all at once, and the next change to the store moved each one
along, so the models came back a seat to the left, the first in the last cell. A
row dropped on a cell still swaps that cell's model **in place**, which is the other question: the
eye is a model asking for a cell, the drop is a cell being given a model. **The eye follows the
deck, however the deck changed**: a cell closed from its own heading darkens its row's eye, and a
row dropped on a `+` or an empty cell lights it, the moment the cell is drawn. The card used to ask
the deck only when its own eye was pressed, so a closed cell left its row lit and a dropped model
left it dark. **A structure cell's heading is its model's name**, and it is edited there: a name
typed into it renames the row on the Structures card and every other place the model is named, as a
map's heading renames the map (§16.10); an empty box keeps the name it had, since a model with
no name is a row the card cannot tell from its neighbours. The *3D structure* card
has no picker for it: it said the second thing in the place a reader looks for which cell the card
sets, which its title line says instead (below). And **the row the cell is drawing, removed from the card, empties
the cell**, which says so, rather than quietly showing the next model along — however the cell came
to be drawing it, whether the reader picked it, the session restored it, or it was simply the only
one there was (a remembered choice whose row is already gone when a session opens falls back to the
first, since no cell was drawing it) — with three.js, which is loaded when the first cell is built and never with the page: a chunk of its own
on the web, folded into the one file of the standalone build. **Beads, sticks and a tube as three
toggles that combine** (the tube alone by default); a **dashed run of ink across every gap** in a
chain, always, so a chain with a missing bead reads as one chain with a hole and not as two — and
faded with the chain it belongs to, as a stick is, so a ghosted sequence's gaps are ghosted too; a
halo on the hovered bead; a **dashed chord of ink** across a hovered contact and the loops as chords
of ink, both drawn as cylinders rather than one-pixel lines so they are seen at the size of the tube
they cross — the loops, like the gaps' dashes, at **half its radius**, since a line drawn *about* the
model that is as thick as the model reads as a piece of it, and the hovered chord a little wider, on
top of them; **a fog tied to the slab**: it begins at the centre of rotation — the plane the slab is centred on,
which ⌘-click moves — and reaches the page exactly where the slab cuts, so what the fog says is
*how close this is to being cut away*, its slider weakening it by pushing that plane out (at 1 the
far face of the slab is the page, at a half it is half way there). Measured from the camera alone,
as it was, a thin slab left every one of the few beads it kept already half dissolved: the fog was
describing the whole model while the slab was showing a slice of it. Lit, always; **orthographic,
always** — a model has no horizon, and perspective made the same distance read shorter at the back;
the camera remembered per file and seat. What is **outside the window, or ghosted from the key, is drawn at
the ghost opacity** — 0.1 by default, a trace — and that slider is the one opacity there is:
everything else is drawn whole. It is a **real transparency**: a ghosted bead keeps its own hue and
lets whatever is behind it through, and at **0 it is gone** — not drawn, and not in the way of the
model behind it either. It used to be a colour mixed towards the page, which on a white page reads
as *pale* rather than as *faint*, still hid what was behind it, and at zero left a page-coloured bead
punching a hole in the picture; the 2D painter always had it right, so the same model on screen and
in an exported PDF disagreed about what ghosting meant. *Outside window* has three answers: *ghost* (the default),
*hide*, and *show* — the window ghosts nothing, and only the key's own ghosting is left, which is
how a whole genome is looked at while the maps look at one window of it. The map's *legend* switch (§7) hides the key here too, so one switch
says what a figure carries. On/off settings are icon toggles, **lit when on** (§26.3): drawn as, chords, fog,
overlays. Every slider carries a **readout of the number it is at** beside it — a bead radius with
its value nowhere on screen is a figure nobody can reproduce — and a slider whose setting does
nothing is **greyed with its reason in its tooltip**: the ghost opacity while *outside window*
is *hide*.

**A setting is one row.** A select sits on one line with its label wherever the card is wide enough
to read the value, and drops the label above it below about 15 rem — asked of the *card* through a
container query rather than of the window, because this card is drawn both in a 200-pixel Aesthetics
column and in the enlarged dialog's sidebar, which is twice that and resizable. And a slider that
only **shapes** something a toggle or a select **arms** shares that control's row: *fog* carries its
depth and *outside window* its opacity, where each was two rows and the second carried a label
that repeated the first. A slider that is the whole setting — bead radius, tube radius, depth slab —
keeps a row of its own.

The card's rows are in one order, choices before the things that modify them: compare with (and
its RMSD note), in the frame of, drawn as, overlays, colour by, colour scale, bead
radius, tube radius, haplotype, outside window (with its ghost opacity), loops as chords, fog
(with its depth), depth slab, shared (below), measurements, camera, frame, export. *Overlays*
follows *drawn as* because the two are one question asked twice: what the model is drawn as, and
what is drawn over it. *In the frame of* follows *compare with* because the two are one question
asked twice as well — the same superposition, drawn or not (§25.5).

**A star on each cell says which one the card is about.** The column holds **one** *3D structure*
card — a second copy of eighteen controls is a column nobody can read, and §26.3 wants a control
offered once per column — and a deck may hold several models, so the card follows a cell the reader
names. It was whichever cell was built first, which a reader with two models discovers by dragging
a slider and watching the *other* picture change, and which left the second model's settings
unreachable. The same glyph and the same radio behaviour the maps' star has, because it is the same
idea: one of several pictures singled out for something that can only be about one of them. It is
its **own** star and not the maps' — a starred map is the file an analysis runs against and the
map the *Map* card sets, a starred cell is the picture this column's *3D structure* card is for, and
one deck can want both at once. A filled star is **live**, as the maps' is: pressed, it leaves **no
cell starred**, and the card then sets **every structure cell at once** — the first cell's values
shown, *every structure — all N* under its title in the warn colour, and each change written to
every cell's row, camera presses and the turntable included. The rows that are about one cell's own
picture are not offered then — *compare with*, *in the frame of*, the measurements and the
export — since one model compared with itself, or one file saved for five
pictures, is not a setting that can be made to all of them. While a cell is starred, **the card says which under its title** — `★ Yeast_structure`, the
filled star and the name the cell's own heading wears — which is the *Map* card's line for the
starred map, in the same place, words and colours: a reader who has learned where to look for which
map a card sets knows where to look for which model. It appears only where there is a choice, so a
deck of one structure cell has none, and neither star nor line; it follows the cells when the
starred one is closed, so the card is never about a picture that is gone; *none* holds while there
are cells for it to be about and goes with the last of them; and a cell that opens does **not** take
it, because a model arriving should not move a control out from under the reader who was using it.

**The settings are a card of the Aesthetics panel** — *3D structure*, in the view's own column of
cards right after its *Map* card and before *Tracks* and *Groups*, built from the same field
primitives, placed by the session whenever the deck has a structure cell and taken out when it has
none, the column scrolling over all of them as one — and not a menu in the cell: a view's settings are in that column, and the model is a
view. The cell keeps **five corner buttons** — mark a bead, mark a loop, measure (§25.4), frame the
window, enlarge — the frame wearing the same mark the Map card's refit does and the enlarge its own,
since two corner-bracket glyphs side by side were told apart only by hovering them; the dialog
borrows the card into its sidebar — the card alone, its *camera* and *frame* rows being the dialog's
camera controls — and gives it back where it was.

**And it carries the settings that are not the row's own.** `legend`, `crosshair` and `tooltip` are
preferences about every picture in the app (§26.3), kept in one store; which picture each of them is
about is declared once, in `ui/plotOptions.ts`, beside the matrix's list and the tracks' —
`STRUCTURE_OPTIONS` is the model's, and a list copied into the cell is a list that stops being the
answer the day a fourth preference is one the model honours. They appear as a **shared** row on the
card, and what is in it is **whatever no other card in the column offers**:

- **Enlarged**, all three. The model is the window and every card that owns one of them is *behind*
  the dialog, so the one switch for the key the reader is looking at is not the one they cannot
  reach.
- **Beside a map**, none: the *Map* card offers all three, and §26.3 wants a control offered once per
  column — two copies ten lines apart read as two settings.
- **Beside the 1D browser**, the key alone. That card offers the crosshair and the hover card but no
  *legend*, a browser having no key of its own to hide, so the model's key was reachable only by
  enlarging it.

Exactly the three this picture reads; a fourth would be a control that does nothing to the thing it
was pressed beside.

The card also carries a **depth slab** (two clipping planes either side
of the centre of rotation along the line of sight, at a fraction of the model's reach, the way into a
dense globule, and **the depth the fog is measured against** — see below; measured in the scene's
own units, against the model's reach, rather than in the file's), a **genomic ruler** (a tick of ink at the first bead of every step along each chain —
the first of 10 kb, 20 kb, 50 kb, 100 kb… at least ten beads wide and no more than about forty
ticks over the whole model, so a genome at 5 kb is read at 500 kb — labelled `500 kb`, `1.5 Mb`,
at most eighty labels, and no zero tick: a chain's start is where its name is),
**camera presets** (front, top, side), a **turntable** that turns the model slowly by itself, **turn
together** and **replant the axes** on the same row, and **frame** (the window, everything) with the
two **mirrors** beside them — all of them **bordered buttons** like every other action in the
column (§26.6), since a quiet word beside a bordered toggle reads as a caption for it.

**Turn together** is a link between cells and not a setting of the model, so it is the cell's and
not the row's: every cell with it lit shares the camera's two angles, so one drag turns them all,
and **only the angles travel** — each cell keeps its own centre, zoom and projection, which is what
makes two synced cells two views rather than one view drawn twice. Pressed on, a cell **leads**: the
others come round to it, since any other reading depends on which cell is touched next. With
*in the frame of* (§25.5) under it, this is how two models are compared without either being drawn
over the other — each turned into one frame, side by side, turning as one. The cell's actions are **commands** in the palette with keys —
`f` frame the window, `a` everything, `1` `2` `3` beads, sticks, tube, `l` names, `r` turntable —
**bound only while the model is enlarged**, and listed in the palette either way; there they come
before the app's own, so `a` is the whole model in the dialog and the reader's marks everywhere else
(§8.1); the three modes
have none at all (§25.4), which is three letters — `e`, `o`, `m` — handed back to the breaks toggle,
the new tab and the Aesthetics panel that each already had one of them (the panel has since moved to
`3`, `e` to the O/E and the breaks to `m`). They are single keys and so are the app's own (`1` `2`
`3` fold the General, Annotations and Aesthetics panels, §26.6, as `f` and `a` folded Files and
Annotations once); a cell sits *beside* a
map and its commands come first in the palette's list, so binding them there would take those keys
from the panels for as long as a model was on screen. In the dialog the model is the whole window and
there is nothing else a letter could mean. And a key is **printed on a control only where it is
bound**, through `withKey` (§26.4): the corner's *frame* and the card's *frame* and *turntable* are
retitled when the dialog opens and closes, because a card beside a deck reading `(f)` was offering a
letter that folds a panel instead. A phased file draws both homologues,
and the key's chips solo one. The picture takes the whole cell — a map's cell is its plot and its
lanes together, and a model has no axis to line up — and a **bar under it sets the cell's height**,
dragged, nudged with the arrow keys, and double-clicked to give the height back to the row;
remembered per seat. A model has no axis to line up with the map's, so its height is the reader's
business — as a stack of tracks' is, whose cell has the same bar (below): a deck one across put the
model in a 16 rem band under a map that could be shrunk to a thumbnail, and nothing done to either of
them gave the model any more room. A button in its corner **enlarges** it into
a dialog with every setting in a sidebar beside it, **dragged wider or narrower by the grip between
them** and remembered per file, as a panel column is; the cell's own canvas, key and labels are
moved into the dialog and back, so the camera, the colouring and the pin the reader left it with are
what the cell shows afterwards; a button in the stage's bottom corner hides the sidebar and brings it
back. A **legend in the top-left corner** lists what the hand can do, **one row per control, the key
on the left and what it does on the right**, and **the live row is lit**: *drag* to turn (a drag
orbits, **without limit** — neither angle stops, so the model turns over the top and keeps going
rather than hitting a wall halfway through a drag; the clamp that used to hold the horizon level was
a turntable's convention and a structure has no horizon), *scroll* to zoom, *⇧* to move (a drag
pans the whole model, as a drag with the right button does; a right click that does not drag opens
the cell's menu, whose *Copy this* puts the model alone on the clipboard, §7.2), the centre key — ⌘ on a Mac, Ctrl elsewhere — for *centre* (a click on a bead
makes it the centre of rotation), and *space* for *fog* (the wheel brings it forward or pushes it
back, which the slider on the card's *fog* row also sets, 0 to 1, 0.6 the depth the cell always had). A
**sticky mode** — *mark*, *loop* or *measure* (§25.4) — takes a row at the top while it runs, lit in
the accent, because it is a state the cell is *in* rather than a key being held, and a click will do
that and not what the rows below describe. It was one chip naming the current gesture, which told a
reader who already knew the keys which key they were holding and everybody else nothing: that Shift
moves the model, that ⌘ puts the centre somewhere and that Space and the wheel are the fog were
facts discoverable only by pressing things. It is a **readout and not a control** — no border and no
pill, the translucent backing the map's key has — because a bordered pill three pixels from five
bordered buttons is a button a reader presses and nothing happens; and the **readout of where the
pointer is** sits under it in the same column, since the legend is five rows or six and a readout
pinned below it by a number would sit on top of it half the time. **In a small cell it is the live
row alone**, and the rest come back while the pointer is on the picture: five rows of keys over a
cell 330 pixels wide is a caption taking the corner of the thing it captions, a reader four cells
across is looking at shapes rather than learning keys, and the moment the keys *are* wanted is the
moment the hand is already there. Asked of the **cell** through a container query and not of the
window, for the settings card's reason (§25.3): the same cell is 330 pixels in a four-across deck
and thirteen hundred in the enlarged viewer. A **tap** of the centre key alone
shows or hides the **centre of rotation**, which the card's *overlays* row also does; the keys act
only while the pointer is over the cell, its canvas is focused or its dialog is open. The arrow keys
turn the model too while its canvas has the focus, and a pinch zooms it. The three **sticky**
modes — *mark*, *loop* and *measure* — stay on until pressed again, so each button is lit while its
mode runs (§26.3) and the legend's top row names it. It opens when a structure is dropped or named
by URL while a map or the browser is on screen, from the bar's add row, from a g3d dropped on an
empty cell, from a link's `3d`, or by **dragging a row of the Structures card into an empty cell**
(or onto a `+` edge, §16.9); a second structure opens a cell of its own beside the first rather than
replacing its picture (above). Every row of that card carries a **grip** for it, because a reader
with three models loaded has the row's eye — which says *which* model and leaves *where* to the
deck — and no way to say *that one, there*; dragging says where as well as which, and an empty cell
is a place somebody already made room in. The drag carries the row's id
under a type of this application's own, so an empty cell can tell a model from a file while the drag
is still in the air, and the cell's hint offers both.

**The tracks cell** is the session's own browser over the lead file's sequences — the same store,
client, groups and marks — drawing only the tracks **placed on it**: the location control lists
it beside the maps, with its one edge live and the other three greyed and saying why, and a track
file let go anywhere on it — off the disk, out of the Files column or a store — is drawn in it, at
its foot (§16.9). It follows
the maps and the maps follow it without joining the lock, whose currency is cells of a block: the
deck hands the cell the lead's window as loci, one way and never reported back, and a pan in the
cell takes the lead's *column* axis there (`MatrixPanel.showLocusOnColumns`), which the lock
spreads to every other map. The chain in its heading unhooks both roads. **It is its axis and its
lanes**, with no locus box, zoom steps or summary line of its own: where to look is the maps'
question, asked in the lead's bar above the grid, and it is still panned and zoomed in place — by a
drag, the wheel and the keys — like any 1D browser. **Its heading is a name the reader can change**,
and the change is the cell's alone: it names the stack in its heading and in the location control's
list of places, and renames no track on it — the tracks are the session's, named on the Tracks card,
and a cell is where they are drawn. Until then it is `tracks`, and `tracks 2`, `tracks 3` for the
ones after it counting from the left, in the heading as in the control — two headings both saying
`tracks` over a list saying `tracks` and `tracks 2` left a reader guessing which line was which
cell — renumbered as cells come and go. Two stacks side by side are what a name is for, *G1*
beside *G2M*; an empty box, or the default typed back, hands the cell back to its default. **A bar
under the stack sets the cell's height**, the structure cell's bar and gesture — dragged, nudged
with the arrow keys, double-clicked to give the height back to the row: a column of cells under a
map gave a stack of tracks the 16 rem floor and no more, and the stack scrolled inside it. The names
and the heights are remembered by **seat**, a tracks cell's place among the tracks cells counting
from the left, written from the live cells on every change to the deck, so a reload names and sizes
each cell as it was and a cell moved or closed takes both with it rather than leaving them on a seat.

**The browser as lead.** A session showing its 1D browser can open a deck: the browser stays the
session's view, re-parented into a cell as a map's is — moved and hidden as a map's is (§16.9) — and
the cells beside it are tracks and the structure. The deck learns a lead that is not a map — the
browser's windows as loci, a way to be taken somewhere, and its tracks as a cell of the deck's
figure — pixels for its PNG, paths for its PDF (§16.5) — so the deck's figure has them in their
cell where it used to leave a gap — and the browser reports every
move of its window, a link's included. Its Export card saves and copies the deck's figure while a cell
beside it has a picture, as the map's does (§16.5). A map may not join such a deck: the bar refuses
it in words, the add row puts its map roads away, a map a link names is held as the cell it would
have been, under its name, and the two presses that match maps' scales and resolutions are not
offered, having nothing to act on. The deck's count of maps says nothing of a deck with none.

### 25.4 Hover, both ways

A bead under the pointer is a place on every map and every lane: the maps draw it as a **dashed line
down and across the heatmap** on each axis the place is on — on a turned map, whose rows are
separation, as the dashed **V** the place makes, the two 45° rays of contacts it anchors, as a line
the reader drew is (§17.4), where a straight line up the band ran through contacts between two other
places — and as the tick at the edge of the stacks the lanes already give a pointer on another
panel's track; the status bar names the bead, **and so does the cell's own corner**, which is where
a reader looking at the model is looking — one place for a bead, the pair and their distance for a
contact named by a map. The corner is not gated with the *tooltip* switch: that switch is about the
card that follows the pointer, not the line in the corner. The other way, a place pointed at on a map or a lane
lights its beads and, for a contact, joins the two with a chord; the **ball** on a lit bead is
translucent and depth-tested, so it sits in front of the bead or tube it marks and behind any part
of the model nearer the eye, as a ball at that place would. The ball and the chord, and the halo on
a bead under the cell's own pointer, go with the *crosshair* switch, as the map's guide lines do; a
pinned bead keeps its halo.

**Three modes, a button each**, in the cell's corner and in the palette — and **no key**, because a
bare letter that arms a mode is a letter pressed by accident while the pointer happens to be over
the model. One is on at a time — arming the next disarms the
one that was on, pressing the one that is on turns it off — and the legend in the top-left corner
says which, in its top row (§25.3). They are three buttons and not one mode that counts clicks
because marking a place and marking a loop are two things a reader means, and a mode whose first
click might be either is a mode whose first click cannot be taken back by stopping.

**Mark a bead** turns every click into one of the reader's own marks (§8.1's manual annotations):
a **line** at the bead's locus on both axes, kept in the Manual annotations card and drawn by every
map, lane and tracks cell. On the model it is the bead again, **twice the radius, in the mark's own
colour** — a place is a thing on the model, so it is drawn as a bigger bead rather than as one more
line over one. **Mark a loop** holds the first bead clicked, names it in the status bar and closes
an **arrowhead** — the map's loop mark — on the second; Esc lets the held bead go. An arrowhead made
here is a chord on the model, since *loops as chords* switches to *manual annotations* when nothing else is
chosen. **Measure** is a **drag**: press on one bead, travel to another, let go, and the
measurement is made — the line follows the pointer on the way, so what is about to be measured is
what is drawn. The model does not turn under a measuring drag, because the hand is pointing rather
than steering; a press that lands on nothing turns it as ever. A press and release on the same bead
holds it instead, so the two-click gesture still closes a measurement for a reader who prefers it.
The card lists each one — the two loci, the distance in the model's units and the genomic separation
along the sequence, or *across sequences* — until its × removes it; each is drawn on the model as
dashed ink with the distance written at the middle, and in the figure the same.

**A card under the pointer** names the bead's sequence and where along it, in the same shape the
map's card has and under the same switch (§7's *tooltip*): a reader who turned the card off beside
the map meant it off. The line in the corner and the status bar are not gated, exactly as they are
not beside the map.

A store of one place (`ui/hoverLocus.ts`): one locus from a track, a bead or the browser's axis,
two from a map's cell — **one** while a span modifier is held, because that is the gesture the hand
is in the middle of: the crosshair has already stood up as a single line and the readout has already
stopped naming a contact, so a model still joining two beads would be the one surface left answering
a question the pointer stopped asking. The one place is the position along the diagonal, which is
what the line is drawn at and what the readout names. Each saying which surface it came from, every
subscriber ignoring its own.
A pointer on a map lights the bead at each end and joins the two with a chord, and puts **a guide
at each end** on every tracks cell — the pair the lanes beside that map mark, where a tracks cell
marked the first of the two and left the other anchor with no line; a pointer on a bead is a mark on
every map's column axis and a guide on every tracks cell; a pointer on a tracks cell is the same on
the maps and the structure. The deck's own cell-to-cell echo between maps is
untouched, and a map's hover is not relayed to the maps twice.

What the maps are looking at reaches the cell as loci on every pan; beads outside the window are
ghosted, hidden or shown, at the reader's choice, and the frame button puts the camera on what is
lit. **The pointer aims for you.** A bead is a few pixels across and a fibre is thinner, so the ray is
cast first — exact, and respecting what is in front of what — and where it hits nothing the nearest
bead whose centre falls within fourteen pixels is taken instead, the nearest to the eye winning
where several do, and never one the slab has cut away. **The cursor becomes a cross** whenever a
bead is being aimed at, either way, so the slack is visible rather than a surprise when the click
lands somewhere the hand did not press. A click pins a bead; Shift-click puts a mark at its locus
that every map and track then draws; a double-click on a bead takes the maps there; on the air, it frames. A picking mode armed
by the marks card or an analysis form takes a click on a bead as the place, on both axes at once,
as a track's does.

### 25.5 Colour, chords, names

**The key is a control.** Under *colour by sequence*, each sequence's row carries its swatch as a
colour picker — click it to choose the sequence's colour, kept with the row by name over the
palette's — and its name as a button: a **click ghosts** that sequence (drawn as the beads outside
the window are, and hidden with them under *outside window: hide*), a **double-click shows it
alone** (every other ghosted; a second double-click brings all back). Ghosting stacks with the
window's: a ghosted sequence stays ghosted whatever the maps look at.

**And under *colour by manual annotations* the key lists the marks**, a row each, named as the
Manual annotations card names them (`│ IV:1,200,000`, `▭ IV:1,100,000-1,150,000`), with the same
three gestures: the swatch is **the mark's own colour**, written to the marks' store, so a colour
picked on the model is the colour on the card and on every map; a **click** hides that mark, and a
**double-click shows it alone** (a second brings back the ones it put away). Both are the mark's own
eye on the card (§8.1), so the mark goes from the model and from every map, lane and track at once,
and its row's eye on the card goes dark with it; a hidden mark stays listed on the key, faded, to be
clicked back. A click used to take the mark off the model's colouring alone, held in the model's
style, which was a second meaning of *hidden* for one mark — off the model and still on every map,
with nothing on the card to say so; a style saved with that list reads without it. With no marks yet
the key says where they are made. This colouring used to have no key at all, so a model coloured by
six marks was six colours nobody could name.

**A feature set's names are a colouring of their own.** Every interval set whose features carry a
name — a BED4 or wider, a bigBed, a task's segments — is offered twice in the picker: *· features*,
the lane's own ink where a bead overlaps a feature, and right under it **· names**, the names as
categories — a compartment call's `A` and `B`, a segmentation's states. Each bead takes the name
that overlaps it by the **most base pairs**, summed per name, so a compartment called as two
touching intervals is still one compartment; a tie goes to the name the file gives first, and a bead
no named feature overlaps keeps the neutral grey. This is not E1's ramp: a name is a level, not a
value, so the colour-scale picker is not offered. The colours are the set's (§8.16): `A` red and `B`
blue where those are the only names, the categorical palette by base pairs covered otherwise, and
past twenty-three names one `other` bucket that the key says the size of. **The key lists the names
some bead is under** — a legend naming a colour nothing on the model is drawn in is a legend for
another model — and its swatches are pickers, as a sequence's and a mark's are. What a swatch writes
is the **set's** colour for that name, kept on the set's row with the session, for the reason a
mark's colour is the mark's: `A` is a fact about the call, so `A` picked green here is green on the
next model coloured by the same call and on its lane coloured by name.

The reader's own

**arrowhead marks** are offered under *loops as chords* as *manual annotations*, beside the loaded loop
sets, so a loop marked on the map or in loop mode is a chord on the model. The row is *label, toggle,
set* on one line, and **the toggle is absent while the set is `none`**: lit with nothing chosen it
was a *show the chords* that could not show one, and a reader pressing it could not tell which of
the two controls was why the model stayed bare (§8.5).

The homologue picker on a phased model is labelled **haplotype** and the row of name, ruler,
telomere and centre marks **overlays** — the word the Map and Tracks cards use for the same kind of
row. Both read *show* before, which is one name for two questions on one card.

**Telomeres.** A toggle under *overlays* puts a **yellow bead on every telomere** — the palette's own
yellow, drawn through the same channel a reader's mark is and therefore at the same larger radius,
in the same place under every drawing and every colouring, and in the vector export without a second
road. What counts as one is **both ends of every chain**, with nothing asked of the session: a chain of
one bead gets one mark rather than two, and beads the file left unplaced are skipped, so a chain
that opens with a gap is marked at the first bead that is actually somewhere.

An earlier rule asked, and the argument for it was sound — the end of a *chain* is not the end of a
*chromosome*, so the start was claimed only from a first bead at base zero, the far end only against
a length the *file itself* declared, and neither for a sequence ticked **circular** (§8.15). It was
also useless in practice, and the reason is worth keeping: a model's own lengths are a lower bound,
a lower bound cannot establish an end, and a whole yeast genome came out with five marks where a
reader was looking for thirty-two. The mark is a **chain end** and claims no more than that.

**A mark fades with the bead it is on.** Every mark — a telomere, a reader's own place, a tick of the
genomic ruler — is drawn at the **ghost opacity** when the bead under it is outside the window or
ghosted from the key, exactly as that bead is. A place is a fact about a bead, so a mark on a bead
that is barely there is barely there. They used to be drawn at full strength whatever the model was
doing, so a window of one chromosome was read against a constellation of solid yellow telomeres
nowhere near it — the brightest thing in a picture of somewhere else. The vector export had it right
from the start (`structure/painter.ts` reads the same `lit` array the beads do), so the screen and
the exported PDF disagreed about the same model; this is the screen catching up.

**The centre of rotation, and the frame it is read in.** *Overlays* shows a **ball at the camera's
target with three arms out of it** — one per axis, each a shaft with a **head** on the positive end
and a short stub on the negative, in the colours every 3D tool uses (x red, y green, z blue),
sized to the view so it reads the same at every zoom and drawn over the model, since a centre inside
a tube is still the centre. **On by default**: it is where every drag turns about and where ⌘-click
puts the next one, and a reader who cannot see it is turning the model about a point they have to
infer from the motion. It was six half-lines crossing in a dot, which said neither which way an axis
went nor which end was the centre.

The arms carry a **frame the reader plants**. The identity is the model's own axes, and **replant**
(on the *camera* row) lays them along **this view** — x across the screen, y up it, z out of it — so
every turn after that is read against the view they were planted in, which is the question anybody
asks of a gizmo: *how far have I come from where I was looking*. **Neither the model nor the centre
moves**; only the frame they are read against. ⌘-click **replants as it re-centres**, because a
centre put somewhere new is a reader saying *read the model from here*, and arms left pointing along
the frame the file happened to be written in answer a question nobody asked.

**Mirrors.** Two toggles on the *frame* row reflect the model **across the screen** or **up it**. A
reconstruction from contacts is determined **only up to reflection** — a model and its mirror image
explain the same counts equally well, and which one a solver returns is an accident of where it
started — so two models of one map routinely come out in opposite hands and no rotation will ever
bring one onto the other. This is how one is brought into the other's hand. The reflection is
applied to the **built coordinates**, not to the camera, so picking a bead, measuring between two,
the labels and the vector export all follow it; a mirror at the camera would flip the picture and
leave the numbers under it describing a model nobody is looking at. Which means the renderer has to
**rebuild its geometry when a model moves**, and not only when its style changes: what is built is
keyed on the counts and the drawing — how many beads, drawn as what, how wide — which is everything
that could change back when nothing ever moved a bead. A reflection hands over the same counts and
the same style at new coordinates, so the key matched, the buffers were left alone, and the fibre
stayed exactly where it was while the chain **names**, drawn from the model every frame, flipped:
the picture and its labels disagreed about which model was on screen. Both at once is a half turn
rather than a reflection, which is the one combination that changes nothing about the fold; it is
allowed because seeing a model the other way up is a reason on its own.

**In the frame of.** A select beside *compare with*, naming another model: this model is turned into
**that one's frame**, over the beads the two share and by the same superposition, and **the other is
not drawn**. The two are one question asked twice — a reader asking *where do these differ* wants
both on screen, and a reader asking *is this the same fold* wants them in one frame — and asking one
control to do both put a second model in the picture of everybody who only wanted the first. The
reflection is applied **first**, since mirroring is what makes the fit possible at all and fitting
first would reflect the answer instead of the question. Two cells each *in the frame of* one row,
*turning together* (§25.3), are two models in one frame showing the same face of each.

**Contacts from the pin.** With a bead pinned, *colour by contacts with pinned bin* puts the
map's row through it onto the beads: each value through the map's own transform, clipped to its
`vmin`–`vmax`, in its colormap — the virtual 4C of the pin, read in space and agreeing with the
picture beside it cell for cell. **A pair the map never counted is the bottom of that scale**, not
`log10(0) → 0`: that clamp is numpy's and it is right on a map, whose scale starts at zero, but the
scale here is the map's *transformed* range and a balanced map's runs from about −3.6 to about 0 —
so the clamp drew every uncounted pair at the dark end, and a 4C in space came out with its darkest
beads exactly where there was no contact at all.

The same row was also drawn as **chords** from the pinned bead, under a *pin contacts* toggle and a
threshold. That is gone: the colouring says the same thing in the representation the model is
already in, and a cage of coloured cylinders over a globule was a second answer to a question the
first had answered.

**Compare with.** Another structure row — the loaded model against the reconstruction, or two
solvers' models of one map — is **superposed** on this one: the beads the two share are matched by
locus (and haplotype where both are phased), the other is rotated, scaled and moved onto this by a
similarity fit (Horn's closed form for the rotation, Umeyama's scale; `structure/align.ts`, held
still by a model asked back from a turned, scaled and shifted copy of itself), drawn in grey as a thin
tube in this model's frame, and the card says how many beads matched and the root-mean-square
distance between them. *Colour by displacement* colours each bead of this model by its distance to
its bead in the other, on a ramp, which is where the two disagree. Fewer than four shared beads is
no fit, and the card says so.

**The colour scale is the reader's**, where the colouring has one: a picker under *colour by* lists
every colormap this application carries, and *the colouring's own* — the default — keeps the rule
below, that a track's beads take the lane's colormap and contacts the map's, so a bead and the
picture beside it cannot disagree at the same value. It is offered only for a **ramp**: a colouring
by sequence or haplotype is levels and has no scale to change, and a control that does nothing under
the default colouring is one a reader tries and then distrusts. The key follows the choice, because
a legend naming one ramp over a model drawn on another is a legend that lies. Under a **track**
the picker also offers **white to the track's colour**: a ramp from white to the colour the track's
lane is drawn in, so a model coloured by H3K27ac is drawn in its lane's orange (`TRACK_TINT_RAMP`,
`structure/colour.ts`; a colouring with no colour of its own keeps its own ramp under it).

**And under a track the key's two ends are numbers to type into**, as the lane's own range is
(§8): a click on either puts a caret in it, Enter or a click away commits, Escape leaves it alone,
Tab goes from the bottom to the top and Shift+Tab back (§26.8),
and a number that is not one or an end past the other is refused in place. What is typed is
written to **the lane's limits**, the one pair the lane and the beads are drawn against, so the
lane beside the map changes with it; once fixed, an arrow after the range puts the track back on
autoscale, here and on the lane.

One picker, on the picture, and the model's own five lead it in the order a reader goes through
them: **sequence**; **linear position along the sequence**; **manual annotations** — the reader's
marks, a line colouring its bead and a rectangle its run; **spatial distance to pinned bin**, in the
model's units; and **contacts with pinned bin** — the lead map's own row through it, read out of the
block in hand on the map's own transform, range and colormap, the virtual 4C drawn in space. *Linear*
and *spatial* because the picture beside the model measures a distance too, in base pairs, and the
two words say which one each colouring is. After them, **haplotype** where there are homologues,
any column the file carries, and from the session **a track's values** at each bead — read
through the same sample cache the lanes use at one bucket per bead and on the lane's own limits, so
a bead coloured by a bigWig agrees with the lane at every value — and **a feature set's** colour
where a bead overlaps one, or its **names** as categories (above). The file's **score column** was a colouring and is not now: a g3d carries
none worth a ramp, so the row was a column of nothing, and a session stored coloured by it opens by
sequence. Any other colouring the list no longer has stays named in the picker rather than silently
becoming the first option. Two rules carried from the modules reused: fit the
colouring to the file, not to the window, so turning the model never changes what a colour means;
and use the lane's scale.

A **pairs row** — BEDPE, loops — can be drawn as chords between its anchors' beads, kept to the
loops touching the window and capped at six hundred, past which a model is a cage. The reader's
**bookmarks** are named on the model at their middle beads, with the sequence names.

### 25.6 Analysis

Three tasks, on the *3D tasks* card of the Analysis panel (§18.8), which *Model from the map* opens.
The other two are listed greyed until a map is open and a structure loaded. **Model versus
map** bins the beads to the map's bins per sequence and answers the validation picture: the
model's distances as a matrix and as `1/d^α`, the mean distance at each separation beside the
map's own P(s) over the same bins with the log-log slope, and a table of Spearman correlations
between `1/d` and the observed contacts per sequence and haplotype — rank-based, so the exponent
enters the picture and not the number. **Spatial tracks** turns the model into three profiles on
the map's bins — radial position, distance to a chosen locus, local compaction — which "a
synthetic track is a track" (§18.5) makes lanes, colourings of the model itself, and inputs of
every track task. Both are `structure/versusMap.ts`, pure over arrays, held still by tests.

**Model from the map** needs no structure: it makes one. It is the reversal of §25.8's refusal, and
the §18.9 bar is met the way it was met for chromosight — by porting a published method rather than
inventing one. **Method** offers the two positions the literature takes on what a contact count
*is*, because they are not two settings of one algorithm and they give different models of the same
map: **pastis-NB**, where a count is a count drawn from a distribution, and **ShRec3D**, where a
count measures a distance. pastis-NB is the default. One control is shared and is never hidden —
**Exponent α**, 3 by default, the same number *Model versus map* assumes and the one α is *not*
fitted by either method, so that a model made here and a model made by either published tool mean
the same thing by it.

**pastis-NB** (Varoquaux, Ay, Noble & Vert 2014 for the Poisson models; Varoquaux, Noble & Vert
2023 for the overdispersed one) reads a pair of beads `d` apart as having been counted
`c ~ NegativeBinomial(mean β·bᵢ·bⱼ·d^(−α), dispersion r)` times, and the model is the one that makes
the counts most probable. Two things follow, and they are why it is the default. **A zero is
evidence** — weak evidence, that the beads are far apart — rather than a distance of `0^(−1/α)`
that has to be dropped or invented, so **nothing is filled in**; on a map that is three-quarters
zeros this is the difference between a model and a guess. And **a count's precision is in the
likelihood**, so a pair seen ten thousand times holds its beads ten thousand times as firmly with
nothing weighted by hand.

**It is solved on the raw counts**, whatever the view is balanced with, and the balancing weights go
where pastis puts them — into the mean, as `bᵢ = 1/wᵢ`. This is not a preference: a balanced value is
a count times two weights, and **overdispersion is a statement about a count**. `variance > mean`
compares a squared quantity with a linear one, so scaling the data scales the two sides differently
and a balanced map is never found overdispersed whatever it actually is; handed balanced values the
negative binomial would silently become a Poisson. The coverage is still corrected — in the mean
rather than in the data — and the run says so, in a note and in the table. A bin the balancer
**rejected** (a `NaN` weight) is left out of the model, because the balanced view of the same map
does not draw it either and reading raw counts would otherwise put it back; it is counted in the
same note as a gap. A pooled cell's bias is the mean of its bins'. A file with no `/bins/weight` has
no bias to fold and the mean is `β·d^(−α)`. One consequence for the reader: a **balanced view cannot
be borrowed** by this method, so a run on one reads its blocks from the file, and the estimate says
so. The dispersion is **fitted from the counts, per genomic separation**, by
the method of moments (`r = m²/(v − m)`) over log-spaced separation bins — which is pastis-NB's one
claim over pastis-PM2, that overdispersion is not one number for a map but grows as the counts thin
out with distance; a bin with too few pairs to believe takes the nearest that had them, and a
separation whose counts are not overdispersed at all takes `r = 10⁶`, which is a Poisson to six
figures and is reported as *none*. The whole of the negative binomial over the Poisson is one
factor: the force on a pair is the Poisson's own `μ − c`, **shrunk by `r/(r + μ)`**. What is
optimised is three coordinates per bead and `log β`, by **L-BFGS** with a strong-Wolfe line search
— the optimiser pastis reaches for through SciPy — started from the MDS model ShRec3D would have
given, which is pastis' own initialisation and is why this method stands on the other rather than
replacing it. `β` is a variable rather than a constant because the scale of the model and the scale
of the mean are one degree of freedom, and the normalisation below fixes it. Three departures from
the paper are deliberate and named here: the dispersion is a **moment estimate per separation bin**
rather than their parametric fit of dispersion against the mean, and it is taken **once** rather
than alternated with the structure; there are **no restarts**, so the answer is one deterministic
model rather than the best of several local optima; and `α` is the reader's control rather than a
fitted parameter. The **MDS start is sixty SMACOF steps**, fixed, because it has only to land in
the right basin — **Refinement steps** under this method is the likelihood's budget.

**ShRec3D** (Lesne et al. 2014) is the same pipeline with the refinement every MDS toolkit ends
with: a contact count `c` is read as a distance `d = c^(−1/α)` — the law *Model versus map* assumes
the other way round; the pairs the map never counted (a zero, a `NaN`) are filled so the matrix is
complete; classical MDS (Torgerson: double-centred squared distances, three leading eigenvectors by
subspace iteration) gives a start; **SMACOF** (de Leeuw's majorisation, taken one bead at a time as
Gansner, Koren and North's localised stress majorisation) moves the beads until the model's
distances match the map's over the pairs the map counted, **each pair weighted by how often the map
counted it** — a filled pair weighs nothing — stopping at the step count asked for or once a step
improves the weighted stress by less than a millionth. The weighting is the point of refining at
all: the count sets a pair's target, but with every pair weighing the same the stress is the far,
weak, noisy pairs' and the near diagonal, where the map is most certain, is fitted worst. **Weight
pairs by** — shown only under this method, since a likelihood *is* its own weighting — offers the
count (a pair seen a thousand times is a thousand times as sure as one seen once, which is what a
Poisson count's precision says; the default), its square root (a weak pair is still heard on a deep
map), or nothing (every counted pair one vote: the plain SMACOF of every toolkit, kept so a reader
can see what the weighting changes). Three departures from ShRec3D are deliberate and named here:
its shortest-path filling is cubic in the bead count and would not finish in a tab, so the filling
is the mean observed distance at the same separation on the same sequence, walking outward to the
nearest separation with an observation, and the mean observed trans distance across two; ShRec3D
stops at the classical solution, which honours the filled pairs as much as the counted ones; and it
has no refinement to weight. The bead-at-a-time form is what makes the weighting affordable: the
full weighted Guttman transform is a linear solve in the weight Laplacian, and the localised one
costs a pass over the pairs like the unweighted one does, and never raises the stress.

Either way the model is centred and scaled to a unit root-mean-square radius: a map carries no
physical unit, and neither `c^(−1/α)` nor a `β` fitted against it is in one (§25.8).

**What it is solved over** is what the **Sequences** box names, seeded from what the map shows
(a locus, or every sequence on screen): where the view's block **as drawn** covers it — the loaded
locus, drawn one bin to the cell — the block is taken as it is, cis and trans together, one bead per
bin, filed under the sequence holding it. Where it does not — several sequences, a whole file, a
block pooled, balanced the other way or not square — the
file is **read span by span**, one rectangle per pair of named spans (two sequences far apart cost
their two squares and the rectangle between them, never the sequences in between). **One bin of the
resolution the reader has selected is one bead** — never the drawn cell, whose width comes from a
raster cap and the size of the window rather than from anything anybody chose. The block on screen
is borrowed only when it is drawn *one bin to the cell*, where borrowing changes nothing and costs
no read; a pooled block is declined, which is `usableBlock`'s rule and every other task's (§18.4).
A coarser model is a coarser **rung**, selected in the view, which also reads far less: a genome at
5 kb from the 5 kb rung reads a twenty-fifth of what the 1 kb rung does for the same model. The box
**empty is the whole file**. A cell whose row the map counted nothing on — a filtered bin, a gap —
is left out of the model, and the run says how many were.

**There is no ceiling on the beads.** Both the time and the memory are quadratic in the count, and
what the estimate does about it is *say so* — the bead count and its bin width, the seconds per
hundred refinement steps and the gigabytes of matrices — for the reader to confirm before pressing
run. A number chosen in the source could only be a guess about somebody else's machine. What is
still refused is the allocation that cannot succeed: the matrices are asked for inside a `try` and a
browser that will not give them leaves a note naming the size, rather than a tab that dies. **Either
method holds two** dense `n × n` matrices of singles and no more — under ShRec3D the pairs' weights,
under pastis-NB the counts with a zero still distinct from a gap, and in both cases the counts
turned into the distances they imply over the buffer they already occupy, compacted onto the kept
beads in place and then filled over themselves — so twelve thousand beads is about a gigabyte. The
likelihood adds **vectors and not squares**: L-BFGS at depth eight keeps twenty vectors of `3n + 1`
doubles, six megabytes beside that gigabyte, where the Hessian a full quasi-Newton method would
write down is thirty terabytes. What it does cost is time — a likelihood evaluation is about 2.3
passes' worth of a SMACOF step, and a step is a line search of just over one evaluation — and the
estimate prices the method the reader picked rather than an average of the two.
**Every phase reports progress and breathes between units of work**: each rectangle read, each of
the eighty sweeps of the classical start, each SMACOF step, and under pastis-NB each *evaluation*
of the likelihood rather than each step, since a line search is several of them and each is as long
as a SMACOF step. The run's other output is a table, and it says which method ran: where the
contacts came from, the bead count and width, the pairs counted, and then either the law, the
weighting, the steps and the final weighted stress, or — under pastis-NB — the mean's law, how many
zeros were used as evidence, the fitted overdispersion near the diagonal and far from it (or
*none*, where the counts turned out Poisson and the run is a pastis-PM2), the MDS start, the
likelihood steps and evaluations, why the optimiser stopped, the final `−log L` and the fitted `β`.
Both end with Spearman's ρ between `1/d` in the model and the contacts — **against `raw/(bᵢbⱼ)`
where a bias was divided out**, which is exactly the balanced value, since balancing is `raw·wᵢwⱼ`;
ranking against the raw counts would score the model on coverage it was right to have removed. So it
is the same number *Model versus map* would give the row on a balanced map, and a reader can see how
well the model honours the map before believing it.

**Its result is a row**, not a picture: a `structure` row on the Structures card, of kind
`structure`, payload a bed3d-shaped feature set with its `model`, id `analysis:reconstruct3d:
reconstructed-model` (per map on a deck, as every computed row is), labelled `3D model · chrIV`,
`3D model · IV:1,000,001-1,400,000` or `3D model · 16 sequences`, summarised as a loaded one is,
carrying the task and the framing as provenance. **It never replaces the last run's row.** Every
other computed row does — running insulation again with a wider window means the reader wants the
*new* boundaries — and a model is the one thing an analysis makes that is not stored anywhere else
and is made **to be compared**: two methods, two exponents, or two framings of one map (the same
settings twice give the same model, the run being deterministic, above). So a run takes the next
free id in the series `…reconstructed-model`, `…#2`, `…#3`, numbered from what is on the card
so closing the second of three gives that number back, and the label carries the same `(2)` because
two rows under one name are two rows nobody can tell apart on the card, in *compare with* or in
*in the frame of*. It is the model the cell draws the moment it lands, is
what *Model versus map* and *Spatial tracks* read, persists as a recipe and comes back
`detached` with **recompute**, and leaves as a bed3d from the row, from the drawer and from the
shell (§25.7). The golden is the one a reconstruction can honestly have. For ShRec3D
(`structure-reconstruct.test.ts`): a helix whose contacts were made from it by the law comes back
as itself up to a rigid motion, a chain with most far pairs uncounted comes back with ρ above 0.9,
and a helix whose weak far pairs were corrupted keeps its near pairs when weighted by the count
and loses them when every pair weighs the same. For pastis-NB (`structure-negbinom.test.ts`, with
the optimiser held separately in `structure-lbfgs.test.ts` against Rosenbrock and a badly
conditioned quadratic): the gradient agrees with a central difference at every coordinate and at
`log β`; the objective is the Poisson's as `r → ∞`, and is stationary exactly where the mean equals
the count, for every `r`; a counted zero moves the likelihood and an unobservable pair does not; the
pull on a pair is the Poisson's shrunk by exactly `r/(r + μ)`; a helix whose counts were **drawn**
Poisson at the law's own mean, three-quarters of them zeros, comes back with ρ above 0.9 from a
classical start that was below 0.4; and a helix whose far counts were corrupted holds its near
diagonal about twice as well under the fitted dispersion as under a flat Poisson one.

### 25.7 Export

The card's last row is **the export row** (§26.6) — `[resolution] [format] [⭳] [⧉]` with a line
under it — so a model is saved the way a map and a browser are, and at the resolution the reader
chose rather than at a fixed one. The PNG is the picture the GPU lit, at that resolution. The PDF is
**paths, whatever the model is drawn as**, through `structure/painter.ts`, projected through the
same camera the screen was: beads as discs, sticks as segments, and the **tube** as a stretch per
bead along the Catmull–Rom curve the GPU draws it on, each bead's stretch running from half way to
one neighbour to half way to the next — the stretch the GPU colours by that bead — and meeting the
next at one width, the perspective's change of width running along the stretch rather than stepping
at the joint; a run ends round. **Every surface is lit, as the screen's is**, by the screen's own key
light, which rides with the eye: a bead is a PDF radial shading from a highlight up and to the
right of its centre out to a rim in shadow — smooth at any zoom, one shading per bead — and a tube
or a stick, round whose curve no shading can follow, is a stack of bands, eight at the fewest and
none wider than a third of a pixel, each narrower, lighter and nudged towards the light than the
one under it, so a fibre reads as a solid rather than a ribbon. Each of a tube's bands is the ring
of the section that is its own, reaching three bands in under the next: laid whole, the bands of
one stretch put their edges at one line over the lighter ones of its neighbour, and a reader's
anti-aliasing drew a dark hairline across the tube at every bead. The fog mixes every colour of
the shading towards the paper, as it does a flat one. Only what is under three quarters of a pixel
across, and what is ghosted, is one flat colour. The tube used to export
as the raster the GPU drew, on the argument that a lit surface is no `arc`; it is the default
representation, so most models left as a picture of pixels in the one file meant to be a drawing.
Nothing in a model's PDF is a raster now, so the format reads **PDF (vector)** and the row's
resolution is **absent while it is chosen**, as on the map's and the browser's cards (§7.2). The
page holds what the PNG holds, from the same numbers: the dashes across a gap, whatever the model is
drawn as; the centre of rotation when it is shown; the ruler's ticks, the marks and the telomeres;
the measurements; the depth slab and the fog; and the cell's own colours. What is written on the
model — the sequence names and the bookmarks under *names*, the ruler's labels, each measurement's
distance in the file's units — is one function for both files, so the PNG and the PDF name the same
things in the same places. The deck's figure takes the cell's canvas for its PNG, at the figure's
resolution — 300 dpi from the deck's bar, the Export card's own from that card — and the cell's paths
for its PDF (§16.5). The clipboard takes a PNG, as it does for a map.

**An exported model is framed by its cell's edge**: a thin rule round the picture, at the weight and
in the colour of the map's plot border (`--border-strong`, 0.75 px scaled to the export's
resolution), so the two cells of a deck are framed alike. A model zoomed past its cell is cut by the
cell's edge, and on screen the cell's own border says where the cut is; exported without one, the
model floated on the page with a straight side sliced off it for no visible reason. Every export of a
model draws it — the deck's figure, the card's PNG and PDF, the card's copy — as pixels on a raster
and as a path on a page of paths, inset by half its width so the whole of the line is on the page.
The right-click *Copy this* is the model alone, and carries no frame (§7.2).

**A model leaves as a bed3d** — `chrom start end x y z`, the haplotype column for a phased one, a
`#` line naming the row, its framing and when it was made, six decimals — from the **bed3d**
button of its row, from the drawer's result and from the export road a computed row shares with
called intervals. *When it was made* is the run's, on all three roads alike: the row's button asks
the analysis workspace, which holds the run, and a model loaded from a file, which was not made
here, is written with no date. It is the file §25.2 reads, so it reads straight back here and in
`g3dtools`.

**That road includes the shell.** `chromosomix reconstruct3d --out` writes the bed3d beside the
TSV every output carries (§18.7), through this same writer — because the batch is where a model
whose coordinates went missing is least likely to be noticed, and because a reconstruction is the
one task whose whole result is the three columns BED has nowhere to put.

**A model also leaves as a PDB, for PyMOL** and every other molecular viewer — from the **PDB**
button beside the bed3d on its row, from the drawer's result beside the bed3d there, and from
`reconstruct3d --out`, which writes it beside the bed3d — through one writer (`annotations/pdb.ts`),
with a TITLE that says what the bed3d's `#` line says, in ASCII. pastis' own PDB is a list of atoms
in bin order on one chain with no bonds, which PyMOL draws as a cloud joined by guesswork; this one
is the file a viewer can draw as the fibre it is:

- **One HETATM per bead**, a carbon `C` in a residue `BEA`: a bead is no amino acid and no
  nucleotide, and HETATM is the record a non-standard group takes. A bead the model left unplaced is
  no atom.
- **One chain per sequence and haplotype**, the scene's chains in the scene's order, so colouring by
  chain tells chromosomes apart and the homologues of a phased model apart, and residues numbered
  along each chain from 1, so a rainbow by residue runs from one end of a chromosome to the other.
  The chain letters are A–Z, a–z and 0–9, which PyMOL keeps apart by case; a model with more than
  sixty-two chains — a metagenome's contigs — takes them round again, and every chain's segment
  identifier is then its number, which PyMOL selects by too.
- **CONECT between neighbouring beads and nowhere else**: a bond for every step of every run the
